However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), which decomposes the Radix-n FFT matrix into sparse integer matrices and an approximated twiddle-factor diagonal matrix to reduce arithmetic cost.
AI.motivation: Conventional FFT implementations incur heavy non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in large-scale signal processing and machine learning pipelines.
AI.method: SIFT decomposes the 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT into four sparse integer matrices and approximates the complex twiddle-factor diagonal matrix via an optimization strategy.
AI.result: For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces estimated arithmetic cost by 75% with RMSE below 2.3765e-8 and MAPE below 0.01089%; in a numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and 2.536e-6, and in wind turbine fault diagnosis it extracts compact spectral features that reduce classifier input dimensionality.
AI.conclusion: Approximating twiddle factors alongside sparse integer matrix decomposition enables substantial arithmetic savings for FFT-based feature extraction with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables. Preprint of the technical part of an MSc thesis (Politecnico di Milano). Code and pre-registrations are held privately until venue submission
summary: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

AI.tldr: This case study investigates whether decision models (Clef-flash on Qwen3.5-9B and Clef on Qwen3.8-27B) localize the industrial anomalies they detect, finding that their decision heads do not localize defects.
AI.motivation: Decision models output option probabilities without generating text, but it is unclear whether their internal attention mechanisms actually localize the anomalies driving their predictions.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Clef-flash and Clef on MVTec AD and MVTec AD 2, probing decision-head routing attention, backbone attention under question perturbations, and token-masking interventions.
AI.result: Clef-flash achieves 0.924 image AUROC on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2, yet its decision head yields only 0.391 pixel AUROC and is unaffected by hiding image tokens; backbone attention points to defects but drops below a center prior when questions change, and region-specific prompting or retraining still lags dedicated few-shot localizers.
AI.conclusion: High image-level anomaly detection accuracy in decision models does not imply spatial localization in the decision head, limiting their out-of-the-box interpretability.

title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges closest-world counterfactual explanations and formal XAI (AXps/CXps) by introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps) and showing how to compute them using existing AXp/CXp machinery.
AI.motivation: Closest-world counterfactuals require reasoning over all minimally distant counterexamples, whereas formal XAI relies on abductive (AXp) and contrastive (CXp) explanations with efficient hitting-set duality.
AI.method: The authors characterize closest-world counterfactuals as a disjunctive normal form over minimally distant counterexamples, define CFXps as conjunctions of feature literals guaranteeing prediction change, and prove structural links showing every CXp plus a witness AXp induces a CFXp.
AI.result: Experiments on tree ensembles and neural networks demonstrate that CFXp extraction is practically efficient, requires no more feature changes than point-based explainers, and guarantees counterfactual predictions beyond a single instance.
AI.conclusion: Connecting formal AXp/CXp duality to counterfactuals enables efficient, provably valid conjunctive counterfactual explanations.

title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
summary: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format using two multiplications and a 64-byte table that achieves near-optimal rate-distortion and is implemented in AWS Trainium 4.
AI.motivation: Scalar quantization formats like INT4 and FP4 waste bits relative to information-theoretic limits, while prior trellis decoders require either large lookup tables or restrictive hash functions.
AI.method: CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and sums the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table, supporting 1 to 6 bits with a single decoder and reproducing standard integer/float formats.
AI.result: CPTC comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits, outperforms all QTIP codebooks (reducing KL divergence on Llama 3.1 8B/70B Instruct by up to 27% without fine-tuning), runs at native FP4/FP8 throughput on AWS Trainium 4, and quantizes an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: CPTC delivers hardware-friendly, near-optimal trellis quantization for LLM weights with negligible area overhead.

title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
summary: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MemGP, a unified theory of working memory that casts memory as Gaussian-process variational inference and analytically maps the algorithm onto recurrent neural circuits.
AI.motivation: Working memory research remains divided across computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels over discrete slots versus continuous resources, attention effects, and persistent versus activity-silent states.
AI.method: MemGP models working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function with a Gaussian-process prior, approximates the posterior with a finite set of shared inducing points, and analytically maps this algorithm onto a recurrent circuit without training.
AI.result: In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional maintenance benefits, inter-item attraction/repulsion, and delay-dependent neural drift, while analytically deriving center-surround connectivity and a mix of persistent activity and synaptic weights.
AI.conclusion: A single probabilistic inference objective can simultaneously account for behavioral and circuit-level signatures of working memory, reconciling competing theories.

title: Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: 28 pages. Includes supplementary material. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes exogenous variability in cooperative MARL as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP) and proposes LEICA, a CTDE algorithm using influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards.
AI.motivation: Cooperative MARL agents often fail when uncontrollable episode-level exogenous regimes (such as opponent strategy shifts) alter environment transition dynamics.
AI.method: ED-POMDP partitions global state into action-responsive and non-action-responsive components to expose mediated influence, and LEICA learns history-conditioned context representations for both while shaping policy updates with agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards.
AI.result: Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and zero-shot generalization to unseen opponent strategies over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Modeling mediated influence and shaping rewards via counterfactuals improves cooperative MARL robustness under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
summary: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MedGuardBench, a 5,001-scenario medication safety benchmark, and develops personalized reasoning guardrails that condition safety verdicts on patient profiles.
AI.motivation: Existing safety guardrails judge content generically without considering individual patient facts, even though medication safety depends critically on who is affected.
AI.method: The authors release MedGuardBench (5,001 drug-disjoint scenarios across 87 medications and 17 risk categories) and propose personalized reasoning guardrails combining Personalized Reasoning Distillation, Context Unrolling (CU) to check each patient field, and rule-based guided GRPO.
AI.result: Standard guardrails rely on surface cues rather than patient facts; CU reduces false alarms on most backbones, guided GRPO improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection on some backbones, and the combined models outperform base models and no-profile controls in accuracy while reducing false alarms.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning guardrails on structured patient-field checks and personalized reasoning substantially improves patient-specific medication safety.

title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR) and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), plug-and-play objectives that reformulate generative reconstruction as discriminative ranking to avoid gradient conflicts.
AI.motivation: Combining contrastive learning and generative reconstruction in MLLM visual encoders often causes optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference.
AI.method: AUCGR and pAUCGR maintain perceptual reconstruction while adding a ranking-based constraint that orders matched versus mismatched reconstruction outputs in the generative manifold, optimizing AUC or partial AUC without architectural changes.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes generalization guarantees, and extensive experiments show improvements in both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating generative reconstruction as AUC-based ranking unifies discriminative and perceptual representation learning without loss competition.

title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
summary: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LoCaR, a training-free framework for localized text-to-image retrieval using SAM2 object proposals encoded by frozen vision-language models, alongside a new benchmark LOCFG.
AI.motivation: Whole-image embeddings from frozen vision-language models underrepresent small objects and local attributes needed for localized text-to-image retrieval.
AI.method: LoCaR generates independent object proposals with SAM2 and encodes each region separately using a frozen visual encoder, optionally adding paired-support residual adaptation from matched text-region exemplars without updating encoder weights.
AI.result: Evaluated on the newly introduced Visual Genome-derived LOCFG benchmark and across multiple VLM backbones, improving region-level representation is the primary driver of retrieval gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling region proposals and encoding them independently with frozen VLMs enables effective, training-free localized retrieval.

title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted manuscript of the article published in J. Inf. Commun. Converg. Eng. 24(2), 155-164 (2026)
summary: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a nonlinear Cucker-Smale flocking model with dynamic networks and the discrete p-Laplacian, deriving a quantitative link between flocking time constraints and graph volume.
AI.motivation: Understanding how strict finite-time flocking constraints drive network connectivity mobilization in multi-agent systems remains underexplored both theoretically and experimentally.
AI.method: The authors prove finite-time flocking for a discrete p-Laplacian (p in (1, 2)) Cucker-Smale model, derive a lower-bound relationship between flocking time and graph volume, and train a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each step.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds and PPO experiments show that tighter flocking time constraints and larger initial velocity variance force higher graph volume, with a sharp threshold increase in average connections under the strictest time constraint.
AI.conclusion: Strict convergence-time constraints quantitatively induce network connection mobilization in nonlinear flocking dynamics.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
comment: Accepted manuscript. 13 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (supplementary text, Tables S1-S2, Figures S1-S5). Published in Antiviral Research 222 (2024) 105818
summary: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a deep RL molecule design platform to discover two non-sialic acid-like compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021, that inhibit influenza A and B neuraminidases in vitro and protect mice in vivo.
AI.motivation: Discovering new antiviral agents effective against both influenza A and B viruses, including oseltamivir-resistant H275Y mutants, is an urgent therapeutic need.
AI.method: A deep RL platform generated 60,291 candidate compounds targeting influenza neuraminidase; after computational filtering, nine non-sialic acid-like candidates were tested in vitro, in molecular dynamics simulations, in cell assays, and in mouse infection models.
AI.result: 86.5% of generated compounds showed superior physicochemical properties to oseltamivir; DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV, IBV, and H275Y mutants with cell-based EC50 values of 0.29-2.31 uM, and conferred 65%/85% protection against IAV (H1N1 pdm09) and 65%/100% protection against IBV (Yamagata) in mice.
AI.conclusion: Deep RL-driven de novo molecule generation can successfully identify novel, in vivo-active antiviral candidates against diverse influenza strains.

title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary video in the ancillary files. Dataset: this https URL
summary: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

AI.tldr: This paper trains thermally aware RL locomotion policies for a Unitree Go2 quadruped without temperature observations by minimizing predicted steady-state motor temperatures from a 13-node RC thermal model, shifting endurance from thermal-limited to battery-limited.
AI.motivation: Legged robots often suffer thermal shutdown in a few joint motors long before battery depletion, and thermal time constants are far too long for standard RL credit assignment.
AI.method: The authors fit a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network (under 1 C mean RMSE across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds) and use a reward penalizing the hottest predicted steady-state motor asymptote, which responds within a single gait cycle to torque and joint speed.
AI.result: On a Unitree Go2 with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, the baseline hits thermal shutdown at 19 min (1.1 km) while the policy runs until battery depletion at 174 min (10.0 km) with 14 C thermal margin; on an unloaded factory circuit, it completes 47 laps (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 C margin versus 25 laps (6.2 km) for the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Penalizing predicted steady-state thermal asymptotes enables RL policies to distribute heat and achieve battery-limited endurance without requiring temperature sensors.

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
comment: Under review at ACM IMWUT. 30 pages, 4 figures and 6 tables
summary: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OAK-Mind, a zero-training, multi-agent, knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline that infers mental health changes from passive smartphone and wearable sensing data, matching or outperforming supervised baselines without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Inferring mental health outcomes from passive sensing has traditionally relied on supervised models that require labeled data and offer limited interpretability, while existing LLM-based approaches still depend on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining.
AI.method: OAK-Mind organizes passive sensing data into behavioral dimensions (sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use), orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes, and synthesizes their assessments with questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline with human-readable rationale.
AI.result: Across datasets and prediction tasks, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples, consistently improves over direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones, and ablations confirm the value of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, domain-specific agents, and domain knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs enable effective, interpretable, training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation, along with the HH-Bench benchmark, outperforming baselines in simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: Multi-humanoid collaboration requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots, which are difficult to achieve in decentralized settings without network communication.
AI.method: Heave-Ho combines a low-level multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions using only local observations, and a high-level vision-language planner with a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism for network-free synchronization.
AI.result: Trained with two identical humanoids, Heave-Ho scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining, consistently outperforming baseline methods across the 12 tasks of HH-Bench and demonstrating robust decentralized collaboration in real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: Combining decentralized multi-agent tracking adaptation with speech-coordinated vision-language planning enables scalable, long-horizon multi-humanoid collaboration without network communication.

title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
summary: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces XM-Sparse, a sparse-attention LLM serving system over scale-up memory pools that offloads both KV caches and K-index caches with pattern-matched I/O mechanisms, achieving up to 4.98x higher decode throughput than PCIe-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Production sparse-attention LLMs must retain the full KV history, and even with scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem), decode throughput remains bounded by GPU HBM capacity because hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM while exhibiting distinct access patterns.
AI.method: XM-Sparse aggressively offloads both KV and K-index caches to scale-up memory pools, fusing TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline for dynamically selected KV entries while prefetching predictable K-index pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA coordinated to avoid interfering with decoding.
AI.result: Implemented atop SGLang and evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool across 16K-1M contexts, XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98x and 4.52x higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34x over a naive integration on the same platform.
AI.conclusion: Tailoring I/O mechanisms to the distinct access patterns of KV and K-index caches unlocks high-throughput sparse-attention LLM serving over scale-up memory pools.

title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
summary: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ConfGuard, a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance LLM agents that uses conformal monitoring and a deterministic physics-policy validator to defend against prompt injection and sensor perturbation attacks.
AI.motivation: Predictive-maintenance LLM agents face both injected text in retrieved documents and bounded sensor perturbations that corrupt remaining-useful-life estimates, while existing defenses police data provenance and tool privilege without checking whether prognostic quantities are physically plausible.
AI.method: ConfGuard pairs a conformal monitor that tests each prediction against degradation physics (capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle, calibrated over whole asset trajectories) with a physics-policy validator that checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against a deterministic policy derived from the same interval.
AI.result: On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows, ConfGuard cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0) while escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target; behind a Qwen3-14B planner, it holds urgency-class injection to 0.00 and universal sensor attack to 0.12 (vs. 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt), whereas an adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485.
AI.conclusion: Physics-grounded conformal monitoring and deterministic policy validation substantially improve the robustness of predictive-maintenance LLM agents against both text-injection and sensor-perturbation attacks, though an attack class missed by the projection remains.

title: PVTSizing 2.0: A Fast and Reliable Analog Circuit Sizing Operator for Agentic EDA Workflows
summary: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

AI.tldr: This paper presents PVTSizing 2.0, a human-agent analog circuit sizing workflow built around a standalone numerical optimizer with optional LLM-guided parameter relationships, achieving a 7.3x runtime speedup over the original PVTSizing.
AI.motivation: Analog circuit design automation requires coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search, but finding a single sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains computationally costly.
AI.method: PVTSizing 2.0 embeds an independently usable numerical optimizer—which reduces unnecessary training via loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement for cross-corner conflicts—within an agentic workflow, optionally using an LLM adviser to supply parameter relationships while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies them via simulation.
AI.result: Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs with a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing at a comparable mean sample count, and the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.
AI.conclusion: Combining a fast, standalone numerical optimizer with optional LLM-supplied circuit knowledge provides a reliable and much faster operator for agentic analog circuit sizing.

title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
summary: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a multistage contextual optimization approach and a parallel block evaluation algorithm for ride-hailing vehicle repositioning, achieving 7.7% to 9.1% higher business benefit than MSE-trained predictors on NYC data.
AI.motivation: Ride-hailing vehicle repositioning is a prediction-driven multistage problem where forecasts affect the objective, constraint matrix, and right-hand side of coupled stage linear programs, and serial forward propagation across many stages makes training slow.
AI.method: The authors formulate a multistage linear program with a macroscopic fundamental diagram, derive the exact gradient and an equivalent reverse vector-Jacobian adjoint covering forecast, inherited-state, and context-shift effects, and propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel.
AI.result: On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms baselines from five paradigms and realized demand fed to the same policy, and parallel block evaluation with eight workers shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without losing decision performance.
AI.conclusion: Decision-focused multistage contextual optimization with parallel block evaluation significantly improves vehicle repositioning performance while accelerating training.

title: From Constraints to Causality: Petri net Encodings for Explaining Binary Neural Network Inference
summary: Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) are attractive for resource-constrained hardware and on-device components in autonomous systems. However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. Finally, we outline two directions this opens: a correctness-of-translation theorem, and a causal-trace analysis of where two trained BNNs diverge in their decisions, a structural question that constraint-based verifiers cannot express.

AI.tldr: This early work introduces a compositional translation from trained Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) to 1-safe Petri nets, enabling causal-trace explanations of BNN inference decisions.
AI.motivation: Existing SAT and SMT verifiers treat BNNs as monolithic constraint systems, revealing only whether an input-output property holds without explaining how the computation reaches its result.
AI.method: The authors translate the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN into a 1-safe Petri net where each computation step is an explicit transition and each firing sequence forms a causal trace of the decision.
AI.result: On a worked example, the translation establishes faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation and shows how contrasting firing sequences localize where a single-feature change alters the prediction.
AI.conclusion: Petri net encodings provide a discrete-event, causal-trace perspective for BNN explainability, opening avenues for formal translation-correctness theorems and structural divergence analysis between trained BNNs.

title: Do Diffusion Models Learn to Generalize Basic Visual Skills?
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Diffusion models generate high-quality images, but how well they generalize is hard to measure. Current evaluations rely on human preference and prompt-following benchmarks for text-to-image models and on distribution-level metrics such as Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) for class-conditional models, but these cannot tell whether models learn basic visual skills or largely match training patterns. To address this gap, we introduce the Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled experimental framework for studying how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, including size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions. By generating synthetic training data for each skill from explicit rules, VGL allows precise measurement of generalization with task-specific, rule-based metrics. Training models from scratch on these data reveals three patterns in this controlled setting: (1) with our default design, extrapolation is limited: size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy on out-of-range counts, and rotation extrapolation accuracy varies widely across seeds; (2) for compositional generalization, the number of distinct basic visual skill combinations matters more than dataset size; (3) skills mostly fail independently, except position. Code and data-generation scripts: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Visual Generative Lab (VGL), a controlled synthetic framework for measuring how diffusion models learn and generalize basic visual skills, revealing sharp limits in extrapolation and compositional generalization.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluations such as human preference, prompt-following, FID, and IS cannot distinguish whether diffusion models genuinely learn basic visual skills or merely match training patterns.
AI.method: VGL generates synthetic training data from explicit rules for size, position, rotation, count, color, shape, and their compositions, enabling precise evaluation with task-specific, rule-based metrics on models trained from scratch.
AI.result: Controlled experiments show that (1) extrapolation is limited (size and position degrade within a few pixels of the training range, count reaches only about 50% accuracy out of range, and rotation extrapolation varies widely across seeds), (2) the number of distinct skill combinations matters more than dataset size for compositional generalization, and (3) skills mostly fail independently except for position.
AI.conclusion: Controlled rule-based testing exposes systematic generalization limits in diffusion models that distribution-level metrics obscure.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

AI.tldr: This review systematically analyzes efficiency strategies for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) by representing diverse architectures within the canonical Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and GRACE frameworks.
AI.motivation: Efficiency is the primary purpose of MLIPs relative to quantum mechanical calculations, yet strategies for achieving efficient MLIPs have not been systematically reviewed on a common footing.
AI.method: The authors map classical potentials and modern MLIPs (including equivariant transformers) into the ACE and graph-generalized GRACE basis expansions, analyzing how cost scales linearly with system size and model complexity at fixed tensor decomposition rank, and comparing accuracy-cost trade-offs on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard.
AI.result: Models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models on Matbench Discovery, and a single basis truncated along the error-speed Pareto front spans more than two orders of magnitude in computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Apparent architectural diversity in MLIPs largely reflects differences in non-linearity, layer coupling, and optimization rather than representable interactions, while training data ultimately determine model quality.

title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
summary: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free decoding framework that mitigates cross-modal hallucinations in Omni-LLMs, achieving up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free decoding methods for Omni-LLMs can suppress correct unimodal predictions and fail to resolve erroneous consensus due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors.
AI.method: PACD uses two paths: Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration resolves non-consensus cases using task-relevant unimodal evidence, while Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery applies the outranking principle to evaluate layer-wise modality evidence consistency and strength to selectively correct erroneous consensus under confidence constraints.
AI.result: Across four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding on CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average 7.7% relative improvement over the best baseline on OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Separating consensus and non-consensus cases with provenance-aware evidence evaluation effectively reduces cross-modal hallucinations in Omni-LLMs without training.

title: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models
summary: Latent generative models synthesize images by decoding generated latents, yet their decoder is trained only to reconstruct encoder latents and never sees the latents it decodes at test time, so the residual errors of the generator are rendered directly into the final image. Existing remedies retrain the generator, add cost at every sampling step, or make the decoder robust to perturbed real latents, assuming that generator errors resemble such perturbations. We find that they do not. Generated latents lie on the encoder latent manifold as closely as real ones, yet follow a different distribution. The decoder should therefore be adapted to the distribution of generated latents, which raises two challenges: (1) unpaired supervision, since a generated latent has no ground-truth image, and (2) latent-space drift, since a decoder freed from paired targets forgets the latent space it must decode. We propose Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator at no inference cost. Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment matches decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space, and Encoder Anchor Preservation keeps the decoder close to the original one on encoder latents. Our analysis shows that the alignment is effective only on generated latents, where it corrects each sample in proportion to how much more often the generator produces such latents than the encoder; on encoder latents it can only work against the anchor. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, e.g., FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E, complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our code and models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), a post-training framework that fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen latent generative model on generated latents, improving ImageNet FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98 for REPA-E at zero inference cost.
AI.motivation: Latent generative decoders are trained only on encoder latents and never see generated latents at test time, which follow a different distribution despite lying close to the encoder manifold, causing generator residual errors to appear in final images.
AI.method: SAD fine-tunes only the decoder using Generated-Sample Distribution Alignment—matching decoded generated latents to unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space—and Encoder Anchor Preservation to prevent latent-space drift on encoder latents.
AI.result: SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers (e.g., reducing REPA-E FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98), complements discriminator guidance, and extends to text-to-image generation.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the decoder directly to the generated latent distribution with an encoder anchor eliminates distribution mismatch at no extra inference cost.

title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
summary: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a planner-hardware co-design for JEPA-style latent world-model planning that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity via reference forest sampling, achieving 1.28-1.80x speedup and 38-52% energy reduction over a dense accelerator.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based model predictive control with JEPA-style world models repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, making planning too slow for real-life embodied control even on high-end GPUs.
AI.method: The co-design pairs reference forest sampling—which couples sampled action sequences in each group to a shared root to manufacture differential bit-level sparsity across candidates—with a bit-exact hardware accelerator that exploits this exposed sparsity structure.
AI.result: Across three JEPA world models, the co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster and uses 38-52% less energy than a dense accelerator, and is 1.22-1.58x faster with 16-36% less energy than a prior bit-sparse design at the same area.
AI.conclusion: Jointly designing the planner to manufacture differential bit-level sparsity and the hardware to exploit it substantially accelerates JEPA-style world-model planning.

title: Efficient Self-Supervised Adaptation of 3D Abdominal Vision-Language Model for Institution-Specific HCC Classification via Full Fine-Tuning and PEFT
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables, including appendices. Corrected author revision of the MIDL 2026 paper. Revised preprocessing yields lower HCC classification performance; the main findings on temperature initialization and better VerSe performance retention with PEFT remain supported
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) capture cross-modal relationships between image and text, yet their adaptation to institution-specific clinical tasks remains underexplored. In this study, we fine-tuned a pretrained 3D medical VLM for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution with acquisition characteristics that differ from the model's original pretraining corpus. We compared two adaptation strategies: full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), motivated by the common use of PEFT to reduce computational cost and enable adaptation under limited-data constraints. Both approaches achieve strong downstream HCC classification performance despite the cross-institutional domain shift, with PEFT reaching an AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70, and full fine-tuning achieving an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71. Although these results remain below the performance reported by supervised HCC classification approaches, our method achieves improvements over the pretrained model through CT-report contrastive learning without requiring lesion-level annotations or HCC classification labels as training targets. Full fine-tuning converges rapidly but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) attains comparable performance while updating approximately 1% of the model parameters, although requiring more training steps. We also examine the role of contrastive temperature, observing that temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance. This study demonstrates that a 3D medical VLM can be efficiently adapted to institution-specific HCC classification using self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning, while highlighting the practical trade-offs between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for adapting a pretrained 3D abdominal vision-language model to institution-specific hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification via self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning.
AI.motivation: Adapting medical VLMs to institution-specific clinical tasks with different acquisition characteristics remains underexplored, particularly without lesion-level annotations or classification labels.
AI.method: Using paired abdominal CT scans and radiology reports from a different institution, the authors adapt a pretrained 3D medical VLM via CT-report contrastive learning, comparing full fine-tuning against PEFT (ConvLoRA for the image encoder and LoRA for the text encoder) and examining contrastive temperature initialization.
AI.result: Full fine-tuning achieves an AUC of 0.82 and F1 of 0.71 but overfits within a few epochs, whereas PEFT reaches a comparable AUC of 0.79 and F1 of 0.70 while updating approximately 1% of parameters (requiring more training steps), and temperature initialization significantly affects classification performance.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised CT-report contrastive learning enables effective cross-institutional adaptation of 3D medical VLMs for HCC classification, with PEFT offering strong parameter efficiency and reduced overfitting compared to full fine-tuning.

title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $α$-Stable MIMO Channels
summary: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $\alpha$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $\alpha$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $\alpha$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.

AI.tldr: This work studies diffusion-based signal and channel estimation under Gaussian and symmetric alpha-stable MIMO fading channels, showing that temporal reconstruction and alpha-stable priors improve both channel estimation and image recovery.
AI.motivation: Most diffusion models assume Gaussian distributions that fail to accurately represent heavy-tailed data encountered in alpha-stable fading channels.
AI.method: The authors develop standard and score-based diffusion models for Gaussian and alpha-stable distributions, guide reverse diffusion with observation likelihoods (allowing single-model reuse across the location-scale family), combine separate image and channel diffusion models for blind MIMO recovery, and compare independent versus temporal reconstruction.
AI.result: Temporal reconstruction using previous observations improves both channel estimation and reconstructed image quality under time-dependent channels, and an alpha-stable diffusion prior outperforms a Gaussian diffusion prior on heavy-tailed channel data.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating alpha-stable diffusion priors and temporal dependence significantly enhances joint signal-channel estimation in heavy-tailed MIMO channels.

title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
comment: 39 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL. Extends an earlier version presented at the non-archival CoLoRAI workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a U(1)-symmetric Tensor Train (TT) framework for constrained combinatorial optimization, using expressibility enhancement and graph-based diversity selection to improve solution quality and runtime over baselines.
AI.motivation: Incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based generative optimization is challenging because existing interpolation and sampling methods often fail when feasible points are rare.
AI.method: Built on U(1)-symmetric tensor networks, the framework introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure to guide sample selection during training.
AI.result: On assignment benchmarks, both expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their baselines; the diversifying strategy extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning with larger gains in higher-tensor-rank families, and runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads.
AI.conclusion: U(1)-symmetric tensor trains with expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection provide a practical, scalable approach to constrained combinatorial optimization.

title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
summary: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. To address this credit-assignment conflict, we introduce PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a training framework that combines reference-aligned plan protection and plan-aligned action repair without altering the original scalar action reward. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark.
