Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PACT (Plan-Action Consistency Training), a credit-assignment framework for GUI agents that protects verified plans and repairs erroneous actions, raising AndroidWorld success from 60.34% to 68.97%.
AI.motivation: GUI agents often generate a correct immediate plan but emit a mismatched action, and standard outcome-supervised RL broadcasts negative advantages across all tokens, unfairly penalizing valid planning.
AI.method: Using annotated reference actions to detect execution gaps, PACT masks negative policy-gradient contributions across the verified plan's token span and uses a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights to favor the reference action over the erroneous action while keeping the reasoning unchanged.
AI.result: Compared to the outcome-only baseline, PACT improves AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), AndroidControl High plan-action consistency from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp), and OSWorld desktop task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling plan protection from action repair resolves credit-assignment conflicts and improves GUI agent execution across mobile and desktop environments.

title: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
summary: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), a single-run pixel-sparse adversarial attack that matches or beats individual members of sparse-AutoAttack (sAA) while running 3.7 to 5.0 times faster on CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Pixel-sparse robustness is currently evaluated using the sAA ensemble because sPGD relies on a first-order model broken by full pixel changes while Sparse-RS ignores informative gradients.
AI.method: Derived from a Taylor bound and empirical state measurements, GRS follows five rules: use gradient sign to set a new pixel's value, follow candidate-pixel rankings loosely and removal rankings more closely, avoid proposing a pixel twice before acceptance, and accept moves solely based on the loss.
AI.result: Across 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA, is within one point of sAA or stronger on 17 of 18 settings (and significantly stronger on 8), uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than full sAA members on CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: Combining gradient-guided proposal rules with loss-only acceptance yields a fast, single-run pixel-sparse attack that rivals or surpasses ensemble-based evaluation.

title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
summary: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents COTTI, an industrial recommendation framework combining contrastive training and time-aware inference for promotional drift, achieving +3.14% conversion rate and +2.68% revenue per mille in a 10-day online experiment.
AI.motivation: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and conversion probability scales across time horizons, degrading standard recommendation models.
AI.method: COTTI separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment via Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) on paired user histories, Active Re-weighting (RW) based on historical-interest distance, and Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) to adjust logits at inference with fixed predictor parameters.
AI.result: On Fliggy data, COTTI achieves 0.8127 offline AUC (vs. 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN+ABA) with 38.9 ms p99 latency and 14,700 requests/s throughput (ABA adds 2.2 ms); in a 10-day online experiment against HDR, it yields relative gains of 3.14% in conversion rate and 2.68% in revenue per mille, though cross-category analysis shows declines in paid-item recall for novel categories.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling contrastive historical alignment from time-aware logit adjustment improves promotional recommendation performance at low serving cost, while highlighting a trade-off with novel-category recall.

title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
summary: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an inference-time refinement framework for flow-matching robotic policies that uses parallel physics rollouts and constrained CMA-ES to enforce task-level progress funnels, boosting PushT success from 31.3% to 88.5%.
AI.motivation: Generative robotic policies can produce plausible motion chunks that nonetheless stall or undo earlier task progress because they lack guarantees of task-level convergence.
AI.method: The framework evaluates candidate action chunks via parallel physics-based rollouts, enforces task-level performance funnels verified with interval-wise Lipschitz bounds, and refines flow source seeds using CMA-ES constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution for both Euclidean and Riemannian Flow Matching policies.
AI.result: On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%, respectively; on PushT, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% over endpoint-only constraints, and the radial band keeps out-of-distribution motion windows at 11.3% (vs. 34.1% for unconstrained search).
AI.conclusion: Funnel-constrained inference-time source-seed refinement ensures task convergence in flow-matching policies while preserving the learned motion prior.

title: DAQ: Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Transformers
summary: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ) for spiking transformers, aligning quantized membrane variables with reference firing regions to achieve 58.8% AUC and 90.9% PR on FE108 while reducing energy by 66.2%.
AI.motivation: Spiking transformers still incur substantial storage and computation overhead from weights and membrane variables, and standard post-training quantization struggles to preserve neuronal firing decisions across recurrent time steps.
AI.method: DAQ analyzes how quantization errors affect firing at decision boundaries and propagate over time, then calibrates quantizers with an objective that keeps quantized membrane variables within reference floating-point firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory.
AI.result: Evaluated with 4-bit weights and membrane variables across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking, DAQ achieves 58.8% AUC and 90.9% PR with SDTrack on FE108 while reducing energy by 66.2%.
AI.conclusion: Aligning quantizer calibration directly to neuronal firing decisions along the quantized trajectory enables accurate, energy-efficient 4-bit spiking transformers.

title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
summary: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.

AI.tldr: This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data, showing that ZZFeatureMap_1 achieves an average R2 of 0.991 under 90% missingness.
AI.motivation: Vessels in the Internet of Ships generate large volumes of data with persistent missing values, yet existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning.
AI.method: The authors compare classical SVR (with RBF and other kernels) against QSVR models using different quantum feature maps to estimate main-engine fuel-flow rate on real-world Panamax bulk carrier data (37 variables across six categories) under exploratory, scalability (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluations.
AI.result: Both classical and quantum approaches maintain strong imputation performance under severe data scarcity, with ZZFeatureMap_1 achieving the highest average R2 (0.991 with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features) and lowest aggregate errors, while the RBF kernel is the strongest classical baseline.
AI.conclusion: QSVR with appropriate quantum feature maps is a viable and accurate alternative to classical SVR for imputing missing ship performance data.

title: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow
summary: Canopy height models (CHMs) - per-pixel maps of vegetation top height - are essential for forest carbon accounting, wildfire fuel mapping, and tree-level ecology, yet sub-meter CHMs require airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year national cycles. We produce 0.5 m CHMs from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a 20$\times$ cross-modal super-resolution task where optical reflectance must predict geometric height it does not directly observe. Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, we derive two operating points with shared conditioning. A deterministic regressor (Anchor) targets low distortion; a conditional flow matching model, trained on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space (AR-flow), targets perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles spanning 69 ecoregions across the contiguous United States and evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only free satellite input. The AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from the Anchor's 1.13 to 0.208, at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. Crown-scale statistics improve, but strict individual-tree detection remains weak: generated sub-pixel detail represents plausible structure rather than measured individual trees. Quarterly continental refresh becomes tractable, letting satellite monitoring inform timing and extent for more expensive data acquisitions.

AI.tldr: This paper produces 0.5 m canopy height models (CHMs) from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery using a deterministic Anchor regressor and a conditional flow matching model (AR-flow), achieving 2.83 m MAE across 2,530 held-out US tiles.
AI.motivation: Sub-meter CHMs are critical for carbon accounting and wildfire fuel mapping but typically require expensive airborne LiDAR refreshed on multi-year cycles.
AI.method: Motivated by the perception-distortion trade-off, the authors train a deterministic regressor (Anchor) for low distortion and a conditional flow matching model (AR-flow) on the Anchor's residual in a learned CHM latent space for perceptual fidelity, using 197k LiDAR-paired tiles across 69 US ecoregions.
AI.result: Evaluated on 2,530 held-out tiles against eight baselines, the Anchor achieves 2.83 m MAE using only Sentinel-2 input, while AR-flow reduces sliced Wasserstein distance from 1.13 to 0.208 at a higher MAE of 3.68 m, improving crown-scale statistics though individual-tree detection remains weak.
AI.conclusion: Dual-operating-point synthesis enables tractable quarterly continental CHM updates from free satellite imagery to guide targeted LiDAR acquisitions.

title: Social Signal Bench: Evidence-Weighted Evaluation of Co-occurring Social Signals in Video and Audio
summary: Recognizing social signals such as interest and hesitation requires interpreting context-dependent behaviors that may co-occur in conversation. Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate such co-occurring signals, and conventional multi-label F1 overlooks semantic relationships and annotator disagreement. We introduce Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour densely annotated benchmark for the evaluation of social signal recognition and engagement, comprising two datasets: Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours), covering ten social signals in audiovisual recordings, and Social Signal Bench Audio (22 hours), covering six signals in audio-only recordings. Each dataset pairs a public training set of online conversational video, of which 10 hours are expert-annotated and the remainder pseudo-labeled, with a private expert-labeled test set spanning four conversational domains. We also propose Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions through optimal per-clip matching. Controlled perturbations demonstrate that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones, unlike conventional F1. Under a shared evaluation protocol, 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Social Signal Bench, a 47-hour audiovisual and audio-only benchmark for co-occurring social signals, along with Evidence-Weighted F1 (EW-F1), showing that post-trained 7B open models match or outperform frontier models.
AI.motivation: Existing affective computing benchmarks rarely evaluate co-occurring social signals, and conventional multi-label F1 ignores semantic relationships and annotator disagreement.
AI.method: The authors construct Social Signal Bench Video (25 hours, 10 signals) and Audio (22 hours, 6 signals) with public training sets and private expert-labeled test sets, and propose EW-F1, which weights reference labels by annotator evidence and assigns graded credit to semantically related predictions via optimal per-clip matching.
AI.result: Controlled perturbations confirm that EW-F1 distinguishes semantically related errors from unrelated ones unlike conventional F1, and 7B open models post-trained on Social Signal Bench outperform general-purpose frontier models on video and match them on audio.
AI.conclusion: Social Signal Bench and EW-F1 provide a nuanced evaluation framework for co-occurring social signals, demonstrating strong performance from specialized 7B open models.

title: LoopZip: Visual Token Compression for Efficient Looped Vision-Language Models
summary: Looped vision-language models (VLMs) deepen computation by reusing shared layers, approaching larger models' capabilities with fewer parameters and easing the storage and deployment burden of stacking independent layers. However, repeatedly processing long visual sequences still incurs substantial compute and GPU memory costs. Visual token compression reduces these costs by shortening sequences. Existing methods mainly select original tokens directly or combine selection with aggregation. In looped models, the former may overlook changing token importance across calls and discard information needed later; the latter lack joint consideration of output changes across calls, limiting information preservation. We propose LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm addressing both issues. Visual aggregation builds a compact candidate pool before the looped backbone, and cross-invocation selection averages instruction attention from the first two existing calls of the same shared attention layer to retain tokens needed by both states. Weight-tied value correction then jointly fits shared visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs, reducing output deviations across states. To validate LoopZip's effectiveness, we conduct extensive experiments covering two open-source looped VLMs, eleven benchmarks, and three pruning ratios. On LoopVL-1B, LoopZip retains 97.16% of the original model's performance at 50% pruning ratio and exceeds the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning ratio. Across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, LoopVL-1B with LoopZip reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups over the original model.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LoopZip, a training-free visual token compression algorithm for looped vision-language models (VLMs) that retains 97.16% of LoopVL-1B's performance at 50% pruning while reducing peak GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98% and achieving 2.01-2.47x speedups.
AI.motivation: Looped VLMs reuse shared layers to save parameters, but repeatedly processing long visual sequences incurs high compute and memory costs, and existing token compression methods fail to account for changing token importance and output deviations across shared-layer invocations.
AI.method: LoopZip builds a compact candidate pool via visual aggregation before the looped backbone, selects tokens by averaging instruction attention across the first two calls of the same shared attention layer, and applies weight-tied value correction to jointly fit visual-value adjustments to both pre-selection layer outputs.
AI.result: Evaluated on two open-source looped VLMs across eleven benchmarks and three pruning ratios, LoopZip on LoopVL-1B retains 97.16% performance at 50% pruning, beats the strongest baseline by 5.36% at 87.5% pruning, reduces peak GPU memory by 58.36%-58.98%, and achieves 2.01-2.47x end-to-end speedups across Hugging Face Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for cross-invocation attention and output consistency enables effective, training-free visual token compression for looped VLMs.

title: Proximal Targets: Training Looped Refiners on Problems with Many Correct Answers
summary: Looped refiners such as HRM and TRM apply one small network repeatedly to a draft answer, and deep supervision trains every pass toward one stored answer per puzzle. We prove that when a puzzle has many correct answers this target sets a loss floor that no model capacity removes, and that the loss-minimising pass blends the answers into an invalid grid. We propose the proximal target: train each pass toward the correct answer nearest to its own input, found by scanning a list of answers, by a search solver started at the draft, or within a band of quality set by a knob; correct answers become fixed points, and a pass only has to make fewer errors than its input has for the loop to converge, which its training loss bounds. With the same 1.7M-parameter network and 5 seeds, the proximal target solves 98.8% of Sudoku puzzles with 2-64 answers (standard target: 2.5%), 93.8% of sparse puzzles with more than 10,000 answers without any list of answers (0.0%), and 90.9% of 200-node 3-colourings after training on graphs of at most 50 nodes (36.9%), and different random starts end at different answers. Against GRAM, a stochastic-latent reasoner, a single run is correct far more often (98.8% vs. 57.7%) and twenty runs find more of the answers (53.6% vs. 37.4%), while GRAM is slightly ahead on its own 10-node colouring benchmark; in Scrabble the knob becomes a calibrated strength dial.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes training looped refiners toward a "proximal target"—the correct answer nearest to each pass's input—raising 1.7M-parameter Sudoku solving on multi-answer puzzles from 2.5% to 98.8%.
AI.motivation: Standard deep supervision trains every pass of a looped refiner toward a single stored answer, which creates an unremovable loss floor and causes the model to blend multiple valid answers into an invalid grid when puzzles have many correct solutions.
AI.method: The proximal target trains each pass toward the closest valid answer to its current draft (found via answer-list scanning, a solver, or a quality band), making correct answers fixed points so the loop converges whenever a pass reduces errors relative to its input.
AI.result: With a 1.7M-parameter network across 5 seeds, proximal targets solve 98.8% of Sudoku puzzles with 2-64 answers (vs. 2.5% standard), 93.8% of sparse puzzles with >10,000 answers without an answer list (vs. 0.0%), and 90.9% of 200-node 3-colourings after training on <=50-node graphs (vs. 36.9%), while outperforming GRAM on single-run accuracy (98.8% vs. 57.7%) and 20-run answer diversity (53.6% vs. 37.4%).
AI.conclusion: Training toward the nearest valid solution eliminates multi-answer blending and enables small looped refiners to generalize strongly on under-constrained reasoning problems.

title: Stochastic Diversity Windows: Diagnosing Noise Influence in Robotic Diffusion Sampling
summary: Diffusion models are increasingly adopted in robotics and control due to their capability to express multiple feasible solutions to a given task. However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic for robotic diffusion sampling, identifying compact stochastic diversity windows (SDWs) that guide targeted amplification and DDIM-skipping hybrids for up to 40-60% fewer network evaluations and 85% wall-clock speedup.
AI.motivation: The role of sampler stochasticity across denoising steps in robotic diffusion models is poorly understood, limiting principled control over solution diversity and sampling speed.
AI.method: The authors apply a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic across five model-sampler configurations on three robotics benchmarks to measure temporal sensitivity profiles, define compact SDWs where stochasticity most affects outputs, and test targeted stochastic amplification and an SDW-hybrid sampler that replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions.
AI.result: The SDW-hybrid sampler reduces network evaluations by up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85% with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.
AI.conclusion: Identifying stochastic diversity windows enables principled acceleration and diversity control in robotic diffusion sampling without degrading task performance.

title: OICycle: Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle for Belief-State Learning in Longitudinal Clinical Decision Making
summary: Clinical care is a closed loop: clinicians observe partial evidence, infer the patient's state, and intervene, and each intervention determines what is observed next. This makes clinical decision making a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which a belief over a latent patient state must be updated from irregular, multimodal, and incomplete records. Yet most deep clinical models predict from a single snapshot or from coarsely aggregated history, while POMDP-based clinical methods need hand-specified discrete state spaces and transition models that real electronic health records cannot supply. We introduce OICycle (Observe, Infer, and Intervene Cycle), which learns a stochastic belief state directly from retrospective trajectories. At every episode, a learned recurrent operator fuses a sample of the previous belief with the new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them. The resulting Gaussian belief is trained to predict clinicians' next interventions, the time to the next episode, and next-episode mortality. To enable reproducible evaluation, we release a benchmark derived from MIMIC-IV, MIMIC-IV-Note, and MIMIC-CXR that organizes 72,075 hospital admissions (5.4M laboratory, microbiology, radiology, prescription, and note records) into temporally ordered therapeutic--diagnostic episodes. Compared with an otherwise identical history-free model, OICycle improves next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649. Analysis shows that the learned belief encodes intervention type and trajectory position and evolves smoothly across episodes, and that the benefit of history is concentrated in interventions whose ordering depends on prior findings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OICycle, a recurrent belief-state model for longitudinal clinical decision making, along with a 72,075-admission MIMIC-IV benchmark, improving next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347.
AI.motivation: Clinical care is a closed-loop POMDP, yet most deep clinical models rely on single snapshots or coarse history aggregation, while traditional POMDP methods require hand-specified discrete states and transitions unavailable in real EHRs.
AI.method: OICycle learns a stochastic Gaussian belief state directly from retrospective trajectories using a recurrent operator that fuses a previous belief sample with new multimodal observations and the intervention that produced them, trained to predict next interventions, time to next episode, and next-episode mortality.
AI.result: On a newly released benchmark of 72,075 MIMIC-IV admissions (5.4M records), OICycle outperforms an identical history-free model, improving next-intervention adaptive recall from 0.253 to 0.347, time-to-next-episode macro-F1 from 0.293 to 0.351, and next-episode mortality macro-F1 from 0.585 to 0.649.
AI.conclusion: Learning continuous stochastic belief states over therapeutic-diagnostic episodes captures clinically meaningful history and substantially improves longitudinal clinical prediction.

title: TabDAG: Structured Evolutionary Search for Tabular Feature Engineering
summary: Feature engineering can improve tabular prediction, but useful transformations are compositional, data-dependent, and subject to leakage constraints. We present TabDAG, a framework that combines evolutionary search with a graph representation of feature-engineering programs. Nodes implement row-wise or data-fitted transformations; edges encode dependencies among raw variables, intermediate values, and final features. The representation supports interactions, statistical encodings, clustering- and neighborhood-based features, and multi-stage compositions in a single executable program. Mutations are structured edits constrained by a parent-specific schema and checked before evaluation. In our experiments, no structurally invalid program reached evaluation, although proposals could be rejected and valid graphs could still fail at runtime. Across ten regression and classification datasets and three tabular model families, evolved features improve predictive performance over raw inputs. TabDAG and its combination with OpenFE achieve the two best mean ranks among the compared methods; pairwise rank differences between feature-engineering methods do not survive multiple-testing correction. The LLM-based searches use the same backbone and candidate-evaluation budget. A controlled ablation compares free-form Python, whole-graph JSON, and constrained graph edits with the search engine, budget, and backbone held fixed. Constrained edits yield fewer failed evaluations than either rewrite baseline. The resulting graphs expose the transformations and dependencies selected by search, enabling feature-level analysis of the observed gains.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TabDAG, an evolutionary search framework over directed acyclic graphs of feature-engineering programs, achieving the top mean ranks alongside OpenFE across ten tabular datasets while eliminating structurally invalid proposals.
AI.motivation: Tabular feature engineering requires compositional, data-dependent transformations subject to leakage constraints, which free-form code generation often violates or fails to execute reliably.
AI.method: TabDAG represents feature-engineering programs as executable DAGs of row-wise and data-fitted transformations with dependency edges, applying schema-constrained structured edits checked before evaluation.
AI.result: Across ten regression and classification datasets and three model families, no structurally invalid program reached evaluation; TabDAG and TabDAG+OpenFE achieved the two best mean ranks (though pairwise rank differences did not survive multiple-testing correction), and constrained graph edits yielded fewer failed evaluations than free-form Python or whole-graph JSON baselines.
AI.conclusion: Schema-constrained DAG representations make evolutionary feature engineering more reliable and interpretable while maintaining competitive predictive performance.

title: Outcome-Balanced PPO and Policy-Induced Flow Rectification for Flow-Based VLA Policies
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper combines Outcome-Balanced PPO with policy-induced flow rectification for RL post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies, improving success rates across simulated manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RL post-training of flow-based VLA policies faces two challenges: policy updates alter the velocity-field geometry used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts produce uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs.
AI.method: Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs, while policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs from the current policy to refresh the score-approximation representation.
AI.result: Evaluated on simulated manipulation benchmarks and a Real2Sim2Real task, the combined framework improves task success rates over the evaluated baselines.
AI.conclusion: Balancing multi-task advantage signals and periodically rectifying the policy-induced flow stabilizes and improves RL post-training for flow-based VLA policies.

title: Is model self-assessment enough for diverse LVLM ensembles?
summary: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates training-free candidate response selection for diverse LVLM ensembles across 34 confidence estimators, 24 configurations, and 20 datasets, finding that simple self-assessment can outperform constituent models but depends heavily on confounding factors.
AI.motivation: LVLM ensembles typically rely on training, parameter fitting, or complex pipelines, and prior evaluations are too limited to establish fair comparisons or generalizability.
AI.method: The authors build a unified candidate response selection pipeline that picks the best answer from diverse LVLMs using each model's uncalibrated self-assessment confidence, evaluating 34 confidence estimation methods, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications.
AI.result: Simple training- and parameter-free self-assessment approaches can outperform constituent models and compete with more involved alternatives, including on open-ended tasks; however, dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording significantly confound results, sometimes causing ensembles to underperform their best single model.
AI.conclusion: Training-free LVLM ensembles via self-assessment are effective when deployment conditions are well characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models serving as a solid starting point, though sensitivity to confounders limits general-purpose use.

title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
summary: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), an end-to-end pixel-space diffusion model that progressively groups related tokens, achieving 1.48 FID on ImageNet 256x256 with ~40% of JiT's training FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Plain pixel-space Transformers trail two-stage latent diffusion models in quality and efficiency because they retain one token per patch throughout the backbone rather than building a visual hierarchy.
AI.method: HiT progressively groups related tokens into single compact group tokens for the main Transformer bottleneck and ungroups them back to image positions, using a batch-level compression budget that lets group memberships and counts vary across images and timesteps.
AI.result: HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet 256x256 at ~40% of JiT's cumulative training FLOPs, exceeds UniLiP's average text-to-image score across five benchmarks with ~6x fewer denoiser parameters and ~3x fewer forward FLOPs, and exhibits emergent semantic grouping of objects and caption words without labels.
AI.conclusion: Learning an internal visual hierarchy closes the efficiency and quality gap for end-to-end pixel-space diffusion without external visual pretraining.

title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
summary: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a residual-guided lightweight RL framework for risk-aware trajectory selection with a frozen world model, reducing nuScenes open-loop L2 error by 3.99% with only 11,725 deployed parameters.
AI.motivation: Fixed trajectory selection rules in world-model-based automated driving cannot easily adapt to scene-dependent trade-offs.
AI.method: The framework uses PPO to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals (16,106 parameters across actor and critic), training a context-conditioned ranking network from local perturbation feedback; at inference, only the 11,725-parameter ranking network is deployed alongside predicted risk ranks to select an unmodified candidate.
AI.result: On the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average L2 trajectory error by 3.99% over the RiskWorld baseline without RL selection, by 0.83% over categorical PPO without residuals under matched budgets, and maintains lower L2 when risk features are removed or shuffled.
AI.conclusion: Residual-guided RL exploration enables ultra-lightweight, risk-aware trajectory selection over frozen world models.

title: When Anchors Shift the Target: Advantage-Gated Adaptation for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
summary: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets. Because negative advantages induce concave updates with unbounded repulsive gradients, existing methods stabilize training using cached predictions from a moving policy copy, yet these anchors also alter what positive feedback teaches the model to fit. We formalize this conflict as anchor coupling: after separating frozen-reference regularizers, affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target. We propose Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA) to decouple these roles. Positive samples retain standard target fitting, whose self-limiting update vanishes at the observed target independently of the moving anchor. Negative samples instead use the first-order tangent of the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction, preserving the local repulsion direction with a prediction-independent gradient. Within the quadratic-anchor family, these requirements uniquely determine the parameter-free gate $\omega(a)=\max(-a,0)$. Because the moving copy provides local linearization rather than retention, AGA assigns long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference regularized at its operating classifier-free guidance scale, interpreted through an implicit-reward lens. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, our experiments show that displacing positive targets degrades visual quality and heightens sensitivity to policy-copy schedules, whereas AGA consistently improves the reward--quality trade-off.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes anchor coupling in forward-process diffusion RL and proposes Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA), a parameter-free gating rule that decouples positive target fitting from negative-sample repulsion.
AI.motivation: Moving-policy anchors stabilize negative-advantage updates in forward-process diffusion RL, but they also displace positive regression targets, degrading visual quality and increasing sensitivity to policy-copy schedules.
AI.method: AGA retains standard target fitting for positive samples and linearizes the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction for negative samples, yielding the unique parameter-free gate omega(a) = max(-a, 0) within the quadratic-anchor family, while delegating long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference.
AI.result: Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, AGA consistently improves the reward-quality trade-off compared to moving-anchor baselines that displace positive targets.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling positive target fitting from negative-sample linearization via advantage gating resolves anchor coupling and improves diffusion RL alignment.

title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates opportunistic screening of MRI-verified soft-tissue pathology (synovial effusion) from routine dental CBCT scans using physics-guided 3D self-supervised learning, achieving 0.793 ROC AUC.
AI.motivation: Routine CBCT is optimized for mineralized tissues, burying soft-tissue abnormalities beneath photon noise and below human visual perception, which normally forces secondary MRI scans.
AI.method: The authors pre-train a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes using the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware PhysLoss targeting the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window, followed by automated condylar zenith localization and deterministic 3D cropping on N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI temporomandibular joints.
AI.result: Under patient-isolated 3x10-fold cross-validation, the PhysLoss+GCond representation achieves 0.793 ROC AUC for MRI-verified synovial effusion, captures 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001), and maintains 0.791 intra-patient structural consistency, whereas identical architectures pre-trained with L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition collapse to random guessing.
AI.conclusion: Physics-guided 3D self-supervised learning can extract sub-visual soft-tissue pathology signatures from routine low-contrast CBCT scans under severe paired-data scarcity.

title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
comment: 41 pages. Ancillary files contain the measurement and verification scripts. Prepared with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude for drafting, revision and the verification scripts; OpenAI ChatGPT for a critical reading of a draft); all measurements were produced and verified by the author, who is responsible for the content
summary: For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $\Delta = [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not. We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $\pi$ to $\pi \circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $\Delta(\pi) = -\Delta(\pi \circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in. The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $\sigma$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques recent fixed-text "entropy production" and assembly-order measures in language models, proving that neither represents thermodynamic entropy production on a single text.
AI.motivation: Recent work evaluates fluctuation-theorem expressions on single fixed texts by comparing forward and reversed text probabilities, treating them as entropy production separating causal from arbitrary prose without a theoretical zero.
AI.method: The authors establish an exact zero for sentence-order reversal via an antisymmetric involution over all n! sentence permutations, evaluate five autoregressive models (124M to 4B parameters) using midrank statistics, and analyze a masked-model assembly-order comparison between left-to-right and right-to-left generation.
AI.result: Across the five autoregressive evaluators, only 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order (with the rest reflecting production order), while the masked-model assembly-order quantity vanishes identically when conditionals come from a joint distribution, meaning non-zero values measure evaluator incompatibility rather than text properties.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-text reversal scores lack a thermodynamic zero and cannot serve as fixed-text entropy production, and masked-model assembly comparisons merely diagnose model inconsistency.

title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project page: this https URL
summary: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of a neural controller at 4 kHz without hardware-software co-design.
AI.motivation: Industrial 6D magnetic levitation systems typically rely on hardware-software co-design to enable compact, hand-crafted electromagnetic force approximations at kilohertz rates, which restricts operating workspaces and supported mover topologies.
AI.method: Magflow computes the underlying electromagnetic physics directly in a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator to train a neural controller purely from simulated physics.
AI.result: The learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware, meets hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz, achieves qualitatively new behaviors, and levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable physics simulation removes the need for restrictive hardware-software co-design in industrial 6D magnetic levitation control.

title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
summary: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that routes per-question frame budgets under a fixed average budget, improving long-video QA on Video-MME-v2 and other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-video QA benchmarks evaluate models with a uniform frame budget per question even though queries vary widely in visual evidence demand, and uniformly increasing frames does not reliably improve all metrics.
AI.method: FrameRouter pairs an evidence-demand router with a budget-constrained allocation rule and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies, varying per-question frame counts while keeping the dataset-wide mean budget equal to a uniform reference.
AI.result: Across Video-MME-v2 and several other long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves question-answering accuracy using the same average visual budget as uniform baselines.
AI.conclusion: Allocating frame budgets selectively per question at test time is an effective, training-free complement to query-aware frame selection.

title: Event-Based Dynamic Lip Region Estimation During Speech
summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. These include automatic lip reading, audiovisual speech analysis, and human-robot interaction, particularly in challenging environments characterized by low illumination or high dynamic range. Event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and voice activity detection, however, mostly operate on a cropped region of interest (ROI), by hand or by the dataset, and no event-based method supplies that ROI as a spatial region; existing event-based face analysis gives the mouth as landmarks, which presents a mismatch between application and localization. The present work predicts a dense heatmap over the lip region from the full event "frame". Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed at every location by a two-pathway continuous-time recurrent network (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on the real elapsed time of each bin: a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway, utilised for refining and anchoring the prediction. The model reaches 69.5% on lips on four unseen speakers and switches target only 2.1 times per second, against 8.9 and 11.0 for convolutional baselines with more parameters. Adding a spatial encoder improves precision but fails on a new face scale. On a real event sensor, trained only on simulated events, the proposed model reaches 58.0% on lips against 43.2% for the CNN, with fewer than half its target switches.

AI.tldr: This paper predicts a dense lip-region heatmap directly from full-frame event-camera streams using a two-pathway continuous-time RNN, achieving 69.5% on unseen speakers and 58.0% on real event sensors with far fewer target switches than CNNs.
AI.motivation: Event-based speech applications mostly rely on manually or dataset-cropped lip ROIs, while existing event-based face analysis outputs mouth landmarks rather than the spatial region required downstream.
AI.method: Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed per location by a two-pathway continuous-time RNN (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on real elapsed bin times, combining a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway.
AI.result: The model reaches 69.5% on lips across four unseen speakers with 2.1 target switches/s (vs. 8.9 and 11.0 for larger CNNs), and when trained only on simulated events and tested on a real sensor, reaches 58.0% vs. 43.2% for the CNN with fewer than half its target switches.
AI.conclusion: A two-pathway CT-RNN provides stable, scale-generalizable dense lip ROI localization from raw event streams without spatial cropping.

title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D
comment: 39 pages, 13 figures, 20 tables. Code and data: this https URL and this https URL. Extends arXiv:2611.02699 with robot-level experiments
summary: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper audits the Robotic World Model (RWM) and RWM-U for ANYmal D without a GPU, finding that one-step accuracy misjudges rollout skill, ensemble uncertainty is severely under-covered, and simulator accuracy does not reliably predict walking policy success.
AI.motivation: Learned robot simulators are typically trained and evaluated one step ahead even though policies unroll them for 100+ steps, leaving open whether standard metrics actually predict downstream control performance.
AI.method: The authors rebuilt RWM/RWM-U to match released outputs, losses, and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies, and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and tested policies trained inside these simulators in a MuJoCo ANYmal D model.
AI.result: Rollout training beat one-step training at 368 steps on all 10 held-out episodes despite worse one-step error; pruning 30% of weights kept 90% one-step skill but only 39% at 2 s; ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps) yet covered only 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma (vs. 68% calibrated); and all 18 fine-tuned copies improved 1- and 8-step prediction yet 13 produced failing walking policies.
AI.conclusion: One-step and short-horizon prediction metrics do not reliably rank learned robot simulators by downstream walking policy quality, underscoring the need for policy-level evaluation.

title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
summary: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how training history length (6, 12, 24 months) and sampling/validation policies interact with forecast horizon (5 to 120 minutes) in intraday equity Transformers, finding no single policy dominates all horizons.
AI.motivation: Longer historical training windows can improve parameter estimation but may introduce outdated market relationships that transfer poorly to current conditions.
AI.method: Using a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set in a monthly walk-forward setup (264 refits) from January 2025 to October 2026, the authors test 12 configurations combining four sampling/validation policies and three history lengths across eight cumulative return horizons (5-120 minutes), evaluated by cross-sectional Spearman IC against five-factor residual returns.
AI.result: Six-month recency sampling leads at 5-15 minutes, multi-recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes, and uniform configurations lead at 60-120 minutes; increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy, while an equal-weight ensemble of all 12 models beats every individual mean at 15, 20, and 25 minutes.
AI.conclusion: Historical data selection should be evaluated jointly with forecast horizon, as optimal recency depends on horizon length rather than a universal policy.

title: RSI-Prime: Training Models to Train Models
summary: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RSI-Prime, a dataset of 350 complete model-training trajectories, and a decision-level loss-masking method that improves GLM-5.3's autonomous post-training performance on PostTrainBench by 31.95% relatively.
AI.motivation: Enabling LLMs to autonomously conduct training for recursive self-improvement requires dedicated study and systematic development of their model-training capability.
AI.method: The authors construct RSI-Prime with 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories, perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, and apply decision-level loss masking to exclude low-quality behavior from supervision.
AI.result: Training GLM-5.3 on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight a path toward recursive self-improvement systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.

title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
summary: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a barrier-guided diffusion sampling method that composes single-agent trajectory models into cooperative heterogeneous team trajectories without requiring cooperative demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Generating cooperative team trajectories usually requires costly demonstrations of agents cooperating, which may not exist for new tasks.
AI.method: Known physical cooperation conditions are encoded as trajectory constraints and enforced during sampling from generative models trained on individual agent demonstrations alone.
AI.result: The authors prove the method can generate every team trajectory satisfying the constraints, demonstrate its effectiveness numerically on two cooperative tasks without retraining when agents join or leave, and implement it on a multi-robot testbed.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables flexible capability composition in heterogeneous teams using only single-agent demonstrations.

title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
summary: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Déjà View, a shared working-memory model for visual tasks that combines dynamic activity with temporary feature associations to perform five distinct tasks using explicit response cues.
AI.motivation: A working-memory model must both remember stimuli and flexibly use that memory across different tasks.
AI.method: A single model combining dynamic activity and temporary associations between image features is trained on five visual working-memory and categorization tasks, guided by explicit cues indicating the required response.
AI.result: Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance, whereas seeing more images increases false alarms; on sample-memory-plus-categorization, the probability of answering all questions correctly drops as more questions are asked, while performance remains stable across 40 brief trials per task.
AI.conclusion: A single working-memory system can be flexibly reused across multiple tasks, with error patterns shaped by both image history and task demands.

title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
comment: Accepted at the 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations.
