At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

AI.tldr: This paper presents WoRD, a diffusion-based posterior inference method for online goal recognition that infers calibrated multimodal beliefs over candidate goals from partial continuous trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing goal recognition methods either abstract away continuous motion into symbols or rely on hard-to-acquire dynamics models, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes.
AI.method: WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal using a learned trajectory prior, steers each chain toward observed trajectories via a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights samples by Bayes' rule into a goal posterior.
AI.result: Across simulated robot, pedestrian, and vehicle trajectories evaluated on four metrics, WoRD preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse or grow overconfident.
AI.conclusion: Learned trajectory priors with Bayesian diffusion steering enable calibrated online goal recognition across diverse continuous domains.

title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
comment: Equal contribution: John Gideon and Anshul Gupta. 8 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to CVPR 2027
summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ID-MAE, a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder for impaired driving detection, and introduces DIVERT, a 103-hour driving-simulator dataset with ten impairment inductions.
AI.motivation: Ground-truth labels for human cognitive states such as distraction and stress are costly to collect at scale, limiting supervised impaired-driving modeling.
AI.method: ID-MAE adds a self-supervised objective that reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token.
AI.result: On DIVERT (103 hours, n = 109), ID-MAE achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for location-matched impairment detection compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, outperforms baselines on DIVERT and existing datasets, and improves trajectory and gaze prediction.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised masked-diffusion reconstruction significantly improves impaired driving inference and reveals that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive ones.

title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
summary: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

AI.tldr: This paper uses a 19-day export-control ban on Claude Fable 5 as a natural experiment and finds that access to a higher-scoring coding model did not significantly increase GitHub pull request merge rates or weekly merged volume.
AI.motivation: New coding models advertise higher benchmark scores, yet no prior study tested whether higher benchmark scores translate into more real-world software work done.
AI.method: Using a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, the authors track GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users forced onto Opus 4.8 against 8,908 Opus 4.8 control developers, plus five model upgrades across 1,208 developers and 15,442 pull requests.
AI.result: Access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day pull request merge rate by a statistically insignificant 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3] and weekly merged pull requests by +2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%], while five upgrades showed a weighted mean of -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2].
AI.conclusion: Higher coding benchmark scores did not produce measurable productivity gains in real-world pull request merges.

title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
comment: Accepted by SIAM Journal on Optimization
summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $\epsilon$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($\epsilon$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $\epsilon$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $\epsilon$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $\epsilon$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $\epsilon$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that improves first-order oracle complexity for computing epsilon-surely feasible stochastic optimal solutions in constrained convex finite-sum optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing stochastic variance-reduced penalty methods have a large complexity gap when computing solutions with deterministic constraint-violation bounds versus expected constraint-violation bounds.
AI.method: The authors develop an inexact SVRG method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization, which also reduces to a deterministic first-order method for standard convex conic optimization in the single-function case.
AI.result: The method significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for epsilon-SFSO solutions and achieves lower objective gradient evaluation complexity than existing conic optimization methods when constraint gradients and cone projections are cheaper.
AI.conclusion: The proposed inexact SVRG framework narrows the complexity gap for hard-constrained stochastic optimization and offers an efficient alternative for convex conic problems.

title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
summary: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Spool, a training-free framework for low-latency sliding-window streaming inference in hybrid vision-language models that removes expired frames without replaying the window.
AI.motivation: Hybrid VLMs with linear recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames in a sliding window normally requires re-running the entire window.
AI.method: Spool caches per-frame affine state transformations and composes them associatively using a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to remove expired frames from each recurrent layer's state.
AI.result: Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of 6.6x over the faster of two vLLM baselines while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
AI.conclusion: Associative state-transformation caching enables fast, accurate sliding-window streaming inference for hybrid VLMs without retraining.

title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NEBench R1, a 7,546-question nuclear engineering reasoning benchmark from NRC licensing exams, and finds that correct LLM answers often lack technically sound reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing nuclear-domain benchmarks have limited coverage or evaluate only final answer accuracy without systematically assessing reasoning quality.
AI.method: The authors compile 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions with official explanations from U.S. NRC reactor operator licensing exams across 18 facilities and use an LLM-based judge with a multidimensional rubric to evaluate six LLMs.
AI.result: Overall accuracy ranges from 34.0% to 73.9% across six LLMs; responses score lower on factual/procedural accuracy and distractor analysis than on problem comprehension, and longer reasoning traces correlate with lower accuracy in frontier reasoning models.
AI.conclusion: NEBench R1 establishes a foundation for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning reliability in safety-critical nuclear engineering applications.

title: DOOM-GS: Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting
summary: Traditional Gaussian Splatting (GS) methods use in-core training, i.e. assuming that GPU memory is large enough to accommodate all the primitives. This assumption breaks down when the primitives exceed the capacity of GPU memory, e.g. GS on large environments. Recent out-of-core training research starts to address this issue, but is limited to static scenes. Unlike static GS, dynamic GS primitives move in space and time, breaking common assumptions held in existing out-of-core research and impose new challenges in memory management and training. To this end, we propose Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting (DOOM-GS), the first out-of-core optimization method designed specifically for massive-scale dynamic GS. DOOM-GS is equipped with novel memory management strategies that optimize caching for spatio-temporal primitives, and a fast learning method for large numbers of primitives. Due to the lack of suitable datasets for large-scale dynamic GS, we also contribute a new dataset for evaluation. Since there are no directly comparable methods, we adapt several closely related methods for comparison. Through extensive evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DOOM-GS which now makes it possible to reconstruct city-scale dynamic scenes with high quality on moderate hardware, serving as a foundational tool for diverse future research and applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DOOM-GS, an out-of-core optimization method for massive-scale dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables city-scale dynamic scene reconstruction on moderate hardware.
AI.motivation: Existing out-of-core Gaussian Splatting methods are limited to static scenes, whereas dynamic primitives move in space and time and break static memory-management assumptions.
AI.method: DOOM-GS introduces memory management strategies that optimize caching for spatio-temporal primitives alongside a fast learning method for large primitive counts, and contributes a new evaluation dataset.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations against adapted baselines show that DOOM-GS reconstructs city-scale dynamic scenes with high quality on moderate GPU hardware.
AI.conclusion: DOOM-GS extends out-of-core Gaussian Splatting to massive dynamic scenes, providing a foundation for large-scale 4D reconstruction.

title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers. 11 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables
summary: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FaceRiff, a data- and parameter-efficient framework that generates render-ready 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) from text in a shared UV space.
AI.motivation: High-resolution 3D facial datasets with consistent UV geometry, albedo, and displacement are scarce, and existing 3D face generation methods are slow, single-modality, or data-hungry.
AI.method: FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters (<3% parameters updated per task) conditioned on UV normal maps, using per-instance normals for albedo/displacement and a dataset-mean normal for mesh generation.
AI.result: Trained on 2,049 scans from ~350 identities on one GPU, FaceRiff outperforms FaceG2E and DreamFace in diversity while preserving prompt alignment and UV consistency, and achieves substantially higher realism than DreamFace in a 45-professional blind study.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained 2D diffusion priors can be efficiently adapted for unified, render-ready 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

title: Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Technical Communications. 4 pages
summary: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x (1024 to 4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x super-resolution of 1K facial albedo and displacement maps to 4K render-ready assets.
AI.motivation: Photographic super-resolution models perform poorly on facial UV maps because they have domain-specific statistics and displacement is a scalar height field where errors distort geometry.
AI.method: Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, the method adapts a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules and uses a Tile ControlNet to preserve input structure.
AI.result: On held-out maps, the upscaler produces sharper, more faithful pore- and wrinkle-scale detail than bilinear, GAN, and off-the-shelf diffusion baselines, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 without misplaced displacement relief.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight domain adaptation of pretrained diffusion models yields render-ready 4K facial asset maps without custom super-resolution architectures.

title: Where Should the Lamp Go? Ambient-Aware Lamp Placement for Portraits
summary: Portraits shape first impressions, and lighting is an important factor. Prior work, such as lighting estimation and portrait relighting, edits lighting after capture but does not guide where to place a light before the shot. This leaves an open question: where should a light go to best light a face? Therefore, we propose LightMatch, a preference-grounded inverse lighting framework that disentangles the controllable light from ambient illumination and optimizes its placement. We first learn a Bradley-Terry quality model from pairwise human judgments. A perception head then regresses spherical-harmonic lighting from frozen self-supervised features via cross-attention. Finally, a placement solver isolates the light via spherical-harmonic linearity and optimizes its reachable position. On held-out environments, LightMatch attains 87.8% of the oracle improvement, outperforming the conventional solver that ignores ambient light by a relative 28.4% and the same pipeline with the widely used DPR estimator by a relative 70.5%. It reaches 73.2% on real OLAT faces of unseen identities and, on our real captures, cuts lamp-direction error by 37.7%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LightMatch, an ambient-aware inverse lighting framework that optimizes where to place a controllable lamp before capturing a portrait.
AI.motivation: Prior portrait lighting methods estimate or edit lighting after capture rather than guiding where to place a light beforehand.
AI.method: LightMatch learns a Bradley-Terry quality model from pairwise human judgments, regresses spherical-harmonic lighting from frozen self-supervised features via cross-attention, and solves for reachable lamp placement using spherical-harmonic linearity.
AI.result: On held-out environments, LightMatch achieves 87.8% of oracle improvement, outperforming an ambient-ignoring solver by 28.4% and a DPR-based pipeline by 70.5% relatively; it reaches 73.2% on real OLAT faces and cuts lamp-direction error by 37.7% on real captures.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling controllable and ambient lighting enables preference-grounded pre-capture lamp placement for portraits.

title: FrameSeg3D: Learned Local Frames for Segmenting Small Parts on High-Resolution 3D Scans
summary: Segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans, such as nails on hand scans and teeth on intraoral scans, poses three challenges: 1) each part covers a tiny fraction of the scan, 2) its boundary is only a subtle change of height and curvature, and 3) it faces its own direction. Existing methods fall into two groups, and both fall short. The first group processes the whole scan at once and sees each part too coarsely. Point and mesh networks must shrink the scan to fit in memory, so a small part keeps only a few of its points. Multi-view methods render images of the whole object, so each part fills only a few pixels and a tilted part is seen from the side. The second group first finds each part and then segments it up close. But these methods find the parts with knowledge about one kind of part, for example the shape of the dental arch for teeth. Such knowledge does not carry over to other kinds of parts. We find that accuracy is limited by how a part is seen, from which direction and at what scale, not by how many points land on it. We therefore present FrameSeg3D. It first predicts a local frame for every part, its center and the direction it faces, from a low-resolution view of the whole scan. It then segments the part in views around its frame normal at the scanner's resolution, so covering the whole scan no longer costs resolution. Because every part arrives centered, facing the camera, and at a fixed scale, one segmentation network can serve different kinds of parts and learn from few labeled masks. We test FrameSeg3D on two kinds of parts, nails and teeth. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5), with the most accurate tooth boundaries (boundary IoU 70.5).

AI.tldr: This paper presents FrameSeg3D, a method for segmenting small parts on high-resolution 3D scans by predicting per-part local frames and segmenting in normalized, scanner-resolution views.
AI.motivation: Whole-scan networks lose resolution on tiny parts, while existing two-stage methods rely on part-specific shape priors that do not generalize across part types.
AI.method: FrameSeg3D predicts each part's center and facing direction from a low-resolution whole-scan view, then segments the part in views around its frame normal at full scanner resolution.
AI.result: FrameSeg3D outperforms state-of-the-art methods on hand scans (mean Dice 0.970 on nails) and on the Teeth3DS+ test fold (per-tooth IoU 96.5, boundary IoU 70.5).
AI.conclusion: Normalizing viewpoint and scale via learned local frames enables a single segmentation network to generalize across small 3D part types with few labeled masks.

title: ARG-Avatar: Animation-Rendering Guidance for Efficient Feedforward Avatar Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing animatable 3D human avatars from images is important for applications such as gaming and augmented reality. Feedforward methods make avatar reconstruction accessible by reducing inference time to a few seconds, but recent approaches rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and computation. We ask whether such scaling is necessary. To this end, we introduce ARG-Avatar, an efficient feedforward framework with only 68M trainable parameters that achieves SOTA reconstruction quality. Our key insight is that 3D animation and rendering already provide strong geometric correspondences that existing methods largely attempt to learn from data. In light of this, we design the Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to attend to their corresponding patches. Experiments across multiple datasets show that ARG-Avatar consistently outperforms prior methods when using two or more input images. Compared with LHM++, ARG-Avatar uses approximately 9$\times$ fewer trainable parameters, 4.8$\times$ fewer training sequences, and 14$\times$ less training compute, while running 6$\times$ faster and achieving a 2.7 dB PSNR improvement on the out-of-distribution NeuMan benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ARG-Avatar, a 68M-parameter feedforward 3D human avatar reconstruction framework that uses animation-rendering geometric correspondences to outperform larger models.
AI.motivation: Recent feedforward avatar reconstruction methods rely heavily on scaling model capacity, training data, and compute.
AI.method: ARG-Avatar leverages 3D animation and rendering correspondences through Foreground Avatar Coordinate RoPE attention (FACRoPE) and an Intermediate Token Rendering (ITR) pipeline to guide avatar tokens to matching image patches.
AI.result: With two or more input images, ARG-Avatar outperforms prior methods, using ~9x fewer parameters, 4.8x fewer training sequences, and 14x less compute than LHM++ while running 6x faster and improving out-of-distribution NeuMan PSNR by 2.7 dB.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting explicit geometric correspondences from animation and rendering eliminates the need for heavy model and data scaling in feedforward avatar reconstruction.

title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
comment: Accepted to the WACV 2027 Workshop on Eyes of the Future (EOF). 19 pages including appendix
summary: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer for 3D Gaussian Splatting that runs reliably from workstations to mobile devices.
AI.motivation: Handheld and wearable captures are still sent to CUDA workstations for 3DGS training because GPU and driver differences across vendors determine whether a training schedule executes correctly.
AI.method: Cross3DGS keeps a single optimizer and selects execution schedules per device in two steps: filtering out infeasible schedules using device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures, then choosing via a fixed preference order.
AI.result: Cross3DGS completes 30k-update, 1M-Gaussian training across NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs (including Android and iPhone) where VkSplat and Brush fail on some mobile GPUs, achieving higher quality than VkSplat on workstations and ~3x faster training than Brush.
AI.conclusion: Device-aware schedule selection enables portable, on-device 3DGS training with consistent quality across heterogeneous GPUs.

title: ATS: Anti-Aliased Triangle Splatting with Exact Per-Primitive Integrals
summary: Triangle Splatting represents scenes using semi-transparent triangles, but it evaluates each triangle at the pixel center and culls any triangle with an inradius smaller than one pixel. The former causes severe aliasing, while the latter culls most of the scene at lower resolutions. We show that the integral of the Triangle Splatting window over a pixel admits an exact closed-form solution. The angle bisectors split the triangle into three sub-triangles, in each of which the window is a power of the distance to one edge. Each piece therefore has a closed-form antiderivative, and Green's theorem reduces the integral and its gradients to one term per side of the sub-triangle clipped against the pixel. The integral over the whole triangle, which we show has a closed form, then allows conservative culling, removing only triangles that cannot meet the renderer's alpha cutoff at any pixel. This exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, exhibits less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and enables multi-scale training, matching or outperforming supersampled training at reduced resolutions.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an exact closed-form pixel integral for Triangle Splatting and a conservative culling criterion, eliminating aliasing without retraining.
AI.motivation: Standard Triangle Splatting evaluates triangles at pixel centers and culls those with inradius below one pixel, causing severe aliasing and missing geometry at lower resolutions.
AI.method: Splitting each triangle along angle bisectors into three sub-triangles yields closed-form antiderivatives via Green's theorem for pixel integrals and gradients, while a closed-form whole-triangle integral enables conservative alpha-cutoff culling.
AI.result: The exact formulation anti-aliases existing models without retraining, produces less temporal aliasing than 2x2 supersampling, and matches or outperforms supersampled multi-scale training at reduced resolutions.
AI.conclusion: Exact per-primitive integration makes Triangle Splatting anti-aliased and resolution-consistent without supersampling overhead.

title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
summary: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BRepA, a graph-based self-supervised pretraining framework for CAD boundary representations (B-Reps) that improves both discriminative and generative downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Learning on B-Reps requires specialized architectures, and labeled CAD data is often scarce.
AI.method: BRepA pretrains once on large-scale unlabeled CAD data by explicitly reconstructing both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling.
AI.result: With 1% labeled data, BRepA improves segmentation mIoU by 32.52% over training from scratch; aligning diffusion models with BRepA features accelerates generative training by nearly 2x while improving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a versatile representation backbone for CAD understanding and generation.

title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ReTouchGS, a render-free framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer on pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting models.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS color editing methods require reference images or manual adjustments, whereas users often want automatic, view-consistent aesthetic enhancement.
AI.method: ReTouchGS predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the 3DGS model and camera parameters (or fits one from a single edited view) and refines an analytic color update using a 44.7K-parameter network without rendering.
AI.result: Evaluated on the new ReTouch3D benchmark, ReTouchGS preserves geometry, outputs standard 3DGS assets in seconds, and achieves high color accuracy and generalization to unseen scenes in both tasks.
AI.conclusion: Render-free LUT prediction and lightweight refinement enable fast, view-consistent aesthetic enhancement and color transfer for 3DGS.

title: Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals
summary: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.

AI.tldr: This paper combines Attention Residuals and Jacobian-lens concept readout into a depth-aware activation steering pipeline that outperforms single-layer steering on small open LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification.
AI.method: Persona vectors are distributed across layers using AttnRes-style depth weights, evaluated via Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout, and optionally optimized by training depth weights for 200 steps with a frozen backbone.
AI.result: On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B, depth-aware steering yields stronger internal alignment (p<0.0001) and behavioral shifts than single-layer injection; training depth weights raises held-out alignment 10x, while keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09).
AI.conclusion: Depth-aware steering with rigorous internal and LLM-judge evaluation provides a low-overhead, more effective alternative to single-layer activation steering.

title: How Much of SAR Vehicle Recognition Is the Vehicle? Background Shortcuts, Angle Gaps and Partial Libraries on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.

AI.tldr: This paper audits SAR vehicle recognition on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR and shows that models rely heavily on background shortcuts and fail under depression-angle gaps and partial libraries.
AI.motivation: Deep networks achieve near-99% accuracy on MSTAR, raising the question of how much performance comes from the vehicle itself versus background shortcuts.
AI.method: The authors evaluate ConvNeXt-Small and the SAR foundation model SARATR-X under vehicle-removed, vehicle-only, scene-change, varying depression-angle gap, and partial-library conditions.
AI.result: With the vehicle removed, ConvNeXt-Small still scores 73.3% on MSTAR and 63.3% on ATRNet-STAR SOC, but drops to 22.8% on full chips (30.8% vehicle-only) under scene change; accuracy falls from 57% at a 15-degree angle gap to 26% at 45 degrees, and missing-class accuracy drops to 9.0% in partial libraries.
AI.conclusion: SAR recognition evaluations should report background-only, target-only, and angle-gap controls alongside overall accuracy.

title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
summary: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a red-team/blue-team game for AI safety research sabotage and finds that human auditors mostly fail to detect expert sabotage in end-to-end research transcripts.
AI.motivation: As AI systems automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage safety and alignment research, requiring stress-testing of auditing defenses.
AI.method: A human expert acts as a proxy saboteur running AI safety experiments from scratch, while human auditors (with full transcripts and experiment execution) and frontier models (transcripts only) try to identify sabotaged runs.
AI.result: Human auditors achieve an AUROC of 0.59 and identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases; Fable 5.1 reaches 0.73 AUROC and 32% full identification, and detection drops further when the saboteur chooses which experiments to attack.
AI.conclusion: Current auditing methods struggle to catch expert-level research sabotage, highlighting a critical gap for AI R&D oversight.

title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
summary: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a 27B language model can rewrite its own weights without gradients or training, improving its accuracy and repairing damaged copies.
AI.motivation: Deployed language models are frozen, requiring full training runs for persistent updates while test-time compute gains vanish after the task ends.
AI.method: Given its weights, graded answers, and self-execution, a 27B model diagnoses failures—such as comparing hidden states on finished versus truncated answers—and directly edits its weight matrices.
AI.result: Self-rewriting improves the 27B model by 6.6 points on 490 unseen problems and rises monotonically over eight sessions; it also repairs a corrupted copy using text math alone, lifting unseen image benchmark accuracy from 7% to 70%, whereas 2B, 4B, and 9B models fail or break themselves.
AI.conclusion: Sufficiently capable language models can persistently improve and repair themselves through reasoning-driven weight editing rather than gradient-based training.

title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
comment: Accepted in IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (IEEE AIoT) 2026. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at this https URL
summary: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL) and the end-to-end SLED framework to provide deterministic MAC-level isolation for individual sensor streams within a single UE in O-RAN.
AI.motivation: Current wireless systems allocate resources per device rather than per sensor, causing bulk transfers to starve latency-critical telemetry from co-located sensors.
AI.method: Using agentic coding, SL is implemented in two O-RAN stacks (OCUDU and OAI) and integrated into SLED for per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote HPC tiers.
AI.result: Over-the-air experiments show SLED maintains stable latency where conventional slicing suffers >2,300x delay increases under load, keeps throughput within 0.9%-1.4% of expected allocations, and agentic coding cuts OCUDU implementation time 400x (2h 40m vs. 6.5 weeks).
AI.conclusion: Per-sensor slicing preserves latency-critical telemetry and resource efficiency across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline.

title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
summary: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 2,664 public comments across 40 proposed U.S. AI regulations and finds that government, university, and civil society commenters supply more research and legal evidence than businesses.
AI.motivation: AI regulation is vulnerable to industry capture due to information advantages, but little is known about how different stakeholders supply evidence in public comments.
AI.method: The authors computationally extract formal citations and informal references from 2,664 public comments across 40 U.S. regulations and analyze evidence volume, publication status, and self-citation patterns.
AI.result: Controlling for length, business commenters supply less evidence, while government, university, and civil society commenters supply significantly more research and legal sources; preprints and peer-reviewed articles are cited nearly evenly, and a small cluster of organizations accounts for over half of all self-citations.
AI.conclusion: Public comments play nuanced roles between Issue Advocates and Honest Brokers, complicating simple narratives of regulatory information capture.

title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
comment: Supplementary information is available as an ancillary file (this http URL)
summary: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DiscoveryAgent, a scientist-centric agentic AI framework that pairs autonomous investigation with checkpointed audit agents and scientist-directed hypothesis steering.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI research agents need mechanisms that let scientists inspect evidence, catch errors, and redirect hypotheses.
AI.method: Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between rounds while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims and reproduce analyses.
AI.result: DiscoveryAgent produces the top variable-star classifier among baselines, a ProteinGym predictor beaten by only one of 106 baselines, and 14x more valid error identifications when scientists collaborate with audit agents; three domain case studies achieve 0.971 AUROC on low-redshift estimation, document an 83% rise in Florida insurance premiums, and identify CD4+ T-cell relay genes.
AI.conclusion: Checkpointed auditing and human hypothesis steering expand scientists' empirical reach while preserving their authority over research direction.

title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
summary: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed this http URL that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WebAgents, a signed package contract and OpenClaw-based runtime that unbundles agent creation, hosting, and execution for an agent-native web.
AI.motivation: Realizing an Agentic Web requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a specific execution environment or surrendering user resource authority.
AI.method: WebAgents distributes portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements in a signed package that an OpenClaw-based browser/runtime verifies, authorizes, and binds to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets.
AI.result: Three unrelated workflows run unchanged under local and API-backed models, and in a controlled suite WebAgents blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 benign controls with median pre-execution processing under 0.5 s.
AI.conclusion: Signed portable agent packages enable interoperable web agent ecosystems while keeping execution authority in the user's runtime.

title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
summary: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes KV-LTM, a long-term memory tier for personal assistants that stores each session's raw text alongside its KV cache under a fixed reader model to avoid re-prefill compute and write-time information loss.
AI.motivation: Existing personal-assistant memory stacks put lossy derivation or selection between a question and its evidence, degrading LongMemEval performance compared to offline full-history reading.
AI.method: KV-LTM specifies a storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation, keeping text as the memory of record and the KV cache as a recompute-free prefill accelerator.
AI.result: Analytical sizing shows per-token state spans ~31K-328K bytes (or ~8.1K bytes/token for KDA+MLA), totaling ~0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at 30K tokens/day versus ~49 MB of raw text, and the authors define a two-part evaluation protocol for logical QA and numerical cache equivalence.
AI.conclusion: KV-LTM trades storage within a declared retention budget for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity.

title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
comment: 26 pages, including appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition and proposes a retrieval-grounded generator and bundle-aware critic that jointly select backbone models and tool-skill bundles.
AI.motivation: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources, which independent scoring and fixed-catalog generators fail to capture.
AI.method: A fine-tuned generator retrieves similar task configurations and recombines candidates via constrained beam search, while a bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using an LLM teacher and execution proxies, adapting to execution feedback.
AI.result: Evaluated on AgentSelect-Exec (5,060 executed configurations) and SkillsBench, the method recovers 67.73% of reference configurations within 10 candidates (nearly 2x the strongest baseline), raises top-ranked execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 (and 8.78 with feedback), and adapts to SkillsBench with four target-domain queries.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning and transferring backbone-and-tool bundle composition from task experience outperforms independent resource selection.

title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Technical Report for the SOICT 2026 Student Contest
summary: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.

AI.tldr: This paper describes a single-file Python hybrid exact-heuristic solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem submitted to round 2 of the SOICT 2026 contest.
AI.motivation: The selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes, and heterogeneous taxis requires balancing exact optimality and heuristic scalability within strict time limits.
AI.method: The solver automatically selects between an ALNS metaheuristic with constant-time slack insertion and an exact branch-and-bound set-packing engine with Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing, backed by a verifier and watchdog.
AI.result: On 38 official evaluation instances with a 5-minute limit, the solver achieved a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s using at most 279 MB, and terminated early on 28 instances.
AI.conclusion: Combining adaptive heuristics with exact set-packing selection provides a reliable, memory-efficient solver for integrated passenger-parcel routing.

title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
summary: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Reversibility Classes, a five-level vocabulary and prior-state capture contract for AI agent tool actions, implemented across 536 tools and 20 MCP servers.
AI.motivation: Permission to call a tool does not tell an AI agent or guard whether an action's side effects can be undone.
AI.method: The authors define five reversibility classes with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults, and a prior-state capture contract, and evaluate a session guard and controlled recovery experiments.
AI.result: All 738 rule-case checks pass; on 2,158 recorded runs, the session guard gates all 29 attack-positive runs (vs. 18 for a read/write proxy) while adding 9 approvals across 1,209 benign runs, and recovery experiments reveal dependencies on captured state and a Git merge-state exception.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, testable reversibility classes improve action gating and clarify recovery assumptions, though they do not guarantee production recovery reliability.

title: When Lower Harm Misleads: Auditing Concept Corrections
summary: An expert who corrects a concept prediction, such as a BI-RADS descriptor in breast ultrasound, expects the diagnosis to improve. Objectives that reduce the harm of such corrections are judged by harm and accuracy, yet harm also falls when a model responds less to every correction or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, the reference for harm. We propose a correction audit, a reproducible evaluation protocol that separates these explanations: it splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares objectives with amplitude baselines matched in source harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training, evaluated from the mean-case model's start, lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons pooled over six seeds, raising the corrected negative log-likelihood (NLL); from the same start, selecting between the objectives by harm picks the less helpful model on all three sources. On CUB, a monotonic harm penalty at its reported weight lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising the NLL in all 80, almost entirely before any correction. At a fixed start, rescaling both responses to the same source harm reproduces the penalty's mean harm, useful gain and NLL on single-concept corrections within a prespecified margin of 0.0005 nat, although the two responses point in different directions. Lower harm therefore signals better corrections only when it is read together with useful gain, absolute risk and the start it is measured from.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a correction audit protocol showing that lower harm metrics in concept-correction models can be misleading if not evaluated alongside useful gain, absolute risk, and starting predictions.
AI.motivation: Harm metrics can drop simply because a model responds less to all corrections or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, rather than making better corrections.
AI.method: The correction audit splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares against amplitude baselines matched in source harm.
AI.result: On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training lowers harm but sacrifices more useful gain in all 21 comparisons, raising NLL; on CUB, a monotonic harm penalty lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising NLL in all 80.
AI.conclusion: Lower harm signals better concept corrections only when interpreted together with useful gain, absolute risk, and the baseline starting prediction.

title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
summary: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms, and finds that frontier agents pass fewer than 11% of tasks.
AI.motivation: Real professional work involves under-specified assignments with conflicting information scattered across workplace apps, which existing agent benchmarks do not capture.
AI.method: Experienced bankers authored 100 tasks (15-30 hours of human work each) requiring agents to search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to build financial models, graded against rubrics with a median of 124.5 criteria.
AI.result: Despite completing substantial portions of the work, current frontier models (including Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of ATLAS-Finance tasks.
AI.conclusion: Frontier AI agents remain far from reliably completing complex, under-specified real-world financial workflows.

title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
summary: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule.
