A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EvoDisco, an evolutionary strategy discovery framework that learns which semantic memory operator to apply, when, and how to instantiate it for evolving LLM agent memory.
AI.motivation: Existing online agent memory methods rely on fixed memory-update operators and static selection rules.
AI.method: A learnable policy selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators (Abstract, Refine, Bridge, Reframe) based on memory state and task history, updated via bi-level fitness combining retrieval-quality gain and strategic regret.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench, EvoDisco outperforms MemP and MemRL, achieving up to +8.8 online and +12.9 frozen-transfer points over MemP (+16.4 / +17.9 over MemRL) on ALFWorld.
AI.conclusion: Learning dynamic memory-evolution strategies significantly improves online and transferable agent performance over static memory update rules.

title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated Lean proof scripts into verified proofs using angelic proof checking and MaxSAT-based obligation selection.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated Lean proofs often capture high-level structure but abort early on minor missing side conditions or misapplied lemmas.
AI.method: Angelic proof checking replaces failing fragments with placeholders to isolate unresolved obligations, and residual analysis over a proof dependence graph uses MaxSAT to select a minimal set of essential obligations for a mathematician to answer in natural language.
AI.result: On 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra, MathEye solves 93.3% of problems while reducing required user interactions by 55%.
AI.conclusion: Combining optimistic symbolic execution with minimal human-in-the-loop obligation resolution effectively repairs LLM-generated formal proofs.

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
summary: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval update streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RegimeCouncil, an online paired-evidence router that arbitrates between local and global memory-suppression policies under delayed feedback in LLM agents.
AI.motivation: When stored agent memories go stale, existing systems fix either a local (per-fact) or global (cross-fact) suppression scope at design time, neither of which is sufficient alone.
AI.method: Using paired comparisons against a no-memory anchor, a Local Advisor tracks per-fact outcomes and a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes, while a Meta Governor defaults to local and switches to global only when global utility margin is strictly positive.
AI.result: Across LongMemEval, TempLAMA, and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings.
AI.conclusion: Online arbitration between local and global feedback scopes enables robust memory conflict governance without retraining the LLM.

title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
summary: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

AI.tldr: This report details the architecture, Ascend-based pretraining infrastructure, and TeleGym agentic post-training platform behind the Xing 4 series of large language models.
AI.motivation: Scaling frontier reasoning and agentic models on domestic Ascend chips requires coordinated co-design of model architecture, distributed pretraining, and asynchronous agentic post-training.
AI.method: The authors study sparse activation, attention, depth/width, and speculative decoding; pretrain a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards using MindSpore HyperParallel; and build TeleGym with disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout.
AI.result: The infrastructure supports stable pretraining of a 285B model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards and continuous policy optimization across heterogeneous-duration agentic tasks in TeleGym.
AI.conclusion: Xing 4 establishes a full-stack Ascend-oriented training foundation for large-scale reasoning and agentic models.

title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
summary: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Pupavision, a $45-$75 DIY physical AI instrument running a frontier coding agent on a single-board Linux computer to monitor Drosophila pupariation.
AI.motivation: Biology experiments are often bottlenecked by costly or hard-to-use monitoring instruments, requiring manual tracking of lifecycle transitions like fruit fly pupariation.
AI.method: A deterministic capture service records an image every 10 minutes independently of the agent, while an on-device coding agent (thinking in the cloud) assists capture, repairs code errors, and alerts researchers on failures.
AI.result: A 26-day pilot in a fly incubator captured ~3,580 frames—including 11 days while the agent was logged out—and informed a layered design after a 51-hour outage, enabling backward-traced pupariation curves.
AI.conclusion: Pairing deterministic capture with an on-device coding agent provides a low-cost blueprint for DIY agentic scientific instruments.

title: Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents
summary: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further shows that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies evidence hijacking in tool-augmented medical agents and proposes CIEG, a training-free framework that filters tool outputs outside the reasoner.
AI.motivation: Frozen reasoners cannot ignore noisy or silently failing medical tool outputs once they enter context, flipping previously correct answers to wrong.
AI.method: Grounded in V-information theory, Context-Independent Evidence Governance (CIEG) writes each tool output as a card, uses an independent checker seeing only the raw input and cards to admit evidence, and restricts the reasoner to admitted cards.
AI.result: On medical QA, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, CIEG achieves the highest accuracy at comparable scale and outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using and multi-agent baselines at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Separating evidence admission from final reasoning prevents evidence hijacking in tool-augmented medical agents without any training.

title: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents
summary: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires. In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes quickly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Readie, a code sandbox system that learns a set of compact startup snapshots from workload history to cut agent code-execution latency.
AI.motivation: Existing code sandboxes suffer slow startup because a single snapshot cannot be both compact and cover the diverse packages and datasets required by agent-generated code.
AI.method: Readie formulates multi-snapshot construction as an optimization problem over historical workloads and solves it with an approximation algorithm so each small snapshot initializes fast and together they cover most scripts.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, Readie reduces startup latency by 3-22x and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3x compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.
AI.conclusion: Learning a portfolio of compact startup snapshots resolves the compactness-coverage trade-off for low-latency AI agent code sandboxes.

title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
summary: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RecPo, a framework for reconfiguring procedural knowledge into executable robot skill sequences under sparse task specifications, achieving 91.9% ordered completion on an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark.
AI.motivation: General-purpose behavior models internalize broad procedural knowledge, but adapting them to new goals and skill interfaces under sparse governing information leaves concrete bindings and compositions underdetermined without costly retraining.
AI.method: RecPo represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views in a knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, then interprets task specifications through those same views to resolve compositional queries and bind skills at deployment.
AI.result: On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity, and real-robot studies demonstrate adaptation via local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
AI.conclusion: Reconfiguring stored procedural transitions across multiple views enables fast, data-efficient robot skill adaptation without retraining.

title: The Only Edge Was Memorized in Training: LLM Trading Agents Around Earnings and Bad News
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Original empirical study of LLM trading agents before scheduled earnings announcements and after bad-news drops, run on the rta-bench-1 benchmark (arXiv:2611.19530)
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.

AI.tldr: Testing LLM trading agents on a look-ahead-free benchmark around earnings announcements and bad-news drops shows that no agent beats simple baseline bets, and any apparent edge comes from training-data memorization.
AI.motivation: Prior studies of LLMs on earnings or market reversals either use post-announcement documents or monthly portfolio sorts, leaving unclear whether LLM agents can profitably trade before scheduled earnings or after bad-news drops without look-ahead bias.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five models from four vendors on a look-ahead-free benchmark covering 598 earnings announcements and 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks, comparing staged agents, single calls, simple rules, and logistic regression with inputs cut at the decision close, both with and without stock names.
AI.result: No LLM agent beats simple baseline bets: before earnings, agents mostly bought and matched buying before every announcement, while after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called nearly every drop an overreaction; a GPT-based model given only ticker and dates predicted 59.2% of earnings directions before its training cutoff versus 53.3% after it.
AI.conclusion: Event-trading LLM agents should be benchmarked against simple bets and evaluated blind after their training cutoff to separate genuine skill from memorization.

title: CorrectCast: Selective Multimodal Context for Scale-Aware Residual Correction in Precipitation Nowcasting
summary: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CorrectCast, a lightweight decoupled residual correction framework that refines frozen precipitation nowcasting models using selective multimodal context, improving mean CSI across six base nowcasters.
AI.motivation: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from intensity, location, and spatial structure errors, while retraining nowcaster backbones is computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications.
AI.method: CorrectCast keeps the base nowcaster frozen and trains a lightweight corrector on predicted precipitation fields conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, using selective multimodal context and scale-aware modulation.
AI.result: On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with average absolute gains in mean CSI of 0.0233 and 0.0290, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled residual correction with selective multimodal context provides a unified, low-cost interface for improving diverse precipitation nowcasting models.

title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Main Conference
summary: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that BRIDGE, a minimal RAG memory, matches or beats complex agentic memory systems on standard recall benchmarks, and introduces five adversarial probes demonstrating that memory designs differ in what actions they enable rather than what they retrieve.
AI.motivation: Agentic memory systems have added extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of RAG, but standard benchmarks only score retrieval rather than whether memory enables an agent to act on remembered rules or patterns.
AI.method: The authors build BRIDGE, a minimal RAG memory using chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, and evaluate memory architectures on five adversarial probes judged by a cross-vendor verification chain across 5 probes by 20 scenarios.
AI.result: BRIDGE reaches parity within bootstrap CI with prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader; on the adversarial probes across four domains, three graders, and three reader families, atomic-fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction.
AI.conclusion: Agentic memory should be evaluated on what behaviors it enables an agent to execute rather than recall alone, as different memory designs fail and succeed for complementary reasons.

title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
summary: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that reasoning-importance attribution for pruning language models is fragile across token selection, neuron granularity, and contrastive isolation, proposing three measurement rules for reliable pruning.
AI.motivation: Attribution-guided pruning is increasingly used to compress reasoning language models without harming chain-of-thought performance, but it assumes reasoning importance can be faithfully measured.
AI.method: The authors audit attribution-guided pruning across four small reasoning models by testing final-answer versus reasoning-token scoring, single-neuron versus group-level causal ablation, and contrastively isolated reasoning-specific importance versus raw importance.
AI.result: Scoring final-answer tokens saturates (answer-token NLL of 10^-4 to 10^-3) and costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points compared to scoring reasoning tokens on two 5-seed models while perplexity barely moves; single-neuron effects sit at the noise floor with 90% sign disagreement against group ablations until groups reach ~100 neurons, and protecting contrastively isolated importance performs worse than protecting raw importance.
AI.conclusion: Reliable attribution-guided pruning of reasoning models requires scoring reasoning tokens, attributing at coarse granularity, and evaluating with accuracy rather than perplexity.

title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
summary: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

AI.tldr: Analyzing over 20,000 LLM coding-agent runs under prefix caching reveals that adding retrieved code or removing old tool outputs can substantially increase total token cost even when prompts are shorter.
AI.motivation: Context-management techniques for coding agents aim to reduce cost by adding relevant code or pruning old tool outputs, but their true financial impact under prefix caching and subsequent agent behavior is unclear.
AI.method: The authors measure uncached input, cached input, and output tokens separately across more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench, and Loc-Bench.
AI.result: Retrieved code cuts read and search commands by 18-34% but increases cost by 33-42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input without measurably improving resolution; removing old observations saves 19-36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38-116% with a tenth-price cache, partly because agents take more steps and concurrent runs can share cached prefixes.
AI.conclusion: Context-management methods for coding agents must be evaluated using both token pricing structures and induced changes in agent trajectory length.

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
summary: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for multi-agent memory inconsistency, showing that delegating document review across workers increases evidence retrieval but reduces factual conflict detection.
AI.motivation: Distributing evidence collection across LLM worker agents with separate contexts risks losing facts during handoffs to a lead agent, yet how factual conflicts disappear in multi-agent workflows has not been systematically measured.
AI.method: The authors construct controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks and use an evidence-flow profiler to compare single-agent execution against multi-agent delegation across three models at comparable generation spending.
AI.result: Delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection drops from 16.2% to 13.2% because workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, with detection dropping specifically when claims are split across workers.
AI.conclusion: Worker-to-lead handoffs are a primary bottleneck for conflict detection in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
summary: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only. Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings. Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types. Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular multimodal LLM system with human-in-the-loop dual-model validation for extracting fields and scores from scanned cognitive and behavioral assessments, achieving 97.5% accuracy while cutting manual work by 63.8%.
AI.motivation: Paper-based clinical assessments such as MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog, and NICHQ Vanderbilt are difficult to digitize at scale due to handwriting and scanning artifacts.
AI.method: The system uses a form classifier followed by a schema-based score extractor, and engages human annotators only when two LLMs disagree on a scanned page.
AI.result: End-to-end accuracy reached 88% on cognitive assessments and 97.5% on NICHQ Vanderbilt; adding dual-model human-in-the-loop review raised cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual effort by 63.8%, cutting processing time 10-20x and costs over 12x, with 62.3% of Mini-Cog Clock Drawing errors stemming from ambiguous drawings.
AI.conclusion: Dual-model validation with selective human oversight offers an accurate, scalable, and cost-effective way to structure handwritten clinical forms.

title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop "Sim2Science: ML with Imperfect Scientific Models"
summary: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $\alpha{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: This paper defines fidelity regret to measure how cheap simulators and topological verifiers misrank physical designs, showing positive regret in nearly all tested genetic-circuit cells and evaluating a budget-aware re-scoring remedy.
AI.motivation: Verifiable design workflows assume the verifier or simulator reflects the true physical objective, but in domains like genetic-circuit design, cheap simulators can misrank candidates on physical properties such as growth burden.
AI.method: The authors measure reference simple regret over a 21,362-design subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms, and test an in-sample fixed rule that spends a fraction alpha=0.34 of a matched modeled-cost budget to re-score top cheap-simulator designs.
AI.result: Mean normalized regret is 0.369 across 72 cells with only 6 having zero regret, and yeast library SC1C1G1T1 shows mean regret of 0.113 for cytometry quality versus 0.801 for growth burden; spending alpha=0.34 on re-scoring yields mean excess regret of 0.016 versus 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving over cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells.
AI.conclusion: Measuring fidelity regret before optimization detects simulator-to-physics gaps and guides budget-aware re-scoring strategies across verifiable design domains.

title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
summary: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework for LLM safety alignment that pairs a strategy-level coverage reward for the attacker with a Bayesian replay pool for the defender.
AI.motivation: Existing co-evolutionary safety alignment frameworks suffer from attack strategy collapse, where the attacker overfits to narrow rewrites, and defense adversarial forgetting, where the defender loses robustness to earlier attacks.
AI.method: On the attacker side, the framework uses a two-dimensional strategy space (risk category by attack style) with a normalized marginal coverage gain reward; on the defender side, it maintains a Bayesian adversarial replay pool with time-decayed Beta-Bernoulli threat posteriors sampled via Thompson sampling.
AI.result: Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, the framework improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks, broadens attacker strategy coverage, and preserves general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Jointly addressing strategy-level exploration and uncertainty-aware replay stabilizes adversarial co-evolution for LLM safety alignment.

title: SeasonRainBench: Global Seasonal Precipitation
summary: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SeasonRainBench, a global 1-to-5-month seasonal precipitation benchmark, along with a simulation-to-Earth transfer model that outperforms operational and data-driven baselines on ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position.
AI.motivation: Operational seasonal precipitation forecasting relies on costly, drifting numerical ensembles, while transitioning to data-driven models lacks a global benchmark, operationally relevant metrics, and long observational records for training.
AI.method: SeasonRainBench pairs global 1-degree satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, seven operational centers, 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models, and two new metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position; the proposed model transfers simulation knowledge via climate background alignment (SimForced), a pretrained history encoder (SimMemory), and simulated analog labels (SimAnalog).
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that the proposed model improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0%, 3.6%, 2.9%, and 0.3% over the strongest operational or data-driven baseline.
AI.conclusion: Transferring physical knowledge from climate simulations bridges the short observational record and advances data-driven seasonal precipitation forecasting.

title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
comment: Accepted to AIAS+ 2026, ACM ICPS proceedings. 9 pages
summary: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) for climate downscaling, finding that post-sampling projection eliminates non-negativity and mass-conservation violations while training penalties add no clear perceptual gain over a penalty-free baseline.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow-matching climate downscalers can generate sharp fields that violate physical conservation laws, raising the question of whether training-time physics penalties or post-sampling projections are responsible for physical validity and skill.
AI.method: The authors compare PC-RF, which uses training penalties for wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift plus post-sampling projection, against a penalty-free rectified-flow baseline (RF-base) with the same projection and an unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation on synthetic data and ERA5 (2019-2021).
AI.result: On a corrupted synthetic field, projection drives Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero; on ERA5, both PC-RF and RF-base achieve zero NVR and MCE (up to float32 rounding) with indistinguishable perceptual scores (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772), whereas unprojected CorrDiff leaves 45% of ensemble-mean precipitation cells negative.
AI.conclusion: NVR and MCE require no fine reference and should serve as first-pass pass-or-fail checks alongside divergence error as a diagnostic, since post-sampling projection suffices for exact conservation.

title: Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities
comment: 27 pages (10 main + references + appendix), 1 figure, 8 tables
summary: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper learns constrained regions of attraction for transverse feedback linearization (TFL) controllers under singularities by decomposing the Zubov value function and combining fitted value iteration with interval branch-and-bound verification.
AI.motivation: TFL controllers achieve exact path-following error linearization but become undefined on singular sets (such as zero speed or zero thrust), requiring an accurate estimate of the constrained region of attraction where activation is safe.
AI.method: Exploiting exact linear error dynamics, the authors decompose the state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a learned safety value function trained via fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels, combining an interval-verified inner layer with a sample-tested outer layer.
AI.result: On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, the method covers on average 72.0%, 83.4%, and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction, compared with at most 11.3%, 4.0%, and 0.0% for the quadratic cost-to-go and two PINN Zubov solvers.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing the Zubov value function and learning only the safety component substantially expands verified regions of attraction for singular TFL controllers.

title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine and Jev-based predictor that optimizes speculative decoding configurations across GPUs and workloads, achieving 1.36x throughput over vLLM speculative decoding with full calibration and 1.30x without held-out GPU calibration.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding speedups vary sharply with concurrency, output length, and GPU hardware (for example, DFlash drops from 3.50x to 0.76x AR throughput on an RTX 5090), making static configurations suboptimal.
AI.method: SpecSearch uses an analytical memory-and-compute cost model to prune feasible decoding strategies, draft lengths, and precisions, collects multi-GPU calibration measurements, and trains a Jev-based predictor (adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B with LoRA and a linear correction layer) to select configurations on unseen GPUs.
AI.result: Across NVIDIA RTX 5090, H100, L40, and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration averages 2.01x AR throughput and 1.36x vLLM SD throughput, while the Jev-based predictor achieves 1.30x over vLLM SD (retaining 97.36% of full-calibration throughput) without held-out GPU calibration.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware configuration search and cross-GPU performance prediction unlock consistent speculative decoding speedups across diverse serving regimes.

title: Streaming On-Policy Distillation: Decoupling Three Clocks for Stage-Wise Supervision Consumption
summary: In on-policy distillation (OPD), response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates need not share the same granularity. We develop streaming OPD by decoupling these three clocks: a response repeatedly delivers newly generated segments while generation continues, retaining the full causal prefix at each delivery and computing loss only on new positions. A consumption protocol then organizes supervision budgets, position selection, staleness handling, and update scheduling, allowing control over quantity, coverage, and version lag across training stages. In GSM8K experiments distilling Qwen3-4B into Qwen3-0.6B with VERL, supervised-budget matching reduces the early gap between best test accuracies over seven common candidates from 4.55 to 2.42 points. Synchronous continuation from the same checkpoint reaches 73.39% best test accuracy over seven common candidates at u=384,...,576, versus 74.30% synchronous and 71.95% budget-matched (differences -0.91 and -2.35 points); an unpaired extended record reaches 76.12%. Freshness filtering and disagreement-overlap selection improve local peaks but do not establish sustained advantages. A system prototype shows lower data-supply waiting times without establishing an equal-update speedup. Quality recovery and supply-side benefits are assessed separately; end-to-end gains must account for continuation cost.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes streaming on-policy distillation (OPD), decoupling response completion, supervision delivery, and parameter updates, and evaluates its quality-versus-supply trade-offs on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation couples response generation, supervision delivery, and parameter updates at the same granularity, creating data-supply waiting times during training.
AI.method: Streaming OPD delivers newly generated segments repeatedly while generation continues, retaining the causal prefix and computing loss only on new positions, governed by a consumption protocol for budgets, position selection, staleness, and update scheduling.
AI.result: In GSM8K experiments distilling Qwen3-4B into Qwen3-0.6B with VERL, supervised-budget matching narrows the early best-accuracy gap across seven common candidates from 4.55 to 2.42 points, and synchronous continuation reaches 73.39% versus 74.30% synchronous and 71.95% budget-matched, while a prototype lowers data-supply waiting times without establishing an equal-update speedup.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the three clocks in OPD reduces supply-side waiting, though end-to-end efficiency gains must weigh continuation cost against synchronous baselines.

title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses
summary: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. This runtime, the agent harness, manages context and memory, steers multi-turn control, executes tool actions in sandboxes, and verifies work before stopping. Because models differ in how they use tools and how they fail, a static harness tuned for one model or task often stalls, wastes tokens, or regresses on another. This bottleneck has driven a shift from prompt tuning to self-improving agent harnesses: systems that inspect their own execution traces, separate runtime bugs from model limits, and rewrite their own code. We present a unifying architectural and design framework for self-improving agent harnesses. The framework pairs four editable runtime components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, and verification and recovery) with a four-stage loop that diagnoses failures, proposes code patches, validates candidates, and deploys updates. Using this framework, we show how optimizers trace errors across long trajectories and discover reusable runtime mechanisms such as pre-stop verifiers, loop breakers, and persistent memory. We further show why full-harness rewrites overfit or break across modules, and how modular updates with validation gates generalize across models while bounding token cost. To keep self-modification safe, we establish practical defenses against recurring failure modes including prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering. Finally, experiments on SWE-bench Lite validate this framework, showing that gated modular evolution outperforms prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites across models and repositories at a fraction of the token cost.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unifying framework for self-improving agent harnesses that pairs four editable runtime components with a four-stage diagnosis-and-patching loop, outperforming prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites on SWE-bench Lite.
AI.motivation: Static agent harnesses tuned for one foundation model or task often stall or regress on others, while naive full-harness self-rewrites tend to overfit, break across modules, or incur high token costs.
AI.method: The framework structures runtime software into four editable components (context and state, agent control, action interfaces, verification and recovery) and updates them via a four-stage loop (failure diagnosis, code patch proposal, candidate validation, deployment) with defenses against prompt bloat, benchmark gaming, and evaluator tampering.
AI.result: Experiments on SWE-bench Lite show that gated modular evolution generalizes across models and repositories and outperforms both prompt reflection and full-harness rewrites at a fraction of the token cost.
AI.conclusion: Gated modular self-improvement provides a safer, more cost-effective path to adapting agent runtime harnesses than prompt tuning or monolithic rewrites.

title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
summary: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies visit-count fragmentation across paraphrased reasoning branches as a bottleneck in MCTS for LLM reasoning and introduces Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), improving mathematical reasoning and search accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard UCT in MCTS assigns independent visit counts to distinct textual formulations of the same reasoning strategy, causing redundant exploration and higher cumulative regret.
AI.method: LPC-MCTS replaces standard visit counts in UCT with a lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations to estimate representation coverage and share exploration evidence across related branches.
AI.result: Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, replacing MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across the 5 math benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B, while using LPC-MCTS in both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS.
AI.conclusion: Sharing exploration counts in representation space rather than over raw text branches substantially improves MCTS exploration efficiency for LLM reasoning.

title: Learning to Edit IFC Building Models: Verifiable Checkers as the Training Signal for Dependency-Aware Editing Agents
summary: Editing a building information model in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) schema requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities. Existing language-model agents for IFC editing use prompted models without learning from edit outcomes. Target-file comparisons do not specify which alternative edits are allowed or which unrelated entities must remain unchanged. We present IfcGym, a CodeAct environment in which a language model edits IFC through executable code and four checkers verify validity relative to the input model, intent, dependency and preservation against a task specification. Their conjunction is strict success. IfcEdit distils verified teacher episodes into a Qwen3.5-9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with strict success as the reward. On IfcEditBench, 1,990 editing tasks on 13 held-out real projects, the final student reaches 86.78% strict success, from 79.15% after SFT. The paired confidence interval for the difference from its teacher includes zero; the same recipe on a 27B model reaches 91.76% and exceeds the teacher. On the public benchmarks BIM-Edit and BIBIMBAP the final student scores 55.19 and 54.50. On IfcEditBench, the students outperform all prompted models except the teacher under matched tool access; both evaluated frameworks also score lower. Rewarding all four checkers yields 4.83 points more strict success than rewarding intent and validity alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IfcGym and IfcEdit, a verifiable CodeAct environment and SFT+GRPO training recipe for dependency-aware IFC building-model editing, reaching 86.78% strict success on IfcEditBench with a 9B student model.
AI.motivation: Editing Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) building models requires propagating changes to dependent elements while preserving unrelated entities, which prompted agents and target-file comparisons fail to learn or verify reliably.
AI.method: IfcGym executes language-model code edits and evaluates strict success as the conjunction of four verifiable checkers (validity, intent, dependency, preservation); IfcEdit distills verified teacher episodes into Qwen3.5-9B via SFT and then optimizes strict success with GRPO.
AI.result: On 1,990 tasks across 13 held-out real projects in IfcEditBench, the 9B student improves from 79.15% after SFT to 86.78% strict success (matching its teacher within the paired confidence interval), a 27B student reaches 91.76% and exceeds the teacher, and rewarding all four checkers adds 4.83 points over intent and validity alone, with strong results on BIM-Edit (55.19) and BIBIMBAP (54.50).
AI.conclusion: Training on the conjunction of verifiable dependency and preservation checkers enables compact models to perform reliable, dependency-aware IFC editing.

title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
summary: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Trie-Head and shared-context attention in SGLang for wide-beam generative retrieval, improving closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over a Python custom logit processor and 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec.
AI.motivation: Wide-beam trie-constrained decoding in generative retrieval incurs heavy serving costs from vocabulary-wide score buffers, CPU-GPU Python constraint callbacks, and repeated attention over the shared prompt.
AI.method: Trie-Head stores the semantic-identifier trie as validated GPU tensors to score compact codebook candidates and stream the full-vocabulary normalizer without retraining, while shared-context attention reuses prompt key/value blocks across beams with private decode tails.
AI.result: Evaluated in SGLang on LinkedIn Hiring Assistant candidate sourcing and Qualification Retrieval Platform workloads at beam width 200, the combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the Python CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec.
AI.conclusion: Model-native GPU trie decoding paired with shared-context attention eliminates serving bottlenecks in wide-beam generative retrieval without altering model outputs.

title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
summary: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EviDA and EviDARL, a dual-agent framework trained with alternating reinforcement learning for multi-table question answering, outperforming open-model and multi-table baselines on MMQA and TQA-Bench.
AI.motivation: Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over dispersed evidence and complex table relationships, where existing methods lack verifiable intermediate traces and struggle under constrained budgets.
AI.method: EviDA pairs an Evidence Construction Agent that executes table-manipulation programs to produce verifiable intermediate evidence with a Reasoning and Answering Agent, while EviDARL optimizes each agent alternately with fine-grained rewards while holding the other fixed.
AI.result: Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench show that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.
AI.conclusion: Alternating reinforcement learning over explicit evidence-construction and reasoning agents improves multi-hop multi-table QA.

title: Reliable Evaluation of AI Agents for Investment Research: A Framework for Performance and Validity Assessment
summary: We consider the problem of evaluating AI agents undertaking investment-research tasks, where agents interact with external information sources and computational tools to produce financial analyses and research reports. An important challenge is that the quality of an agent's final output does not necessarily reflect the quality of its execution process, while the reliability of the resulting assessment also depends on the validity of the evaluation procedure. Furthermore, investment-research tasks differ considerably in their requirements for numerical accuracy, information retrieval, financial analysis and supporting evidence, making it difficult to assess agent performance using a uniform set of criteria. We propose a domain-oriented evaluation framework that distinguishes outcome quality from execution quality and accommodates these differences through task-specific criteria, deterministic validators and independent large language model judges. We also introduce an evaluation-validity mechanism that examines the integrity of evaluation inputs, reference information, supporting evidence and grading outputs, with expert review used to resolve identified deficiencies and significant grading disagreements. Numerical results show that the proposed framework can distinguish differences in agent performance across evaluation dimensions, while identifying potential reliability issues in the evaluation process. The associated implementation and evaluation materials will be made available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain-oriented evaluation framework for investment-research AI agents that separates outcome quality from execution quality and audits evaluation validity itself.
AI.motivation: Evaluating investment-research agents is difficult because final report quality does not guarantee sound execution, tasks vary in numerical and retrieval demands, and flaws in reference data or grading can undermine assessment reliability.
AI.method: The framework combines task-specific criteria, deterministic validators, and independent LLM judges to score both execution and outcome quality, alongside an evaluation-validity mechanism that checks input, reference, evidence, and grading integrity with expert review for disagreements.
AI.result: Numerical results show the framework distinguishes agent performance across evaluation dimensions while surfacing reliability issues in the evaluation process.
AI.conclusion: Separating execution from outcome assessment and auditing grading validity provides a more trustworthy evaluation methodology for financial AI agents.

title: HealthCLBench:Evaluating Context Learning in Health Conversations through Controlled Case Clusters
summary: Complex health conversations require answers grounded in individual information and currently valid evidence. We evaluate health context learning: acquiring, integrating, and applying relevant context during inference with fixed model parameters to answer health questions and respond appropriately to changes in facts, evidence, or task goals.
