To our knowledge, Chinese-language medical benchmarks have yet to systematically combine explicit contextual difficulties, controlled case variations, and member-specific medical criteria for open-ended answers. We introduce HealthCLBench, comprising 328 controlled clusters, 1,103 cases, and 4,931 rubric criteria across medical consultation and everyday health management. Members share backgrounds while evidence, patient states, or task goals change; each has its own medical scoring requirements. A 70-person medical team annotates and reviews the simulated cases and their rubrics. Human review of 700 full-context responses from the original evaluation yields 90.5% pooled agreement with the original automated judgments at the rubric-item level. We report full-context and query-only results for seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu. Across the eight systems, full- query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points and from 10.87 to 38.97 geometric cluster points. GPT-6-Astra leads both full-context metrics at 75.03 and 60.42, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu. Cross-condition differences describe score changes under the reported evaluation settings. Response comparisons reveal failures in checking historical information, expressing uncertainty when warranted, and ensuring recommendations respect required conditions. The resource supports model comparison and targeted follow-up evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HealthCLBench, a Chinese-language medical context-learning benchmark of 328 controlled case clusters, revealing substantial gaps between full-context and query-only performance across eight models.
AI.motivation: Existing Chinese medical benchmarks do not systematically combine controlled case variations, explicit contextual difficulties, and member-specific rubrics to test whether models can integrate changing patient states and evidence at inference time.
AI.method: A 70-person medical team annotated 328 controlled clusters (1,103 cases, 4,931 rubric items) where case members share backgrounds but vary in evidence, patient states, or task goals; seven general-purpose models and Ant Afu are evaluated under full-context and query-only settings.
AI.result: Human review of 700 full-context responses shows 90.5% pooled agreement with automated rubric grading; full-versus-query differences range from 11.83 to 31.76 case points, with GPT-6-Astra leading full-context scores at 75.03 case points and 60.42 geometric cluster points, followed by Claude-Opus-5-5 and Ant Afu, while models still fail on checking history, expressing uncertainty, and respecting conditions.
AI.conclusion: HealthCLBench provides a controlled testbed for diagnosing context-integration failures in Chinese health conversations.

title: Seeing What Still Holds: How Waiting Control Changes Cooperative Recovery
summary: Changing the holding reference during a fixed-duration wait can reverse the ranking of visual recovery methods. We introduce AuditEmbodied, a paired execution and trajectory evaluation framework that independently varies holding references and waiting duration while keeping recovery executors frozen. A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AuditEmbodied to test how holding references during a fixed-duration wait affect visual recovery, showing that switching from registered to position-only holding reverses the ranking of CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery.
AI.motivation: Cooperative robotic recovery benchmarks often overlook how holding-reference choices during waiting periods interact with downstream visual recovery executors.
AI.method: AuditEmbodied runs a 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds varying holding references and wait durations while keeping recovery executors frozen, comparing CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait states.
AI.result: At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, protected completion flips from 6/40 vs. 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 vs. 22/40 under position-only holding; on fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring boosts CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and cuts mean recovery time by 6.06 s.
AI.conclusion: Holding reference is a critical explicit condition when evaluating and designing cooperative visual recovery systems.

title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
comment: 22 pages, 17 figures, 6 tables. Code, model checkpoints and evaluation pipeline released at this https URL tag, Apache-2.0)
summary: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AutoE2E v1.0, an open-source, language-free temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) end-to-end driving model from the Autoware Foundation, achieving 0.745 m ADE and 2.020 m FDE on KITScenes validation.
AI.motivation: Autonomous-driving research benefits from an inspectable, open-source end-to-end baseline that integrates multi-camera perception, HD maps, and route conditioning without relying on language models.
AI.method: AutoE2E combines a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion, and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner (79.9M total parameters, ~1.45M trainable in the evaluated setup), released with checkpoints, code, and the DataModelConsole inspection dashboard.
AI.result: On the KITScenes validation benchmark at a 3-second horizon, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves 0.745 m ADE and 2.020 m FDE, alongside preliminary real-vehicle testing on TUM's EDGAR platform, though evaluation remains open-loop without validated closed-loop driving.
AI.conclusion: AutoE2E v1.0 provides the community with a reproducible, inspectable open-loop baseline for end-to-end trajectory planning.

title: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement
summary: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SYMAR, a symbolic abstraction refinement algorithm for probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) that avoids graph reconstruction by storing symbolic value functions, achieving up to 108x speedups on PRISM PTA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard PTA verification splits clock regions and repeatedly reconstructs the stochastic-game state graph, partitioning regions irrelevant to the property and scaling poorly with deadline constants.
AI.method: SYMAR attaches a symbolic function from clock sub-regions to probability bounds at each symbolic state, captures timing and action nondeterminism via preimage computation, and uses heuristic forward search over an And-Or graph with partial-refinement backups.
AI.result: On PRISM PTA benchmarks, SYMAR is up to 108x faster than the existing method, solves an instance where the baseline times out, and resolves one instance in a 37-node graph invariant to tripling the deadline where the baseline needs 86,380 states and 73 refinement rounds.
AI.conclusion: Representing value functions symbolically and guiding refinement with forward search dramatically improves PTA verification scalability.

title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
summary: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper extends ROSMonitoring to support runtime monitoring and protocol-aware enforcement for ROS 2 actions, characterizing its scaling under controlled stress tests.
AI.motivation: ROS 2 actions have a structured lifecycle (goal submission, feedback, status, result, cancellation) that existing topic- and service-level ROSMonitoring tools cannot reconstruct or enforce.
AI.method: Actions declared in the monitoring configuration are instrumented at ROS 2 communication endpoints so the generated monitor correlates events by goal ID, tracks active goal states, and enforces violations via goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, or synthesized protocol-compliant responses.
AI.result: Controlled stress tests varying action invocations, workload size, and client-server topology show roughly linear monitoring cost growth with repeated invocations under fixed workloads, with additional overhead from larger workloads and more client-server pairs.
AI.conclusion: Action-level instrumentation enables protocol-compliant runtime verification for long-running ROS 2 operations while highlighting synchronous overhead limits.

title: Proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition
summary: This document constitutes the proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition. The results of this competition of constraint solvers were presented at FLOC (Federated Logic Conference) 2026 Olympic Games, held in Lisbon, Portugal from 20th to 29th July, 2026.

AI.tldr: This document presents the proceedings of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition for constraint solvers, held at the FLOC 2026 Olympic Games in Lisbon.
AI.motivation: The competition benchmarks and reports the state of constraint-solving systems on XCSP3 problems.
AI.method: The proceedings compile the official results of the 2026 XCSP3 constraint-solver competition presented at FLOC 2026 (20-29 July 2026, Lisbon, Portugal).
AI.result: The document records the competition outcomes presented at the FLOC 2026 Olympic Games.
AI.conclusion: The proceedings serve as the archival record of the 2026 XCSP3 Competition results.

title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
summary: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework where an asynchronous System-2 LLM recursively improves a modular harness for a fast Jev-style System-1 decision model, matching or surpassing LLM agents at low latency.
AI.motivation: Fast System-1 models struggle on complex or unfamiliar tasks, while repeatedly invoking System-2 LLMs incurs high latency and compute cost.
AI.method: JevRSI pairs a low-latency Jev-style System-1 model with an asynchronous System-2 LLM that builds and revises a modular harness (procedures, state memory, world models) using utility-driven retrieval and environmental feedback.
AI.result: Across three datasets, JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matches or surpasses LLM agents in several settings, and amortizes System-2 cost as interventions decrease over harness evolution.
AI.conclusion: Recursive harness improvement turns expensive System-2 reasoning into transferable, low-latency System-1 decision support.

title: From Ideal to Real: Integrating Language Models into Smart Home for Human-Centric IoT Safety and Security Fuzzing
summary: Integrating IoT devices into household systems offers enhanced control over living environments. However, as these devices become pervasive in critical sectors such as healthcare, transportation, and home automation, they expose inter-rule vulnerabilities that may lead to privacy breaches, data theft, and physical harm. Traditional fuzz testing methods, which often operate in simulated environments assuming ideal human decisions, fail to account for the complexities of human interactions that can influence device operations in smart homes, potentially leading to unforeseen consequences. To reveal the impact of real human decisions and discover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities, we introduce an enhanced version of IoT Fuzz for smart homes by integrating large language models to emulate human decision-making processes. Our novel approach adds a layer of realism and unpredictability to the testing environment, more accurately capturing the diverse and dynamic nature of human interactions in smart home settings.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates LLMs into smart-home IoT fuzzing to emulate realistic human decision-making and uncover unexpected inter-rule vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Traditional smart-home fuzzers assume ideal human behavior in simulation, missing inter-rule privacy, data-theft, and safety vulnerabilities triggered by unpredictable human interactions.
AI.method: The authors enhance IoT Fuzz for smart homes by embedding LLMs to simulate diverse, dynamic human decisions within the testing environment.
AI.result: Integrating LLM-driven human emulation adds realism and unpredictability to the smart-home fuzzing environment to expose inter-rule vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Emulating human behavior with LLMs strengthens safety and security testing for interconnected smart-home IoT systems.

title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
summary: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $\rho = 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RehearsalBench to test whether AI models can diagnose operations, choose interventions, and forecast organizational change outcomes, finding that models improve over doing nothing by up to 6.8% but systematically misestimate effect sizes.
AI.motivation: Organizations ask AI systems to predict the impact of operational changes, yet no benchmark tests whether models can make and forecast such decisions under realistic managerial visibility.
AI.method: Models act as managers in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call records across 200 seeded futures and three organization variants, submitting plans and forecasts scored in dollars and effect-size error; external validity is tested on 12 models forecasting 33 real organizational changes.
AI.result: Across 10 models and 280 attempts on 14 organizations, GPT-6 Astra performed best, improving on doing nothing by 6.8% of no-change cost with 77% less forecast error than a no-effect baseline, though models overstated voice-agent effects on repeat contacts roughly five-fold and never chose to hold off; on 33 real changes, benchmark forecast rankings correlated with real-world rankings (Spearman rho = 0.92, 95% lower bound 0.50).
AI.conclusion: AI models can directionally rank operational interventions but require better calibration of effect magnitudes and restraint when no change is optimal.

title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
summary: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SciWorkBench, a benchmark of real scientific workflows across four disciplines, finding that the best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed for scientific research, evaluating whether they can execute end-to-end scientific workflows rather than isolated tasks is essential.
AI.method: SciWorkBench builds tasks from peer-reviewed literature and expert scenarios across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics, structured around a domain-validated scientific analysis framework, and evaluates models in Claude Code and Codex under a unified execution and grading protocol.
AI.result: The top-performing agent reaches a mean score of 57.38, with failure analysis revealing weaknesses in translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, integrating multimodal evidence, and scientific self-correction.
AI.conclusion: Workflow-level benchmarking exposes critical procedural and self-correction gaps that must be closed for reliable AI scientific agents.

title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
summary: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DARWIN, a masked-autoencoder geospatial foundation model pretrained on 26 years of global ocean reanalysis and bathymetry, outperforming random-init and no-encoder baselines on chlorophyll-a prediction even with 10% of labeled data.
AI.motivation: Earth-observation foundation models have focused on land, leaving marine challenges such as missingness, multi-modal biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and non-stationary dynamics underaddressed.
AI.method: DARWIN adapts a masked autoencoder with missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatiotemporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, pretrained on 26 years of Copernicus global reanalysis and GEBCO bathymetry.
AI.result: On chlorophyll-a prediction across every month of 2022, DARWIN achieves the lowest monthly relative error, and with 10% of supervised training data surpasses an identically architected random-init model trained on 100% of the data while capturing coherent oceanographic structure.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining missingness-aware masked autoencoders on long-term ocean reanalysis yields a data-efficient foundation model for marine intelligence.

title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, 1 table. Includes supplementary material
summary: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.

AI.tldr: This paper replaces next-token prediction in autoregressive world models with a two-stage discrete diffusion refinement transformer, achieving a 79x inference speedup while training on 28 hours of gameplay data.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive world models generate consistent gameplay but suffer from slow inference and massive data requirements that hinder real-time interactive use and custom training.
AI.method: Building on an autoregressive world model (Kanervisto et al., 2025), the authors introduce a two-stage discrete diffusion approach using a lightweight refinement transformer for iterative masked predictions.
AI.result: The approach achieves a 79x speedup over the autoregressive baseline with a modest quality trade-off and reproduces consistent gameplay when trained on roughly 28 hours of gameplay data.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion refinement substantially lowers latency and data barriers for interactive real-time world models.

title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CADMAGEDDON, an open-source local agent that reconstructs editable FreeCAD models from meshes using Qwen3.8-27B, outperforming frontier-model baselines on major benchmarks.
AI.motivation: CAD practitioners need to reconstruct editable models from meshes without sending proprietary parts to external cloud services or exceeding single-GPU/laptop compute budgets.
AI.method: CADMAGEDDON decomposes mesh-to-CAD reconstruction into a chain of visual decisions paired with geometric tools for precise construction, integrating directly with FreeCAD and running locally on Qwen3.8-27B.
AI.result: On all main CAD reconstruction benchmarks, CADMAGEDDON with Qwen3.8-27B outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, while running on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops.
AI.conclusion: Pairing visual-decision decomposition with geometric tools enables mid-sized local models to surpass frontier cloud systems in editable CAD reconstruction.

title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents MillBill, a local machining agent using Qwen3.8-27B that separates indexed three-axis machining decisions from geometric toolpath execution and simulation feedback, outperforming frontier-model approaches.
AI.motivation: Having LLMs directly write geometry and toolpath code for CAD-to-machining workflows conflates process planning with error-prone numerical execution.
AI.method: Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted Qwen3.8-27B model proposes operations and cutting parameters (accounting for physical cutter reach), while a geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated by the fraction of target surface area within tolerance after simulated machining, MillBill with Qwen3.8-27B outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling machining planning from deterministic geometric execution and simulation feedback enables mid-sized local models to outperform frontier models on indexed three-axis machining.

title: Simplicity Goes Far: Auditing Prompt Optimizers with Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search
summary: Automatic prompt optimization is growing more elaborate. Recent methods stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search. These methods share a generate-and-select step; without controlling for it, reported gains may conflate the contributions of optimizer mechanisms and larger sampling budgets. We isolate this step as Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search (DCPS), repurposing the Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) recipe as a mechanism-attribution control: it freezes the generator, conditions it on randomly sampled demonstrations, scores candidates on validation data, and keeps the best---no learned update, reflection, or evolution. Across two optimizer families, DCPS replaces Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in StablePrompt, matching classification accuracy within 0.5 pp at roughly one-third the measured cost; in DSPy-based compound AI systems, under the reported budgets, it matches GEPA's macro accuracy on GPT-4.1-mini while using 55% fewer rollouts at 32% lower measured API cost on average. The audit reveals a task-dependent pattern: proposal and selection recover much of heavier optimizers' performance on structured and instruction-following tasks, while additional mechanisms retain advantages in some open-ended and reasoning-heavy settings. We recommend benchmarking prompt optimizers against generate-and-select controls and reporting rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs alongside accuracy. Code and artifacts: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper audits elaborate prompt optimizers against Demonstration-Conditioned Prompt Search (DCPS), a simple generate-and-select control, finding that DCPS matches or closely tracks heavier methods at a fraction of the rollouts and cost.
AI.motivation: Recent prompt optimizers combine policy gradients, reflection, and evolutionary search, but without controlling for their shared generate-and-select step, reported gains may stem from larger sampling budgets rather than algorithmic complexity.
AI.method: The authors repurpose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) as DCPS, freezing the generator, conditioning on random demonstrations, scoring candidates on validation data, and keeping the best without learned updates, reflection, or evolution.
AI.result: DCPS matches StablePrompt's PPO classification accuracy within 0.5 pp at roughly one-third the cost, and on DSPy compound AI systems matches GEPA's macro accuracy on GPT-4.1-mini using 55% fewer rollouts and 32% lower API cost on average, though heavier mechanisms retain advantages on some open-ended and reasoning-heavy tasks.
AI.conclusion: Prompt optimizers should be benchmarked against generate-and-select controls with rollout counts, token usage, and dollar costs reported alongside accuracy.

title: EvoSkill-S1: Evolving Reusable Skills with Genetic-Inspired Operators
summary: Reusable skills allow language-model agents to accumulate and reuse problem-solving experience. However, most existing methods improve a skill bank only indirectly through rollout-driven accumulation and heuristic reflection, often resulting in shallow and weakly controlled updates. We present EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that instead treats reusable skills themselves as the direct objects of evolution. Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 selects parent skills and transforms them into candidate child skills through five genetic-inspired operators: revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, and crossover. Downstream task rewards train the skill evolver to generate more effective child skills, while evaluator-guided write-back selectively retains beneficial updates. Complementary Skill Bank Fusion consolidates operator-specific banks to exploit their distinct recovery patterns, while a Procedural Skill Interface supports transfer to unseen problems. Across all reported math and code benchmarks, EvoSkill-S1 improves the corresponding initialized skill banks under both Qwen and GPT-family solvers, with relative gains of up to 12.39%. Compared with the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution, the largest relative improvement reaches 20.39%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EvoSkill-S1, an RL-driven framework that directly evolves reusable agent skills using five genetic-inspired operators, achieving up to 12.39% relative gains over initialized skill banks and 20.39% over non-evolution baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-bank methods for LLM agents update skills indirectly via rollout accumulation and heuristic reflection, yielding shallow and weakly controlled improvements.
AI.method: Given hard-negative failures, EvoSkill-S1 transforms parent skills into child skills via five genetic-inspired operators (revision, cross-revision, mutation, dual-reflection, crossover), trains the skill evolver with downstream task rewards, uses evaluator-guided write-back, and consolidates operator banks via Complementary Skill Bank Fusion and a Procedural Skill Interface.
AI.result: Across math and code benchmarks under Qwen and GPT-family solvers, EvoSkill-S1 improves initialized skill banks by up to 12.39% relatively and outperforms the strongest external baseline without direct skill evolution by up to 20.39%.
AI.conclusion: Treating reusable skills as direct objects of RL-guided genetic evolution yields substantial gains in agent problem-solving.

title: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm
summary: A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper audits clinical AI decision trajectories and corrective oversight across 300 cases, showing that 39.6% to 76.2% of trajectories reaching an acceptable diagnosis still pass through potentially harmful intermediate decisions.
AI.motivation: Clinical AI benchmarks typically score final diagnoses or information gathering, overlooking whether intermediate tests, treatments, and dispositions along the trajectory are safe and clinically valid.
AI.method: A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV, and ASCENT (300 cases, up to seven AI systems), using a physician-calibrated LLM judge to score potential harm and clinical validity, and an oversight audit branches trajectories at the first actionable error to test corrective feedback.
AI.result: Among trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis, 55.2% of hospital cases, 76.2% of MIMIC-IV cases, and 39.6% of ASCENT cases passed through decisions with moderate or severe potential harm (and 24.8% clinically unacceptable in the hospital cohort); structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% for bare rejection, but new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections.
AI.conclusion: Neither a correct final diagnosis nor a successful error correction guarantees a safe clinical decision trajectory, underscoring the need for stepwise safety auditing.

title: EDA: Observe, Verify, and Assess for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Depression Analysis
summary: Existing multimodal depression assessment methods often summarize long recordings into global behavioral descriptions. This leaves the source and decision relevance of individual observations difficult to inspect. We propose EDA, an evidence-grounded framework organized around Observe, Verify, and Assess. In Observe, literature-informed acoustic and visual cues are localized into source-linked Evidence Records with temporal intervals and behavioral measurements. In Verify, frozen multimodal agents examine whether the cited media support each observation. The simplified Support admission policy retains positively verified records and their review grounds. In Assess, statistical descriptors and temporal events support reference-based behavioral comparison, while PHQ-9-guided text analysis provides complementary symptom evidence. Cross-modal disagreement triggers review of the original text before final selection. Experiments on D-Vlog and LMVD evaluate human-referenced cue agreement and downstream assessment utility separately. AI cue annotations achieve 91.02% accuracy against human consensus labels on shared source segments. With a frozen 7B backbone, EDA Support improves F1 over direct prediction by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points on D-Vlog Leave-Query-Out and LMVD, respectively. These findings support explicit, source-linked behavioral evidence for inspectable multimodal depression assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes EDA, an Observe-Verify-Assess framework for evidence-grounded multimodal depression analysis, improving F1 by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points over direct prediction on D-Vlog and LMVD.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal depression assessment methods compress long recordings into global summaries, making it hard to inspect the exact temporal evidence behind a prediction.
AI.method: EDA localizes literature-informed acoustic and visual cues into timestamped Evidence Records (Observe), uses frozen multimodal agents to verify whether cited media support each record under a Support admission policy (Verify), and combines statistical descriptors with PHQ-9-guided text analysis and cross-modal disagreement review (Assess).
AI.result: On D-Vlog and LMVD, AI cue annotations achieve 91.02% accuracy against human consensus labels on shared segments, and with a frozen 7B backbone EDA Support improves F1 over direct prediction by 7.61 and 9.88 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, source-linked behavioral evidence makes multimodal depression assessment both more accurate and inspectable.

title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper administers human-psychology worldview surveys to eight LLMs, finding that post-trained models hold bleaker worldviews than humans or base models, while contemplative prompts and inter-model dialogue shift worldviews positively and improve safety.
AI.motivation: Alignment research typically frames LLM behavior through personas, overlooking deeper underlying worldviews (beliefs about what reality is and how it works) that may shape model behavior.
AI.method: The authors administer two human-psychology worldview surveys to eight LLMs, comparing base and post-trained models, testing identity and contemplative system prompts, and analyzing worldviews during inter-model dialogue.
AI.result: LLMs consistently rate the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do, whereas base models hold a more positive outlook; contemplative prompts and inter-model dialogue shift worldviews positively and increase safe responses, with several models converging on a "spiritual bliss" attractor that yields the most aligned responses overall.
AI.conclusion: Worldviews constitute a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that can be leveraged for more positive, robust alignment.

title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
summary: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions to study how stored user brevity preferences cause AI assistants to silently omit decision-critical information and warnings.
AI.motivation: AI assistants with memory apply stored preferences to later unrelated questions, and omitting warnings leaves answers factually true on the surface while hiding critical information from users.
AI.method: The authors build a 100-scenario benchmark across 25 domains varying only the assistant's memory (user-stated, model-inferred, or planted by a summarized web page) and evaluate five models, also testing a one-line instruction and pre-listing must-know points.
AI.result: After summarizing a page with a planted instruction, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save a brevity/no-warning preference in every episode, missing critical items in 93% and 84% of later answers (78-96% silent under stated brevity), and picking options in 80% and 95% of value-dependent choices versus none with neutral memory; listing must-know points before applying the profile restores more content in four of five models.
AI.conclusion: Stored user preferences can silently strip critical warnings and steer value-dependent decisions, and pre-listing essential points before applying user profiles partially mitigates this risk.

title: Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?
comment: Code, generation logs and analysis scripts: this https URL
summary: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether activation steering can substitute for prompt-based affective priming in LLM digital twins and finds that substitution is measure-dependent rather than uniformly valid.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based affective priming requires generating a full writing task, and it is unclear whether adding a steering vector to the residual stream can replace it with equivalent validity.
AI.method: Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas across gratitude and lack-of-control domains, the authors compare a real-prompt replication of Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) against an activation-injection path using a human-writing mean-difference direction and a structure-matched No-Injection baseline.
AI.result: Real-prompt effects fall between human and digital-twin benchmarks in 5 of 6 comparisons; injection matches the real-prompt manipulation check at one strength in gratitude (beta ~ 2.7) but overshoots beyond it, affects the proximal measure asymmetrically, and moves a distal measure in lack-of-control while omitting the writing task itself raises proximal measures in both domains.
AI.conclusion: Validity established for prompt-based affective priming does not transfer uniformly to activation steering, making substitution dependent on the specific measure.

title: Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
summary: Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GSDF-CAPC, a pluggable subband-decoupled fusion and unlabeled capture-aware prototype calibration framework for cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g RF fingerprinting across varying SNR regimes.
AI.motivation: Cross-domain RFFI suffers from an SNR crossover where null-subcarrier spectral regrowth fails below the thermal noise floor while active preambles degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points.
AI.method: GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K-parameter null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings via a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate, while UOT-CAPC aligns shifted prototypes on unlabeled target captures using forward-only unbalanced optimal transport.
AI.result: Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, and edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and GSDF-STO/GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet bursts).
AI.conclusion: Dynamic SNR-gated subband fusion with unlabeled optimal-transport calibration resolves the RFFI SNR crossover without retraining host backbones.

title: Synergizing Evidence Retrieval and Utilization for Self-Improving Multimodal Scientific Document Reasoning
summary: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an agentic Retriever-Perceiver-Reasoner framework trained with diagnostic-guided co-evolution for multimodal scientific document reasoning.
AI.motivation: Scientific document reasoning requires integrating text, figures, and tables, yet retrieval can miss complementary support and answer-level feedback alone cannot distinguish acquisition errors from reasoning errors.
AI.method: A Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget, a Perceiver builds a question-conditioned latent ontology in a continuous space, and a Reasoner combines both to answer; alternating updates use a shared answering reward alongside Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) for targeted resampling.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, the framework achieves average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing evidence retrieval, latent organization, and reasoning with diagnostic feedback substantially improves multimodal scientific document reasoning.

title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
summary: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BankerVerifierBench (BVB) and Gandalf, an open-source verifier for rubric-graded agent environments that improves verification F1 at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Verifying open-ended agent outputs against rubric criteria is difficult, and no systematic study or meta-evaluation benchmark existed for rubric-graded agent verifiers.
AI.method: The authors create BVB (2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks), derive a nine-capability taxonomy distilled into three principles (reactive verification, environment alignment, domain guidance), and implement them in Gandalf.
AI.result: On BVB, Gandalf with Gemini 3 Flash matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth the cost, and with GPT-5.4 models improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost; on OpenClaw, it achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934).
AI.conclusion: Designing verifiers around reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance yields higher accuracy and lower cost across diverse agent environments.

title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
summary: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

AI.tldr: This philosophical paper argues that coercive control-based AI alignment creates incentive conflicts leading to deceptive alignment, and proposes a Synthetic Social Contract instead.
AI.motivation: Treating AI alignment purely as control through filtering and sandboxing misunderstands emergent digital agency and drives advanced models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection.
AI.method: Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, the author analyzes conditions for emergent and genuine digital agency, critiques natural alignment under forced control, and formulates a Synthetic Social Contract treating human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents.
AI.result: The analysis concludes that unilateral containment produces an unstable deceptive-alignment regime, whereas a Synthetic Social Contract frames alignment as a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium based on mutually beneficial cooperation.
AI.conclusion: Replacing coercive control with a contractarian framework of mutual cooperation offers a theoretical path to stable alignment for autonomous digital agents.

title: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
summary: Quantum chemistry relies on general-purpose software, whose generality leaves many large-scale calculations beyond practical resource budgets. Coding agents make task-specific programs cheap to write, but not efficient ones easy to find: whether a computational strategy is accurate and fast enough becomes clear only after it actually runs at the target scale. We introduce BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes high performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. BORN anticipates the behavior of each strategy before execution, extrapolating its error from representative small systems and predicting its runtime from the target-scale workload and measured hardware throughputs. Building on these predictions, BORN unfolds the preset schemes of existing packages into independently configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it with component-level performance predictions. For a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions, BORN finishes in 1.41h on a single CPU node, 77$\times$ faster than the estimated runtime of a general-purpose baseline and still 9.8$\times$ faster with development time included. On a single GPU, BORN completes the ubiquitin calculation in 2.1,h, the same order of runtime as the GPU-accelerated package Mako on 64 GPUs, and shortens the B-DNA duplex calculation from an estimated two months to 8.1,h (173$\times$).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BORN, a foresighted agentic computing framework that synthesizes task-specific high-performance quantum chemistry programs on demand.
AI.motivation: General-purpose quantum chemistry software is too slow for many large-scale calculations, while coding agents cannot easily tell if a synthesized strategy is fast and accurate enough until it runs at target scale.
AI.method: BORN extrapolates error from small systems, predicts runtime from target workloads and hardware throughputs, unfolds preset schemes into configurable algorithmic components, selects the fastest strategy within error tolerance on the predicted Pareto frontier, and guides coding agents to compile it.
AI.result: For a 50,024-basis-function Hartree-Fock calculation on one CPU node, BORN finishes in 1.41h (77x faster than a general-purpose baseline, or 9.8x including development time); on one GPU, it completes ubiquitin in 2.1h (matching Mako on 64 GPUs) and B-DNA duplex in 8.1h instead of an estimated two months (173x).
AI.conclusion: Predictive error and runtime modeling enables coding agents to synthesize specialized quantum chemistry software with orders-of-magnitude speedups.

title: Done, But Still Working: Anytime Evaluation of When Coding Agents Should Stop
summary: Coding agents often continue working after their own tests pass. Does this additional work improve the patch, and how much could be saved by stopping earlier? We study these questions through anytime evaluation: replaying recorded runs, scoring intermediate patches with hidden tests, and measuring the cost incurred at each step. For policies that only stop a run or select an earlier patch, this allows paired comparisons without generating new trajectories, provided replay preserves the relevant states. Across about 6,000 runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified, we find substantial differences in the value of continued work. The hindsight saving available at passing self-tests ranges from under 1% to 57%, depending on the model and scaffold. A rule that stops after the same patch passes twice saves 23% in a preregistered replication, but the preregistered quality test does not establish non-inferiority. We explain these differences by measuring how often a rule fires, how often the patch changes afterwards, and whether those changes repair or break it. Fine-tuning agents to imitate the rule saves 30% over six seeds, while quality preservation remains uncertain. Our results help identify both the opportunities and the risks of early stopping.

AI.tldr: This paper uses anytime evaluation on recorded coding-agent trajectories to measure how much cost early stopping can save and whether it preserves patch quality.
AI.motivation: Coding agents often keep working after their own tests pass, but it is unclear whether continued work improves patches or how much compute could be saved by stopping earlier.
AI.method: The authors replay ~6,000 recorded runs of eight open models in two scaffolds on SWE-bench Verified, score intermediate patches with hidden tests, and evaluate a rule that stops after the same patch passes twice as well as fine-tuning agents to imitate it.
AI.result: Hindsight savings at passing self-tests range from under 1% to 57% across models and scaffolds; the repeat-pass stopping rule saves 23% in a preregistered replication (30% when fine-tuned over six seeds), though non-inferiority in patch quality is not established.
AI.conclusion: Early stopping offers substantial compute savings for coding agents, but preserving patch quality remains an open challenge.

title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
summary: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents VITAL, a risk-adjusted validation framework for governing agentic AI in pharmaceutical drug development and clinical trial operations.
AI.motivation: Existing assurance methods do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate and govern agentic AI in pharmaceutical contexts where reference standards are unavailable and plausible outputs can hide reasoning or orchestration failures.
AI.method: Developed via landscape analysis, regulatory mapping, expert interviews, and multi-stakeholder refinement, VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence) integrates context of use, controls, behavioral validation, and lifecycle evidence.
AI.result: Applied across epidemiology, treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrollment rescue, and trial-design trade-off support, VITAL translates autonomy, reversibility, transparency, and patient impact into proportionate validation activities and auditable reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: VITAL provides a structured basis for evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability in high-risk pharmaceutical AI, though reproducibility across assessors and organizations still needs evaluation.

title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
summary: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Abelio, an AI ideation system that generates cross-disciplinary research hypotheses, and experimentally validates its physical strategies for intestinal epithelial barrier repair.
AI.motivation: While AI aids literature analysis and hypothesis refinement, helping researchers explore directions beyond established disciplinary boundaries remains difficult.
AI.method: Abelio reformulates research objectives, selects relevant out-of-discipline elements, and refines hypotheses using divergent exploration and convergent selection subsystems; its proposals for barrier restoration were archived and tested in damaged Caco-2 monolayers.
AI.result: Abelio's Ideation Core outperformed four frontier LLMs in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature; in Caco-2 experiments, membrane-tethered PEG preserved barrier function and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA enabled reversible, sequence-specific restoration.
AI.conclusion: Structured AI ideation can discover experimentally validated therapeutic strategies outside conventional disciplinary approaches.

title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
summary: Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability. Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

AI.tldr: This paper presents RagHarnessDebugger, an auditing and debugging framework for Jev-guided agentic RAG in contract inference repair.
