AI.motivation: Agentic RAG systems repair their own answers by gathering evidence and testing policies, but aggregate metrics like accuracy hide whether repairs actually work or where missed repairs are lost.
AI.method: RagHarnessDebugger records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness, verifies trace integrity and validation alignment, and supports labeled error analysis and counterfactual replay on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements.
AI.result: Auditing exposed a policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealized repairs on development and replication sets; a revised harness improved accuracy over the BM25-only baseline by 3.6 and 3.7 points and over full contract access by 1.1 and 2.4 points.
AI.conclusion: Decision-level auditing and replay provide judgment visibility that enables targeted debugging and measurable accuracy gains in agentic RAG.

title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that enforces explicit physical scope and dependency management for multimodal physics reasoning.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models often interpret physics diagrams correctly but apply constraints outside their valid states or conditions, propagating premise errors through calculations.
AI.method: PhysScope links physical scopes to visual observations, constructs derived views, enforces constraints on state distinctions and conditions during reasoning, checks revisions against sources, and invalidates dependent steps when revisions are accepted.
AI.result: On PhysAlign, PhysScope improves solving scores across all six evaluated VLMs, outperforming Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points with Gemini-3.8-flash and substantially improving accuracy on OOD PhysUniBench.
AI.conclusion: Explicit scope management and dependency maintenance at inference time effectively prevent premise propagation errors in multimodal physics reasoning.

title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
summary: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

AI.tldr: This paper presents PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework for tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations from periapical radiographs.
AI.motivation: Interpreting periapical radiographs and writing reports is time-consuming, technical language hinders patient understanding, and existing automated tools often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence.
AI.method: PeriaTrace integrates tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and plain-language explanations with care recommendations, developed and evaluated on 12,877 radiographs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts.
AI.result: Internally, PeriaTrace achieved 85.35% macro Dice, 0.6504 BLEU-4, 94.37% joint tooth localization and FDI identification F1, and 77.93% grounding-tag F1; externally, senior endodontists rated 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or minor revision, averaging 4.41 seconds per radiograph, and 96.4% of 196 lay participants preferred its plain-language reports.
AI.conclusion: PeriaTrace enables fast, evidence-traceable endodontic reporting that supports both clinical review and patient communication.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
summary: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

AI.tldr: This paper reports an end-to-end case study developing, simulating, and deploying a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) controller for an occupied residential heat pump and underfloor heating system.
AI.motivation: Controlling underfloor heating coupled with heat pumps is difficult due to high thermal inertia and slow dynamics, and real-world deployments of DRL controllers in occupied buildings remain rare.
AI.method: The authors run a simulation pilot to select DRL algorithms and configurations, train agents on a digital twin of a real residential building, and deploy the best policy directly in the physical building without online fine-tuning.
AI.result: The deployed DRL controller maintained indoor temperatures within prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting heat pump supply temperature and underfloor heating valve positions.
AI.conclusion: Digital-twin-trained DRL policies can transfer robustly to real occupied buildings, demonstrating practical feasibility alongside sim-to-real deployment challenges.

title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
summary: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether fixed value statements in a self-improving coding agent's persistent instructions affect its performance and the algorithms it builds.
AI.motivation: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for task outcomes, leaving designers with limited ways to shape how agents work on open-ended tasks.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four higher-order values from Schwartz's theory (openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, self-transcendence) held fixed across self-improvement iterations on diverse coding tasks.
AI.result: Openness values improve held-out performance while conservation values score below having no values; values alter solution size, complexity, and approach; allowing agents to revise their own values narrows differences, and literature-distilled values yield no detectable gain over no values.
AI.conclusion: Human-designed value statements can meaningfully shape both what self-improving coding agents build and how well they perform.

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
summary: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher for oracle-based optimization that discovers algorithms and lower bounds, formally certifies them, and maintains a living Complexity Atlas.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery continually reshapes known frontiers, and oracle-based optimization requires systematically closing gaps between achievable algorithmic rates and unavoidable complexity limits.
AI.method: Colombo tracks knowledge gaps in a Complexity Atlas, uses Self-Organization to plan research programs, runs Adversarial Co-Ascent between algorithm design and hard-instance construction, and verifies claims via independent review and Lean-based formal certification with Long-Term Memory.
AI.result: Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Complexity Atlas.
AI.conclusion: Colombo demonstrates a concrete step toward autopoietic science, where validated discoveries continually regenerate and guide further mathematical inquiry.

title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
summary: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that hidden-state activation similarity to the inoculation context, rather than textual similarity, predicts when evaluation prompts re-elicit suppressed misalignment after inoculation prompting.
AI.motivation: Inoculation prompting reduces emergent misalignment from fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks, but suppressed behaviors can reappear when evaluation prompts contain training-context cues, and what makes a trigger effective is unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze prompts that re-elicit suppressed behaviors after inoculation prompting, comparing textual similarity to the inoculation prompt against similarity in model hidden-state activations.
AI.result: Textual similarity is an incomplete predictor, whereas prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context.
AI.conclusion: Activation-space analysis can help detect when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under evaluation-time prompts.

title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
summary: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture using PKI, Zero Trust, and remote attestation for cross-organization AI agents.
AI.motivation: Existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination but lack a common mechanism to verify cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization.
AI.method: ATI establishes federated trust via peer organizational AgentCAs, validates certificates, model/tool/prompt integrity via Entity Attestation Tokens, and request authorization via IETF WIMSE tokens and three policy checks as an external enforcement layer.
AI.result: Evaluated in a simulated eight-organization federation across six frameworks, 14 attack scenarios, and six benign tasks, ATI increases attack containment from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% on 11 consistent scenarios) with approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request.
AI.conclusion: Open-source ATI provides low-overhead, framework-independent identity, attestation, and authorization enforcement for multi-organization agent ecosystems.

title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26)
summary: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed. We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

AI.tldr: This staged systematic literature review synthesizes research on AI coding assistants and developer productivity, revealing 187 fragmented markers and calling for more comparable, multidimensional evaluation.
AI.motivation: Despite many studies on AI coding assistants, heterogeneous productivity markers, settings, and reporting styles prevent a clear cumulative picture.
AI.method: The authors conduct a two-stage systematic review, first synthesizing explicit productivity studies and then extending to human-centered outcomes using the SPACE framework, analyzing operationalizations, confounders, and effect distributions.
AI.result: The review identifies 187 unique markers while individual studies typically use five; explicit studies focus on time, output, and artifact proxies, whereas SPACE-aligned studies highlight satisfaction and well-being, with positive effects stronger in perceived findings than in objective evaluations.
AI.conclusion: AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence is context-dependent and requires standardized, multidimensional measurement for cross-study comparability.

title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
comment: Accepted at 1st International Workshop on LiveWriting @ ASE 2026
summary: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.

AI.tldr: This position paper proposes a research agenda for static human-AI alignment metrics in hybrid software engineering teams, validated using declarative business process monitoring (BPM) tools.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for human-AI collaboration in software engineering focus on dynamic run-time performance and lack systematic static measurements of early alignment between AI actions and human expectations.
AI.method: The authors outline an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing on software architecture, organizational psychology, and HCI, paired with a validation methodology and static assessment tools using declarative BPM languages to check project constraint adherence.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual research agenda and validation framework rather than empirical results.
AI.conclusion: Static alignment metrics grounded in declarative BPM offer a promising early indicator for effective human-AI collaboration in software engineering.

title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.

AI.tldr: This pre-registered within-subject experiment (N = 128) finds that multimodal LLM-generated textual explanations significantly improve perceived understanding and perceived trust in XAI visualizations.
AI.motivation: Many explainable AI (XAI) visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret, and it is unclear whether LLM-generated textual explanations can bridge this gap.
AI.method: Participants (N = 128) evaluated five XAI methods across seven decision scenarios with and without multimodal LLM-generated textual explanations, analyzed alongside a mediation analysis.
AI.result: LLM explanations increased perceived understanding by 0.35 points and perceived trust by 0.26 points on five-point scales (both p < .001) across all seven scenarios, with the largest gains for users with the least prior XAI exposure and an indirect effect on trust mediated by understanding.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal LLMs can serve as an effective interpretive layer that makes XAI visualizations more understandable and trustworthy for non-expert users.

title: FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts
comment: 5 figures, 13 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which verifies LLM-generated artifacts against the original request by separating formal conformance from requirement fidelity.
AI.motivation: When an LLM writes both an artifact and its tests, passing tests are weak evidence because a single misreading of the request produces both a faulty artifact and a test that accepts it.
AI.method: FCP uses model checkers and SMT solvers to decide formal conformance, while turning eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement into mechanical witness checks and surfacing unresolvable ambiguities as concrete questions for the author across hardware, text, agents, and code.
AI.result: On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements whereas FCP certified none; on ten code tasks across three LLMs, code passed its own tests while violating the request every time (33/33 violations certified by tests vs. 3 by FCP).
AI.conclusion: Separating conformance from fidelity with mechanical witness checks catches false certifications that self-written tests and model agreement miss.

title: EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary
summary: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper summarizes the EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026, which benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence across social reasoning in video and interactive tool-mediated service tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing egocentric benchmarks focus on visible objects and activities, leaving social cue interpretation, visually grounded reference resolution, and closed-loop tool-mediated action under-evaluated.
AI.method: EgoLink comprises Track 1 (social reasoning in egocentric video using a multi-stage MCQ and CoT pipeline) and Track 2 (interactive agents completing service tasks via dialogue and tool use), combining answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation.
AI.result: The top Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, and the top Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy; strong systems relied on candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction.
AI.conclusion: Process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning are key to reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

title: From Top to Bottom: Quark Mass Hierarchies in Heterotic String Theory
summary: Standard Model fermion masses exhibit large hierarchies, spanning more than five orders of magnitude in the quark sector alone. In this paper, we study whether these hierarchies can be generated perturbatively at tree level in smooth heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications, where the supergravity approximation remains under computational control. In such backgrounds, physical Yukawa couplings combine holomorphic superpotential integrals with matter field Kahler metrics. The former can be computed algebraically, while the latter require solving a coupled system of partial differential equations for the Ricci-flat metric, Hermitian Yang-Mills connections, and harmonic bundle-valued forms. Within this framework, we identify two new tree-level mechanisms by which complex structure moduli can generate fermion mass hierarchies and show analytically and numerically that both mechanisms are obstructed for previously studied tetra-quadric models. Motivated by these obstructions, we scan the existing databases of tens of thousands of complete intersection Calabi-Yau line bundle models and find a unique smooth quotient admitting a rank-three up-quark Yukawa matrix at tree level. Evaluating the physical couplings on this manifold and evolving them under the renormalization group, we obtain realistic mass hierarchies for the top, charm, up, and bottom quarks in the smooth supergravity regime.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies two tree-level mechanisms for quark mass hierarchies in smooth heterotic Calabi-Yau compactifications and finds a unique quotient manifold yielding realistic up, charm, top, and bottom quark hierarchies.
AI.motivation: Standard Model quark masses span over five orders of magnitude, and it has been unclear whether realistic hierarchies can arise perturbatively at tree level in computationally controlled smooth heterotic supergravity.
AI.method: Combining algebraic superpotential integrals with numerical solutions for Ricci-flat metrics, Hermitian Yang-Mills connections, and harmonic forms, the authors analyze complex structure moduli mechanisms and scan tens of thousands of complete intersection Calabi-Yau line bundle models.
AI.result: Previously studied tetra-quadric models are shown to obstruct both mechanisms, but the scan identifies a unique smooth quotient admitting a rank-three up-quark Yukawa matrix at tree level that yields realistic top, charm, up, and bottom quark mass hierarchies after renormalization group evolution.
AI.conclusion: Realistic quark mass hierarchies can be generated perturbatively at tree level in smooth heterotic string compactifications.

title: LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana
summary: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates LLMs on diagnosing Solana cross-chain bridge vulnerabilities from source code and transaction records, finding low diagnostic accuracy without comments and frequent false alarms on secure code.
AI.motivation: Missing validation checks in Solana bridges have caused major exploits, yet it is unclear whether LLMs can accurately diagnose these flaws rather than merely raising unsupported alarms.
AI.method: The authors build a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants (including Cashio and Wormhole flaws) and paired secure programs, evaluating six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses and 7,200 graded answers.
AI.result: Without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge; transaction diagnosis is high for missing-signer flaws but averages 6% across the other three scenarios, while original comments raise source diagnosis to 60%.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating bridge security tools requires distinguishing true vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms, as current open-weight LLMs struggle on uncommented code and non-trivial transactions.

title: Beyond Reconstruction: A Unified Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable EEG Artifact Removal Evaluation
summary: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TriX-EEG, a three-level evaluation framework for EEG artifact removal that assesses signal validity, removal faithfulness, and explanation reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG denoising evaluation relies on reconstruction metrics that measure similarity to clean EEG but fail to show whether artifacts are suppressed, neural activity is preserved, or explanations are reliable.
AI.method: TriX-EEG evaluates Level 1 Signal Validity (reconstruction and band-power preservation), Level 2 Removal Faithfulness (artifact error and residual/neural leakage), and Level 3 Explanation Reliability (temporal alignment, causal relevance, stability) across nine neural denoisers and three benchmarks.
AI.result: Across EEGDenoiseNet and PhysioNet motion-artifact benchmarks (EOG, EMG, motion) plus external EEG/EOG and BCI Competition IV-2a validation, reconstruction metrics alone miss residual artifact versus neural suppression trade-offs, while TriX-EEG yields consistent rankings under dataset shift and correlates with downstream task preservation.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evaluating signal validity, removal faithfulness, and explanation reliability provides a more trustworthy basis for assessing EEG denoisers.

title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
summary: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the post-merge survival of AI-agent-attributed code across 88 survival specifications and shows that measurement choices can reverse the verdict for fully autonomous agents.
AI.motivation: Prior studies disagree on whether AI-generated code survives longer, shorter, or about as long as human code, and the sensitivity of these conclusions to measurement choices was unknown.
AI.method: Using 854,139 lines from 2,802 merged PRs across 215 repositories in AIDev, the authors vary nine measurement choices across 88 survival analyses, three variance estimators, multiple observation windows, permuted labels, and intent classifiers.
AI.result: For supervised agents (mostly GitHub Copilot), choices affect effect size but not direction; for Devin, 15 of 22 cross-repo specifications find faster modification under independent lines, dropping to 3 when clustered by repository (no more than permuted labels), and LLM intent classifiers match human agreement (kappa = 0.69-0.72 vs. 0.38 for keyword rules).
AI.conclusion: Post-merge code survival verdicts depend heavily on measurement design, motivating the operationalization checklist provided by the authors.

title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
summary: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks coding agents on writing and transpiling unit tests, finding high coverage driven by test volume alongside sharp quality degradation on larger projects and unreliable translation.
AI.motivation: Trust in coding agents often relies on passing agent-written tests, yet the reliability of agent-generated and transpiled unit tests across project scales is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three popular coding agents, each paired with a native frontier model at high reasoning effort, across unit test generation and cross-language test translation metrics.
AI.result: Coding agents exceed human-written suites on traditional coverage metrics mainly by writing more tests, but test quality degrades sharply with project size and agentic test translation remains inconsistent and unreliable despite strong aggregate numbers.
AI.conclusion: High coverage from coding agents does not guarantee reliable test suites or accurate test translation, especially in larger codebases.

title: Evaluating the Evaluation of Music Generation Models with Generative Psychometrics
comment: Accepted to the 2nd Latin American Music Information Retrieval (LAMIR) workshop
summary: Subjective user studies are one of the major methods for evaluating music generation models. However, subjective evaluation protocols vary widely and are rarely specified in enough detail to be reproduced, hindering comparison across studies. In this paper, we map subjective evaluation methods in ISMIR music generation papers from 2020-2025 and apply generative psychometrics to assess the stability of their items. We extract 284 items from the papers' methodological descriptions, using an LLM and manual validation to standardize them. We represent these items as contextual embeddings and apply Unique Variable Analysis to remove redundant, locally dependent items and Bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis to estimate their latent dimensions. Results show the network converges onto a taxonomy of six stable quality dimensions: Rhythm, Melody, Audio, Composition, Structure, and Lyrics, pointing to a unified methodology for conducting user studies to evaluate music generation models.

AI.tldr: This paper applies generative psychometrics to 284 subjective evaluation items from 2020-2025 ISMIR music generation papers, deriving a stable six-dimension taxonomy for user studies.
AI.motivation: Subjective user studies for music generation vary widely and lack reproducible specifications, hindering cross-study comparison.
AI.method: The authors extract and standardize 284 evaluation items from ISMIR papers (2020-2025) using an LLM with manual validation, represent them as contextual embeddings, and apply Unique Variable Analysis and Bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis.
AI.result: The network converges onto six stable latent quality dimensions: Rhythm, Melody, Audio, Composition, Structure, and Lyrics.
AI.conclusion: This six-dimension taxonomy provides a unified psychometric foundation for designing reproducible subjective evaluations of music generation models.

title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
comment: 22 pages. Conceptual framework for continuous compliance monitoring, behavioral drift detection, and operational authorization of autonomous robotic systems. Extends ARC-1 (arXiv:2609.12932)
summary: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment. This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification. Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. Third, a graduated safe transition protocol separates withdrawal of operational authorization from physical shutdown, consistent with established safety standards and EU AI Act requirements. Fourth, environmental delta is introduced as a distinct baseline validity condition: environmental drift beyond the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD) triggers recertification or ODD revision rather than automatic authority contraction. Together, these extensions transform ARC from a deployment-time certification architecture into a continuous framework for monitoring, evaluating, and enforcing compliance throughout the operational lifecycle of autonomous systems. The framework addresses the continuous compliance obligations established by EU AI Act Article 72(2).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Delta Management (ARC-2), a continuous post-deployment compliance framework that monitors operational and environmental deviations against a certified baseline region.
AI.motivation: ARC-1 established deployment-time governance for autonomous systems, but did not address how to maintain continuous compliance after deployment as required by EU AI Act Article 72(2).
AI.method: ARC-2 defines the certified baseline as a region rather than a point and adds four extensions: worst-case CRAB deviation tracking with outlier quarantine, a layered trigger taxonomy, a graduated safe transition protocol separating authorization withdrawal from shutdown, and environmental delta tracking against the Operational Design Domain.
AI.result: The framework operationalizes continuous monitoring, proportionate response triggering, and recertification workflows throughout an autonomous system's lifecycle.
AI.conclusion: Delta Management extends ARC from static deployment certification to continuous post-deployment compliance aligned with EU AI Act Article 72(2).

title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
summary: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

AI.tldr: This paper presents EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment, and EmbedGym-Bench (598 tasks), showing that interactive hardware testing substantially improves coding-agent firmware pass rates.
AI.motivation: Compiled embedded firmware often fails on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that text-terminal coding agents cannot observe without physical hardware.
AI.method: EmbedGym pairs instruction-level MCU emulators with 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/BLE endpoints, and evaluates eight models across >14K trajectories on EmbedGym-Bench synthesized via a five-stage multi-agent workflow.
AI.result: Despite a 99.7% compilation rate, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets); interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym raises pass rates by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31%), outperforms prior frameworks, and lets lightweight models match frontier models at 30-70x lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop interactive virtual hardware execution bridges the gap between compilation and runtime correctness for embedded coding agents.

title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
summary: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents AR-WAM, a causal streaming world-action model for autonomous driving that uses single-pass future conditioning and reinforcement learning to achieve state-of-the-art NAVSIM-v1 performance.
AI.motivation: Video foundation models help anticipate traffic, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them too costly for real-time autonomous driving.
AI.method: AR-WAM uses a causal video backbone to update visual context incrementally, computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, and refines the policy with reinforcement learning on driving rewards.
AI.result: Using a single front camera on NAVSIM-v1, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 PDMS after reinforcement learning, outperforming strong end-to-end world-action baselines in both standard and continuous driving settings.
AI.conclusion: Causal incremental encoding with single-pass future conditioning enables fast, high-performing streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving.

title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
summary: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

AI.tldr: This large-scale agentic capture-the-flag study audits 363 OpenRouter LLMs and finds that 296 leak a secret 16-character flag stored in their system prompt.
AI.motivation: Instruction-hierarchy enforcement is critical for keeping system-prompt instructions above user requests, yet its prevalence across deployed models is not systematically known.
AI.method: An AI agent (OpenCode powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) steered by a human researcher attempts to persuade 363 text-in/text-out models (plus four newer models) to emit a 16-character flag embedded in the system prompt.
AI.result: The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of 363 catalog models (300 total captures), with 170 captures using a non-English language pivot, most often French.
AI.conclusion: System prompts cannot safely hold secrets, and practitioners should enforce critical behavior outside the model using deterministic checks and output validation rather than relying solely on LLM judges.

title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables (8-page main text with appendices). Code: this https URL
summary: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PathoDraw, a contrast-agnostic generative model for brain MRI with synthetic pathology that enables zero-shot anomaly detection across diverse clinical scans without training on real pathology.
AI.motivation: Clinical brain MRI archives contain diverse pathologies across varied contrasts and resolutions, but existing pathology detectors still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators.
AI.method: PathoDraw samples lesions conditioned on healthy anatomy before contrast-agnostic rendering, and trains a single contrast-agnostic 3D UNet to estimate healthy anatomy and signed intensity deviation directly.
AI.result: Tested zero-shot on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets plus archived clinical data across T1w, FLAIR, and T2w scans, PathoDraw matches or exceeds contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans while preserving healthy anatomy, and also trains super-resolution and pathology-aware registration networks.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic pathology randomization enables a single contrast-agnostic model to unlock uncurated clinical MRI archives for zero-shot detection and downstream tasks.

title: FM-Mamba: An Efficient Native 2D Selective State Space Model with Stability-Aware Discretization
summary: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $\Delta_1(i,j)$, $\Delta_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FM-Mamba, a native 2D selective state space model based on the Fornasini-Marchesini model with stability-aware discretization and a dual-diagonal wavefront scan.
AI.motivation: Applying 1D Mamba to 2D features via flattening breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies compute, while existing 2D recurrences use fixed rescaling, single anti-diagonal aggregation, and lack 2D stability constraints.
AI.method: FM-Mamba uses coupled 2D recurrence with a diagonal-predecessor term and two input-dependent step sizes projected onto a closed-form stability bound, executed via a dual-diagonal wavefront scan without flattening.
AI.result: The proposed formulation enforces per-position 2D stability without global damping and avoids feature-map flattening during both training and inference.
AI.conclusion: Grounding 2D selective state space models in Fornasini-Marchesini stability theory provides a principled, native 2D alternative to flattened multi-scan Mamba architectures.

title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
summary: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that directly regresses rooftop photovoltaic capacity from aerial imagery without coupling predictions to mask-derived area-density products.
AI.motivation: Conventional image-based PV capacity estimators segment arrays, convert masks to area, and multiply by power density, tightly coupling capacity estimates to mask area errors.
AI.method: Direct Head retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors, evaluated across three runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under original and department-holdout splits.
AI.result: Compared to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces MAE by 8.7% and 12.5% and sMAPE by 14.0% and 20.7% on the original and holdout splits, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Using segmentation as spatial guidance rather than a hard area-density bottleneck substantially improves rooftop PV capacity estimation.

title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HyCoInfer, a cloud-edge collaborative LLM serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLM decoding is memory-bound and underutilizes cloud GPU arithmetic units, while edge FPGAs offer decoding efficiency but cannot sustain high-concurrency workloads alone.
AI.method: HyCoInfer integrates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode partitioning, schedules requests by queue load, prompt length, and network state, and combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and residual-vector-quantization KV cache compression.
AI.result: Evaluated on two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 over 100-1000 Mbps links, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11x the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1% at 500 Mbps while lowering per-request energy.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs with bandwidth-adaptive KV compression substantially increases LLM serving capacity and energy efficiency.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
summary: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an analog RF semantic communication framework where edge devices compute semantic encoder latents in their RF front-end mixers and allocate energy via semantic-aware water-filling.
AI.motivation: Computing semantic encoders on resource-constrained edge devices incurs high energy and memory costs.
AI.method: A base station broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, edge devices reuse passive mixers to compute latents, and the authors derive a second-order task-posterior semantic distortion decomposition to optimize energy allocation, broadcast beamforming, and multi-task noise-aware training.
AI.result: In MNIST simulations at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2%-19.2% over uniform precision and 5.1%-13.1% over client-blind allocation, with noise-aware co-design yielding a further 46% reduction.
AI.conclusion: Executing semantic encoding in analog RF hardware paired with semantic-aware energy allocation enables ultra-low-energy edge semantic communication.

title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
summary: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RoboTeam, a real-time vision-only benchmark for controlling 4 to 16 robot arms on long collaborative tasks, revealing high token/time costs and reliability gaps in current multimodal agents.
AI.motivation: Existing robot benchmarks typically test one or two arms on short tasks, pause the world during agent thinking, and provide ground-truth object positions.
AI.method: RoboTeam evaluates adaptive, single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized multi-agent systems across 36 long collaborative tasks using only camera images in a non-pausing simulated world.
AI.result: With the adaptive system, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 of 36 tasks (four other models at most 3), but gpt-6.1-sol averages 3.5 hours and 218M input tokens per task with one-third of steps failing and requiring retries; fixed architectures trade off speed versus tokens without solving reliability.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal agents cannot yet achieve fast, cheap, and reliable real-time multi-arm control from vision alone.

title: EgoHandWAM: Probing the Role of Hand Motion in Egocentric World Action Modeling
summary: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EgoHandWAM to probe how much hand motion predicts future first-person visual features and evaluates whether human demonstrations aid robot manipulation.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how strongly 3D hand motion informs what an egocentric camera will see next, or whether aligned human examples consistently improve simulated robot policy learning.
AI.method: Trained on 751,065 EgoDex windows with a frozen DINOv2 encoder, EgoHandWAM forecasts 3D wrist/fingertip trajectories and future visual features from current images and hand states, tested via trajectory probes and two RoboTwin tasks.
AI.result: The action-only model reduces 2-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48 mm; recorded hand history reduces visual smooth L1 error by 1.32% (erased by shuffling), and adding recorded future displacements with tracking-validity masks cuts visual error by 3.93%, whereas substituting aligned human examples on RoboTwin yields no consistent task-success gain across three seeds.
AI.conclusion: Recorded hand motion provides measurable but modest predictive signal for future egocentric visual features, and human-to-robot data substitution does not consistently improve simulated manipulation success.

title: CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
summary: A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CueClash to test whether frontier vision-language models judge 3-D relations from 2-D picture cues or 3-D ground layout, finding a +18 to +37 percentage point shortcut gap on Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash.
AI.motivation: In natural photographs, 2-D picture cues and 3-D ground layout usually agree, making it hard to tell which one vision-language models rely on when judging 3-D spatial relations.
AI.method: The authors construct CueClash, rendered scenes where the 2-D cue for five 3-D relations is correct on exactly half of the statements, and evaluate models with and without ground coordinates, pixel measurements with camera depths, and top-down map drawing.
