AI.result: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash (at low reasoning effort) exhibit a +18 to +37 percentage point shortcut gap (+7 to +29 excluding confounded items), but achieve 99% to 100% accuracy given ground coordinates and relation definitions; they also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs with misleading 2-D cues.
AI.conclusion: The failure lies in mapping from the picture to the 3-D layout, as models' top-down maps shorten depth and retain picture-plane biases.

title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
summary: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a solver-free online scheduling rule inspired by dual decomposition for AI data center tasks, achieving lower energy cost and much less computation time than a multi-timescale optimization benchmark.
AI.motivation: AI data centers receive tasks continuously while electricity is priced per settlement period, creating a timing gap that slow solver-based optimization cannot bridge in real time.
AI.method: The proposed solver-free online rule assigns each arriving task a start period to optimize energy cost under operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks to low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule.
AI.result: Simulations on an A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show the rule keeps GPU and CPU usage within capacity while achieving lower cost and much lower computation time than a multi-timescale optimization benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Dual-decomposition-inspired online scheduling offers a practical, low-overhead alternative to solver-based methods for cost-aware AI data center management.

title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
summary: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that philosophical efforts to formulate uniform decision rules for physician-AI disagreement are fatally flawed because they abstract away context-specific empirical medical factors.
AI.motivation: Philosophers have attempted to create general epistemological rules for resolving cases where physicians' judgments diverge from medical AI recommendations.
AI.method: The author analyzes the physician-AI disagreement debate through the distinction between useful "anticipation" (exploring plausible futures under irreducible uncertainty to inform present action) and wasteful "speculation" (developing formal solutions to stipulated scenarios disconnected from the present).
AI.result: The analysis classifies crisp philosophical decision rules for physician-AI disagreement as speculation because algorithmic performance and appropriate use depend on determinative empirical and clinical contexts.
AI.conclusion: Technology ethics should ground futures thinking in the messy, uncertain present rather than stipulating abstract, context-free formal rules.

title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
summary: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Popcornn, a framework that finds chemical transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths on machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), recovering more correct transition states than nudged elastic band and growing string methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional double-ended transition state search methods rely on discretized path representations designed for expensive density functional theory, failing to exploit the low cost and automatic differentiation of MLIPs.
AI.method: Popcornn optimizes continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP using a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator and second-order potential-energy-surface information to eliminate discretization artifacts and overcome local features.
AI.result: Across thousands of organic reactions and multiple MLIPs, Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, with reduced hyperparameter sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Popcornn provides a robust, automation-ready, and flexible platform for high-throughput transition state search on MLIPs.

title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
comment: 83 pages. Project page: this https URL. GitHub: this https URL
summary: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys agentic intelligence for the physical world, examining how coding agents write, test, and learn from programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers where the physical world acts as the test suite.
AI.motivation: Unlike software engineering, physical-world programs lack built-in test suites and must be validated through costly, potentially noisy execution on robots, simulators, or policy training.
AI.method: The authors organize the field around three questions—how agents write physical-world programs (policies, rewards, tasks, training worlds), how those programs are tested (physical trials, traces, learned judges, simulators, formal checks, safety), and how agents learn from results (skill libraries, model weights)—and review benchmarks and open challenges.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes how language models for robots and software engineering agents converge, maps each program by its relation to the actuator and its judge, and identifies verification cost and reliability as the primary bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Advancing physical-world agentic intelligence requires a physical counterpart to continuous integration: verification that is cheap, trustworthy under search, and maintained alongside learned experience.

title: FIRE-Drive: Feasibility-Informed Risk Evaluation for End-to-End Diffusion Planning
summary: Diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving models have shown strong potential in generating multimodal planning trajectories. However, their performance still depends heavily on trajectory initialization, mode evaluation, and supervision quality. Weakly constrained noisy initialization may introduce infeasible proposals and increase the burden of denoising. Moreover, selecting the optimal mode remains challenging when candidate trajectories are geometrically similar but differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end autonomous driving. FIRE-Drive improves diffusion-based planning through dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. This design aligns the initial support, risk-aware scoring, and multimodal supervision of trajectory modes under a unified planning objective. It enables the diffusion decoder to focus on refining plausible trajectories while the scorer distinguishes modes using local risk evidence. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 show that FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone. Additional closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes yields a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. Component ablations and a scorer comparison under matched candidate inputs support the contributions of feasible initialization, auxiliary supervision, and risk-informed selection. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end diffusion planning in autonomous driving, achieving 91.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 71.43 Driving Score on Bench2Drive.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based autonomous driving planners suffer from infeasible noisy initializations and difficulty distinguishing geometrically similar candidate trajectories that differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress.
AI.method: FIRE-Drive combines dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement under a unified planning objective.
AI.result: On NAVSIM v1, FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone; on 220 closed-loop Bench2Drive routes, it reaches a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%, with ablations confirming each component's contribution.
AI.conclusion: Aligning feasible initialization, local risk scoring, and multimodal supervision enables diffusion decoders to refine plausible trajectories more effectively.

title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
comment: 3 pages, submitted to ICSE2027 AMPLIFY Workshop this https URL
summary: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

AI.tldr: This position paper proposes analyzing observable autonomous software agent trajectories alongside specifications and generated artifacts as evidence for targeted software quality assurance (QA).
AI.motivation: Autonomous software agents make decisions with limited human oversight that can introduce implicit assumptions not exposed by final code or passing tests.
AI.method: The authors advocate combining execution trajectories with software/agent specifications and AI-generated artifacts to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, diagnose software problems, and improve specifications and development practices.
AI.result: Drawing on industrial experience and existing execution records, the paper outlines how trajectory analysis can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, while noting that trajectories alone cannot prove decisions are justified or outcomes acceptable.
AI.conclusion: Developing and evaluating trajectory-based QA requires interdisciplinary input from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors.

title: An AI-Driven Assistant for Human-Centric Building Digital Twin Systems: Design, Implementation, and Comparative User Evaluation
comment: 43 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to Developments in the Built Environment
summary: Smart buildings generate streams of operational data, yet this richness rarely translates into accessible, decision-ready information for stakeholders who inhabit and manage them. Current Building Digital Twin Systems (BDTS) often remain oriented toward technical specialists and rely on static, one-size-fits-all interfaces. This paper presents the design, implementation, and comparative user evaluation of an AI-driven conversational assistant integrated into a human-centric BDTS for Indoor Environmental Quality monitoring, combined with adaptive information presentation and auto-suggest functionality. The prototype was deployed at New York University Abu Dhabi. A controlled, two-arm, between-subjects, quasi-experimental study with wave-based, non-randomized assignment compared the Baseline interface with the Experimental interface. Results showed significant reductions in task-completion time and perceived workload, while accuracy and usability improved but did not meet the adjusted significance criterion. The study contributes an implemented and empirically evaluated architecture that separates generative interaction from deterministic environmental assessment and coordinates conversational responses with adaptive visual presentation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an AI-driven conversational assistant integrated into a human-centric Building Digital Twin System (BDTS) for Indoor Environmental Quality monitoring, significantly reducing task-completion time and perceived workload in a controlled user study.
AI.motivation: Current BDTS platforms target technical specialists with static, one-size-fits-all interfaces, failing to turn smart-building data streams into accessible, decision-ready information for occupants and managers.
AI.method: Deployed at New York University Abu Dhabi, the system separates generative conversational interaction from deterministic environmental assessment and pairs responses with adaptive visual presentation and auto-suggest functionality.
AI.result: In a controlled, two-arm, between-subjects, quasi-experimental study, the Experimental interface significantly reduced task-completion time and perceived workload compared to the Baseline interface, while accuracy and usability improved without meeting the adjusted significance criterion.
AI.conclusion: Separating generative dialogue from deterministic assessment and coordinating it with adaptive visual presentation makes building digital twins more accessible and efficient for human stakeholders.

title: FailureGen: Scalable Robot Failure Data Generation with World Models
summary: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FailureGen, a four-stage world-model pipeline that generates synthetic robot failure videos with temporal event annotations by transferring recorded failure motions into successful host contexts.
AI.motivation: Collecting robot failure data at scale is difficult, which limits the diversity of failure scenarios available in robot learning datasets.
AI.method: FailureGen fine-tunes an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed executions, identifies failure donor segments and compatible successful hosts, transfers donor motion into host contexts with optional spatial offsets, and filters rollouts by observed events and visual quality.
AI.result: Evaluated on two robot implementations, a visual failure detector trained on real plus generated data achieves 0.51 average precision (vs. 0.41 on real data alone) and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals (vs. 28 of 36).
AI.conclusion: Reusing observed failure trajectories in new contexts via world models provides a scalable way to expand robot failure datasets for downstream learning.

title: Every Camera Grows Up: Camera-Height Regression in Interactive Video World Models
summary: Interactive video world models serve as simulators for embodied agents: from a starting image and an action trajectory, they generate the views the agent would see. The starting image fixes how high the camera is, for example 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m for an overhead camera, and a faithful simulator must keep this height as the camera moves. We show that six recent open-weight models fail to do so: as motion replaces the starting view with generated content, they move the camera toward human eye level, a failure we call camera-height regression. Our benchmark, EyeHeight, pairs six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation. All six models lose their initial height during a $180^\circ$ turn-and-walk rollout: initialized at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips end within $1.3\times$ of the starting height as inferred viewpoints converge to human heights of 1.1 m to 1.5 m, whereas ground-truth renders remain within a few percent. In Matrix-Game models, homography-tracked floor motion stays consistent with constant elevation during rotation even as newly outpainted room geometry yields a higher reconstructed viewpoint. Regression grows with rotation angle, begins while the start frame remains in context, and largely reverses in SANA-WM when a $360^\circ$ turn restores the initial view. We trace this pull to human-centric video priors in which floor-level views are nearly absent: in SANA-WM, textual height cues and dense floor-disparity maps do not prevent it, whereas classifier-free text guidance during the first half of denoising strengthens it. Combining unguided sampling with height-balanced fine-tuning recovers more retention but costs 5 MUSIQ points, a loss fixed during those same early steps. Viewpoint drift alone shifts the paths predicted by visual navigation policies.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers camera-height regression in interactive video world models, showing that six open-weight models drift from initial camera heights toward human eye level (1.1 m to 1.5 m) during 180-degree turn-and-walk rollouts.
AI.motivation: Embodied agent simulators must maintain the camera height fixed by the starting image (e.g., 0.15 m for a floor robot or 2.2 m overhead) as the agent moves, but whether video world models preserve this height is unknown.
AI.method: The authors build EyeHeight, pairing six rendered elevations (0.15 m to 2.2 m) and four calibrated real-world rig heights with scale-free multi-view height estimation, and test six open-weight models under 180-degree and 360-degree turns, homography tracking, and height-balanced fine-tuning.
AI.result: Starting at 0.15 m, only 0-20% of clips from the six models end within 1.3x of the initial height, converging to 1.1-1.5 m; unguided sampling plus height-balanced fine-tuning improves retention in SANA-WM but costs 5 MUSIQ points, and viewpoint drift alters downstream visual navigation paths.
AI.conclusion: Human-centric video priors pull generated viewpoints toward eye level, degrading physical faithfulness and downstream navigation in interactive video world models.

title: Sketch, Don't Paint: Allocating Test-Time Compute in Generative Visual Reasoning
summary: Multimodal models increasingly reason by synthesizing pixels, sketching maze paths within interleaved chains of thought or rolling out video solutions frame by frame. Each visual thought runs the full diffusion schedule inherited from photorealistic synthesis, so iterative denoising dominates inference cost. We study how to allocate test-time compute along two axes: when to render visual thoughts rather than thinking in text or answering directly, and how many denoising steps each thought requires. Controlled interventions that vary only how the thought is rendered uncover three regimes. Causal thoughts carry the plan and become legible early: an 8-step sketch nearly matches a 50-step render in accuracy, commits to the same plan as often as two independent full renders agree, and in video models mostly fails by stalling short of the goal, so the rollout abstains. Decorative thoughts can be omitted without loss, whereas harmful thoughts lower accuracy. Because the regime depends on both model and task, always drawing is suboptimal. Across 14 model-benchmark pairs of three interleaved reasoners, answering directly, without any thinking, wins 9 pairs, and choosing among direct, text-only, and visual tiers from ten labeled examples per pair raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%. Where drawing pays, we propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches (a step count chosen without labels) from independent noises until one answer reaches three votes. With this one setting, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer denoising steps on an image reasoner and two video reasoners, by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and by 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies test-time compute allocation in generative visual reasoning, showing that an 8-step sketchNearly matches 50-step rendering and proposing sketch-and-vote to outperform full rendering with fewer denoising steps.
AI.motivation: Interleaved and video-based visual reasoners run full diffusion schedules for every visual thought, making iterative denoising dominate inference cost even when drawing is unnecessary or harmful.
AI.method: Through controlled rendering interventions, the authors identify three regimes (causal, decorative, harmful), evaluate adaptive selection among direct, text-only, and visual tiers using 10 labeled examples per pair, and propose sketch-and-vote, which samples 8-step sketches until one answer reaches three votes.
AI.result: Across 14 model-benchmark pairs, direct answering wins 9 pairs and adaptive tier selection raises mean accuracy from 60.7% (always drawing) to 65.1%; where drawing helps, sketch-and-vote beats full rendering with fewer steps by 8.6 points on VSP spatial planning and 9.6 and 22.1 points on mazes.
AI.conclusion: Allocating test-time compute between non-visual reasoning and fast low-step sketches yields higher accuracy at lower denoising cost than always rendering full-quality visual thoughts.

title: Rethinking Perceptual Similarity for Remote Sensing: Multi-Layer Attention Scoring and Human Preference Benchmarking
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027). 9 pages
summary: Perceptual similarity metrics for natural images transfer poorly to remote sensing (RS), where severe geospatial and semantic failures can remain visually plausible while still being decisively wrong for downstream use. To address this, we develop a novel human-aligned perceptual quality metric for generated RS imagery and evaluate it across several generation tasks. We first conduct a controlled perturbation study where we progressively increase the severity of common synthetic perturbations. Using the layer-wise Aligned Attention Score (AAS) responses in RemoteCLIP, we find that different RS artifacts are best captured at different depths. Based on these findings, we introduce Remote Sensing Perceptual Distance (RSPD), a pairwise metric that averages seven independently calibrated layer distances without tuning on human-preference labels. To evaluate our metric on realistic RS generation tasks, we construct a blind, reference-conditioned two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) benchmark with five 300-triplet subsets spanning synthetic artifacts, airborne and spaceborne super-resolution, SAR-to-optical translation, and timeseries controls. We also construct a 300-triplet ordered misregistration benchmark with deterministic labels. Using the same RemoteCLIP checkpoint, RSPD substantially outperforms simple cosine distance with the final global embedding and is competitive with the strongest generic baselines across the realistic RS generation tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Remote Sensing Perceptual Distance (RSPD), a training-free metric using seven RemoteCLIP layers that outperforms global-embedding cosine distance on a new 2AFC remote sensing benchmark.
AI.motivation: Natural-image perceptual similarity metrics transfer poorly to remote sensing, where severe geospatial and semantic errors can look visually plausible.
AI.method: Using layer-wise Aligned Attention Score responses in RemoteCLIP under controlled synthetic perturbations, the authors design RSPD by averaging seven independently calibrated layer distances without human-preference tuning, and evaluate it on a new blind 2AFC benchmark (five 300-triplet subsets) plus a 300-triplet misregistration benchmark.
AI.result: Using the same RemoteCLIP checkpoint, RSPD substantially outperforms cosine distance on the final global embedding and is competitive with the strongest generic baselines across synthetic artifacts, super-resolution, SAR-to-optical translation, and timeseries tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer attention-based distances in domain-pretrained encoders capture remote sensing perceptual quality without requiring human-preference supervision.

title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection
summary: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using prediction residuals from a frozen-encoder, LoRA-adapted V-JEPA 2.1 world model with a Latent Consistency Head (LCH) for cross-dataset deepfake detection, achieving 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 when trained only on FF++.
AI.motivation: Existing deepfake detectors rely on generator-specific artifacts and suffer severe performance drops when evaluated on unseen datasets.
AI.method: The authors keep the V-JEPA 2.1 encoder frozen, adapt the predictor with rank-16 LoRA (8.25M trainable parameters, 2.47% of 334M), and feed the prediction residuals into a lightweight LCH that separates residual magnitude from direction under a consistency-margin prior.
AI.result: Trained solely on FF++, the model reaches 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across other cross-dataset benchmarks, while reversing the margin objective widens the cross-dataset generalization gap.
AI.conclusion: Natural-video prediction residuals provide a generalizable consistency-margin signal for cross-dataset deepfake detection.

title: Temporal Pseudo-RGB Encoding for Label-Free Detection of VEEV Infection in Human Brain Endothelial Cells
comment: 20 pages. Supplementary material is included as an ancillary file
summary: Label-free detection of viral infection is central to antiviral screening and pathogen surveillance. Most deep-learning methods analyze individual frames and do not model temporal progression. We evaluate temporal pseudo-RGB encoding, which stacks three time-offset brightfield frames ($t{-}6$ h, $t{-}3$ h, $t$) as the red, green, and blue channels of a single image so that morphological change becomes color and an ImageNet-pretrained convolutional neural network (CNN) can be trained on infection trajectories without architectural modification. In human brain microvascular endothelial cells (HBMVEC) infected with Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) TC-83, a multi-task network predicts infected-versus-mock status and time post-infection in one forward pass. Across three experimental runs under leave-one-row-out cross-validation, with all 36 wells scored out of fold, the encoding reaches 91.6% accuracy against 87.4% for the single-frame model (paired difference $+4.2$ percentage points, 95% CI $[+2.5, +6.1]$; sign-flip $p = 3\times10^{-5}$; well-level inference, conditional on three runs). At the late-phase endpoint (40-48 h), where floating cells and debris can make conventional brightfield images difficult to interpret, the advantage widens to $+23.9$ points (95% CI $[+19.2, +28.9]$). Time post-infection is recovered on the fixed row split with MAE = 1.31 h ($R^2 = 0.975$). Among the temporal models tested the encoding has the highest mean accuracy, at a fraction of the cost of the recurrent and 3D convolutional alternatives, though only its margin over the single-frame model is resolved; the tested ViT-B/16 backbone showed no corresponding gain, so the finding is limited to convolutional backbones and this virus-cell system.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates temporal pseudo-RGB encoding—stacking three time-offset brightfield frames as RGB channels—for label-free VEEV infection detection in human brain endothelial cells, reaching 91.6% accuracy vs. 87.4% for single-frame CNNs.
AI.motivation: Most deep-learning methods for label-free viral infection detection analyze individual frames and ignore temporal progression, struggling with late-phase debris and floating cells.
AI.method: Three time-offset brightfield frames (t-6 h, t-3 h, t) are stacked as R, G, and B channels so morphological changes become color, allowing an ImageNet-pretrained CNN to predict infection status and time post-infection in one forward pass.
AI.result: Under leave-one-row-out cross-validation across three runs (36 wells), temporal pseudo-RGB achieves 91.6% accuracy vs. 87.4% for single-frame (+4.2 percentage points, p = 3e-5), widening to +23.9 points at 40-48 h, and recovers time post-infection with MAE = 1.31 h (R^2 = 0.975); ViT-B/16 showed no corresponding gain.
AI.conclusion: Temporal pseudo-RGB encoding offers a simple, low-cost way for convolutional backbones to capture infection trajectories without recurrent or 3D architectures.

title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
summary: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes REEL, a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank framework for fMRI-to-video decoding that reranks pretrained video generator candidates using linear semantic decoding and three neural encoding streams, improving 50-way accuracy on CC2017 and BMD.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing videos from fMRI is difficult because rapid video stimuli mismatch slow BOLD dynamics, and existing pipelines are increasingly complex.
AI.method: REEL combines a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts (and learned pooling in two streams) to propose and rerank video candidates.
AI.result: Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking improves mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-and-rerank with linear decoding and encoder embeddings offers a conceptually simple, complementary direction for fMRI video reconstruction.

title: GridDriver: On-Board BEV-Based Language Planning and Reasoning
summary: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

AI.tldr: This paper presents GridDriver, an onboard BEV-conditioned LLM framework that combines trajectory prediction, driving indicators, navigation, explanations, and QA, achieving 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 32.7 ms standalone planning latency.
AI.motivation: Onboard deployment of BEV-conditioned LLMs for language-interactive driving requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation.
AI.method: GridDriver pairs lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens with a shared LLM, using frame-wise scheduling to interleave trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation.
AI.result: GridDriver achieves 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared checkpoint, outperforms Q-Former compression in geometric retention, and runs at 32.7 ms standalone planning latency (9.4 plans/s in ROS 2), with open-loop onboard vehicle validation.
AI.conclusion: Spatially structured BEV tokens and frame-wise scheduling enable real-time onboard planning alongside language reasoning.

title: SCAN: Site-Aware Collaborative Privacy-Preserving Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Neurological Disease Classification
summary: Worldwide neuroimaging data could strengthen diagnostic foundation models, but privacy rules often prevent centralizing brain MRI scans. We present SCAN, a site-aware collaborative adaptation framework for Neurological Disease Classification that lets new sites adapt a 3D medical vision-language model (VLM) without retraining or sharing patient scans. Each site keeps exact class prototypes for local prediction and can share privacy-protected class summaries: norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise. Using 7,641 scans from 67 sites across 12 countries, covering Alzheimer's disease (AD), stroke, epilepsy and controls, we assess local adaptation, cross-site benefits, and effects on existing sites. At seven unseen sites, the frozen VLM's zero-shot AUCs were 0.833-0.945 for AD and stroke. Training-free local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863, nearly matching a classifier trained at each site (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759). With differential privacy ($\epsilon$ = 4), new sites contributed without materially reducing accuracy at existing sites (AUC change $\leq$0.2%), although gains from sharing were limited, and membership attacks performed near chance. SCAN offers hospitals a worldwide framework to adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging scans or retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SCAN, a training-free, privacy-preserving framework for adapting 3D medical vision-language models across 67 neuroimaging sites without sharing patient scans, nearly matching per-site trained classifiers.
AI.motivation: Privacy regulations prevent centralizing worldwide brain MRI scans, limiting the adaptation of diagnostic foundation models to local clinical sites.
AI.method: Each site maintains exact local class prototypes for prediction and optionally shares differentially private class summaries (norm-bounded sums and counts perturbed once with calibrated noise) without retraining the 3D VLM.
AI.result: Across 7,641 scans from 67 sites (AD, stroke, epilepsy, controls), local prototypes improved epilepsy AUC at three unseen sites from 0.598/0.625/0.508 to 0.684/0.729/0.762 and AD AUC at one site from 0.833 to 0.863 (mean AUC 0.757 vs. 0.759 for per-site trained classifiers); with epsilon = 4 DP, existing-site AUC changed by at most 0.2% and membership attacks performed near chance.
AI.conclusion: SCAN enables hospitals to collaboratively adapt and share brain MRI VLMs without exchanging raw scans or retraining models.

title: How Many Persistent Features Does a Biometric Need? A Law Linking Equal Error Rate to Feature Count and Persistence
summary: A biometric designer controls the number of features and their temporal persistence. Earlier empirical work linked the equal error rate (EER) to persistence and to the required number of features by straight lines. We derive the law behind these regularities. For $N$ independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation $\rho$, scored by cosine similarity, Fisher's $z$-transform turns the genuine and impostor scores into two normals, giving $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{atanh}\rho)$ and, inversely, $N=(2q/\operatorname{atanh}\rho)^2$ with $q=\Phi^{-1}(1-\mathrm{EER})$; intercorrelated features enter through an effective count $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The central extension lets persistence vary across comparisons with spread $\tau$ on Fisher's scale: $\mathrm{EER}=\Phi(-m/(\sqrt{\tau^2+v}+\sqrt{v}))$ with $v=1/(N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2)$, which for a normal spread has a floor $\Phi(-m/\tau)$ that no number of features can lower. With no fitted parameter the simple law reproduces published simulations and the EER-ICC line, and predicts the KCC-EER relation of eye-movement embeddings on GazeBase ($R^2=0.88$), though less well on GazeBaseVR ($0.63$). Read from the genuine and impostor scores, the general form matches the EER of eye movements, keystroke dynamics, the ECG and face embeddings over 101 conditions with $R^2=0.98$ and a median error of $0.6$ points, against $0.87$ and $1.9$ points for the simple law. The 61 eye-movement, keystroke and ECG conditions check consistency on the same scores; the 40 face conditions use held-out subjects, with the same accuracy. The product $\tau\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2}$ gives a design rule: adding or decorrelating features pays fully while it is well below one and little once it exceeds about three, where only higher or more uniform persistence helps.

AI.tldr: This paper derives analytical laws linking biometric equal error rate (EER) to feature count N and temporal persistence rho, matching empirical EER across 101 conditions of eye-movement, keystroke, ECG, and face embeddings with R^2 = 0.98.
AI.motivation: Earlier biometric studies observed empirical linear relationships between EER, feature count, and temporal persistence, but lacked a unified theoretical derivation.
AI.method: Modeling N independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation rho scored by cosine similarity, the authors apply Fisher's z-transform to derive EER = Phi(-0.5 * sqrt(N) * atanh(rho)) and extend it to handle intercorrelated features (effective count N_eff) and varying persistence spread tau.
AI.result: Without fitted parameters, the simple law predicts GazeBase eye-movement EER-KCC (R^2 = 0.88) and GazeBaseVR (R^2 = 0.63); the general form matches EER across 101 conditions (eye movements, keystroke, ECG, face embeddings) with R^2 = 0.98 and 0.6-point median error, revealing an irreducible floor Phi(-m/tau).
AI.conclusion: The product tau * sqrt(N_eff - 2) provides a concrete design rule showing when adding or decorrelating features helps versus when only higher or more uniform persistence can lower EER.

title: Beyond Appearance: Where Forest Visual Place Recognition Actually Fails
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, accepted to the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA)
summary: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context against an appearance-only baseline (MegaLoc) for forest visual place recognition on WildCross, finding that only score-space sequence matching consistently helps.
AI.motivation: Repetitive vegetation, illumination, season, and viewpoint changes make forest visual place recognition difficult, and it is unclear which contextual representations actually improve over appearance-only descriptors.
AI.method: Using MegaLoc on the WildCross benchmark, the authors compare score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction, extended, and reverse traversals.
AI.result: On same-direction revisits, score-space sequence matching raises recall at 100% precision from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% (94.1% Recall@1), whereas descriptor-space matching drops it to 36.5%; captions, reranking, scene graphs, and LiDAR stem graphs yield no consistent improvement.
AI.conclusion: Current linguistic, structural, and geometric context representations are limited by weak place-specific discrimination and candidate shortlists, leaving score-space sequence matching as the most reliable enhancement in forests.

title: BATMoS: Budget-Aware Guidance Allocation for Efficient Video Diffusion
summary: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes BATMoS, a training-free temporal guidance allocation policy for video diffusion that routes between fresh and cached classifier-free guidance, matching full guidance within 0.10 VBench points using 20% fewer branch evaluations.
AI.motivation: Denoiser evaluations dominate video diffusion inference cost, and equal-budget configurations span 4.80 VBench points, showing that where guidance computation is spent along the trajectory matters.
AI.method: BATMoS uses a magnitude-based temporal rule with a single integer budget parameter to assign cached guidance to low-magnitude blocks and fresh guidance to remaining blocks, requiring no router training or threshold search.
AI.result: Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B (4,720 videos per configuration across 16 VBench dimensions), BATMoS achieves the highest total score among eight equal-budget policies, stays within 0.10 points of full CFG with 20% fewer branch evaluations, and composes with feature reuse (80 to 62 evaluations, -0.11 points).
AI.conclusion: Temporal guidance allocation provides a simple, training-free mechanism to preserve video generation quality under tight inference budgets.

title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
summary: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a three-stage transfer learning pipeline (ImageNet-1K to water bodies to algal blooms) with SCSE-enhanced Swin Transformer U-Net and model-assisted annotation, reaching 0.919 mIoU on a 256-image test split.
AI.motivation: Automated segmentation of harmful algal blooms in freshwater imagery is hindered by scarce pixel-level annotations.
AI.method: The authors adapt a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body datasets (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, while using model-assisted annotation to expand the labeled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images.
AI.result: On a 41-image validation split, corpus expansion is the largest driver (+11 mIoU), water-body pretraining adds +1.1 mIoU on the expanded corpus, SCSE adds 0.3, and adding 476 images cuts non-water false-positive area from 22.6% to 4.9%; on a 256-image test split, checkpoint S2-A13 reaches 0.919 mIoU and 0.902 algae IoU, though a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap.
AI.conclusion: Data expansion and domain-staged pretraining substantially improve algal bloom segmentation and reduce false positives, though benchmark overlap must be accounted for when interpreting test scores.

title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
summary: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CueSplat, a post-training sparse deformation scheduling framework for 4D Gaussian splatting that achieves up to 6.74x and 8.15x speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX with at most 0.16 dB PSNR drop.
AI.motivation: Evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame in 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) is too compute-intensive for edge devices.
AI.method: Keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history, uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within an offline-calibrated budget based on reliability and rendering contribution, reuses indices across nearby frames, and triggers three full-deformation frames via drift signals to rebuild history.
AI.result: Across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat delivers up to 6.74x speedup on Jetson AGX Orin and 8.15x on Orin NX while limiting dataset-average PSNR loss to at most 0.16 dB.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting local temporal regularity with drift-controlled sparse routing enables real-time 4DGS rendering on edge hardware without retraining the backbone.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Skin-Tone Color Casts in Ultra-Lightweight Photo Retouching Networks
comment: Accepted to ACCV 2026. 32 pages including supplementary material
summary: Color casts are expected to come from the scene or camera, and a retouching model removes them. We report a case where the model leaves one: an ultra-lightweight retouching network renders human skin greener than the original because it under-restores the skin chroma that a degradation removes and, even on clean inputs, adds a small hue shift of its own. A common paired-data-free recipe, synthetic self-supervision (degrade high-quality images, learn to restore them), silently produces this cast while whole-frame PSNR/SSIM stay essentially unchanged. In a representative 6,825-parameter histogram-conditioned network, the cast appears in 52 of 70 portraits under a ground-truth-anchored, white-balance-free protocol. Both a histogram-conditioned and a CNN-conditioned network develop the cast under synthetic self-supervision, yet both are near-neutral in-domain when trained on MIT-Adobe FiveK expert pairs. Image-level objectives miss it: a global-mean green loss worsens the cast (52/70 to 57/70). With zero added parameters, our per-pixel, skin-masked, asymmetric green-excess loss reduces the cast to 1/70 across stratified skin tones (68.1% to 2.2% over the 70,000-image FFHQ corpus; 64.4% to 0.8% on held-out CelebA-HQ photos). In-domain FiveK PSNR/SSIM are unchanged (+0.13 dB, +0.004), at the cost of a small whole-frame CIEDE2000 increase (8.77 to 9.69) and a magenta over-correction where skin is nearly neutral (skin Delta a* -1.5 to +4.4 and CIEDE2000 5.6 to 6.4 on clean inputs): the loss targets the signed green-magenta axis, not total skin-color fidelity. The same loss suppresses the cast across three ultra-light architectures. A whole-frame green metric correlates with skin-region CIEDE2000 at the method level (Spearman rho = 0.89). The final network exports to a 35 KB TFLite model.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses a green skin-tone color cast caused by synthetic self-supervision in ultra-lightweight photo retouching networks and fixes it with a zero-parameter, skin-masked asymmetric green-excess loss.
AI.motivation: Ultra-lightweight retouching networks trained with synthetic self-supervision render human skin greener than the original, a failure missed by whole-frame PSNR/SSIM and worsened by global-mean green losses.
AI.method: The authors introduce a per-pixel, skin-masked, asymmetric green-excess loss with zero added parameters to penalize green casts specifically on skin regions.
AI.result: In a 6,825-parameter histogram-conditioned network, the cast drops from 52/70 portraits to 1/70 (68.1% to 2.2% on 70,000 FFHQ images; 64.4% to 0.8% on CelebA-HQ), while in-domain FiveK PSNR/SSIM remain unchanged (+0.13 dB, +0.004) at the cost of a small whole-frame CIEDE2000 increase (8.77 to 9.69) and slight magenta over-correction on neutral skin; the final model exports to 35 KB TFLite.
AI.conclusion: Skin-masked asymmetric color losses effectively eliminate synthetic self-supervision color casts across ultra-lightweight architectures without increasing model size.

title: RetiDual-Select: Reliability-Aware Specialist-Generalist Routing for Retinal OCT under Image-Quality Shift
comment: 4 figures, 4 tables, 42 references. Submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Main article only; the separate Supplementary Information is not included
summary: Adaptive fusion can repair a static ensemble's errors, but can also overturn correct decisions. RetiDual-Select combines retinal specialist RETFound with the image encoder of the medical vision-language model MedSigLIP, separating candidate fusion, routing safety and predictive review. Calibrated product-of-experts (PoE) fusion is the static reference, a small gate proposes an alternative for each image, a validation-frozen harm guard decides whether that candidate may replace the reference, and a separate score prioritizes review. Static PoE reached the highest or joint-highest clean accuracy on all three datasets. At a clean 2% accepted-error target the review policy accepted 94.3% of Kermany-4 images at 99.89% selective accuracy, and 92.4% of OCT-C8 at 98.65%. Both branches were correct on 95.0% and 91.8% of clean images; only 4.4% and 6.2% had exactly one correct branch. Across 15 prespecified synthetic conditions, adaptive gains were concentrated in severe contrast reduction, where this routing opportunity widened roughly ninefold; percentile rescaling largely removed the effect, linking it to compressed dynamic range. In post-hoc validation-only analyses, gain was higher when the gate followed the more reliable branch, and a frozen guard cut the worst-condition OCT-C8 loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points. Adaptive routing was useful when image quality created a reliability opportunity and the gate followed it; otherwise the system retained Static PoE or deferred for review. The findings are bounded by the synthetic perturbations evaluated and do not establish robustness to natural acquisition or scanner shift.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RetiDual-Select, a reliability-aware routing framework combining RETFound and MedSigLIP for retinal OCT classification, which cuts worst-condition OCT-C8 accuracy loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points under severe contrast reduction.
AI.motivation: Adaptive ensemble routing can fix static ensemble errors under image-quality shifts, but it can also overturn correct decisions when no reliability gap exists.
AI.method: RetiDual-Select uses calibrated product-of-experts (PoE) fusion as a static reference, a small gate to propose per-image alternatives, a validation-frozen harm guard to block risky replacements, and a separate score to prioritize predictive review.
AI.result: Static PoE achieves the highest or joint-highest clean accuracy on all three datasets, with 99.89% selective accuracy at 94.3% coverage on Kermany-4 and 98.65% at 92.4% on OCT-C8; across 15 synthetic perturbations, adaptive routing gains concentrate in severe contrast reduction, where the frozen guard cuts worst-condition OCT-C8 loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Separating candidate routing, harm-guarded acceptance, and review prioritization preserves clean-image accuracy while safely exploiting reliability gaps under severe contrast degradation.

title: Text-Guided Modality Correction for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) is essential for detecting objects beyond the categories seen during training. Establishing vision-language associations is crucial for recognizing unseen categories, while integrating complementary visual features across levels supports detection at different scales. However, existing methods often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment strategies, and underuse complementary features across levels, limiting their ability to detect unseen categories and objects of varying scales. To address these limitations, we propose a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network (TMCNet) that incorporates textual guidance into region feature extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding to strengthen region-category semantic correspondence and promote complementary feature fusion across levels. First, a text-guided modality encoder incorporates textual semantics into queries to guide regional feature aggregation, reducing semantic ambiguity in object representations. Second, a cross-modal alignment module strengthens the correspondence between region representations and category semantics through interactions between visual and textual features. Finally, a progressive text correction decoder combines a top-down pathway with lateral connections to progressively fuse text-guided deep semantic features with shallow visual features at the corresponding scales, preserving both semantic information and spatial detail for objects of different sizes. Experiments on two public datasets, COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD, demonstrate that TMCNet achieves strong performance in open-vocabulary object detection using simple text queries as guidance. Extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields performance gains, demonstrating its cross-task applicability and extensibility.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces TMCNet, a Text-Guided Modality Correction Network for open-vocabulary object detection that integrates textual guidance into region extraction, cross-modal alignment, and multi-scale decoding, improving performance on COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary object detectors often provide insufficient textual guidance for object regions, rely on limited cross-modal alignment, and underuse multi-scale complementary features.
AI.method: TMCNet combines a text-guided modality encoder (injecting text semantics into queries), a cross-modal alignment module for region-category correspondence, and a progressive text correction decoder that fuses text-guided deep features with shallow visual features via top-down and lateral connections.
AI.result: Experiments on COCO-OVD and LVIS-OVD show strong open-vocabulary detection performance using simple text queries, and extending TMCNet to open-vocabulary segmentation also yields gains.
AI.conclusion: Injecting textual guidance throughout region encoding, alignment, and multi-scale decoding strengthens semantic correspondence and spatial detail for unseen categories.

title: CEVA: Complementary Evidence Verification via Frame-Level Reorganization for Short-Video Fake News Detection
summary: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CEVA, a short-video fake news detection framework that reorganizes frames by evidential role before multimodal fusion, achieving state-of-the-art results on FakeSV and FakeTT.
AI.motivation: Existing short-video fake news detectors pool frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity, overlooking that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim while less dominant context frames challenge it.
AI.method: CEVA's Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames before applying cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization.
AI.result: On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among compared methods; under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors.
AI.conclusion: Organizing frames by evidential role prior to multimodal fusion is an effective and transferable strategy for short-video fake news detection.

title: Unsupervised Multi-modal Medical Image Registration via Invertible Translation
summary: In medical imaging, the alignment of multi-modal images plays a critical role in providing comprehensive information for image-guided therapies. Despite its importance, multi-modal image registration poses significant challenges due to the complex and often unknown spatial relationships between different image modalities. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised translation-based multi-modal registration method, termed Invertible Neural Network-based Registration (INNReg). INNReg consists of an image-to-image translation network that converts multi-modal images into mono-modal counterparts and a registration network that uses the translated mono-modal images to align the multi-modal images. Specifically, to ensure the preservation of geometric consistency after image translation, we introduce an Invertible Neural Network (INN) that leverages a dynamic depthwise convolution-based local attention mechanism. Additionally, we design a novel barrier loss function based on Normalized Mutual Information to impose constraints on the registration network, which enhances the registration accuracy. The superior performance of INNReg is demonstrated through experiments on two public multi-modal medical image datasets, including MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT pairs. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces INNReg, an unsupervised multi-modal medical image registration method using an Invertible Neural Network (INN) with local attention for geometry-preserving translation and an NMI-based barrier loss, outperforming baselines on MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT datasets.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal medical image registration is challenging due to complex, unknown spatial relationships across modalities, and translation-based methods risk distorting anatomical geometry.
AI.method: INNReg translates multi-modal images into mono-modal counterparts using an INN with dynamic depthwise convolution-based local attention to preserve geometric consistency, then aligns them with a registration network constrained by a Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) barrier loss.
AI.result: Experiments on public MRI T1/T2 and MRI/CT datasets demonstrate that INNReg achieves superior registration performance compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Invertible translation with local attention and NMI barrier constraints enables accurate, geometry-preserving unsupervised multi-modal medical image registration.

title: HandRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Hand Pose Estimation
comment: Technical report. 25 pages, 17 figures, 18 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework where coding agents refine an executable inference harness and selectively distill a video hand pose estimator, reducing MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC.
AI.motivation: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators suffer from border misses, occlusion errors, and jitter, which are typically addressed by separately tuning hand-written inference refinements and model fine-tuning.
AI.method: In each round, coding agents refine the inference harness and accept changes only if a composite of ten held-out metrics improves without regression; the accepted harness then guides selective distillation of the estimator on unlabeled frames for presence and temporal consistency alongside ground-truth pose supervision.
AI.result: Starting from ACE-Ego-Hand, five rounds of HandRSI cut MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D (16% below fine-tuned ACE-Ego-Hand) and 11% on ARCTIC, roughly halve jitter, and outperform nine published methods across all ten metrics on both benchmarks, yielding Lite, Medium, and Heavy models at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Tightly coupling agent-driven harness refinement with selective distillation creates a self-reinforcing loop for egocentric hand pose estimation.

title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
summary: In computational pathology, high-magnification whole-slide image analysis preserves tissue detail but requires encoding many patches, whereas lower magnification reduces computation by covering a higher field of view per patch while sacrificing detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation matches features that often encode detail unreachable by low-magnification input, sometimes requiring slide-level labels that limit scalability. To address those issues, we introduce Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation (SRED), which transfers regional event occurrences that encode reachable high-level interactions between details without slide-level labels. We use a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to learn an event dictionary from 20x teacher features. Logical OR pooling records whether each event is detected in any spatially aligned patch, retaining both localized and shared evidence within the corresponding 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional targets without slide-level labels. Visual analysis identifies dictionary components responsive to recognizable histological patterns, supporting target interpretation. Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification and grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts. Runtime matches native 5x, with an average 11.58x speedup over 20x.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SRED, a label-free cross-magnification distillation method for whole-slide imaging that transfers sparse autoencoder event occurrences from 20x to 5x encoders, achieving an 11.58x speedup over 20x while improving over native 5x features.
AI.motivation: High-magnification whole-slide analysis is computationally expensive, while existing cross-magnification distillation methods match features that may be unreachable at low magnification or require slide-level labels.
AI.method: SRED learns an event dictionary from 20x teacher features using a sparse autoencoder (SAE), applies logical OR pooling over spatially aligned patches to form regional targets, and fine-tunes a pretrained 5x encoder to predict these targets without slide-level labels.
AI.result: Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification/grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts, matching 5x runtime with an 11.58x average speedup over 20x.
AI.conclusion: Distilling sparse regional event occurrences bridges high- and low-magnification pathology representations without slide-level supervision.

title: MIRAGE: Motion Identity Reduction via Autoregressive Generative Encoding for Privacy-Preserving Skeleton-based Motion Data
summary: Skeleton motion identifies people through body proportions and movement style, and skeleton streams are increasingly passed to third-party analytics that run action classifiers trained on raw data. A prior adversarial anonymizer adds a per-frame residual in the raw coordinate space but sees one frame at a time; motion retargeting needs a target skeleton and complete sequences, which rules out online use. We present MIRAGE, a target-free, causal anonymizer that adds an identity-reducing residual to each incoming frame in the raw coordinate space, computed by attention over past frames.
