One causal, optionally windowed mask governs every attention in a rotary-position encoder-decoder, and key/value caches let the trained function run frame by frame; on all 56,578 NTU 60 sequences, batched and streaming outputs differ by at most 7.2e-6 m. Reported results use an unbounded window, so per-stream state grows with stream length. We evaluate against a passive adversary that applies raw-trained identity models and an adaptive adversary that trains on the anonymizer's output, treating the adaptive adversary as the headline, on NTU RGB+D 60 over five generator seeds, alongside the per-frame residual anonymizer of Moon et al. trained identically. When consumers retrain on the released data, MIRAGE keeps 83.9% action recognition (raw 89.1%; Moon et al. 88.7%) while a retrained identity classifier reaches 43.4% re-identification (RI) over 40 subjects, against 69.4% for Moon et al. and 75.4% on raw data. The strongest adaptive attacker still reaches 49.3% (chance 2.5%), so MIRAGE reduces identity leakage; it does not anonymize. Against raw-trained (frozen) classifiers, MIRAGE lowers RI below the strongest retargeting baseline (10.36% vs. 22.09%), but frozen action recognition falls to 37.04% (vs. 75.82%), so at full residual scale it is not a drop-in replacement for raw input to existing frozen models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MIRAGE, a target-free, causal autoregressive anonymizer for streaming skeleton motion data that reduces re-identification from 75.4% to 43.4% under adaptive retraining while retaining 83.9% action recognition on NTU RGB+D 60.
AI.motivation: Skeleton motion streams leak user identity, but prior per-frame adversarial anonymizers lack temporal context and motion retargeting requires a target skeleton and full sequences, preventing online streaming use.
AI.method: MIRAGE uses a causal rotary-position encoder-decoder with key/value caches to add an identity-reducing residual to each incoming frame in raw coordinate space based on past frames, with batched and streaming outputs differing by at most 7.2e-6 m.
AI.result: On NTU RGB+D 60 (40 subjects), when consumers retrain on released data, MIRAGE retains 83.9% action recognition (raw 89.1%) and lowers retrained re-identification from 75.4% to 43.4% (vs. 69.4% for Moon et al.), though the strongest adaptive attacker reaches 49.3% (chance 2.5%); against frozen raw-trained models, RI drops to 10.36% but action recognition falls to 37.04%.
AI.conclusion: MIRAGE enables causal, streaming identity-leakage reduction for skeleton data, though it reduces rather than eliminates identity leakage and is not a drop-in replacement for frozen raw-trained classifiers at full residual scale.

title: Joint-ID: Transformer-based Joint Image Enhancement and Depth Estimation for Underwater Environments
comment: 11 pages. (c) 2023 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Underwater imaging is a challenging task due to factors such as scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade image quality and limit visibility. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for enhancing underwater images that leverages the benefits of joint learning for simultaneous image enhancement and depth estimation. We introduce Joint-ID, a transformer-based neural network that can obtain high-perceptual image quality and depth information from raw underwater images. Our approach formulates a multi-modal objective function that addresses invalid depth, lack of sharpness, and image degradation based on color and local texture. We design an end-to-end training pipeline that enables joint restoration and depth estimation in a shared hierarchical feature space. Additionally, we propose a synthetic dataset with various distortions and scene depths for multi-task learning. We evaluate Joint-ID on synthetic and standard datasets, as well as real underwater images with diverse spectra and harsh turbidity, demonstrating its effectiveness for underwater image enhancement and depth estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of Joint-ID to perform feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the visual perception of underwater environments and benefit applications such as oceanography and underwater robotics. Supplements are available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Joint-ID, a transformer-based network for joint underwater image enhancement and depth estimation, demonstrating improved perceptual quality, depth accuracy, and downstream robotic feature matching and saliency detection.
AI.motivation: Underwater imaging suffers from scattering, absorption, and turbulence, which degrade visibility and hinder both visual perception and depth estimation for underwater robotics.
AI.method: Joint-ID uses a transformer-based architecture with a shared hierarchical feature space and a multi-modal objective targeting invalid depth, sharpness, color, and local texture, trained on standard data plus a newly proposed synthetic dataset with diverse distortions and depths.
AI.result: Evaluations on synthetic, standard, and real turbid underwater datasets show effective image enhancement and depth estimation, as well as improved feature matching and saliency detection for visually guided underwater robots.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning underwater image restoration and depth estimation in a shared feature space benefits both visual quality and downstream robotic perception.

title: ExplicitIR: Explicit Spatial Policy Fields for All-in-One Image Restoration
summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover clean images blindly from inputs with various degradation types and levels using a single model. However, the adaptation policy in most existing methods remains implicitly encoded in feature representations, leaving the restoration decision neither explicitly represented nor independently controllable. Since real-world degradations vary spatially, applying uniform updates across the entire image leads to over-smoothing of clean areas and under-correction of localized degradations. To address these limitations, we present ExplicitIR, which represents the restoration policy as two explicit per-pixel fields: Budget, which determines where and how strongly to update, and Style, which selects between narrow and wide context windows. Specifically, ExplicitIR incorporates a Spatial Policy Estimator (SPE) to predict these fields, explicitly representing the restoration policy and capturing spatially-varying degradations, which are then applied by Policy-Adaptive Decoder Blocks (PADB) through adaptive fusion of narrow- and wide-window responses, enabling independent control and precise local modulation. This design enables spatially-adaptive restoration in a single forward pass, without requiring task labels, prompts, or test-time degradation estimators. Extensive experiments on three-task and five-task benchmarks demonstrate that ExplicitIR achieves performance competitive with the strongest all-in-one baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ExplicitIR, an all-in-one image restoration network that represents restoration policies as explicit per-pixel Budget and Style fields, achieving competitive performance on three-task and five-task benchmarks in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Existing all-in-one image restoration models encode adaptation policies implicitly in features, leading to uniform updates that over-smooth clean regions and under-correct localized degradations.
AI.method: ExplicitIR uses a Spatial Policy Estimator (SPE) to predict two explicit per-pixel fields—Budget (update strength) and Style (narrow vs. wide context)—which Policy-Adaptive Decoder Blocks (PADB) apply via adaptive fusion without requiring task labels, prompts, or test-time estimators.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three-task and five-task restoration benchmarks show that ExplicitIR achieves performance competitive with the strongest all-in-one baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit per-pixel policy fields enable controllable, spatially adaptive all-in-one image restoration in a single forward pass.

title: TRIDENT: Efficient Triple-Task Learning of Dehazing, Depth, and Uncertainty Estimation for Underwater 3-D Robot Visual Perception
comment: 13 pages. (c) 2024 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works
summary: Underwater visual systems often suffer from blurry textures and low color contrast due to the inevitable light propagation. These issues can significantly degrade the perception of stable robotic operations. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning-based sensing system that tackles the multidimensional vision tasks in underwater; concretely, we deal with image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty for 3-D visual systems. Also, we propose a TRIDENT model in a fast and lightweight manner; TRIDENT consists of three parallelized decoders and one backbone structure for efficient feature sharing. In addition, it is designed to be trained to express complex parameterization. In experimental evaluation on several standard datasets, we demonstrate that TRIDENT significantly outperforms other existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation. Despite performing three tasks, our model has better efficiency than the others for both memory size and inference time. Finally, our joint learning approach demonstrates robustness in feature matching and seamlessly extends from 2-D to 3-D vision tasks. Supplements are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents TRIDENT, a lightweight triple-task network for underwater image dehazing, depth estimation, and uncertainty estimation that outperforms existing methods in accuracy, memory size, and inference time.
AI.motivation: Underwater 3-D robotic perception is degraded by blurry textures and low color contrast from light propagation, requiring fast, lightweight models that handle multiple vision tasks simultaneously.
AI.method: TRIDENT employs a shared backbone with three parallelized decoders to jointly learn image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty estimation with compact parameterization.
AI.result: On several standard datasets, TRIDENT significantly outperforms existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation while using less memory and faster inference time, and demonstrates robust feature matching across 2-D and 3-D tasks.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a single backbone across parallel dehazing, depth, and uncertainty decoders provides an efficient, accurate perception front-end for underwater 3-D robotics.

title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Project website: this https URL
summary: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM framework, achieving state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality on indoor and cross-session benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent panoramic SLAM faces false loop closures across symmetric rooms under full 3D rotation search, monocular scale drift that splits merged maps, and noisy loop translation directions at short baselines.
AI.method: CoSphere-SLAM performs spherical loop closure via fast Fourier correlation over SO(3) with global Sim(3) consensus to reject symmetric false closures, solves a per-keyframe Sim(3) pose graph with log-scale regularization and decoupled direction/magnitude terms, and fuses omnidirectional Gaussians at maximum ray response.
AI.result: Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks show CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among both single-agent and multi-agent methods.
AI.conclusion: Spherical Fourier loop closure, directional Sim(3) optimization, and omnidirectional Gaussian fusion enable accurate collaborative panoramic mapping.

title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents PhyVGGT, a feed-forward articulated object reconstruction framework built on a frozen 3D foundation model that runs in 6.8 s per 48-frame video and achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing articulated 3D objects from uncalibrated monocular videos is slow with per-scene optimization, while feed-forward 3D foundation models blur moving part boundaries and produce ill-conditioned joint axes.
AI.method: PhyVGGT adds a Part and Motion Decoder anchored to a static-base query to segment 3D parts and predict Bingham priors, followed by a Kinematic Inference Layer that fits a Manhattan frame to static normals, selects the joint axis in closed form, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot.
AI.result: Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT outperforms FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint across five benchmarks, surpasses posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and runs in 6.8 s per 48-frame video compared to hours for Articulat3D.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring part matching and closed-form kinematic inference to stationary base geometry enables fast, accurate feed-forward articulated reconstruction from monocular video.

title: Multispectral-Polarization-Infrared Multi-Aperture Camouflaged Vehicle Detection
summary: Camouflaged vehicle detection is challenging because camouflage suppresses discriminative cues across sensing modalities. Existing multimodal methods often require precise pixel-level registration and feature-level fusion, creating a trade-off between accuracy and latency. We propose a spectral-polarization-infrared tri-modal detection framework co-designed with a multi-aperture imaging setup to exploit complementary imaging physics. A consensus-guided decision-level fusion strategy combines cross-modal detections within bounded registration tolerances, reducing dependence on precise alignment while maintaining accuracy and real-time performance. We construct a tri-modal camouflaged vehicle dataset containing infrared, polarization, and spectral data. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves 82.7% mean Average Precision (mAP) with an end-to-end latency of 16 ms, outperforming representative feature-level fusion approaches. On the public MID-1K dataset, the framework generalizes to RGB-Depth-Infrared modalities without architectural modification and improves mAP@0.5 by 5.7% over state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate the potential of decision-level consensus fusion and multi-aperture sensing for robust and deployable camouflaged vehicle detection.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multispectral-polarization-infrared multi-aperture detection framework with consensus-guided decision-level fusion for camouflaged vehicles, achieving 82.7% mAP at 16 ms latency.
AI.motivation: Camouflaged vehicle detection suppresses cues across single modalities, while existing multimodal feature-level fusion methods require precise pixel registration and trade off accuracy against latency.
AI.method: The framework co-designs a multi-aperture imaging setup (spectral, polarization, infrared) with consensus-guided decision-level fusion that combines cross-modal detections within bounded registration tolerances.
AI.result: On a newly constructed tri-modal camouflaged vehicle dataset, the method reaches 82.7% mAP with 16 ms end-to-end latency, outperforming feature-level fusion baselines; on MID-1K (RGB-Depth-Infrared), it improves mAP@0.5 by 5.7% over state-of-the-art methods without architectural changes.
AI.conclusion: Decision-level consensus fusion with multi-aperture sensing delivers real-time, registration-tolerant camouflaged vehicle detection across diverse modalities.

title: SARVIA: Fast-Adapting the Strong SAR Foundation Models That Are Already in Your MLLMs
summary: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes MLLM visual encoders for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) using self-supervised visual questions, outperforming dedicated SAR foundation models in 2 GPU-hours.
AI.motivation: Developing SAR foundation models typically requires costly large-scale domain pretraining, even though modern MLLMs already possess strong visual encoders.
AI.method: SARVIA constructs computable self-supervised visual questions from unlabeled observations (general spatial tasks plus SAR-specific measurement and SAR-optical correspondence tasks), jointly trains LoRA adapters across visual and language components with loss-driven sampling, and exports the adapted visual encoder.
AI.result: With 600 adaptation steps (2 GPU-hours), SARVIA outperforms compared SAR foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks while cutting domain-training costs by orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight, self-supervised VQA specialization of existing MLLM encoders offers a fast, reusable alternative to from-scratch SAR pretraining.

title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
summary: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), a method that adds a linear pixel-prediction head to diffusion transformers, removing the latent decoder, cutting Wan video warping error by 23%, and improving ImageNet pixel-flow FID from 1.55 to 1.43.
AI.motivation: Latent diffusion models rely on a separate decoder to map latents to pixels, adding architectural complexity and inference cost.
AI.method: DWD separates sampling from pixel decoding: the original denoising head drives the trajectory, while a linear DWD head on the last few finetuned transformer blocks predicts final pixels at the last step using pixel quality losses.
AI.result: Across latent image and video models, DWD removes the decoder and lowers inference cost while maintaining or improving quality, reducing Wan video warping error by 23%; applied to pixel diffusion models without a decoder, it improves texture detail and sets a new state-of-the-art ImageNet FID of 1.43 (from 1.55).
AI.conclusion: Decoupling final-step pixel prediction from the denoising trajectory eliminates latent decoders and improves pixel-level fidelity in both latent and pixel diffusion models.

title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Equal contribution: Xiaoqian Zhang and Zhihao Zhang
summary: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider-carrier framework where multiple MLLMs communicate via projected visual key-value (KV) states rather than text, showing modest task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than text communication.
AI.motivation: Multi-LLM video understanding via text communication introduces an intermediate generation step and can lose visual details needed for downstream reasoning.
AI.method: Provider models observe complementary video frames, and their visual KV states are aligned, projected into the carrier's representation space, and integrated via gated residual updates without extending the carrier KV-cache sequence length.
AI.result: On MLVU and Video-MME, StateKV yields modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, though some categories remain unchanged or drop; increasing provider frame coverage helps selected tasks without growing the carrier cache.
AI.conclusion: Visual KV state injection offers a lower-latency alternative to text-based multi-LLM communication, warranting further study under controlled compute budgets.

title: Inertial Video World Models
summary: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents InertialWorld, an autoregressive video world model that incorporates Inertial Memory (a dense Eulerian grid paired with persistent Lagrangian carriers) to achieve competitive prediction across robotics, 3D games, and navigation.
AI.motivation: Existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for physical inertia, causing repeated frame reconstruction during autoregressive rollouts to accumulate errors and destabilize dynamics.
AI.method: InertialWorld's Inertial Memory maintains a dense Eulerian grid for scene-aligned evidence and persistent Lagrangian carriers bound to canonical coordinates; at each step, carriers are transported by action-conditioned motion, combined with the grid to predict the next state, and gated into the next memory state.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation show that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling inertia as an evolving memory state stabilizes autoregressive video world modeling by carrying forward existing scene evidence.

title: SIDUMN: Self-Supervised Image Denoising Under Symmetric Multiplicative Noise
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Letters
summary: Self-supervised denoising is challenging when the corruption is multiplicative and signal-dependent. In this letter, we propose SIDUMN, a symmetric noisier framework for self-supervised denoising under mean-one symmetric multiplicative noise. Given noisy observations and the noise law, the method samples an independent synthetic noise factor from the same law and constructs two complementary noisier images by applying the factor and its reflection about one. The denoising network is trained to predict one noisier image from the other, and at inference the reconstructions of $K$ such antithetic pairs are averaged. We show that the population target of the training loss is the clean conditional mean minus a multiplicative cross-term. We further prove that, for any trained network, antithetic averaging never increases the expected squared error of a single noisier-input reconstruction. Numerical results validate the theoretical findings and the proposed method.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SIDUMN, a self-supervised denoising framework for mean-one symmetric multiplicative noise that trains on complementary antithetic noisier image pairs and averages K pair reconstructions at inference.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised image denoising is challenging when corruption is multiplicative and signal-dependent rather than additive.
AI.method: Given noisy observations and the noise law, SIDUMN samples an independent synthetic noise factor from the same law and applies both the factor and its reflection about one to form two complementary noisier images. A denoising network is trained to predict one noisier image from the other, and at inference it averages the reconstructions of K such antithetic pairs.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows the training loss population target is the clean conditional mean minus a multiplicative cross-term, and antithetic averaging never increases the expected squared error of a single noisier-input reconstruction; numerical experiments validate both the theory and method.
AI.conclusion: SIDUMN provides a theoretically grounded, self-supervised approach for denoising under symmetric multiplicative noise with provable variance reduction from antithetic averaging.

title: Breaking Visual Conventions: Spectrally Coupled Weight Perturbation for Creative Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models often produce high-quality images that follow familiar visual conventions, even in response to open-ended prompts such as ``a creative [CLS]''. Existing methods encourage novelty by exploring semantic conditions or modifying features and guidance during denoising. Pretrained weights offer a complementary source of creative variation, but unstructured perturbations can have little visual effect or degrade image quality. We introduce Coupled Spectral Perturbation (CosPert), a training-free method that targets attention projections in layers identified by a one-time sensitivity analysis. For each projection, CosPert uses a shared random transformation and its transpose to couple updates to the singular-vector factors while perturbing the spectral gains. A common relative budget calibrates the magnitude of weight changes across projections, and a sigmoid schedule concentrates their influence in early denoising and gradually attenuates them during refinement. CosPert provides plug-and-play creativity enhancement at inference time. Once the perturbations are prepared, sampling requires no auxiliary networks or additional model evaluations. On both FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, CosPert enhances visual creativity, producing more varied object structures while preserving category identity. Across 50 object categories, CosPert achieves the highest mean CREward among the evaluated methods while maintaining strong prompt alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Coupled Spectral Perturbation (CosPert), a training-free inference-time method that perturbs attention projection weights to increase visual creativity in text-to-image diffusion models while preserving category identity.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image models often generate conventional images even for open-ended creative prompts, and existing unstructured weight perturbations either have little visual effect or degrade image quality.
AI.method: CosPert targets attention projections in layers selected by a one-time sensitivity analysis, using a shared random transformation and its transpose to couple updates to singular-vector factors while perturbing spectral gains. A common relative budget calibrates perturbation magnitudes across projections, and a sigmoid schedule concentrates perturbations in early denoising before attenuating them during refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated across 50 object categories on FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5, CosPert produces more varied object structures while preserving category identity, achieving the highest mean CREward among evaluated methods with strong prompt alignment and no extra model evaluations at sampling time.
AI.conclusion: Structured spectral weight perturbation offers a plug-and-play, zero-overhead way to enhance creative diversity in pretrained text-to-image models.

title: M$^3$-Test: Coverage Gaps in Joint-Perturbation Testing of Visual Question Answering
summary: A visual question answering (VQA) model can pass every image-only and question-only test yet fail when the same changes occur together. Standard robustness reports average over conditions and therefore cannot say which accepted requests remain vulnerable. We introduce M3-Test, a coverage audit that aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint library, so that any reduced test suite can be replayed on the same requests. Across 2.6 million responses from four vision-language models, joint failures affect 26-29% of the Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, although fewer than 0.6% of their joint records fail. Passing the 25 maximum-strength corners does not close this gap: 11-14% of the accepted questions still fail elsewhere in the library. Re-executing the archived failures reproduces about 90% of them, against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate among matched passing controls, and re-checking the most fragile failure records supports 80-89% of them. On the evidence examined, neither execution noise nor grading error can fully account for the gap. The same aligned grids make previous evaluations reusable. On held-out images, a risk order learned from other models discovers about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries, compared with 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays. M3-Test thus turns a passing robustness suite into a request-level account of what remains untested, supporting acceptance, regression review and test allocation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces M3-Test, a coverage audit for visual question answering that exposes how models passing all single-modality tests still fail frequently when image and question perturbations are combined.
AI.motivation: Standard VQA robustness evaluations average over conditions and miss request-level vulnerabilities where a model passes every image-only and question-only test yet fails under joint perturbations.
AI.method: M3-Test aligns each clean input with its single-modality variants and a complete 5x5 family, 4x4 strength joint perturbation library, enabling replay of reduced test suites on the same requests and risk-ordered query allocation learned from other models.
AI.result: Across 2.6 million responses from four VLMs, joint failures affect 26-29% of Qwen questions that pass all 40 single-modality tests, and 11-14% still fail even after passing the 25 maximum-strength corners; re-execution reproduces about 90% of archived failures against a 0.3-0.6% flip rate on controls, and a cross-model risk order finds about 80% of affected Qwen questions within 25 additional queries versus 65-68% for maximum-first and 53-57% for pairwise covering arrays.
AI.conclusion: M3-Test turns aggregate robustness suites into request-level coverage audits, supporting acceptance decisions, regression review, and targeted test allocation.

title: DAP-MR: Degradation-Aware Prompt-Magnitude Routing for Real-World Ultrasound Super-Resolution
summary: When super-resolution models designed for natural images are used on ultrasound scans, relying on semantic text prompts can lead to unreliable results. The tags these models generate often do not match the actual restoration needs, and specialized medical terms may be misunderstood by general-purpose text encoders. Instead, prompts focused on common image degradations are more directly useful for guiding restoration. However, using a single prompt to describe both the type and severity of image degradation can entangle these factors, making it hard for the model to know how strong the degradation is. To address this limitation, we introduce Degradation-Aware Prompt--Magnitude Routing (DAP-MR). Each degradation type is represented by a dedicated token initialized from the contextualized EOS embedding of a degradation-oriented prompt and subsequently adapted during ultrasound SR training. A separate magnitude router predicts a continuous, input-dependent magnitude that modulates the corresponding token. Thus, language provides a degradation-aware initialization for what should be restored, while magnitude routing supplies an explicit signal for how strongly it should influence restoration. DAP-MR can be added to both one-step and multi-step diffusion super-resolution frameworks without changing their core structures. Our experiments--on synthetic datasets with both in-domain and under anatomical-domain shift, as well as unpaired real-world ultrasound data--show that DAP-MR delivers better restoration quality and generalizes more consistently across different domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Degradation-Aware Prompt-Magnitude Routing (DAP-MR), which separates degradation type tokens from input-dependent severity routing to improve diffusion-based ultrasound super-resolution.
AI.motivation: Natural-image super-resolution models rely on semantic text prompts that mismatch ultrasound restoration needs, and encoding both degradation type and severity in a single prompt entangles the two factors.
AI.method: DAP-MR represents each degradation type with a dedicated token initialized from the contextualized EOS embedding of a degradation-oriented prompt and adapted during ultrasound SR training, while a separate magnitude router predicts a continuous, input-dependent magnitude to modulate each token. The module plugs into both one-step and multi-step diffusion SR frameworks without altering their core structure.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic datasets (in-domain and under anatomical-domain shift) and unpaired real-world ultrasound data show that DAP-MR achieves better restoration quality and more consistent cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling degradation type initialization from continuous magnitude routing enables more reliable and generalizable diffusion super-resolution for real-world ultrasound scans.

title: PURE: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multi-Granularity Multimodal Identity Matching
summary: Identity matching asks whether two records denote the same identity, yet the answer depends on the target granularity. Two records may match at the base level but not at the variant level: they share an underlying design while differing in attributes such as color or size. Final matching accuracy does not separately characterize the capabilities involved. To study this problem, we use e-commerce as a challenging real-world domain. We introduce PURE, a diagnostic benchmark for multi-granularity multimodal identity matching covering four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment. The benchmark comprises 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks, derived from real-world matching pairs and verified by two domain experts. Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%. Understanding receives the highest mean score and Judgment the lowest, with weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment. Modality ablations show that models benefit from multimodal evidence but can incorrectly identify conflicts between matching records. In direct matching, most models recognize matching pairs more reliably than non-matching pairs at the base level, whereas the reverse holds at the variant level. PURE therefore reveals what aggregate matching accuracy hides: not only whether models judge a pair correctly, but where they struggle to interpret evidence and apply matching criteria.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PURE, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,457 multiple-choice questions across 14 tasks for evaluating multi-granularity multimodal identity matching in e-commerce.
AI.motivation: Identity matching depends on target granularity (base design vs. variant attributes like color or size), and aggregate matching accuracy fails to reveal which underlying capabilities models lack.
AI.method: Built from real-world e-commerce matching pairs verified by two domain experts, PURE evaluates four capability dimensions: Perception, Understanding, Reasoning, and Evidence-grounded Judgment.
AI.result: Across ten recent MLLMs, overall scores range from 47.1% to 86.0%, with Understanding highest and Judgment lowest due to weaknesses in visual difference localization and variant-level rule judgment; modality ablations show models benefit from multimodal evidence but can misidentify conflicts, and in direct matching they recognize matches better than non-matches at the base level but the reverse at the variant level.
AI.conclusion: PURE diagnoses fine-grained failure modes in evidence interpretation and rule application that aggregate matching accuracy obscures.

title: SandBAR: A Band-Asymmetric Architecture for Underwater Image Restoration with Removable Frequency Scaffolding
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Camera-ready version. 9 pages, 6 figures
summary: Light scattering, absorption and turbidity degrade underwater imagery through complementary frequency tendencies: large-scale, channel-dependent appearance distortions and local high-frequency detail loss. This band asymmetry motivates different forms of restoration for global colour and local structure. Our primary contribution is SandBAR, a novel unified band-asymmetric architecture for underwater image restoration. Rather than treating frequency processing as an isolated module, SandBAR organises the restoration pipeline around band asymmetry at the block, encoder and objective levels. Within this architecture, we introduce a novel band-asymmetric sandwich block with a reserved post-attention repair slot and the Split-band Parallel Asymmetric Repair Kernel (SPARK), a novel module that applies channel-aware large-support correction to the low band, which predominantly carries large-scale appearance distortions, and lightweight local refinement to the detail-bearing high band, thereby restoring global colour while preserving fine structure. To deliver the global cast to the depth at which the network represents global structure, a learnable low-frequency guidance path injects a low-pass view of the input into the deep encoder, and a three-scale spatial-frequency objective supervises the same axis throughout the decoder. Building on the reserved post-attention slot, we further introduce Post-attention Scaffold Training (PaST), a novel removable nonlinear scaffolding scheme that trains the permanent SandBAR graph under band-specific capacity and runs it at inference without that capacity. SandBAR reaches 29.89 / 28.92 / 22.77 dB on EUVP / LSUI / UIEB and establishes a new three-domain mean state of the art on the benchmark family, exceeding the strongest published result by approximately 1.0 dB. PaST adds no parameters or FLOPs at inference and preserves matched latency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SandBAR, a band-asymmetric underwater image restoration architecture with removable post-attention scaffolding (PaST), achieving state-of-the-art performance across EUVP, LSUI, and UIEB.
AI.motivation: Underwater light scattering, absorption, and turbidity cause asymmetric frequency degradations, namely global channel-dependent color shifts and local high-frequency detail loss, which require distinct restoration mechanisms.
AI.method: SandBAR integrates a band-asymmetric sandwich block with a reserved post-attention repair slot and the Split-band Parallel Asymmetric Repair Kernel (SPARK) for large-support low-band color correction and lightweight high-band local refinement, alongside a learnable low-frequency guidance path and a three-scale spatial-frequency objective. Post-attention Scaffold Training (PaST) trains with band-specific nonlinear capacity in the reserved slot and removes it at inference.
AI.result: SandBAR achieves 29.89 dB on EUVP, 28.92 dB on LSUI, and 22.77 dB on UIEB, exceeding the strongest published three-domain mean by about 1.0 dB, while PaST adds zero parameters or FLOPs at inference.
AI.conclusion: Structuring the entire restoration pipeline around frequency band asymmetry and removable training scaffolding improves underwater image restoration without inference overhead.

title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ContraSense, a benchmark of counter-intuitive image-text pairs designed to test whether multimodal LLMs rely on visual evidence rather than commonsense priors.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language benchmarks mostly align with human commonsense, allowing MLLMs to score well via statistical co-occurrence and dataset priors instead of genuine visual understanding.
AI.method: ContraSense curates counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, forcing models to ground reasoning in the image content.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations of open- and closed-source MLLMs show a large gap below human performance: the strongest closed-source model reaches only about 60% accuracy compared with 96.04% for human participants.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs still depend heavily on commonsense priors over visual evidence, underscoring the need for more faithful image-grounded multimodal reasoning.

title: Leveraging Segmentation Representations for Efficient Classification: A Self-Configuring Framework Based on nnU-Net
summary: We propose a self-configuring framework that extends the nnU-Net workflow to both segmentation and classification in 3D medical imaging. Building on nnU-Net's self-configuring method, the framework reuses representations learned by a segmentation model for image-level classification. Its encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities are used by a lightweight classifier. Two information-sharing strategies are investigated. In the frozen-backbone branch, features are augmented with region-of-interest information, predicted foreground volume, and segmentation confidence. In the adaptation branch, the final encoder stage is partially fine-tuned for classification, with an auxiliary segmentation loss to preserve segmentation-related information. Additional five-fold experiments showed that more complex configurations did not consistently improve classification performance. On the public validation leaderboard, our selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056. In the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation, our framework ranked first overall, achieving the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, including two hidden testing tasks. Local inference measurements also remained below the challenge limits of $60 \mathrm{s}$ per case and $4 \mathrm{GB}$ GPU memory. These results demonstrate the practical value of reusing segmentation representations for classification while maintaining a simple and efficient framework.

AI.tldr: The paper extends nnU-Net into a self-configuring framework for joint 3D medical image segmentation and classification, winning first place overall in FLARE 2026 Task 2.
AI.motivation: Reusing representations learned by 3D segmentation models for image-level classification can improve efficiency, but effective information-sharing strategies within a self-configuring pipeline need systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The framework feeds nnU-Net encoder features and predicted segmentation probabilities into a lightweight classifier, comparing a frozen-backbone branch (augmented with ROI info, foreground volume, and segmentation confidence) against a partial fine-tuning adaptation branch with an auxiliary segmentation loss.
AI.result: The selected framework achieved an Overall score of 0.8056 on the public validation leaderboard and ranked first overall in the official FLARE 2026 Task 2 final evaluation with the highest DSC, NSD, and AUROC across all four testing tasks, while staying under the 60 s per case and 4 GB GPU memory limits.
AI.conclusion: Reusing segmentation representations in a simple, self-configuring nnU-Net pipeline yields top-ranked 3D medical classification and segmentation performance within strict clinical resource budgets.

title: CoBoVLA: Decoupling Language from Action with Discrete Codes for Robust and Interpretable Robot Manipulation
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, and supplemental material included
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve high success rates on the LIBERO benchmark but remain sensitive to paraphrasing. Existing VLAs ranging from 0.6B to 7.5B parameters experience a 22-52 point performance drop on LIBERO-Para while SmolVLA exhibits an even larger decline, from 83\% to 8\%. Because most VLAs jointly learn language understanding and action generation, it is difficult to determine whether a failure originates from misunderstanding an instruction or executing it incorrectly. To address these challenges, we introduce CoBoVLA, or CodeBookVLA, a 250M-parameter VLA that decouples language understanding, planning, and control through learned discrete interpretable codes. A text encoder maps the instructions to shared step codes, which a visual planner then converts into action code sequences executed by a language-independent actor. This design improves robustness to instruction paraphrasing while allowing failures to be traced to individual stages. It also enables efficient real-time control on resource-constrained hardware by encoding instructions only once and using compact discrete representations to keep each component lightweight. CoBoVLA achieves 91.4\% success on LIBERO-Goal, compared with 82.8\% for SmolVLA, under a matched protocol, with 17 ms per control step latency. On LIBERO-Para, it achieves 81.1\% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases and 78.5\% on matched episodes, compared with 36.5\% for SmolVLA LoRA fine-tuned on paraphrases. Without two-step demonstrations, CoBoVLA completes 48.8\% of 160 free-form two-step tasks. Finally, success reaches 91\% when instructions are correctly encoded but falls to 27.2\% otherwise, identifying language understanding as the main source of remaining failures. Together, these results demonstrate that decoupling language understanding and control can improve instruction robustness while making VLA failures easier to diagnose.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoBoVLA, a 250M-parameter Vision-Language-Action model that decouples language understanding, planning, and control via learned discrete codes to improve paraphrase robustness and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs (0.6B-7.5B) suffer 22-52 point drops on paraphrased instructions (and SmolVLA drops from 83% to 8%), and joint training makes it hard to diagnose whether failures stem from language misunderstanding or execution errors.
AI.method: CoBoVLA uses a text encoder to map instructions once into shared discrete step codes, a visual planner to convert them into action code sequences, and a language-independent actor to execute them.
AI.result: CoBoVLA reaches 91.4% success on LIBERO-Goal (vs. 82.8% for SmolVLA) at 17 ms per control step, achieves 81.1% across 4,092 unseen paraphrases on LIBERO-Para (78.5% on matched episodes vs. 36.5% for LoRA-tuned SmolVLA), completes 48.8% of 160 zero-shot two-step tasks, and shows 91% success when instructions are correctly encoded versus 27.2% otherwise.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling language understanding from action generation with compact discrete codes improves paraphrase robustness, enables real-time edge control, and pinpoints language encoding as the primary remaining bottleneck.

title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: Includes supplementary material. Code available at this https URL
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SpatialMind, a task-adaptive MLLM framework that dynamically fuses multi-level 3D geometric representations via a gated GeoFus module, achieving 72.3 on VSI-Bench.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs use either a single geometric granularity or a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, whereas different spatial reasoning tasks require different geometric granularities.
AI.method: SpatialMind introduces GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module with a gating network conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric features to adaptively modulate shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across LLM decoder layers, trained with a negative-entropy regularization loss to prevent gate collapse.
AI.result: Gate visualizations confirm task-dependent granularity adaptation, and SpatialMind achieves a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically routing multi-level 3D geometric features based on task context is essential for strong 3D spatial reasoning in MLLMs.

title: CutAgent: Creative-Gene-Driven Planning and Experience-Guided Self-Refinement for High-CTR E-commerce Advertising Video Creation
summary: E-commerce advertising video creation requires both high-level creative planning and reliable multi-modal production. However, existing methods often map product attributes directly to scripts or editing decisions without explicitly modeling advertising strategies, narrative structures, and production styles. They also have limited ability to reuse past production failures. To address these limitations, we propose $\textbf{CutAgent}$, a dual-agent framework that formulates advertising video creation as a Plan--Execute--Self-Evolve process. CutAgent comprises two collaborative agents, $\textbf{GeneAgent}$ and $\textbf{VideoAgent}$, connected by a structured creative gene that bridges product understanding and video production. GeneAgent maps multi-modal product inputs---textual attributes together with product images---to creative genes that specify narrative units and production rules. To train GeneAgent, we construct $\textbf{CutAgent-70K}$ with approximately 70K samples of product attributes/images, reverse-extracted creative genes, cleaned clip pools, and real-world CTR, and apply high-CTR supervised fine-tuning followed by CTR-guided GRPO. Guided by the generated gene, VideoAgent retrieves category-then-gene failure--correction experiences from a long-term memory as constraints for shot-script planning, then coordinates material retrieval, narration, subtitles, music, and timeline rendering. Independently, a reflection loop diagnoses quality defects, revises deficient production decisions, and writes verified corrections back to memory for later retrieval. Experiments on $\textbf{CutAgent-Eval}$ show that CutAgent outperforms representative baselines in e-commerce advertising video creation, achieving the highest online CTR of $\textbf{2.21\%}$.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CutAgent, a dual-agent framework for e-commerce advertising video creation that uses structured creative genes and experience-guided self-refinement, achieving 2.21% online CTR.
AI.motivation: Existing ad video generation methods map product attributes directly to scripts without modeling advertising strategies or narrative structures, and cannot reuse lessons from past production failures.
AI.method: CutAgent pairs GeneAgent (trained on CutAgent-70K with high-CTR SFT and CTR-guided GRPO to map product text and images to structured creative genes) with VideoAgent (which retrieves category-then-gene failure-correction experiences from long-term memory to constrain shot-script planning and coordinate rendering), supported by an independent reflection loop that writes verified fixes back to memory.
AI.result: On CutAgent-Eval, CutAgent outperforms representative baselines and achieves the highest online click-through rate of 2.21%.
AI.conclusion: Bridging product understanding and video production through learned creative genes and memory-backed self-evolution improves real-world e-commerce advertising effectiveness.

title: When Neural Collapse Fails to Route: Routing Drift in Continual Learning
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026. 36 pages, including supplementary material
summary: Progressive neural-collapse classifiers can learn strong task-local decision boundaries while failing the global Class-IL decision. We identify the failure as routing drift: under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, a held-out sample can remain separable within its true task block, yet receive its largest global score from another block. This produces high Task-IL accuracy but low Class-IL accuracy, and small replay buffers can mask the problem because stored samples are optimized repeatedly and often remain well routed. We formalize route accuracy directly from the global class argmax and use it to separate within-task discrimination from cross-task score comparability. This decomposition suggests a classifier-level correction: preserve the global ETF frame, but add class-local reliability evidence when transported class measures deviate from the neural-collapse ideal. We develop Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a lightweight post-hoc classifier that composes standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, NC-shrunk class representatives. Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, this NC-consistent correction gives the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six. The largest gains occur in harder routing regimes: up to $+6.75$ FAA over the reported reference, and up to $+8.03$ FAA and $+8.62$ final route accuracy in paired evaluations, while preserving Task-IL performance. These results position routing drift as a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning and show that reliability-calibrated class evidence can repair part of the lost global routing without retraining the representation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies routing drift as a failure mode in progressive neural-collapse continual learning and proposes Reliability-Calibrated Routing (RCR), a post-hoc classifier correction that improves Class-IL accuracy without representation retraining.
AI.motivation: Under an expanding equiangular tight frame (ETF) classifier, held-out samples can remain separable within their true task block yet receive a higher global score from another block, causing high Task-IL but low Class-IL accuracy.
AI.method: RCR preserves the global ETF frame and combines standardized ETF alignment with radial plausibility around transported, neural-collapse-shrunk class representatives to supply class-local reliability evidence.
AI.result: Across three datasets and two fixed replay-buffer budgets, RCR achieves the best Class-IL FAA on five of six settings and reduces Class-IL forgetting on all six, with gains up to +6.75 FAA over the reference (+8.03 FAA and +8.62 final route accuracy in paired evaluations) while preserving Task-IL performance.
AI.conclusion: Routing drift is a measurable failure mode of ETF-based continual learning that can be substantially mitigated post-hoc by calibrating class-local reliability evidence.

title: Where Demand Meets Supply: Spatial Elastic Consensus for Low-Bandwidth Collaborative Perception
summary: Occlusions and limited sensor range make ego-only 3D perception insufficient for safe driving. Collaborative perception addresses this by enabling connected vehicles to share complementary observations, yet it remains constrained by tight vehicular communication budgets. While spatial selection is more flexible than fixed-rate feature compression, existing selectors remain largely sender-driven and waste scarce bandwidth on ego-visible targets. Furthermore, applying convolutions after masking spreads isolated tokens into their neighborhoods, silently violating low-bandwidth constraints. To address this, we propose Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bandwidth-adaptive framework centered on bilateral demand-supply consensus. Instead of unilateral token selection, the ego vehicle formulates a content-aware demand prior while each collaborator evaluates its local supply. This single-round consensus allocates the token budget to critical ego-missed evidence rather than ego-visible redundancy, without transmitting dense maps. To guarantee exact budget compliance, an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline refines features prior to discrete token selection, preventing receptive-field leakage. A lightweight deformable sampler then aggregates these sparse messages with learned local offsets, compensating for the spatial context lost to token selection and mitigating inter-agent pose drift. Evaluated at a stringent 64KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the best AP@0.7 on the simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets and the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset. These results demonstrate that combining bilateral consensus with budget-exact transmission is key to efficient low-bandwidth collaborative perception.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Spatial Elastic Consensus (SEC), a bilateral demand-supply collaborative perception framework with anti-dilation feature refinement that achieves top AP@0.7 under a strict 64 KiB bandwidth budget.
AI.motivation: Sender-driven spatial token selectors waste scarce vehicular bandwidth on ego-visible targets, and applying convolutions after masking causes receptive-field leakage that silently violates low-bandwidth budgets.
AI.method: The ego vehicle forms a content-aware demand prior while collaborators evaluate local supply in a single-round consensus to allocate tokens to ego-missed evidence; an anti-dilation refine-before-mask pipeline prevents receptive-field leakage, and a lightweight deformable sampler aggregates sparse messages with learned local offsets to handle lost context and pose drift.
AI.result: Evaluated at a 64 KiB budget, SEC consistently achieves the highest AP@0.7 on simulated OPV2V and V2XSet datasets as well as the real-world DAIR-V2X dataset.
AI.conclusion: Combining bilateral demand-supply consensus with budget-exact anti-dilation transmission enables accurate low-bandwidth collaborative 3D perception.

title: As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
summary: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

AI.tldr: The paper uncovers that On-Policy Distillation (OPD) of Vision-Language Models is vulnerable to rapid visual backdoor propagation once a critical poisoning threshold is crossed, even without explicit malicious target responses.
AI.motivation: Because OPD supervises student-generated online trajectories with teacher probability distributions rather than teacher-generated malicious responses, it was thought to resist backdoor propagation.
AI.method: The authors combine theoretical analysis with experiments across multiple VLM families and datasets, and design a trigger that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection.
AI.result: Unlike gradual propagation in offline distillation, OPD backdoors rarely appear at low poisoning ratios but surge to nearly 100% attack success rate past a critical threshold, driven by continuous accumulation of anomalous teacher probability mass rather than explicit malicious responses.
AI.conclusion: On-Policy Distillation introduces a previously overlooked, threshold-driven visual backdoor risk that requires dedicated security defenses.

title: MedImgAnnotator: batch wise medical image annotation and preprocessing tool
summary: The curation of large cohort datasets for developing deep learning models demands annotating or editing over the AI-predicted labels. However, openly available annotation tools are time-consuming, as they involve complex navigational steps and do not support batch processing. This study aimed to develop a simple, fast, semiautomated batch-annotation tool named MedImgAnnotator. The tool was created by integrating editing tools, image mask pair matching logic, preprocessing functions, object detection tool, and a plugin management system. Its performance was evaluated in terms of active annotation time and ease of use by the developer and 12 users using open-source MR and CT scans. Additionally, the tool had been used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation best performance winner to annotate liver masks from 6412 MRI volumes. The evaluation results showed that MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 (average active annotation time of openly available tools) seconds to 59 seconds. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test of 12 users evaluation results recorded P values of 0.032 and 0.008 for the active annotation time and higher ease of use rating metrics, respectively, indicating that the current tool significantly reduces annotation time and enhances ease of use. Moreover, the tool utilization for annotating different regions of interest from different modality scans and body regions shows its usability across modalities and areas of interest. MedImgAnnotator, which significantly reduces active annotation time for large imaging cohorts, is available as an executable file and as a Python script. Access link: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedImgAnnotator, a semiautomated batch-processing tool for medical image annotation and preprocessing that cuts active annotation time from 206.5 s to 59 s.
AI.motivation: Existing open-source medical image annotation tools lack batch processing and require complex navigation, making large-cohort label curation and AI-prediction editing slow.
AI.method: MedImgAnnotator integrates editing tools, image-mask pair matching, preprocessing functions, object detection, and a plugin management system, and is distributed as both an executable and a Python script.
AI.result: In evaluations by 12 users on MR and CT scans, MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 s to 59 s (Wilcoxon P = 0.032) and significantly improved ease of use (P = 0.008); it was also used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation winner to annotate 6,412 MRI volumes.
AI.conclusion: MedImgAnnotator substantially accelerates large-scale multi-modality medical image curation and editing.

title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
summary: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MAVE, an agentic framework for reconstructing editable 3D Blender blockouts from film shots, along with MAVEBench and the MAVEData-3K dataset.
AI.motivation: Manually reconstructing animated 3D blockouts from reference videos for previsualization and video-generation conditioning is costly, limiting creator adoption and paired training data.
AI.method: MAVE combines metric observation (recovering cameras, human motion, and geometry in a shared metric coordinate system), agentic modeling (constructing an editable Blender environment under observation constraints), and programmatic verification checks that flag inconsistencies for refinement.
AI.result: On MAVEBench (50 film shots, 416 keyframes), MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over vanilla baselines; with DeepSeek-1017 it scores 73.2 at USD 0.054 per shot while cutting reconstruction time by 53%, and the authors release MAVEData-3K (3,000 blockout-video pairs).
AI.conclusion: Combining metric 3D observations with programmatic verification enables fast, low-cost, editable 3D blockout reconstruction from film footage.

title: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents
comment: 45 pages, 8 in the main text. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Visual token pruning speeds up large vision-language models (VLMs) by keeping only a part of their visual tokens. Most existing methods improve the ranking of the tokens and then answer every question once with the same budget. With strong rankings, pruning hurts only a few questions, and signals computed on the kept tokens see little of what it removed. We find that, on most of these questions, a small VLM given the full image disagrees with the pruned answer, since it still sees the missing evidence. We propose PRUDENT, which first answers with about half the budget and spends the saved tokens on re-answering the disagreeing questions at twice the budget. We show when such re-answering pays and why the small VLM should read the full image. On 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average budget of visual tokens. Its lead widens as the budget tightens, and holds across five InternVL sizes. PRUDENT also has the highest average in two more model families. The disagreement of the small VLM flags most pruning failures of all eight methods, and re-answering on it also improves the two strongest with their own rankings. Other checkers give similar gains, and the extra tokens go where the first pass hurts the answer. These results suggest that identifying which pruned answers are trustworthy provides an additional lever for visual token pruning beyond the ranking of tokens. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PRUDENT, a visual token pruning strategy that uses a small VLM reading the full image to flag likely pruning failures and re-answer only those questions at twice the token budget.
AI.motivation: Standard visual token pruning uses a fixed budget per question, but even strong token rankings hurt a small subset of questions where signals on kept tokens cannot detect the missing evidence.
