AI.method: PRUDENT first answers all questions using about half the visual token budget, then checks each answer against a small VLM given the full image and spends the saved tokens to re-answer disagreeing questions at twice the budget.
AI.result: Across 18 benchmarks, PRUDENT outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average token budget, with larger gains at tighter budgets, holds across five InternVL sizes and two additional model families, and also improves the two strongest baselines when applied to their rankings.
AI.conclusion: Identifying untrustworthy pruned answers via small-VLM disagreement provides an effective, orthogonal lever to token ranking for efficient VLM inference.

title: LeViT-UNet++: Towards Balanced Fine-Grained Details and Context for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Efficient medical image segmentation is essential for clinical applications requiring fast and accurate delineation, such as surgical navigation, radiation therapy, and real-time image-guided intervention. Despite substantial advances in convolutional neural networks and Transformers, attaining high accuracy under limited computational resources remains difficult, because reducing model complexity often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context modeling, yielding an unfavorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. To address this, we propose LeViT-UNet++, an efficient encoder-decoder architecture that better balances local detail preservation and global context modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes feature representations into low- and high-frequency components to extract multi-scale structural information, thereby mitigating detail loss during downsampling. We further develop a depthwise convolution-based decoder that integrates multi-scale global representations from Transformer blocks with local spatial features, enabling progressive feature refinement while reducing computational overhead. Evaluated on four benchmarks (Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart) under both 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and fast inference. On Synapse, for instance, it attains a DSC of 76.57% with only 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS, confirming a favorable accuracy-efficiency balance. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining wavelet-based multi-scale feature extraction with lightweight local-global feature fusion for efficient medical segmentation. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LeViT-UNet++, an efficient medical image segmentation architecture combining Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling and a depthwise-convolution decoder, achieving 76.57% DSC on Synapse at 241.72 FPS.
AI.motivation: Reducing computational complexity in CNN and Transformer medical segmentation models often sacrifices fine-grained structural details and global context.
AI.method: LeViT-UNet++ introduces a Haar Wavelet Multi-Scale Downsampling (HWMD) module that decomposes features into low- and high-frequency components to preserve detail during downsampling, paired with a depthwise-convolution decoder that progressively fuses multi-scale Transformer representations with local spatial features.
AI.result: Evaluated on Synapse, ACDC, LA2018, and MSD Heart in 2D and 3D settings, LeViT-UNet++ achieves competitive accuracy with low overhead, reaching 76.57% DSC on Synapse with 8.025M parameters and 241.72 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Combining wavelet-based multi-scale downsampling with lightweight local-global decoding yields a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off for real-time clinical segmentation.

title: Fast and Strong Image Protection against Diffusion Personalization
summary: Personalized text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce a person from a handful of photographs. Image protection perturbs each image before publication so that fine-tuning on it fails, but it optimizes every perturbation from scratch, so its cost grows with the number of images. We present the protective diffusion model (PDM), which is trained once and samples the perturbation of a new image over many denoising steps. PDM distills an iterative teacher and is then post-trained with the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward, a stronger objective than existing ones. PDM outperforms nine baselines on faces and artworks and nearly matches its teacher at a tenth of the cost.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the protective diffusion model (PDM), a one-time-trained generative model that samples adversarial perturbations to protect images against diffusion personalization at a tenth of the teacher's cost.
AI.motivation: Existing image protection methods against personalized text-to-image diffusion models optimize perturbations from scratch for each image, causing costs to scale linearly with dataset size.
AI.method: PDM distills an iterative optimization teacher into a diffusion model that samples perturbations for new images, and is post-trained using the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward.
AI.result: Across faces and artworks, PDM outperforms nine baselines and nearly matches its iterative teacher at one-tenth of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing adversarial perturbation generation via distilled, reward-post-trained diffusion models makes image protection against personalization practical at scale.

title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
summary: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses motion collapse in video editing reward models and proposes a motion-aware reward model with an RGB frame-difference stream that eliminates motion-suppressed selections on VE-Bench.
AI.motivation: Video editing reward models often favor temporal consistency over actual motion, leading to motion collapse where motion-suppressed candidates are preferred in 97% of VE-Bench cases.
AI.method: The proposed reward model adds an explicit RGB frame-difference stream, trains with preference supervision against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives, and uses a distillation anchor to preserve alignment with human quality judgments.
AI.result: On the VE-Bench motion ladder, the model reduces selection of motion-suppressed candidates from 97% to 0%, achieves a 0.57 Spearman correlation with human quality ratings, detects unseen suppression variants, and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling inter-frame dynamics and training against motion-collapse negatives is essential for reliable video editing reward models.

title: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement
summary: Visual place recognition (VPR) faces critical challenges in handling extreme environmental variations while meeting the computational constraints of practical applications. Current methods predominantly address these challenges by either scaling up model capacity or employing computationally intensive reranking stages, creating a significant efficiency bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, we propose EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework that achieves speed-accuracy trade-offs through two key innovations: i) a scene-aware visual prompt tuning method which adapts pretrained features with less parameters while dynamically adjusting to sample-specific characteristics, and ii) an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module that further reinforces discriminative regions. Comprehensive evaluations on Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime and SVOX demonstrate that our method establishes a new SOTA for DINOv2-small models by outperforming all same-scale competitors, and delivers a $73\times$ speedup with 60\% lower-dimensional features while maintaining competitive (within 2.5% average R@1 gap) against the SOTA DINOv2-large-based two-stage method. Our code will be available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage visual place recognition framework using scene-aware prompt tuning and adaptive local feature enhancement, delivering a 73x speedup over two-stage DINOv2-large methods.
AI.motivation: Visual place recognition methods typically handle extreme environmental variations by scaling up model size or adding expensive reranking stages, creating an efficiency bottleneck.
AI.method: EfficientVPR combines scene-aware visual prompt tuning to adapt pretrained features dynamically with few parameters, and an instance-dependent key local feature enhancement module to reinforce discriminative regions.
AI.result: Across Pitts250k, MSLS, Eynsham, AmsterTime, and SVOX, EfficientVPR sets a new state of the art for DINOv2-small models and achieves a 73x speedup with 60% lower-dimensional features while staying within 2.5% average R@1 of the SOTA DINOv2-large two-stage method.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic prompt tuning and targeted local feature enhancement enable fast, compact, one-stage VPR with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Reliability-Driven Feature Correction for Hyperspectral and LiDAR Classification
summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) and LiDAR data provide complementary spectral and elevation information for land-cover classification. However, the spatially varying class-discriminative reliability of modality features is rarely modeled explicitly, allowing weak or ambiguous features to adversely affect cross-modal interaction and fusion. To address this issue, we propose ReDF, a reliability-driven framework that quantifies the reliability of each modality's features at each spatial location through the strength of class-related evidence they provide, and uses it to guide feature correction and fusion. Specifically, a Reliability-Guided Feature Correction module introduces a class prototype bank for each modality and converts feature-prototype similarities into class evidence for reliability estimation. The estimated reliabilities are used to construct a reliability-weighted shared representation and to guide bidirectional cross-modal feature correction based on neighborhood agreement, refining modality features with weak class evidence through information from the other modality. Building on these outputs, a Reliability-Guided Feature Reweighting module conditions a low-rank modulation on the estimated reliabilities and the cross-modal disagreement, and applies it to the corrected modality-specific descriptors to adaptively rescale each modality's contribution to the fused representation used for final classification. Experiments on three public HSI-LiDAR datasets show higher mean overall accuracy and Kappa than the compared methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ReDF, a reliability-driven framework for hyperspectral and LiDAR classification that estimates per-location modality reliability from class-prototype evidence to guide cross-modal correction and fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing HSI-LiDAR fusion methods rarely model spatially varying class-discriminative reliability explicitly, allowing weak or ambiguous modality features to corrupt cross-modal interaction.
AI.method: A Reliability-Guided Feature Correction module uses per-modality class prototype banks to convert feature-prototype similarities into class-evidence reliabilities, guiding bidirectional cross-modal correction via neighborhood agreement; a Reliability-Guided Feature Reweighting module then applies low-rank modulation conditioned on reliabilities and cross-modal disagreement to rescale each modality's contribution.
AI.result: Experiments on three public HSI-LiDAR datasets demonstrate higher mean overall accuracy and Kappa than compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly quantifying spatial class-evidence reliability improves cross-modal feature correction and fusion for multi-sensor land-cover classification.

title: Fast Training-Free Low-Light Video Enhancement with a Frozen Image Diffusion Prior
summary: Pretrained image diffusion models can enhance low-light video without low-light training data and without retraining for a new camera. ZVRD, the only published training-free method for low-light video, is too slow to use: our implementation needs over a minute per $256 \times 256$ frame. We present a causal, training-free pipeline that adds two temporal components to a frozen MR. Illuminate image prior. Temporal input fusion recursively averages motion-compensated low-light frames before diffusion inversion. Late-start offset propagation runs the full sampling trajectory only on key frames. Each non-key frame inverts the low-noise part of its own trajectory and adds an enhancement offset warped from the latest key frame. At ZVRD's own resolution the pipeline is $261\times$ faster than ZVRD and scores better on all five metrics we report. On 13 held-out SDSD clips at $1280 \times 720$, it improves on framewise eight-step processing by 0.55 dB in PSNR and 0.034 in LPIPS and halves the warping error, in 10% less time. Measurements inside the model show why, and a linear-Gaussian model of inversion explains them. Fusion removes frame-to-frame noise before inversion amplifies it. A flow error perturbs the transported offset ten times less than it perturbs a transported state. The perceptual gain does not transfer to low resolution: at $346 \times 260$, LPIPS is worse by 0.028. At 0.65 frames per second, the pipeline is an offline method.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a causal, training-free low-light video enhancement pipeline using a frozen image diffusion prior that runs 261x faster than ZVRD and improves PSNR by 0.55 dB on 720p SDSD clips.
AI.motivation: ZVRD, the only prior training-free low-light video enhancement method, takes over a minute per 256x256 frame, making it impractical to use.
AI.method: Built on a frozen MR. Illuminate image prior, the pipeline applies temporal input fusion (recursively averaging motion-compensated low-light frames before inversion) and late-start offset propagation (running full sampling only on key frames while non-key frames invert only the low-noise trajectory and add a warped enhancement offset).
AI.result: At ZVRD's resolution, the pipeline is 261x faster and beats ZVRD on all five reported metrics; on 13 held-out 1280x720 SDSD clips, it improves PSNR by 0.55 dB and LPIPS by 0.034 and halves warping error in 10% less time than framewise eight-step processing, though LPIPS degrades by 0.028 at 346x260 resolution and throughput is 0.65 fps.
AI.conclusion: Pre-inversion temporal fusion and offset propagation make training-free diffusion-based low-light video enhancement substantially faster and more temporally consistent at high resolutions.

title: Strong Fused Performance Can Mask Branch Collapse in a Dual-View Heart-Sound Classifier: A Three-Part Diagnostic Protocol
summary: Fusion models are usually judged by their fused score, a practice that assumes that every branch has learned something useful. We show that this assumption can fail silently in dual-view heart-sound classification. In AudioFuse, which fuses a spectrogram transformer with a waveform CNN, the spectrogram branch is unused despite strong fused performance when both branches are trained from scratch. We introduce a three-part diagnostic for branch collapse: whether deleting a branch changes the fused score, whether a linear probe on its features beats an untrained copy of the same branch, and whether the branch can learn its view when trained alone. Deleting the branch has negligible effect, and probing its features shows little improvement over an identically initialised, untrained copy. Yet the same architecture trained alone exceeds 0.9 AUC, so its view is learnable, while the jointly trained model is near chance when it must rely on this branch. Update statistics and an initialisation experiment point to an early optimisation imbalance. Moving a strong artificial label cue from one input to the other can switch which branch the model relies on, even though the branch architectures stay the same. We observe branch collapse on PhysioNet, but the full diagnostic is not met on ICBHI or CirCor. Fused performance alone therefore cannot establish that every branch learned a meaningful representation, and we recommend reporting branch deletion and an untrained-control probe alongside it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a three-part diagnostic protocol for branch collapse in multimodal classifiers, revealing that AudioFuse ignores its spectrogram transformer branch on PhysioNet despite high fused scores.
AI.motivation: Evaluating fusion models solely by fused accuracy assumes every branch learns useful representations, which can fail silently when one branch collapses.
AI.method: The diagnostic checks whether deleting a branch changes the fused score, whether a linear probe on its features beats an untrained copy, and whether the branch can learn its view alone; the authors also test moving an artificial label cue between inputs.
AI.result: On PhysioNet, deleting AudioFuse's spectrogram branch has negligible effect and probing it barely beats an untrained copy, even though the same branch exceeds 0.9 AUC when trained alone; early optimization imbalance drives this collapse, which does not meet the full diagnostic on ICBHI or CirCor.
AI.conclusion: Fused performance alone cannot verify multi-branch learning, so multimodal studies should report branch deletion and untrained-control probes.

title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We address two key questions: (1) when can we trust a world model for planning, and (2) what should we do when we cannot? We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CURE, a certificate-guided framework for action-conditioned world models that diagnoses when a world model can be trusted for planning and reduces regret by 10-64% over baselines.
AI.motivation: World models can generate plausible, realistic videos consistent with training data yet still lead to poor planning decisions when training support is missing.
AI.method: CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore) uses a decision-quality certificate to assess world-model trustworthiness and accordingly decides whether to upweight training data to debias the model, roll out more samples at test time, or explore to collect new data in unsupported regions.
AI.result: Across PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table (sim and real), certified decisions have much lower regret than uncertified ones (0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim; 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), and CURE lowers regret by 10-25% over the best pessimistic decision rule and by 41-64% over world-action models, search, and policy learning.
AI.conclusion: Certifying decision support rather than video perceptual quality is critical for reliable planning with action-conditioned world models.

title: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, yet their good-vs-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. We ask whether these models fail to see quality or fail to say it. Layer-wise probes on five VLMs point to the second: quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and still from the last language layer, far better than the answer reveals, and about a hundred labels recover most of it. The loss lies mainly in the final read-out, which partly reads something else: relative to human opinion, it over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness on all five models. We test this by intervention: if the read-out is at fault, a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron, fitted to many prompts at once, should close the gap and no more. Both hold. Under prompts never used for fitting, the edit recovers 86--100\% of what a ridge head on the last-layer state, fitted under the same prompts, finds beyond the answer on KonIQ. Where that gap is small, it gains little, too little for our transfer criterion on the two largest models; where the head itself is below the answer, it lowers the score; and it works only when written from the middle of the language model on. Unlike unconstrained fine-tuning, the edit leaves perception question answering intact. It does not carry over to yes-or-no or rating questions, and it reverses the good--poor contrast after sentiment-laden sentences. Code will be made available.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that VLMs encode image quality in their internal states but lose it in the final read-out, and a closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron recovers 86-100% of this gap on KonIQ.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot VLMs agree only moderately with human image quality judgments, and it is unclear whether they fail to perceive quality or fail to express it.
AI.method: Layer-wise probes on five VLMs diagnose where quality information is lost, followed by a closed-form edit to a single last-layer neuron fitted across multiple prompts simultaneously.
AI.result: Quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and last language layer, whereas the final read-out over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness; on KonIQ under held-out prompts, the single-neuron edit recovers 86-100% of what a ridge head finds beyond the answer while leaving perception QA intact, though it does not transfer to yes/no or rating questions and reverses after sentiment-laden sentences.
AI.conclusion: The zero-shot image quality gap in VLMs largely stems from a misaligned final read-out rather than visual representation failure, and can be partially corrected via targeted, non-destructive neuron editing.

title: Semantic-Guided Geometric Decoding for Token-Efficient Visual Grounding
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned visual perception. In pixel-to-sequence grounding, autoregressive coordinate generation requires multiple sequential decoding steps per box, increasing inference cost with the number of instances. Pixel-to-embedding methods reduce this overhead but lack explicit spatial encoding when using a shared special token. We introduce SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization. A geometric decoder reuses visual features and hidden states to recover precise discrete box coordinates in parallel. To train proposal generation and box localization together, we introduce Gaussian soft labels that encode coordinate distances during supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Reinforcement post-training further combines box-set rewards with coordinate supervision on model-generated proposals. This stage trains the language model and geometric decoder on their own predictions to mitigate the mismatch between teacher-forced training and inference. Across eight benchmarks spanning object detection, referring object detection, and document layout grounding, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIou among compared MLLMs on six benchmarks. It also delivers $2.07\times$ and $1.25\times$ the mean box-generation throughput of representative grounding baselines under vLLM and Transformers, respectively, while achieving higher accuracy in both comparisons.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SemGeo, a token-efficient visual grounding framework that uses a single grid token per instance plus a parallel geometric decoder, achieving top F1@mIoU on six of eight benchmarks at up to 2.07x throughput.
AI.motivation: Pixel-to-sequence MLLMs decode multiple coordinate tokens sequentially per box, slowing inference, while pixel-to-embedding methods using a shared token lack explicit spatial encoding.
AI.method: SemGeo represents each instance with a single grid token for coarse localization and uses a geometric decoder over visual features and hidden states to recover discrete box coordinates in parallel, trained with Gaussian soft labels during SFT and reinforcement post-training with box-set rewards on model-generated proposals.
AI.result: Across eight object detection, referring detection, and document layout benchmarks, SemGeo achieves the highest F1@mIoU on six benchmarks and delivers 2.07x (vLLM) and 1.25x (Transformers) mean box-generation throughput over representative baselines with higher accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Combining single-token coarse spatial grounding with parallel geometric decoding and on-policy RL post-training improves both speed and accuracy in MLLM visual grounding.

title: Distilling World Action Models for Efficient Bimanual Manipulation via Anchored Path Matching
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly generate future video and robot actions through iterative denoising. Few-step distillation reduces the number of model evaluations, but its coarse updates can move the student away from the teacher's trajectory. We propose Anchored Path Matching (APM), which supervises endpoint and short-transition predictions from states reached by the student. From each state, we continue the teacher to zero noise and use its endpoint and first intermediate state as targets. Modality-routed adapters learn to match both targets from the same starting state. When the two gradients conflict, anchor-priority updates preserve the endpoint gradient and remove the opposing component of the local gradient within each modality. One checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step joint generation. The sampling budget can be chosen at deployment without retraining or teacher queries. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train only on Clean demonstrations and evaluate directly on the domain-randomized Random setting. At one step, APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation at matched inference budgets by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random. Video peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) rises from 30.169 to 32.317 dB, with gains in structural similarity (SSIM) and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). On two real-robot tasks, APM improves success over the one-step teacher and reduces control-cycle latency by $21.3\times$ relative to the eight-step this http URL page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Anchored Path Matching (APM) to distill World Action Models into 1-, 2-, or 4-step generators, improving bimanual manipulation success and cutting real-robot latency by 21.3x.
AI.motivation: Few-step distillation of World Action Models suffers from coarse updates that drift away from the teacher's denoising trajectory.
AI.method: APM supervises both endpoint and short-transition predictions from student-reached states using teacher rollouts to zero noise, with modality-routed adapters and anchor-priority gradient updates that preserve the endpoint gradient when local gradients conflict; a single checkpoint supports 1-, 2-, and 4-step generation.
AI.result: On RoboTwin 2.0 (trained on Clean, evaluated on Clean and Random), one-step APM improves closed-loop success over continued base distillation by 2.0 percentage points on Clean and 1.4 on Random, raises video PSNR from 30.169 to 32.317 dB (with SSIM and LPIPS gains), and on two real-robot tasks improves success over the one-step teacher while cutting latency by 21.3x vs. the eight-step teacher.
AI.conclusion: Anchored Path Matching enables flexible, fast few-step distillation of World Action Models without sacrificing action success or video fidelity.

title: PlaceTally: A Test-Time Memory Model for Constructing Place Graphs
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code, data and supplementary material: this https URL
summary: Counting distinct objects in a video is hard when the camera returns to places it has seen. A vision-language model that reads the whole video answers with a few small numbers, and one that reads it in parts counts an object again in every part that shows it. Object trackers need the category before the video is read, or a fixed vocabulary. We observe that a memory for counting does not need to know what it is looking for, only where it has been: objects rarely leave a room between visits, so parts of a video grouped by place share almost no objects, and a place can be recognised before any question is asked. Building on this, we introduce PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that constructs a place graph for each video. Each video fragment joins the place of its best earlier match or opens a new place, because a strong match is rarely wrong while a true return often matches weakly. A frozen vision-language model counts each place once from at most 128 of its frames, so every read has a bounded input and the memory grows with the number of places; the graph is built 15 times faster than real time. On RevisitCount, our benchmark of real room re-recordings, it scores 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, against 51.2% and 44.3% for the same model reading the whole video. It stays level as rooms return more or less often, while a fixed correction of summed visits moves from 38.5% to 61.4%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that builds a place graph to count distinct objects in revisited-room videos, scoring 62.5% on RevisitCount at 15x real-time speed.
AI.motivation: VLMs undercount when reading whole videos and double-count objects across revisited rooms when reading in chunks, while object trackers require predefined categories or vocabularies.
AI.method: PlaceTally groups video fragments into a place graph by matching each fragment to its best earlier place or opening a new one, then uses a frozen VLM to count each place once from at most 128 frames, building the graph 15 times faster than real time.
AI.result: On the RevisitCount benchmark of real room re-recordings, PlaceTally achieves 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms (vs. 51.2% and 44.3% for whole-video VLM reading), remaining stable across varying revisit frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Organizing video memory by physical place rather than object category provides a fast, bounded-input solution for distinct object counting in long, revisited environments.

title: OVET-Consensus: Rank-Preserving Counterfactual Event Verification for Video Moment Grounding
summary: Modern video moment retrieval systems often propose windows that overlap the target event, yet still select the wrong one. We study this scorer bottleneck on QVHighlights with a fixed QD-DETR-derived temporal expert: the parent-aware temporal expert reaches 64.71 R1@0.5, while diagnostic oracles over the same candidate family reach 75.68 R1@0.5 within the parent-reranked pool and 94.97 R1@0.5 over the full 100-candidate evidence pool. We introduce OVET-Consensus, a rank-preserving counterfactual event verification layer that keeps the temporal expert's ranked list as the default and permits only high-confidence rank-1 overrides from a policy calibrated on held-out training videos. The verifier uses parent-aware interval evidence, structured Qwen3-VL event judgments, VideoLLaMA3 pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence, but never lets those signals freely reorder the top-K list. On QVHighlights validation, OVET-Consensus improves the parent-aware temporal expert from 64.71 to 65.35 R1@0.5 with a positive paired-bootstrap interval, while mAP is largely unchanged, from 42.67 to 42.74; it makes 20 overrides, with 15 helpful corrections and 3 harmful corrections. The results point to a practical constraint on verifier design: semantic compatibility is useful evidence, but temporal grounding still requires deciding where the event starts, changes, and ends inside a visually compatible scene.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OVET-Consensus, a rank-preserving counterfactual event verification layer for video moment grounding that improves QVHighlights R1@0.5 from 64.71 to 65.35.
AI.motivation: Video moment retrieval systems often propose windows overlapping the target event yet rank the wrong one first, while unconstrained reranking can degrade temporal boundaries.
AI.method: OVET-Consensus keeps a QD-DETR-derived temporal expert's ranked list as default and allows only high-confidence rank-1 overrides calibrated on held-out training videos, using parent-aware intervals, Qwen3-VL event judgments, VideoLLaMA3 pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence.
AI.result: On QVHighlights validation, OVET-Consensus improves R1@0.5 from 64.71 to 65.35 (with mAP 42.67 to 42.74), making 20 overrides with 15 helpful and 3 harmful corrections, compared to diagnostic oracle ceilings of 75.68 (parent-reranked pool) and 94.97 (full 100-candidate pool).
AI.conclusion: High-confidence, rank-preserving overrides can safely leverage semantic VLM verification without disrupting the temporal expert's boundary localization.

title: REVEAL: Reconstructing Video Amodal Content via Language and Flow Guidance
comment: Accepted to Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents REVEAL, a diffusion-based video amodal completion framework guided by text queries and optical-flow-warped masks, along with the LAVAT benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based video amodal completion methods lack auxiliary priors to reconstruct heavily occluded regions and maintain temporal consistency over long sequences.
AI.method: REVEAL uses a text query for open-vocabulary visible segmentation and semantic texture guidance, while warping previous visible masks via optical flow to form a shape prior for occluded regions.
AI.result: Evaluated on existing benchmarks and the new long-sequence LAVAT benchmark, REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance with strong temporal consistency under heavy occlusion.
AI.conclusion: Combining optical-flow shape propagation with language-guided texture completion enables coherent video amodal reconstruction over long sequences.

title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore
summary: Must a detector see generated images in order to catch them? Detection of AI-generated images has long faced two problems. The cues a detector learns from the few generators in its training set carry traces specific to those generators and transfer poorly to new ones, which limits generalization. The real and generated training images also differ in format and content, so the detector takes these differences as evidence of authenticity, and its decisions change with factors that have nothing to do with authenticity, which harms robustness as well as generalization. Both problems stem from training on generated images. A detector never trained on them can largely avoid both at the source. Vision foundation models have already learned the concept of "AI-generated" during pretraining, and text can point to it directly. Building on this, we propose SaySee, a training-free detector: Say builds a generation direction from sets of paired descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores an image by the projection of its embedding onto it, and See uses real images to correct the score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets that span standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data and the latest generators, SaySee reaches a mean AUC of 98.2% with MoE-ViE, 4.2 points above the best existing detector. When format is decoupled from authenticity, it remains the best of all methods. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SaySee, a training-free AI-generated image detector using language-defined authenticity directions and real-image offset correction, reaching 98.2% mean AUC across 24 datasets.
AI.motivation: Detectors trained on generated images overfit to generator-specific traces and format/content differences between real and fake training sets, hurting generalization and robustness.
AI.method: SaySee constructs a generation direction in a vision foundation model's embedding space from paired text descriptions differing only in authenticity (Say), and uses real images to correct score offsets caused by format, image type, and content (See).
AI.result: Across 24 evaluation sets spanning standard benchmarks, in-the-wild data, and recent generators, SaySee achieves 98.2% mean AUC with MoE-ViE, outperforming the best existing detector by 4.2 points and remaining top when format is decoupled from authenticity.
AI.conclusion: Detecting AI-generated images without ever training on generated samples avoids dataset-specific artifacts and yields strong cross-generator generalization.

title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OmniTongue, a fine-grained VQA benchmark of 1,351 images and 21,616 instruction pairs for Traditional Chinese Medicine tongue diagnosis, revealing poor MLLM performance.
AI.motivation: Existing TCM tongue diagnosis datasets are coarse-grained, single-dimensional, and ambiguously labeled, preventing rigorous evaluation of MLLMs' regional clinical perception.
AI.method: OmniTongue integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs spanning 16 clinical dimensions, region-specific pathological localization annotations, and 66 fine-grained diagnostic labels.
AI.result: Evaluations of existing MLLMs show large performance gaps, with medical-specific models offering no domain advantage and universally low Macro-F1 scores indicating reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine pathology understanding.
AI.conclusion: OmniTongue establishes a rigorous benchmark for diagnosing MLLM limitations in regional medical perception and advancing automated TCM tongue diagnosis.

title: Unified Residual Translation for Paired Image Restoration
summary: Paired image restoration spans changes in imaging contrast, sensor modality, and spatial resolution. These settings differ in their input channels and target grids, raising the question of how much of the prediction pipeline must be specialized to each task. We present the Unified Residual Translator (URT), which separates fixed channel and scale mapping from learned residual prediction. A deterministic reference uses channel averaging, replication, or bicubic interpolation to match the target dimensions, while a NAFNet encoder-decoder predicts an additive correction from the complete input. Separately trained instances share the prediction rule, $\ell_1$ objective, and optimizer across MRI contrast synthesis, visible-to-infrared translation, SAR-to-optical translation, and real-camera super-resolution. Across six task and scale settings, URT achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the evaluated baselines on IXI, SEN1-2, and RealSR $\times3$ and $\times4$. It reaches 30.774dB on IXI and 13.478dB on SEN1-2, with luminance PSNR of 33.596, 28.742, and 27.342dB at the three RealSR scales. On LLVIP, it ranks second in PSNR and SSIM. A study of four spectral alternatives identifies complementary benefits of fitted references and bandwise residual gains. Together, these results support explicit dimensional alignment and learned residual correction as a common formulation for heterogeneous paired imaging tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Unified Residual Translator (URT), separating deterministic dimensional alignment from NAFNet residual prediction, achieving top PSNR/SSIM across MRI, SAR-to-optical, and RealSR tasks.
AI.motivation: Paired image restoration tasks vary in input channels and target grids, raising the question of how much of the prediction pipeline actually needs task-specific specialization.
AI.method: URT computes a deterministic reference via channel averaging, replication, or bicubic interpolation to match target dimensions, and trains a NAFNet encoder-decoder with an L1 objective to predict an additive residual from the full input.
AI.result: Across six task and scale settings, URT achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM on IXI (30.774 dB), SEN1-2 (13.478 dB), and RealSR x3/x4 (luminance PSNR 33.596, 28.742, and 27.342 dB across scales), and ranks second on LLVIP.
AI.conclusion: Explicit deterministic alignment paired with learned residual correction provides a unified formulation for heterogeneous paired image restoration.

title: SpatialCast: Reading the 3D World via Cast Shadows
comment: 10 pages (main paper), 7 pages (supplementary material), 5 figures and 6 tables in the main paper
summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SpatialCast, a benchmark of 21,000 synthetic and 200 real questions using cast shadows to evaluate 3D physical scene reasoning in MLLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial benchmarks test relations and viewpoints but rarely evaluate whether MLLMs connect physical scene conditions (geometry, illumination, viewpoint) with visual observations.
AI.method: SpatialCast uses cast shadows across three tasks: scene-projection consistency, predicting intervention-induced changes, and inferring physical changes from visual transitions, and also tests GRPO post-training on SpatialCast data.
AI.result: Closed-source MLLMs outperform open-weight and spatial-specialized MLLMs (which score near chance on synthetic questions), though even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments; GRPO post-training improves open-weight MLLM scores on SpatialCast and transfers to external spatial benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Cast shadows offer a controlled diagnostic lens for 3D physical reasoning in MLLMs, and targeted RL post-training can improve transferable spatial skills.

title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VSpark, a speculative decoding method for autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models that achieves 1.28x to 2.10x lossless speedup across four VLAs and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard speculative decoding yields limited speedups for autoregressive VLAs because many action tokens encode similar motions, causing near-correct drafts to be rejected.
AI.method: VSpark trains a lightweight draft model on rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, aligns it to the VLA's hidden features rather than output tokens alone, and reuses VLA predictions along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step.
AI.result: Across four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves a 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping decoding lossless.
AI.conclusion: Noise-augmented rollouts, hidden-feature alignment, and continuation reuse unlock substantial lossless acceleration for autoregressive robot control.

title: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus
summary: Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that fail on underrepresented groups. Existing methods either correct human-specified bias attributes or infer unknown biases from the learned representation space. However, annotated attributes may differ from the shortcuts actually used by a model, while a single representation provides incomplete and potentially noisy evidence. Our key insight is that a bias obscured in one feature space may be clearer in another. In this work, we propose CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing), a multi-view framework that allows samples to "sing in chorus" across diverse representation spaces to achieve robust cross-view consensus. CHORD aggregates aggregates within-class partitions in each view, which is a proxy for specifying candidate biases, to debias the target representation and classifier without bias supervision. Experiments on seven benchmarks across vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy. Code and checkpoints are available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CHORD, a multi-view debiasing framework that aggregates within-class partitions across diverse representation spaces to mitigate spurious correlations without bias supervision.
AI.motivation: Single-representation bias inference provides noisy evidence, while human-annotated bias attributes may not match the actual shortcuts learned by deep models.
AI.method: CHORD (Cross-view Harmonic Outlier Reversal for Debiasing) aggregates within-class partitions across multiple diverse feature views as a proxy for candidate biases to achieve cross-view consensus and debias the target representation and classifier without bias labels.
AI.result: Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning vision, language, speech, and medical imaging show consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Cross-view consensus across diverse representation spaces provides a label-free, domain-general way to uncover and mitigate spurious correlations.

title: Beyond the Camera: A Tri-Modal Driving World Model for Future RGB, Thermal, and LiDAR Forecasting in Adverse Weather
summary: Driving world models forecast what a vehicle's sensors will record next. Most forecast camera video and some add LiDAR, but thermal cameras, which still see in darkness and some adverse weather, are rarely a forecast target, and to our knowledge no world model forecasts all three sensors. We study joint forecasting of RGB, thermal, and LiDAR on real adverse-weather sequences of the DSERT-RoLL dataset. We post-train a pretrained video world model for each sensor and represent LiDAR as a depth video aligned with the RGB camera, with densification and encoding chosen by what the model's video tokenizer can reconstruct. A tri-sensor model sees all three sensors as one video. We score LiDAR in meters against measured returns and compare against persistence baselines passed through the same tokenizer as the model. With this matching, an apparent loss of the thermal model to persistence in fog disappears. On all 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence. Joint training lowers the LiDAR error at 2s by 2.1m at a small cost in camera fidelity, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR forecasts beat persistence in mean error. Blanking one sensor degrades the forecasts of the others more in snow than in fog.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a tri-modal driving world model that jointly forecasts future RGB, thermal, and LiDAR on adverse-weather DSERT-RoLL sequences, beating persistence in all three modalities.
AI.motivation: Driving world models rarely forecast thermal imagery (which sees through darkness and adverse weather), and none jointly forecast RGB, thermal, and LiDAR.
AI.method: The authors post-train a pretrained video world model on DSERT-RoLL, encoding LiDAR as camera-aligned depth video matched to the video tokenizer, and compare against compression-matched persistence baselines.
AI.result: Across 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence; joint tri-sensor training cuts 2 s LiDAR error by 2.1 m at a small camera-fidelity cost, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR beats persistence in mean error, while sensor blanking hurts other forecasts more in snow than in fog.
AI.conclusion: Joint tri-modal video world modeling enables accurate multi-sensor forecasting in adverse weather, with thermal and LiDAR providing complementary resilience.

title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation
summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FVScore, a neuro-symbolic video evaluation framework using soft Linear Temporal Logic over grounded propositions, outperforming holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM and vision-language video evaluators struggle to align with human judgments and cannot trace scores to specific temporal violations.
AI.method: FVScore compiles each video into explicit prompt propositions and implicit physical/temporal/cross-modal constraints, grounds them with specialized perceptual tools, evaluates confidence traces via soft Linear Temporal Logic operators, and applies Significance-Aware Calibration to retain only perceptually significant violations.
AI.result: Across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with leading video models, FVScore achieves higher correlation with human judgments than holistic and agent-based evaluators while producing timestamp- and evidence-grounded reports.
AI.conclusion: Grounded neuro-symbolic verification with temporal logic provides more faithful and interpretable evaluation of generated videos.

title: Classification of Tissues on MALDI-MSI Image Modality for Pancreatic Cancer Studies
summary: Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) spatially maps molecular distributions in tissue sections. Despite the availability of preprocessing tools for MSI data, building end-to-end workflows suitable for deep learning remains challenging. We have developed a fully automated pipeline for transformation of raw Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Mass Spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) data into deep-learning-ready image patches for binary pancreatic tissue classification (tumoral vs non-tumoral) and built individual models for recognition of tumoral regions in spectral images. Images resulting from the proposed pipeline and from reference interactive workflow are very close in terms of image quality metric mean squared error (MSE). The proposed pipeline computational time is of 20 min in average compared to a full working day of the reference interactive workflow. The models achieved 0.94 accuracy on high-resolution spectra and a mean accuracy of 0.59 on lower-resolution spectra.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an automated pipeline converting raw MALDI-MSI data into deep-learning-ready patches for pancreatic tumor classification, cutting processing time from a full day to 20 minutes and reaching 0.94 accuracy.
AI.motivation: Despite existing preprocessing tools, building end-to-end deep learning workflows for Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) tissue classification remains slow and manual.
AI.method: The automated pipeline transforms raw MALDI-MSI spectra into image patches for binary pancreatic tissue classification (tumoral vs. non-tumoral) and trains individual recognition models on the spectral images.
AI.result: Output images closely match a reference interactive workflow in MSE while reducing average computation time from a full working day to 20 minutes, and the classifiers achieve 0.94 accuracy on high-resolution spectra (0.59 mean accuracy on lower-resolution spectra).
AI.conclusion: Automating MALDI-MSI patch generation enables fast, scalable deep-learning tissue classification for pancreatic cancer studies.

title: CascadeJEPA: Enhancing 3D Geometric Representations via Spatially Coupled Cascaded Prediction
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for predictive visual representation learning. However, our analysis of I-JEPA reveals a growing discrepancy between semantic and geometric learning: improved semantic recognition during pretraining is accompanied by degraded 3D geometric representations. We hypothesize that this partly stems from predicting highly abstract latent representations with incomplete spatial context, favoring semantic regularities over fine-grained geometric information. To address this issue, we introduce CascadeJEPA, a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework that promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages, while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition performance. Furthermore, its advantages extend to future feature forecasting and world model planning, highlighting the potential of enhanced geometric representations to support predictive world modeling.

AI.tldr: CascadeJEPA is a spatially coupled cascaded prediction framework for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures that improves 3D geometric representations without sacrificing semantic recognition.
AI.motivation: Analysis of I-JEPA shows that improved semantic recognition during pretraining comes at the cost of degraded 3D geometric representations, likely because predicting abstract latents with incomplete spatial context favors semantics over fine-grained geometry.
AI.method: The framework promotes richer patch-level interactions through full-grid context encoding and cross-attention between prediction stages while largely preserving the original I-JEPA architecture.
AI.result: Experiments show substantial improvements over I-JEPA across multiple 3D geometric tasks while maintaining strong semantic recognition, with gains extending to future feature forecasting and world model planning.
AI.conclusion: Enhancing spatial coupling in JEPA prediction preserves fine-grained 3D geometry and supports downstream predictive world modeling.

title: TANGO: Real-World Unregistered RGB-Guided Hyperspectral Super-Resolution with Two-Camera Acquisitions
comment: 18 pages, 11 Figures, 10 tables. Submitted to CVPR 2027
summary: Unregistered hyperspectral image super-resolution aims to recover a high-resolution HSI from a low-resolution hyperspectral observation and an unregistered high-resolution RGB reference. Although recent methods have begun to address the geometric misalignment between the two modalities, their evaluation is still constrained by the lack of a large-scale public benchmark based on real two-camera RGB--HSI acquisitions with a high-resolution HSI reference. To address this gap, we introduce DUET, the first large-scale public dataset for unregistered RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution, comprising 403 indoor and outdoor scenes captured with two separate RGB and hyperspectral cameras. We further propose TANGO (Two-camera AligNment with Gated Occlusions), which first compensates for the dominant cross-camera displacement through end-to-end global alignment and then refines the remaining inconsistencies with a coarse-to-fine local feature alignment. A learned gating mechanism further attenuates the RGB guidance where the two views cannot be consistently matched. Experimental results show that TANGO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both DUET and REAL across all evaluated scale factors, outperforming the strongest competitor on DUET by up to 2.29 dB in PSNR while requiring 2.5$\times$ fewer FLOPs. The code and dataset will be available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DUET, a real-world two-camera RGB-HSI super-resolution dataset, and TANGO, an alignment and gated-fusion network that achieves state-of-the-art unregistered hyperspectral super-resolution.
AI.motivation: Existing unregistered RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution methods lack a large-scale public benchmark of real two-camera RGB-HSI acquisitions with high-resolution HSI references.
AI.method: DUET provides 403 indoor and outdoor scenes from separate RGB and hyperspectral cameras, while TANGO performs end-to-end global alignment, coarse-to-fine local feature alignment, and learned gating to attenuate RGB guidance in inconsistent regions.
AI.result: TANGO achieves state-of-the-art results on DUET and REAL across all evaluated scale factors, outperforming the strongest competitor on DUET by up to 2.29 dB in PSNR with 2.5x fewer FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Real two-camera benchmarking paired with hierarchical alignment and occlusion gating enables accurate and efficient unregistered hyperspectral super-resolution.

title: Know When to Zoom: How Small Is Too Small for Vision-Language Models?
comment: Accepted to the SENSE workshop at WACV 2027. 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code, data and a plain-language walkthrough: this https URL
summary: Online vision-language models often miss small details in large images, because the service shrinks the image, or rejects it, before the model ever sees it. A car 20 pixels wide in an 8000 by 6000 drone photo reaches Claude about 6 pixels wide, and OpenAI's default rejects the photo outright. We measure how much detail survives for seven models from four vendors, using an eye exam of printed codes and 601 questions about small objects in real photos. The smallest text a model reads half the time grows from 6 pixels or less on a small image to a predicted 10 to 13 pixels on a 7680 by 4320 photo at default settings. Zooming wins much of the detail back. Splitting each photo into up to nine tiles raises accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points for Claude and Gemini, and by avoiding rejections it lifts GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7%. A two-step zoom, in which the model first names the region it needs, matches or beats tiles on Gemini and comes within 2.5 points of them on Claude, with about 40% of their image tokens. When a detail is lost, Claude and Gemini both say they cannot tell about half the time, but they fail differently in the rest: Gemini gives a confident wrong answer in 43% to 48% of these cases, Claude in only 5% to 9%. A check based on detail size, run before the call, misses most of the gain from tiles on Claude and Gemini, but Claude's own reply is a reliable trigger: tiling only after an unsure reply comes within 1.4 points of always tiling with 62% to 70% of the image tokens. We turn these findings into five rules for when an agent should zoom, and release the eye exam, every model answer and code at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This study measures how online vision-language models lose small details in large images due to resizing or rejection and establishes five rules for when and how agents should zoom.
AI.motivation: Online VLM services shrink or reject large images before the model sees them, causing small objects and text to become unreadable.
AI.method: Using printed-code eye exams and 601 real-photo questions across seven models from four vendors, the authors evaluate tiling (up to nine tiles) and a two-step zoom where the model names a region first.
AI.result: Tiling raises accuracy by 11.1 to 14.5 percentage points on Claude and Gemini and lifts GPT-6.1 Sol from 50.7% to 83.7%, while two-step zoom matches or beats tiling on Gemini and comes within 2.5 points on Claude using about 40% of the image tokens; triggering tiles only after an unsure Claude reply comes within 1.4 points of always tiling using 62% to 70% of the tokens.
AI.conclusion: Targeted zooming and model-uncertainty triggers recover lost fine detail in high-resolution images at substantially lower token cost than uniform tiling.

title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
summary: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.

AI.tldr: PCRG is a training-free pruning and caching method for reference-to-video diffusion transformers that accelerates generation by removing or reusing redundant reference tokens.
AI.motivation: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack reference and generated latents into one full-attention sequence where reference tokens form about half the sequence and dominate quadratic attention cost despite mostly being static or irrelevant.
AI.method: PCRG uses low-level VAE latent redundancy and high-level VLM conditioner attention importance to prune unimportant redundant tokens before the first step, cache keys and values for important redundant tokens, and keep non-redundant tokens active.
AI.result: On int8-quantized 8-step MiniMax-H3, PCRG achieves 1.57x end-to-end speedup on V2V-Bench and 1.49x on VACE-Benchmark with VBench quality drops of only 0.24% and 0.17%, and stacks with TeaCache, Spark, and Veda for up to 2.15x speedup.
AI.conclusion: Shortening the reference sequence using existing internal signals provides plug-and-play acceleration that composes cleanly with step caching and sparse attention.

title: Practice in Text, Act in Pixels: Correcting Where Perception Fails
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, 19 tables. Code: this https URL ; aligned reader: this https URL
summary: GUI agents can learn cheaply from a text view of an interface and act on screenshots through a vision-language screen reader. Yet on a simulated mobile platform with a low-cost reader, policies that complete most tasks in text fail on many of the same tasks on screenshots. We ask where a small budget of real screenshots is best spent to close this gap. We find that the reader's misreads are systematic and recur on the same interface elements. Noise matched to the reader's error rates, a natural sim-to-real remedy, misses this structure, and in a pre-specified comparison it did not beat training the policy directly on screenshots. We therefore correct the misreads at their source with reader alignment, which fine-tunes the reader on screenshots paired with their text views. The reader learns to output each screen's text view, as in text practice, and the policy stays unchanged. Spent on the reader, the screenshot budget gives 80.9% full-task success on new task instances, against 55.6% when spent on training the policy. Given the same labeled screenshots, adapting the reader also beats adapting the policy, and a single aligned reader improves every text-trained policy we tried without retraining any of them.

AI.tldr: Reader alignment fine-tunes a GUI screen reader on paired screenshots and text views to close the sim-to-real gap for text-trained GUI agents.
AI.motivation: GUI policies trained cheaply on text views fail on screenshots when paired with a low-cost vision-language screen reader, and matching noise to error rates fails to capture the reader's systematic misreads.
AI.method: Instead of retraining the policy on screenshots, reader alignment fine-tunes the screen reader on screenshots paired with their text views so it outputs the expected text representation while keeping the policy unchanged.
AI.result: Spending the screenshot budget on reader alignment yields 80.9% full-task success on new task instances compared to 55.6% when spent on training the policy, and one aligned reader improves every tested text-trained policy without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Correcting perception errors at the screen reader level is more sample-efficient and reusable than adapting downstream GUI policies directly on pixels.

title: ConserveEdit: Source-Anchored Transactions for Drift-Bounded Iterative Image Editing
comment: 28 pages, 15 figures, 16 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Instruction-driven image editors produce convincing local edits in one pass, but inside an iterative refinement loop every accepted output becomes the next input, so unintended changes outside the requested region accumulate. We present ConserveEdit, an editor-agnostic controller that treats each refinement step as a transaction against a contract compiled once from the source image. The contract separates what may change (the authorized region of each target, with a bounded halo for shadows and reflections) from what must survive (protected content with explicit tolerances). Candidates from a frozen editor are composed through a source-anchored mask and committed only if target progress, drift on protected content, and image quality pass as separate tests; otherwise the step is rolled back and repaired. For any editor, this keeps every pixel outside the authorized region bit-exact and bounds drift independently of the number of iterations, whereas no fixed scalar trade-off reproduces the separate tests. On all 1053 MagicBrush test edits with a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit, masking is necessary but not sufficient. A direct call already alters the rest of the image (12.1 dB PSNR outside the mask); composed through the source-anchored mask, it stays bit-exact there and its DINO similarity to the ground truth rises from 0.67 to 0.85, matching ConserveEdit, so this gain comes from the mask. Next to automatic masks, however, masked direct editing changes a protected face or text on 48% of turns, and masked scalar selection avoids this mostly by abstaining (23% constrained success). Because its drift test names the violated entity, ConserveEdit shrinks the support instead (2% violations, 53% constrained success); in a simulator with known ground truth it raises constrained success from 55.0% to 61.8%. Automatic grounding remains the main bottleneck. Code and logs will be released.

AI.tldr: ConserveEdit is an editor-agnostic transaction controller that bounds drift in iterative image editing by verifying target progress, protected-content drift, and image quality as separate tests.
AI.motivation: Iterative instruction-driven image editing accumulates unintended changes outside the target region because each accepted output becomes the next input.
AI.method: ConserveEdit compiles a source-image contract separating authorized edit regions from protected content, composes frozen-editor candidates through a source-anchored mask, and commits a step only if separate progress, drift, and quality tests pass, rolling back and repairing otherwise.
AI.result: On 1053 MagicBrush edits with Qwen-Image-Edit, source-anchored masking keeps outside pixels bit-exact and raises DINO similarity from 0.67 to 0.85, while ConserveEdit cuts protected face or text violations from 48% to 2% with 53% constrained success (versus 23% for masked scalar selection) and raises simulator constrained success from 55.0% to 61.8%.
AI.conclusion: Treating iterative edits as source-anchored transactions with separate entity-level drift tests prevents cumulative corruption without retraining the underlying editor.

title: SlopeGuard: Towards Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection via Radial Spectral Slope Guidance
summary: AI-generated image detectors often overfit to generator-specific artifacts, hindering generalization to unseen synthesis pipelines. Existing frequency-based methods usually learn high-dimensional spectral patterns that may preserve generator-dependent variations. We explore Radial Spectral Slope, a compact descriptor of global spectral decay that captures transferable spectral trends while suppressing fine-grained variations. Our analysis shows that real and generated images exhibit systematic but generator-dependent slope differences, indicating that slope provides useful forensic evidence but is insufficient as a standalone decision criterion. This motivates combining spectral slope with semantic representations for more robust detection. Based on this insight, we propose SlopeGuard, which couples slope-aware data processing with slope guided feature learning to construct informative patch-based views, integrate Radial Spectral Slope with semantic features, and adapt prior preservation according to spectral atypicality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SlopeGuard achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracies of 97.5% on AIGCDetectBench, 97.8% on GenImage, and 85.1% on AIGIBench, while maintaining competitive performance under blur, cropping, JPEG compression, and additive noise.

AI.tldr: SlopeGuard combines Radial Spectral Slope with semantic features to improve generalization in AI-generated image detection across unseen generators.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-generated image detectors and high-dimensional frequency methods overfit to generator-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to unseen synthesis pipelines.
AI.method: SlopeGuard extracts Radial Spectral Slope as a compact descriptor of global spectral decay and pairs slope-aware patch processing with slope-guided feature learning that integrates spectral slope, semantic features, and atypicality-adaptive prior preservation.
AI.result: SlopeGuard achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracies of 97.5% on AIGCDetectBench, 97.8% on GenImage, and 85.1% on AIGIBench, while remaining competitive under blur, cropping, JPEG compression, and additive noise.
