AI.conclusion: Coupling a compact global spectral decay descriptor with semantic representations yields robust, cross-generator synthetic image detection.

title: Evolve in Panorama, Render in View: Panoramic World State Evolution for Video World Models
summary: Video world models should maintain a world that keeps evolving as the viewpoint changes. Yet when the camera turns away and returns, current models often freeze the unobserved scene, lose objects, or change their appearance, because content outside the view has no representation that keeps changing. We present PanoEvo, which uses a Panoramic Evolver to evolve the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model, where every viewing direction is present at every time step, so the scene evolves whether or not it is observed. Existing panoramic video models are not trained to evolve a scene from a single image or the objects within it, so we build PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360° videos, and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine as an image-to-panoramic-video model. Since each view covers only a small part of the low-resolution panorama, directly projected views are blurry and often show low-quality details or structural errors. A Perspective Renderer, built on a perspective video diffusion model, reads this state via latent-space projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to render sharp, high-quality views. PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench. Code, models, and data will be released.

AI.tldr: PanoEvo maintains evolving unobserved world state in a panoramic video diffusion latent space and renders sharp perspective views for video world models.
AI.motivation: Current video world models freeze, lose, or alter unobserved scene regions when the camera turns away and returns because out-of-view content lacks an evolving representation.
AI.method: A Panoramic Evolver trained coarse-to-fine on a new 360-degree event-centric dataset (PanoEvo-Data) evolves the full 360-degree latent state at every step, and a Perspective Renderer reads this state via latent projection and direction-restricted cross-attention.
AI.result: PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling global panoramic state evolution from perspective rendering enables temporally consistent world dynamics across large camera rotations.

title: RefCloth: Transferable Adversarial Tablecloths for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Closed-loop vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely continuously on multi-view cameras, yet existing visual attacks typically hijack sensor streams with 2D patches or alter target object meshes that require retraining when manipulation objects change. We introduce RefCloth, a framework that optimizes one persistent adversarial tablecloth on a frozen source policy and deploys it zero-shot across unseen tasks and target models without modifying task objects or cameras. Throughout manipulation, static third-person and moving wrist views observe this shared world-bound texture under evolving occlusions. To generalize across shifting surface views while bridging the gap between differentiable and native renderers, RefCloth combines bounded texture parameterization with shared surface UV transformations and a same-path clean reference that removes static rendering offsets at initialization. Across four LIBERO suites in native simulation, one frozen texture transfers from OpenVLA-OFT to $\pi_0$ and $\pi_{0.5}$, reducing success relative to an unoptimized cloth by 62.50 and 43.75 percentage points on average and far exceeding amplitude- and variation-matched random controls. Dual-view audits and target closed-loop camera interventions show that moving wrist exposure drives over twice the standalone drop of the main view with strong synergy, while ablations confirm the roles of UV diversification and path calibration.

AI.tldr: RefCloth optimizes a single persistent adversarial tablecloth that transfers zero-shot across unseen tasks and target vision-language-action (VLA) models.
AI.motivation: Existing visual attacks on closed-loop VLA policies rely on 2D sensor hijacking or object-specific mesh edits that require retraining when manipulation targets change.
AI.method: RefCloth combines bounded texture parameterization, shared surface UV transformations, and a same-path clean reference to optimize a world-bound texture on a frozen source policy across static third-person and moving wrist camera views.
AI.result: Across four LIBERO suites in native simulation, a single texture optimized on OpenVLA-OFT transfers to pi_0 and pi_0.5, reducing success rates by 62.50 and 43.75 percentage points on average relative to an unoptimized cloth.
AI.conclusion: World-bound surface textures can persistently disrupt multi-view closed-loop VLA policies zero-shot across tasks and model architectures.

title: GaussianMamba: Geometric and Relational State Space Scanning of 3D Gaussian Primitives
summary: 3D semantic occupancy prediction requires representing complex spatial structures and modeling contextual relationships across a scene. 3D Gaussian primitives provide a sparse and adaptive representation of scene geometry and semantics, while Mamba offers efficient sequence modeling for capturing dependencies among primitives. However, Gaussian primitives are irregular and unordered, making sequence construction challenging, as conventional spatial ordering may overlook their anisotropic geometry and feature-semantic relationships. In this paper, we present GaussianMamba, a dual-branch Mamba framework that explicitly incorporates Gaussian-specific geometric and feature-semantic relationships into complementary scanning strategies. The first branch refines a locality-preserving traversal using anisotropic Gaussian support derived from primitive scale and orientation. The second branch reorders spatially organized groups according to feature-semantic affinity and adjusts local features using geometry-weighted semantic differences. The resulting sequences are processed by separate Mamba modules, and their features are fused through a support-aware mechanism that incorporates local feature discrepancies arising from the distinct scanning paths. Experiments on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360 demonstrate consistent improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 in both IoU and mIoU.

AI.tldr: GaussianMamba is a dual-branch state space framework that scans 3D Gaussian primitives along both anisotropic geometric and feature-semantic orderings for 3D semantic occupancy prediction.
AI.motivation: 3D Gaussian primitives are irregular and unordered, so conventional spatial scanning overlooks their anisotropic geometry and semantic relationships when modeling scene context with Mamba.
AI.method: One branch refines locality-preserving traversal using anisotropic Gaussian support from scale and orientation, while the second reorders spatial groups by feature-semantic affinity and adjusts local features with geometry-weighted semantic differences before support-aware fusion.
AI.result: Experiments on nuScenes-SurroundOcc and SSCBench-KITTI-360 show consistent improvements over GaussianFormer and GaussianFormer-2 in both IoU and mIoU.
AI.conclusion: Tailoring Mamba scanning paths to the anisotropic geometry and semantic affinity of 3D Gaussians improves 3D semantic occupancy prediction.

title: Teaching What to Look For: Privileged Perception Questions for Agentic On-Policy Distillation in Video Captioning
summary: Detailed video captioning requires comprehensive and faithful descriptions of objects, actions, and temporal events. Fixed-frame sampling, however, can miss brief motions, small objects, and other fine-grained evidence, motivating captioning agents that actively seek relevant moments and inspect local regions. Training such behavior is challenging because, unlike video question answering, generic captioning instructions do not specify what visual evidence should be acquired. We propose Perception-Question On-Policy Distillation (PQ-OPD), which uses training-only Perception Questions (PQs) to guide active video perception. PQs specify what should be inspected without revealing the corresponding answers, encouraging the teacher to explore the video more comprehensively and focus on relevant visual evidence. Along trajectories generated by the student, on-policy distillation transfers this guidance to the student's reasoning, tool calls, and captions; no PQs are required at inference. Across three detailed-captioning and two caption-to-QA benchmarks, PQ-OPD consistently improves the corresponding untrained agents across teacher-student scales and input-frame budgets. Under our evaluation protocol, PQ-OPD achieves the strongest primary-metric results among the compared open-source models on DREAM-1K, CaReBench, ShortVidBench, MotionBench, and VidCapBench-AE. Our ablations, together with analysis of temporal coverage and answer leakage, further indicates that the student internalizes the training-time guidance as a more effective video exploration policy.

AI.tldr: PQ-OPD uses training-only Perception Questions to guide teacher exploration during on-policy distillation, improving active video perception in captioning agents.
AI.motivation: Generic video captioning instructions do not specify what visual evidence to seek, making it hard to train captioning agents to actively inspect brief motions or small objects.
AI.method: During training, Perception Questions specify what to inspect without revealing answers so the teacher explores more comprehensively, and on-policy distillation transfers this exploration, reasoning, and tool-use behavior to the student without needing questions at inference.
AI.result: PQ-OPD consistently improves untrained agents across scales and frame budgets, achieving the strongest primary-metric results among compared open-source models on DREAM-1K, CaReBench, ShortVidBench, MotionBench, and VidCapBench-AE.
AI.conclusion: Privileged perception questions provide an effective training signal for distilling active visual exploration policies into video captioning agents.

title: ForceBody: Force-Paired Parametric Body Motion with Torque Uncertainty
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track
summary: Forces and torques drive human motion, central to biomechanics, robotics, and physics-aware animation, yet they are often absent from learning-based motion pipelines for body reconstruction and generation. Some motion datasets provide force annotations, but the paired motion sequences are incompatible with the parametric body models used in modern learning pipelines. In addition, existing datasets typically obtain joint torques through inverse dynamics, which is inherently sensitive to the quality of the input kinematics; however, they do not quantify the reliability of these torque estimates. We close this gap with ForceBody, the first dataset to bring ground truth force supervision into a parametric body representation, shipped with per-sample torque uncertainty. ForceBody pairs the SKEL body model with ground reaction forces and inverse-dynamics joint torques across 10,386 motion trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects. Each torque label is paired with a per-frame, per-joint uncertainty annotation obtained by Monte Carlo sampling through the inverse dynamics pipeline. We benchmark six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) on ground reaction force and joint torque prediction from SKEL motion. As one example use of the released uncertainty, finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces the MAE of joint torque estimation by 5%. Code and data are at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ForceBody is the first dataset pairing a parametric body model (SKEL) with ground reaction forces and per-sample inverse-dynamics joint torque uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Existing force-paired motion datasets are incompatible with modern parametric body models and lack reliability estimates for inverse-dynamics joint torques.
AI.method: ForceBody pairs SKEL motion with ground reaction forces and inverse-dynamics joint torques across 10,386 trials (9.7M frames, 26.9 hours) from 140 subjects, adding per-frame, per-joint uncertainty via Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.result: The authors benchmark six architectures (MLP, Conv1D, LSTM, GRU, Mamba2, Transformer) and show that finetuning a Transformer with per-sample uncertainty weighting reduces joint torque MAE by 5%.
AI.conclusion: Providing force supervision and torque uncertainty in a standard parametric body format supports more reliable physics-aware human motion modeling.

title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding
comment: 25 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.

AI.tldr: NexSight introduces SightForge, SightLine, and SightLoop to build and evaluate verifiable, evidence-traceable tasks for fine-grained agentic long-video understanding.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained counting and ordering questions in long videos require dense temporal evidence, yet answer-only supervision fails to supervise evidence search and sparse checks miss omitted or double-counted events.
AI.method: SightForge accepts tasks only when a blind verifier reconstructs the answer from densely reacquired video evidence and counterexample checks fail to refute it, producing 310 tasks (SightLine) evaluated in a multiscale harness (SightLoop) whose solver trajectories provide step-level supervision.
AI.result: The strongest model scores 54.52% on SightLine versus 79.35% with annotated evidence, while post-training Sight-35B on under 6K examples nearly doubles its interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), beats its 397B family counterpart, and gains over 8 points on two external benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable evidence-traceable task construction and trajectory supervision substantially improve agentic search and reasoning in long videos.

title: Visual Harness Scales General VLMs to Medical Images
summary: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce \ours, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With \ours, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, \ours improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3\% to 98.3\%), renal search (57.5\% to 71.2\%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0\% to 28.2\%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with \ours. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8\% to 69.2\% with \ours, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.

AI.tldr: A medical visual harness equips general vision-language models with interactive visual tools, lossless evidence memory, and iterative self-assessment to scale performance on medical images.
AI.motivation: General VLMs struggle on specialized medical imaging tasks when relying on single-pass image inspection without structured diagnostic verification.
AI.method: The harness provides interactive visual tools, stores acquired findings in lossless memory, and runs an iterative agentic loop that assesses potential omissions and finding reliability to guide further inspection and answer revision.
AI.result: Across 11 tasks and four modalities, the harness improves Qwen3.8-27B on every task—such as spleen measurement (63.3% to 98.3%), renal search (57.5% to 71.2%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0% to 28.2%)—and boosts GPT-6.1 Sol pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8% to 69.2%.
AI.conclusion: Interactive visual harnesses with structured evidence management offer an effective paradigm for scaling general VLMs to clinical imaging tasks.

title: Pixel is All You Need
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables, including references and appendices
summary: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

AI.tldr: Purely pixel-space generative models trained from scratch without text pathways can read, write intermediate reasoning steps, and solve symbolic tasks directly on a visual canvas.
AI.motivation: Current image, video, and unified multimodal generators fail at symbolic reasoning over rendered text unless an underlying text module supplies the answer.
AI.method: The authors train purely pixel-space generative models from scratch with images as the sole input and output, evaluating scaling behavior, frame-by-frame intermediate step generation, and reinforcement-learning post-training.
AI.result: Performance scales with model size following a power law, frame-by-frame intermediate steps substantially outperform single-frame answering, and RL post-training further strengthens reasoning while enabling cross-modal reasoning on a shared canvas.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic reasoning failures in current visual generators stem from training paradigms rather than pixels themselves, showing that pure pixel-space models can exhibit LLM-like reasoning behaviors.

title: A tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude open-water search and rescue
summary: Large aerial platforms often operate above 1.5 km to improve the efficiency of open water search and rescue (OW-SAR). However, long imaging distances, wide fields of view, and limited sensor resolution reduce objects to a few pixels, increasing their susceptibility to environmental interference and making detection harder than for conventional small objects. To our knowledge, existing datasets focus on low-altitude scenarios and do not support automatic detection at 1.5-2.0 km. We therefore present TinyWOD, a tiny object detection dataset for high-altitude OW-SAR using lifebuoys as detection targets. It comprises 11,359 manually annotated images and 19,505 annotated instances spanning diverse environments, lighting conditions, water colors, and surface ripples. Compared with existing datasets, TinyWOD contains much smaller objects and a substantially higher proportion of tiny instances; its average equivalent side length (ESL) is 12.7 pixels, with 76.96% of in stances having ESLs below 15 pixels, reflecting actual high-altitude water-rescue imaging conditions. We define APtiny, a tiny object detection metric, and benchmark mainstream and state-of-the-art networks using this and conventional metrics. All evaluated networks effectively detect tiny waterborne objects, demonstrating TinyWOD's reusability and utility. We expect this dataset to support research on tiny object detection in high-altitude OW-SAR.

AI.tldr: TinyWOD is a tiny object detection dataset of 11,359 images and 19,505 lifebuoy instances captured for high-altitude (1.5-2.0 km) open-water search and rescue.
AI.motivation: Existing aerial datasets focus on low-altitude scenes and do not support detecting objects reduced to a few pixels in high-altitude open-water search and rescue.
AI.method: The authors curate 11,359 manually annotated images with 19,505 lifebuoy instances across varied water, lighting, and ripple conditions (average equivalent side length 12.7 pixels, 76.96% below 15 pixels) and define the APtiny evaluation metric.
AI.result: Benchmarking mainstream and state-of-the-art detectors on TinyWOD using APtiny and standard metrics shows that all evaluated networks can effectively detect tiny waterborne targets.
AI.conclusion: TinyWOD and APtiny provide a dedicated benchmark for advancing tiny object detection in high-altitude maritime search and rescue.

title: Kolibri: Color Finds the Place, Refinement Sets the Pose for RGB-D Localization in Colored Point Clouds
summary: An agent or robot in a scanned building must locate its camera in rooms that no model saw during training. Point cloud registration methods can align each RGB-D frame with the building's colored point cloud, accurately but at a high cost. We observe that geometric refinement brings nearby initial poses to the same final pose, so the learned component only needs to find the place. Kolibri does this with a graph network of 55,712 parameters that describes 10 cm cubes of points, called cells, by their color, local shape and neighbors. With the same refinement, it matches GeDi on 96 unseen ScanNet rooms (81.4% against 80.3% within 5 cm and 5°) and on a held-out test of 10 further rooms, in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti. The saved time allows for search without a room label. In one point cloud of 100 rooms, Kolibri loses 1.3 points against knowing the room, while retrieving the room first loses 56.0. In a hospital emergency department scene from a real scan, it localizes 86.5% of the frames rendered from the scan in 384 ms each, where GeDi needs 91 minutes per frame on cubes of the scan for a similar recall. The method needs colors that agree between the frame and the point cloud. On gray frames and across cameras with different color responses, point cloud registration methods keep the lead.

AI.tldr: Kolibri is a lightweight 55,712-parameter graph network that localizes RGB-D frames in unseen colored point clouds in 82 ms per frame by finding the place before geometric refinement.
AI.motivation: Point cloud registration methods can align RGB-D frames to building scans accurately, but their high computational cost makes searching across large multi-room buildings impractical.
AI.method: Kolibri encodes 10 cm colored point cells by color, local shape, and neighbors using a 55,712-parameter graph network to retrieve the coarse location, then relies on geometric refinement to recover the exact pose.
AI.result: On 96 unseen ScanNet rooms, Kolibri matches GeDi (81.4% vs. 80.3% within 5 cm and 5 degrees) in 82 ms per frame on an RTX 2080 Ti, loses only 1.3 points when searching 100 rooms without a room label, and localizes 86.5% of hospital scan frames in 384 ms each versus 91 minutes for GeDi, though registration leads on gray or color-mismatched frames.
AI.conclusion: Fast learned place retrieval paired with geometric refinement enables practical room-free RGB-D localization in large colored building scans.

title: Keeping Parts Honest: Isolated Part Graphs for Faithful Vision Transformer Explanations
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material will be added in a later version
summary: Part and prototype-based explanations for Vision Transformers (ViTs) present a decision as evidence from individual image regions. However, self-attention mixes information across patches, so part-level features absorb context from the whole image and consequently fail to faithfully reflect the decision. We show that existing interpretable ViT classifiers depend heavily on this leakage: when each explained region is encoded in isolation, their accuracy collapses, and retraining them under isolation recovers only part of the lost accuracy. We propose a classifier that represents each image as a graph of isolated parts. Each part is encoded only from its own patches by a ViT whose last blocks are fine-tuned under isolation, preventing evidence leakage from elsewhere in the image. Parts are discovered without annotation and refined hierarchically through their sub-parts, making them more consistent and stable across images than those of competing methods. Each edge is computed from part pairs, and recovers evidence that attention previously shared across the object without affecting the parts. Matching the image graph to a learned prototype graph per class makes the prediction a direct combination of node and edge similarities, each computed only from the patches it is credited to, so every explanation is faithful by construction. Across 11 fine-grained and general-object benchmarks, our method exceeds the accuracy of existing explainable methods that rely on leakage, while providing explanations that reflect what the model actually uses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an isolated part-graph Vision Transformer classifier whose explanations are faithful by construction because each part is encoded without cross-patch leakage.
AI.motivation: Existing part- and prototype-based ViT explanations suffer from self-attention leakage across patches, causing accuracy to collapse when explained regions are encoded in isolation.
AI.method: Each image is represented as a graph of unsupervised, hierarchically refined parts whose last ViT blocks are fine-tuned under isolation, with pairwise edges recovering cross-part evidence and predictions formed by matching against learned class prototype graphs.
AI.result: Across 11 fine-grained and general-object benchmarks, the isolated part-graph classifier exceeds the accuracy of existing leakage-reliant explainable methods while guaranteeing faithful explanations.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing part isolation during encoding and explicitly modeling inter-part edges reconciles high classification accuracy with faithful ViT explanations.

title: Propose & Verify: Fast Reflection Symmetry Detection via Harmonic Fields
summary: Detecting multiple reflection symmetries in 3D shapes requires aggregating geometric evidence over a large space of candidate planes, making traditional voting approaches computationally expensive. We introduce the Fourier Accelerated Symmetry Transform (FAST), a training-free framework that combines geometric pair voting with efficient spectral computation. Exploiting the fact that global reflection planes pass through the shape centroid, we reduce the search to plane orientations, while geometric consistency filtering and independent witnesses suppress unreliable pair hypotheses. Our key insight is to represent these votes as a signal over plane orientations and efficiently compute a continuous, smoothed symmetry field in the spherical-harmonic domain. Specifically, we exploit the Funk-Hecke theorem, the spherical counterpart of the Fourier convolution theorem for rotationally symmetric kernels, to transform Gaussian smoothing into multiplication of harmonic coefficients. This enables efficient field evaluation, from which symmetry candidates are extracted, refined, and geometrically verified. Across two benchmarks, including a new benchmark of highly symmetric shapes, FAST achieves the highest clean multi-plane detection $F_1$ scores among evaluated methods (0.861 and 0.947), with GPU inference below 4 ms per shape: over $100\times$ faster than the next-fastest evaluated multi-plane GPU baseline. FAST also demonstrates strong robustness to geometric noise and competitive single-plane detection, achieving 94.9% success on clean single-plane shapes.

AI.tldr: FAST is a training-free 3D reflection symmetry detector that uses spherical-harmonic fields to detect multiple symmetry planes in under 4 ms per shape on a GPU.
AI.motivation: Traditional voting over candidate 3D reflection planes is computationally expensive when aggregating geometric evidence for multiple symmetries.
AI.method: FAST restricts search to plane orientations through the shape centroid, applies geometric consistency filtering and independent witnesses, and uses the Funk-Hecke theorem to compute a smoothed symmetry field in the spherical-harmonic domain before extraction and verification.
AI.result: Across two benchmarks, FAST achieves the highest clean multi-plane F1 scores (0.861 and 0.947) with GPU inference under 4 ms per shape (over 100x faster than the next-fastest GPU multi-plane baseline) and 94.9% success on clean single-plane shapes.
AI.conclusion: Spectral smoothing of geometric pair votes over spherical harmonics enables accurate, real-time multi-plane 3D symmetry detection.

title: Beyond Co-Generation: Rethinking Jointness in Joint Audio-Video Generation
summary: Our aim is to advance the understanding of genuine audio-visual coordination in joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation, with particular emphasis on semantic consistency. Evaluating audio-visual consistency in T2AV generation is nontrivial, as detailed text prompts obscure whether such consistency stems from genuine cross-modal coordination or merely from independent text following. To isolate the former, we introduce intrinsic jointness: the ability of audio and video to produce the same realization for details left underspecified by the prompt. Using semantically underspecified prompts (e.g., "musical instrument playing" rather than "electric guitar playing"), we investigate four recent models and reveal their limited intrinsic jointness. To address this limitation, we propose JointREPA, a simple representation alignment-based post-training method to facilitate cross-modal coordination. Since existing benchmarks use semantically detailed prompts, we introduce UNSAIDBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate intrinsic jointness under semantic underspecification. Experiments across two distinct models and three benchmarks, including UNSAIDBench, demonstrate that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces intrinsic jointness, the UNSAIDBench benchmark, and JointREPA, a representation alignment post-training method to improve cross-modal semantic consistency in audio-video generation.
AI.motivation: Detailed text prompts mask whether audio-video consistency in T2AV models comes from genuine cross-modal coordination or independent text following.
AI.method: Using semantically underspecified prompts in a new benchmark (UNSAIDBench), the authors measure intrinsic jointness across four models and propose JointREPA, a representation alignment post-training method to strengthen cross-modal coordination.
AI.result: Evaluation reveals limited intrinsic jointness in existing models, while experiments across two models and three benchmarks including UNSAIDBench show that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.
AI.conclusion: Testing under semantic underspecification exposes cross-modal coordination gaps that representation alignment post-training can effectively reduce.

title: LOCUS: Causal Support Windows for Attribute Control in Autoregressive Image Generation
summary: Unified autoregressive (AR) image generators struggle to satisfy multiple attribute constraints in a single prompt. Although these attributes are decodable from image-token latents, editing those latents at test time remains difficult. Adding a fixed attribute direction to the prefix can reinforce a requested attribute but rarely overrides a conflicting one, such as turning a car red when the prompt specifies blue. We investigate how the effect of an intervention depends on where it acts in the image-token sequence. We introduce the causal support profile, which measures, for each attribute, how often patching image-token states within a given window flips the rendered attribute. Structural attributes (count and position) are most responsive in early, narrow windows, while appearance attributes (color, size, and material) respond over later, broader windows. A budget-matched comparison of early and middle windows shows that the effect of window location depends on the target attribute, and two-dimensional support maps show that the responsive regions track spatial content. Based on these profiles, we propose LOCUS (Latent Optimization in Causal Support windows), which diagnoses which attribute failed and routes test-time latent optimization to its corresponding support window. With the generator, optimizer, reward, verifier, and token budget held fixed, support-routed windows outperform late windows by 23.6 percentage points in GenEval++ macro accuracy. With the generator frozen, LOCUS raises Janus-Pro's GenEval++ accuracy from 24.6% to 46.8% overall and from 19.5% to 40.5% on multi-attribute tags. On GenEval, LOCUS repairs 48.1% of failed generations in one rollout, compared with 37.4% for prefix optimization, and needs 14% fewer rounds on average to succeed.

AI.tldr: LOCUS routes test-time latent optimization to attribute-specific causal support windows in autoregressive image generators, substantially improving multi-attribute prompt adherence.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive image generators struggle with multi-attribute prompts, and adding fixed attribute directions to prefixes rarely overrides conflicting attributes.
AI.method: The authors measure causal support profiles—showing structural attributes respond in early narrow windows and appearance attributes in later broader windows—and propose LOCUS to diagnose failed attributes and optimize latents within their corresponding support windows.
AI.result: Support-routed windows outperform late windows by 23.6 percentage points in GenEval++ macro accuracy under matched budgets, raise frozen Janus-Pro accuracy from 24.6% to 46.8% overall (19.5% to 40.5% on multi-attribute tags), and repair 48.1% of GenEval failures in one rollout versus 37.4% for prefix optimization with 14% fewer rounds.
AI.conclusion: Targeting test-time latent optimization to attribute-specific causal windows enables reliable attribute control without modifying generator weights.

title: Harnessing Image Diffusion Prior for Photo-Realistic Video Restoration
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Recent image generation models produce photo-realistic results with rich details, but transferring their powerful priors to video restoration remains difficult due to temporal inconsistency from stochastic detail synthesis. Existing video restoration methods improve temporal coherence but often sacrifice visual fidelity, leaving a gap between image-level quality and video-level stability. We propose a generative video restoration method that bridges this gap by enabling temporally consistent detail synthesis from image generation priors. Our method combines noise energy rebalancing to suppress structure-disturbing low-frequency stochasticity, motion-aligned noise warping to propagate details along object motion, a self-supervised denoising encoder to mitigate encoder-induced temporal uncertainty, and decoupled temporal attention to model cross-frame dependencies. Together, these components preserve fidelity, enhance fine-grained realism, and maintain temporal consistency. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially outperforms existing video restoration approaches in visual quality, detail richness, and temporal stability.

AI.tldr: A generative video restoration method transfers rich image diffusion priors to video while maintaining temporal consistency via noise rebalancing, motion-aligned warping, and decoupled attention.
AI.motivation: Transferring photo-realistic image diffusion priors to video restoration introduces temporal inconsistency from stochastic detail synthesis, whereas existing video methods trade visual fidelity for stability.
AI.method: The approach combines noise energy rebalancing to suppress low-frequency stochasticity, motion-aligned noise warping to propagate details, a self-supervised denoising encoder to reduce encoder uncertainty, and decoupled temporal attention.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show substantial improvements over existing video restoration methods in visual quality, detail richness, and temporal stability.
AI.conclusion: Controlling noise stochasticity and aligning temporal propagation bridges the gap between image-level realism and video-level temporal coherence.

title: SlideJev: Order-Stable and Tissue-Grounded Jev Decisions for Whole-Slide Pathology
summary: Whole-slide visual question answering (VQA) offers a natural-language interface to pathology, allowing diagnostic and phenotypic questions to be answered directly from tissue slides. However, current vision-language models (VLMs) rely heavily on linguistic priors: their answers are sensitive to the order of the candidate answers, and can be reached through shortcuts that bypass the tissue evidence. To address these challenges, we introduce SlideJev, a framework that separately verifies candidate answers against the slide and learns to ground these judgments in tissue evidence. To connect parallel candidate evaluation with visual evidence learning, we adopt Jev and score each candidate by the difference between support and rejection log-likelihoods from the original language-model head. We compute these scores in parallel using separate prompts with the same format and no option-position labels, then normalize them for answer selection. To ground these scores in tissue evidence, candidate-conditioned reading and comparison guide gated updates to visual tokens across decoder layers. With the backbone frozen, we train these visual modules through the same scores using question-answer and paired-image supervision. Across three whole-slide pathology VQA benchmarks, SlideJev achieves the highest mean overall accuracy and 100% answer consistency across four option orders. Image-control experiments further show that SlideJev achieves the largest average accuracy gains from correct images over mismatched and image-free inputs across the three datasets. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SlideJev is a whole-slide pathology VQA framework that scores candidate answers in parallel without option-position labels and grounds visual updates in tissue evidence.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs in whole-slide pathology VQA rely on linguistic priors, making them sensitive to candidate option order and prone to bypassing tissue evidence.
AI.method: SlideJev scores each candidate in parallel using support-versus-rejection log-likelihoods from the language-model head without position labels, while candidate-conditioned reading guides gated updates to visual tokens across decoder layers with the backbone frozen.
AI.result: Across three whole-slide pathology VQA benchmarks, SlideJev achieves the highest mean overall accuracy, 100% consistency across four option orders, and the largest accuracy gains from correct images over mismatched or image-free controls.
AI.conclusion: Parallel order-free scoring combined with candidate-conditioned visual gating eliminates option-order bias and enforces tissue-grounded pathology reasoning.

title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

AI.tldr: AgentWorld is an agent-centric vision-language-action world model for autonomous driving that reasons over compact, dynamically grounded discrete agent tokens instead of dense future pixels.
AI.motivation: Pixel-level world VLA models waste capacity generating driving-irrelevant appearance details, creating a bottleneck for trajectory planning.
AI.method: AgentWorld represents future world states using discrete agent tokens grounded to surrounding objects' semantics, 3D geometry, motion, and interactions, trained via explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented SFT, and agent-oriented RL.
AI.result: Open-loop and closed-loop driving experiments show that AgentWorld improves planning performance, exploits visual and agent dynamics effectively, and produces interpretable agent-centric world states.
AI.conclusion: Abstracting world modeling into structured, agent-centric discrete tokens aligns future prediction directly with autonomous driving planning.

title: RoadAnnoter: An AI-Assisted Desktop Tool for Semantic Segmentation Annotation of Road-Scene Images
summary: Accurate semantic segmentation of road-scene images is essential for road safety research; however, polygon-level annotation remains labor-intensive and limits labelled dataset development. This study presents RoadAnnoter v1.0, an open-source desktop application integrating six human-in-the-loop annotation modes: manual polygon delineation, SAM Prompt, Smart Select, Edge Fill, pretrained semantic segmentation using Cityscapes-trained SegFormer models, and task-specific segmentation using TinySegNet, a lightweight MobileNetV3-Small-based network trained with accumulated annotator-generated labels. SAM-based modes use promptable segmentation with SAM and MobileSAM, while Edge Fill combines Canny edge detection with colour-similarity-based flood filling in CIELAB colour space. SegFormer generates suggestions for common road-scene categories, whereas TinySegNet supports adaptation to project-specific features through iterative training. All six modes use a shared mask-to-polygon pipeline comprising morphological processing, Gaussian smoothing, contour extraction, and Douglas-Peucker simplification; annotations are exported in YOLO segmentation format. RoadAnnoter was used to annotate Google Street View images from recorded road accident locations in Bangladesh for a vision-language model-based investigation of free-flow speed estimation. Qualitative assessment across representative scenes demonstrated the complementary applicability of the annotation modes to diverse feature geometries. Visual comparison with Roboflow indicated similar qualitative boundary characteristics for principal road-scene regions, although no quantitative accuracy assessment was conducted. RoadAnnoter provides a locally operated framework for developing road-scene segmentation datasets for transportation engineering and road safety research.

AI.tldr: RoadAnnoter v1.0 is an open-source desktop tool integrating six human-in-the-loop segmentation modes and a shared polygon export pipeline for road-scene annotation.
AI.motivation: Polygon-level semantic segmentation annotation of road-scene images is labor-intensive and slows dataset creation for road safety research.
AI.method: The application combines manual polygons, SAM Prompt, Smart Select, CIELAB Edge Fill, Cityscapes-pretrained SegFormer, and an iteratively trained MobileNetV3-Small network (TinySegNet), feeding a unified mask-to-polygon pipeline that exports YOLO segmentation format.
AI.result: Applied to Google Street View images from Bangladesh accident sites, qualitative evaluation showed complementary mode utility and boundary characteristics comparable to Roboflow, though no quantitative accuracy assessment was conducted.
AI.conclusion: RoadAnnoter provides a practical local workflow for accelerating road-scene segmentation dataset development in transportation research.

title: Wear and Go: Calibration Free Sparse Inertial Motion Capture via Online Sensor Setup Estimation
summary: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC is a calibration-free sparse inertial motion capture framework that estimates sensor anatomical identity and mounting orientation from ordinary motion.
AI.motivation: Sparse inertial motion capture typically requires known sensor identities and mounting orientations or explicit calibration poses.
AI.method: A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention to accumulate assignment and rotation evidence over time, canonicalizing measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators.
AI.result: On real inertial recordings with randomized setups at prescribed body sites, MOSAIC achieves near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets, benefits from temporal accumulation under arbitrary orientations, and transfers across pose networks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling online sensor setup recovery from pose estimation enables calibration-free operation across interchangeable sensors and pretrained motion models.

title: Impact of Pretraining Length, Model Size, and Annotation Budget on Downstream Clinical Tasks of Foundation Models in Radiotherapy
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary Material included
summary: Cone-beam CT (CBCT) scans acquired during radiotherapy capture changes such as tumor shrinkage and radiation-induced tissue changes, offering great potential for foundation models that help monitor individual treatment responses. However, to our knowledge, no large-scale pretrained models for radiotherapy CBCT exist, and evaluating modeling choices is difficult since downstream tasks are not known in advance. We examine how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning strategy relate to downstream clinical performance, and how metrics tracked during pretraining correlate with it. We pretrain vision transformer encoders with masked image modeling on about 150,000 raw 3D radiotherapy CBCT scans, tracking representation quality via validation loss, effective rank, and linear probing. Downstream tasks are classification of feeding tube presence ($n=51,135$ CBCTs, $1,562$ patients) and clinical characteristics (T-, N-stage, sex, age, tumor site; $n=1,278$ patients) in head and neck cancer. We compare low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full finetuning against no pretraining, varying annotated dataset size. Pretext validation loss was the most consistent predictor of downstream performance; effective rank and linear probing were also associated, but not consistently across model sizes and finetuning methods. LoRA performed comparably to full finetuning while training only 0.5-2.5% of the parameters. Fully finetuned models consistently outperformed models without pretraining across all sizes, with AUROC 0.91-0.97 vs. 0.58-0.85 for feeding tube classification and 0.99-1.00 vs. 0.71-0.97 for sex classification. Model size had only a small, inconsistent effect, suggesting smaller models suffice at lower computational cost. Code and pretrained models (non-commercial license): this https URL

AI.tldr: Pretraining 3D ViTs with masked image modeling on 150,000 radiotherapy CBCT scans substantially improves downstream clinical classification, with LoRA matching full finetuning at a fraction of the parameters.
AI.motivation: No large-scale pretrained foundation models exist for radiotherapy cone-beam CT (CBCT), and it is unclear how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning strategy affect unknown downstream clinical tasks.
AI.method: The authors pretrain 3D ViTs on roughly 150,000 raw CBCT scans, track validation loss, effective rank, and linear probing, and compare LoRA, full finetuning, and no pretraining on feeding tube presence (51,135 CBCTs) and head-and-neck clinical traits (1,278 patients).
AI.result: Pretext validation loss best predicts downstream performance; LoRA matches full finetuning using 0.5-2.5% of parameters; full finetuning beats no pretraining (AUROC 0.91-0.97 vs. 0.58-0.85 for feeding tubes; 0.99-1.00 vs. 0.71-0.97 for sex); and model size has only a small, inconsistent effect.
AI.conclusion: Masked image modeling on raw CBCT scans yields strong clinical representations where smaller models and parameter-efficient LoRA finetuning suffice.

title: You Only Encode Once: Sub-Pixel-Shifted Frames for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution with 2D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Arbitrary-scale super-resolution (ASSR) of remote sensing images remains challenging due to the limited high-frequency information in a single low-resolution (LR) observation. While multi-frame SR can exploit complementary sub-pixel information, existing approaches often require real multi-frame training sequences and repeated feature encoding, increasing data acquisition demands and computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose SPS-GS (Sub-Pixel-Shifted Gaussian Splatting), an encode-once framework that learns from multi-phase LR observations synthesized from individual high-resolution images, without requiring real multi-frame training sequences. Specifically, Phase-Coherent Aliasing Demodulation (PCAD) exploits shift-dependent aliasing through Fourier-based alignment, phase-aware residual fusion, and least-squares aliasing estimation, enabling multi-frame information to be integrated before a single deep encoding pass. Gaussian Projection Alignment (GPA) then iteratively refines Gaussian centers and colors using multi-observation back-projection to promote observation consistency. The refined Gaussians support continuous rendering at arbitrary scales. Extensive experiments on five remote sensing datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction performance against single-image and multi-frame SR baselines, while maintaining competitive inference efficiency at common scales. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPS-GS is an encode-once 2D Gaussian Splatting framework for arbitrary-scale remote sensing super-resolution that learns from synthesized sub-pixel-shifted frames.
AI.motivation: Multi-frame super-resolution improves arbitrary-scale remote sensing SR using sub-pixel cues, but existing methods require real multi-frame sequences and repeated expensive feature encoding.
AI.method: SPS-GS synthesizes multi-phase LR observations from single HR images, integrates them before a single deep encoding pass via Phase-Coherent Aliasing Demodulation (PCAD), and refines 2D Gaussians with Gaussian Projection Alignment (GPA) for continuous rendering.
AI.result: Experiments across five remote sensing datasets show strong reconstruction accuracy against single-image and multi-frame SR baselines while maintaining competitive inference speed at common scales.
AI.conclusion: Integrating synthesized sub-pixel aliasing prior to a single encoding pass enables efficient, continuous arbitrary-scale remote sensing super-resolution.

title: SWIR-cGAN: Synthesizing SWIR Bands Using VNIR Imagery from CBERS and AMAZONIA-1
comment: Available on: this https URL. Early Access
summary: Spectral band synthesis is an important research topic in remote sensing. The Brazilian satellites CBERS-4, CBERS-4A, and AMAZONIA-1 provide high temporal resolution (1-3 days) visible and near-infrared (VNIR) imagery through the Wide-Field Imager (WFI), but lack short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands. Recent deep learning methods have shown promising results for spectral synthesis, but challenges remain for cross-satellite generalization and spectrally distant bands. This paper presents a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) with an attention-enhanced U-net generator and a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2/MSI SWIR bands 11 (SWIR-1) and 12 (SWIR-2) from WFI VNIR inputs. Experiments used 4,125 patches for training and cross-validation and 1,026 unseen patches for testing, with hyperparameters optimized using a subset of the training data. On SWIR-1, the model achieved SSIM of 0.900, PSNR of 31.44 dB, and MAE of 0.019 in TOA reflectance. On SWIR-2, it achieved SSIM of 0.917, PSNR of 33.35 dB, and MAE of 0.015. Benchmarking was performed on the test dataset, with each model optimized separately prior to evaluation. SWIR-cGAN outperformed the baselines, particularly for SWIR-2. The ablation study identified the multi-loss as the main performance contributor, while the attention and residual modules provided additional improvements. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of synthesizing SWIR bands from WFI imagery. The SWIR-cGAN is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SWIR-cGAN uses an attention-enhanced U-net cGAN with a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2 SWIR bands from CBERS and AMAZONIA-1 VNIR imagery.
AI.motivation: Brazilian satellites CBERS-4, CBERS-4A, and AMAZONIA-1 provide high-revisit VNIR imagery via WFI but lack short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands, and cross-satellite synthesis of spectrally distant bands remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors train a conditional GAN with an attention-enhanced U-net generator and a multi-loss objective on 4,125 patches to synthesize Sentinel-2/MSI SWIR-1 (band 11) and SWIR-2 (band 12) from WFI VNIR inputs, testing on 1,026 unseen patches.
AI.result: SWIR-cGAN achieves SSIM 0.900, PSNR 31.44 dB, and MAE 0.019 on SWIR-1, and SSIM 0.917, PSNR 33.35 dB, and MAE 0.015 on SWIR-2, outperforming baselines with the multi-loss contributing most to performance.
AI.conclusion: Attention-enhanced cGANs with multi-loss supervision can feasibly synthesize missing SWIR bands from high-temporal-resolution VNIR satellite imagery.

title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
summary: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

AI.tldr: Invoker-Render pairs a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model trained via Progressive Forcing for infinite controllable video generation from visual proxies.
AI.motivation: Practical proxy-driven video renderers must handle varying proxy granularities from coarse layouts to fine geometry while streaming causally in few steps without accumulating rollout drift.
AI.method: Trained on an aligned 200-hour multi-granularity corpus over structural proxies, appearance, and language, Invoker-Render uses Progressive Forcing (ProForcing) to distill a causal predictor into a four-step renderer and then train on continuous self-generated rollouts.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts preserving scene and subject appearance.
AI.conclusion: Combining multi-granularity proxy conditioning with self-rollout Progressive Forcing enables long-horizon, real-time controllable video streaming without drift.

title: Fiberpose: state-of-the-art fiber morphometry and instance segmentation with a distance-transform neural network
summary: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool this https URL. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.

AI.tldr: Fiberpose reformulates SEM fiber morphometry and instance segmentation as smooth distance-transform field regression paired with geometry-based reconstruction algorithms.
AI.motivation: Classical image binarization and post-processing for SEM fiber analysis fail on images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers.
AI.method: Fiberpose regresses a smooth distance-transform field encoding fiber geometry and applies custom geometric algorithms for instance reconstruction, diameter measurement, and orientation analysis in a unified Python desktop and web tool.
AI.result: On an independent fibrous SEM dataset, Fiberpose achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation over SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar, and GIFT, while generalizing qualitatively to unseen microscopy modalities.
AI.conclusion: Direct distance-transform regression with tailored geometric reconstruction provides an accurate, interpretable, and reproducible pipeline for fibrous material characterization.

title: Training-Free Building Change Detection with Example-Induced Discriminants
summary: Building change detection (BCD) relies on dense annotations that are costly to collect across regions. A few annotated examples offer a more economical way to specify the target, but change maps provide incomplete building supervision: they label only changed buildings and leave the building-containing date unspecified. Our key observation is that these annotations nevertheless reveal features that recognize buildings in other images, including unchanged ones. We present Linear INduced Discriminants (LIND), a training-free framework that turns regional feature contrasts into a reusable linear building classifier. Using a single frozen vision transformer, it unifies building recognition and temporal comparison in the same feature space. This approach requires neither text prompts nor an auxiliary segmentation model. Only one parameter is tuned on a single validation dataset and then kept fixed across datasets and shot settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong detection accuracy, cross-dataset transfer, and efficient inference, with extensions to other semantic classes and broader land-cover changes. Change annotations thus provide a compact visual specification for detection in new scenes. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: LIND is a training-free building change detection framework that converts regional feature contrasts from a few change-map examples into a reusable linear building classifier.
AI.motivation: Building change detection requires costly dense annotations, whereas few-shot change maps only label changed buildings without specifying which date contains the building.
AI.method: Using a single frozen vision transformer, LIND turns regional feature contrasts from example change maps into a linear discriminant classifier that unifies building recognition and temporal comparison with only one tuned parameter and no text prompts or auxiliary segmenters.
AI.result: Experiments show strong detection accuracy, cross-dataset transfer, and efficient inference, with extensions to other semantic classes and broader land-cover changes.
AI.conclusion: Regional feature contrasts from sparse change examples suffice to induce a transferable, training-free linear classifier for change detection.

title: MI-Hyper: Generating Multiple Instance Models for Weight Space Transfer Learning in Histopathology via Mixed Tasks Pretrained HyperNetwork
summary: Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction aims to generalize to new pathology tasks without parameter updates at deployment. MI-Zero makes these predictions by pooling patch-text similarities. Conditional weight generation, combined with supervision from diverse pathology tasks, offers an alternative: learning to construct predictive rules from task descriptions. We introduce MI-Hyper, a hypernetwork pretrained across mixed tasks to generate the aggregation and classification weights of multiple instance learning (MIL) models. We first train the generator and a shared MIL basis jointly using source labels. We then freeze the basis and refine the generator. The generated task weights are reused across cases. Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17 and 0.57 percentage points, respectively. On some molecular prediction tasks, both AUC and balanced accuracy improve by more than 20 points. These results support task-conditioned weight generation as a promising approach to weight-space transfer for long-sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: MI-Hyper pretrains a hypernetwork across mixed pathology tasks to generate multiple instance learning (MIL) weights for zero-shot whole-slide image prediction.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot WSI methods like MI-Zero pool patch-text similarities without learning task-conditioned predictive rules from diverse pathology supervision.
AI.method: MI-Hyper jointly trains a weight generator and a shared MIL basis across source tasks, then freezes the basis and refines the generator to produce reusable aggregation and classification weights from task descriptions.
AI.result: Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy, and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17, and 0.57 percentage points, with gains exceeding 20 points in AUC and balanced accuracy on some molecular prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Task-conditioned hypernetwork weight generation enables effective weight-space transfer for zero-shot whole-slide histopathology modeling.

title: Rescaling OLS-Merged Adapters To Improve Personalized Image Generation
summary: Merging multiple adapters into a single image generation model reduces deployment costs while preserving diverse task capabilities or personalization modes. State-of-the-art methods such as RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing fit the outputs of the merged model to those of the individual adapters using ordinary least squares (OLS). We show that this reconstruction objective systematically shrinks task-specific signals whenever the activation distributions of different tasks overlap, producing a merged adapter that is too weak for downstream use. We derive a decomposition that quantifies this shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged update to restore signal strength. On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines. Our approach also improves results on style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM-based text classification.

AI.tldr: Rescaling OLS-merged adapters restores signal strength lost to overlapping task activations, improving multi-adapter personalized image generation and other merging tasks.
AI.motivation: Ordinary least squares (OLS) adapter merging methods like RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing systematically shrink task-specific signals when task activation distributions overlap.
AI.method: The authors derive a decomposition quantifying this activation-overlap shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged adapter update to restore signal strength.
AI.result: On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines, and also improves style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM text classification.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for overlap-induced signal shrinkage via simple rescaling makes OLS-based adapter merging effective at scale.

title: SpikWM: Efficient End-to-End Spiking World Modeling for Visual Planning
summary: Goal-conditioned planning with image observations and goals requires predictions that distinguish visual states and action consequences. Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and merge actions with different physical outcomes. We propose the Spiking Latent World Model (SpikWM), an end-to-end joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) with one simulation step per image and one neural update per latent position. Spiking Regional Encoding retains spatial cues through regional pooling. Bi-Spike Action Encoding combines positive and negative binary responses, while Causal Membrane Prediction carries subthreshold evidence across the latent history with learned group-wise time constants. The encoder and predictor are trained jointly on reward-free image--action trajectories using next-embedding prediction and SIGReg. With a common planner, SpikWM achieves mean success rates of $88.67\%$, $97.33\%$, $99.33\%$, and $86.67\%$ on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, respectively, outperforming two spiking baselines. Push-T ablations support each module, and controlled replays examine responses to appearance and physical state changes. Under a matched planning budget, SpikWM reduces estimated arithmetic energy by $75.6\%$ relative to LeWM. Code will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SpikWM is an end-to-end spiking latent world model using a JEPA architecture that achieves high visual planning success with 75.6% less arithmetic energy than LeWM.
AI.motivation: Spiking neural networks offer sparse computation for visual planning, but single-step spikes can obscure motion cues and conflate actions with different physical outcomes.
AI.method: SpikWM uses one simulation step per image with Spiking Regional Encoding, Bi-Spike Action Encoding, and Causal Membrane Prediction with learned group-wise time constants, trained jointly with next-embedding prediction and SIGReg.
AI.result: SpikWM achieves 88.67%, 97.33%, 99.33%, and 86.67% success rates on Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube, outperforming two spiking baselines while reducing estimated arithmetic energy by 75.6% relative to LeWM under a matched planning budget.
AI.conclusion: Preserving subthreshold membrane history and bi-polar action spikes enables energy-efficient, accurate spiking world models for visual planning.

title: CAST: Calibrating Correspondences for Training-Free Biomedical In-Context Segmentation
summary: Biomedical image segmentation must keep up with new anatomical structures, subjects, imaging modalities, and acquisition protocols, yet dense expert annotations are scarce and models trained on one cohort often struggle to transfer. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers a way out: a new structure is specified by a few annotated exemplars at inference time. However, reliable correspondence remains challenging in biomedical images, where adjacent structures often share similar appearances, and variations across subjects and imaging conditions further obscure their distinctions. We introduce CAST, a training-free framework built on a frozen DINOv3 backbone to calibrate fine-grained correspondences. Its stability test improves feature reliability at both global and patch-specific levels, while its coherence test assesses whether candidate correspondences are supported by consistent local structural context. Together, these tests enable more reliable correspondence across diverse anatomical structures and imaging conditions. Across eight biomedical benchmarks spanning 2D and 3D segmentation, cross-subject, and cross-modality transfer, CAST outperforms the strongest overall baseline by 12.34 percentage points in Dice and ranks first across all six volumetric settings. The versatility of CAST further opens up opportunities for challenging biomedical applications, including 2D-to-3D segmentation and atlas label transfer.

AI.tldr: CAST is a training-free biomedical in-context segmentation framework on a frozen DINOv3 backbone that calibrates correspondences via stability and coherence tests.
AI.motivation: Biomedical in-context segmentation suffers from unreliable correspondences because adjacent anatomical structures look similar and vary across subjects and imaging modalities.
AI.method: Built on a frozen DINOv3 backbone, CAST applies a stability test to improve global and patch-level feature reliability and a coherence test to verify consistent local structural context for candidate correspondences.
AI.result: Across eight 2D and 3D biomedical benchmarks spanning cross-subject and cross-modality transfer, CAST outperforms the strongest baseline by 12.34 percentage points in Dice and ranks first across all six volumetric settings.
AI.conclusion: Training-free correspondence calibration unlocks accurate few-shot biomedical segmentation across modalities, including 2D-to-3D and atlas label transfer.

title: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams
comment: Manuscript, 9 pages, Computer vision, AI-generated video detection, compressed-domain analysis, video coding,
summary: Most AI-generated video detectors analyze decoded pixels and overlook how videos are produced. We show that causal video autoencoders leave an architecture-specific rhythm in compressed bitstreams: their temporal stride concentrates unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, so rate-distortion optimized encoders allocate bits periodically. Without decoding pixels, we observe four-frame pulses in CogVideoX and Wan2.2 and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, which are absent from content-matched camera footage. Passing camera footage through a generator's autoencoder alone induces the pulse, supporting its proposed origin. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video (AUC 0.84-0.94) and persists across tested quantization settings and H.264/H.265 encoding. Frame-size traces also identify four commercial generators, with 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating the pixel-based UnivFD baseline (72.7-73.6%). Our results directly link generative architecture to measurable coding demand.

AI.tldr: Causal video autoencoders leave periodic frame-size pulses in compressed bitstreams, enabling training-free AI-generated video detection and generator attribution without decoding pixels.
AI.motivation: Most AI-generated video detectors inspect decoded pixels and ignore architectural artifacts introduced during latent video generation.
AI.method: The authors analyze compressed bitstreams for periodic bit-allocation pulses caused by causal autoencoder temporal strides (4-frame pulses in CogVideoX/Wan2.2, 8-frame in LTX-Video) and use a training-free peak-ratio statistic and frame-size traces for detection and attribution.
AI.result: The peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video with 0.84-0.94 AUC across quantization and H.264/H.265 settings, while frame-size traces identify four commercial generators at 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating UnivFD (72.7-73.6%).
AI.conclusion: Latent chunking in causal video autoencoders creates measurable bitstream signatures that support fast, codec-level synthetic video forensics.

title: Tracking Ethological Behaviors of Broiler Chickens Through Computer Vision (YoloV11) Using an Android Mobile Device
summary: This study developed and evaluated a computer vision model for automated ethological behavior classification of broiler chickens in climate-controlled poultry houses. Using publicly available videos preprocessed and manually annotated into three classes (sitting, standing, and feeding), the YOLOv11 model was trained and deployed on an Android application via TFLite conversion. Exploratory analysis ensured dataset consistency and visual quality, while evaluation showed class-dependent performance: higher robustness for static postures (sitting, AP=0.531; precision=100%) and lower accuracy for dynamic behaviors (feeding, AP=0.292; recall=0.20). Tests with unseen images demonstrated significant improvements, achieving accuracies of 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding. The model showed effective generalization in real farm environments, supporting its potential for continuous behavioral monitoring, early welfare assessments, and decision-making in precision poultry farming. These findings establish a technical foundation for future mobile-based applications at commercial scale, reinforcing the role of computer vision in automated animal welfare evaluation.

AI.tldr: A YOLOv11 model deployed via TFLite on an Android device classifies broiler chicken sitting, standing, and feeding behaviors in real farm environments.
