AI.motivation: Automated, portable monitoring of broiler chicken ethological behaviors is needed for continuous welfare assessment and decision-making in precision poultry farming.
AI.method: Publicly available videos were manually annotated into sitting, standing, and feeding classes, used to train a YOLOv11 detector, and converted to TFLite for deployment on an Android mobile application.
AI.result: On validation, sitting achieved AP=0.531 (100% precision) while feeding had AP=0.292 (recall=0.20); on unseen test images, accuracies reached 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding.
AI.conclusion: Mobile-deployed YOLOv11 demonstrates practical generalization for real-time poultry behavior monitoring and automated animal welfare evaluation.

title: When a Larger Guidance Scale Repairs Text-to-Video Failures and When It Does Not
summary: When a text-to-video diffusion model ignores part of a prompt, the usual first fix is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. This paper is a measurement study of when that fix works. On Mochi, the same increase repairs failures on rare compositions ("a snowy beach") beyond what generating again does, does not repair negations ("a highway with no vehicles"), where it fixes fewer failures than generating again does, and changes nothing for events that must happen late in a clip ("a sandcastle that a wave washes flat"). Which of these happens can be known in advance, from the prompt and one inexpensive score. The score, which we call demand, measures how strongly the denoiser reacts to the part of the prompt that the failed video leaves out, and it is read from the first quarter of denoising, before any video exists. Our main finding is a condition: raising the scale is effective only when the prompt contains no negation and no event tied to a specific time, and when demand is sufficiently high, with recovery clearly higher above a fitted threshold than below it. Published corrections for the three failure types, used as fixed probes, behave as this account predicts. A short decision rule follows: before generating again, a user can tell whether the most common fix is worth trying, and what to use when it is not.

AI.tldr: This measurement study characterizes when raising the classifier-free guidance scale repairs text-to-video prompt failures on Mochi and introduces a demand score to predict it early.
AI.motivation: Users commonly raise the classifier-free guidance scale when a text-to-video model ignores part of a prompt, but it is unclear when this works versus when it fails.
AI.method: Testing rare compositions, negations, and late-occurring events on Mochi, the authors define a "demand" score measuring denoiser reaction to the omitted prompt part during the first quarter of denoising.
AI.result: Raising guidance repairs rare compositions beyond re-rolling, underperforms re-rolling on negations, and has no effect on late-timed events; guidance scaling is effective only without negations or timed events and when demand exceeds a fitted threshold.
AI.conclusion: Checking prompt structure and early denoising demand lets users predict before full generation whether increasing guidance will fix an omitted concept.

title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
summary: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.

AI.tldr: Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) probes a planner with hypothetical objects to focus high-resolution verification only on decision-relevant regions, reproducing full-frame actions with a quarter of the pixels.
AI.motivation: Adaptive-resolution perception relies on image cues that cannot reliably spot missed low-resolution objects or determine which objects actually affect the planner's action.
AI.method: DGSP treats the low-resolution scene and action as a draft, probes the planner by inserting hypothetical objects to map a decision-sensitivity field, and iteratively verifies only that field and current action support at high resolution until the action stabilizes.
AI.result: Proven exact for two planner classes under matching crop detections, DGSP reproduces whole-frame high-resolution actions on about 98% of frames across three driving datasets using roughly a quarter of the pixels, reducing false braking and recovering missed decision-relevant objects.
AI.conclusion: Querying the planner's decision sensitivity turns perception into a targeted, action-driven verification loop that cuts pixel cost without sacrificing driving safety.

title: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) enables a single student to absorb the skills of several domain teachers by learning from its own generated responses. We present Multimodal Model Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation Reasoner (M3OPD-Reasoner), a fully open recipe for post-training vision-language models (VLMs) over three reasoning domains: image STEM, image perception, and video. We curate two datasets, M3OPD-SFT-1.35M for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and M3OPD-RL-193K for reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. On these data, we compare post-training recipes that start from Qwen3.5-9B: training one model on the mixed data of all domains (MixSFT and MixRL), and training one teacher per domain with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), directly or after an SFT warm-up, and distilling the teachers into one student with MOPD. We evaluate on 21 image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning benchmarks after we decontaminate the training data against them. The comparison establishes MOPD of teachers trained with GSPO directly from Qwen3.5-9B as the best recipe: the student closely matches each teacher on its own domain and is on average above the mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Since MOPD already merges the domain capabilities that MixRL would otherwise have to learn, its student is a stronger starting point for RL, and we ask whether the same data can carry the model further from there: we add MixRL on top of the MOPD student, on the same prompts and with the same settings, which, to our knowledge, no prior VLM recipe has studied. The same prompts still improve the MOPD student, with no collapse, and give our main model, M3OPD-Reasoner-9B. MOPD and MixRL can therefore work as consecutive stages that get more out of the same data. We release all data, the training code, and the checkpoints of every stage.

AI.tldr: M3OPD-Reasoner is an open post-training recipe for vision-language models across image STEM, image perception, and video reasoning that combines Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) with a subsequent mixed reinforcement learning stage.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training recipes either train a single model on mixed domain data or distill domain teachers, leaving open how to best combine domain-specific reinforcement learning teachers and whether further mixed RL can still improve a distilled student.
AI.method: The authors curate M3OPD-SFT-1.35M and M3OPD-RL-193K, train per-domain teachers from Qwen3.5-9B using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO), distill them into one student with MOPD, and then apply MixRL on top of the MOPD student using the same prompts.
AI.result: Evaluated on 21 decontaminated benchmarks, MOPD of GSPO teachers trained directly from Qwen3.5-9B outperforms mixed-training baselines on average, and adding MixRL on top of the MOPD student further improves performance without collapse to yield M3OPD-Reasoner-9B.
AI.conclusion: MOPD and MixRL can serve as consecutive post-training stages that extract more capability from the same data, and all data, training code, and checkpoints are released.

title: Automated Annotation-Free Synthetic Data Generation for Underwater Litter Detection: A Comparison of Generative Approaches
summary: Underwater object detection is often limited by scarce and imbalanced training data and by strong appearance variations caused by turbidity, lighting, and differences between sensors. Existing data augmentation strategies, such as geometric or color augmentation or fully synthetic image generation with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), either lack semantic realism, fail to respect scene physics, or require additional annotations. In low-data domains like underwater environmental monitoring, the need for additional annotations is often the core bottleneck. Collecting new footage is hard, but labeling this dataset is even more time-consuming and costly, which limits how quickly a usable dataset can be constructed. We propose a unified fully automated zero-annotation pipeline that inserts class-conditioned trash objects into real underwater frames while preserving the original background context. Starting from sampled bounding boxes, each box is converted into an insertion mask and the object is pasted or generated within it, while the same box coordinates are automatically written as the corresponding annotation. Because labels are derived directly from the sampled boxes, the pipeline generates fully labeled training data for low-data settings without any manual annotation. Within this single pipeline we compare three strategies: copy-paste, Stable Diffusion inpainting, and DALL-E image-conditioned generation. We evaluate bounding-box faithfulness, visual realism, and the impact of the generated samples on downstream detector performance on the SeaClear underwater debris dataset. Results show that DALL-E improves detection performance in four of five domains, with relative gains of up to 96 percent over the real-only baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified, annotation-free pipeline that inserts class-conditioned trash objects into real underwater frames to generate labeled training data for underwater litter detection.
AI.motivation: Underwater object detection suffers from scarce, imbalanced data and appearance variations from turbidity, lighting, and sensors, while existing augmentation or GAN-based methods lack realism, violate scene physics, or require costly manual annotations.
AI.method: The pipeline samples bounding boxes, converts each box into an insertion mask, and inserts or generates objects within the mask while preserving the background and automatically using the box coordinates as labels, comparing copy-paste, Stable Diffusion inpainting, and DALL-E image-conditioned generation.
AI.result: On the SeaClear underwater debris dataset, DALL-E image-conditioned generation improves downstream detector performance in four of five domains, achieving relative gains of up to 96 percent over the real-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Automated zero-annotation synthetic object insertion provides an effective way to build labeled training data for low-data underwater monitoring settings.

title: Wall-to-wall maps of canopy height and aboveground carbon across the Atlantic Forest
comment: 56 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables, 2 supplementary tables. Submitted to Scientific Data. Maps and code openly available via Zenodo and GitHub
summary: Global canopy height maps are increasingly used to estimate forest carbon, yet their regional accuracy is rarely tested. We present wall-to-wall maps of canopy height (10~m) and aboveground carbon density (30~m) for the Brazilian Atlantic Forest in 2024. Height was predicted by a deep learning network fusing Sentinel-2 reflectance, Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR backscatter and ALOS elevation, trained on 7{,}179 and tested on 1{,}793 patches (58{,}800~km$^2$) from a statewide airborne LiDAR campaign over São Paulo state, Brazil. On held-out test patches, the root mean square error is 3.05~m at 10~m and 2.58~m at 30~m, and the model was validated at two LiDAR sites outside São Paulo. Over the same pixels, the Meta and World Resources Institute global product has more than twice this error. A power law fitted to 124 inventory plots converted canopy height to above ground carbon density. The remaining forest holds 1{,}944~Tg~C over 28.3~Mha. Global products therefore need local validation before use in carbon accounting.

AI.tldr: This paper produces wall-to-wall 2024 maps of canopy height (10 m) and aboveground carbon density (30 m) for the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, revealing large errors in existing global canopy height products.
AI.motivation: Global canopy height maps are widely used for forest carbon estimation, but their regional accuracy is rarely validated against local measurements.
AI.method: A deep learning network fuses Sentinel-2 reflectance, Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR backscatter, and ALOS elevation, trained on 7,179 and tested on 1,793 airborne LiDAR patches over Sao Paulo state, and a power law fitted to 124 inventory plots converts height to aboveground carbon density.
AI.result: The model achieves an RMSE of 3.05 m at 10 m resolution and 2.58 m at 30 m resolution on held-out patches, whereas the Meta and World Resources Institute global product has more than twice this error; the remaining Atlantic Forest is estimated to hold 1,944 Tg C over 28.3 Mha.
AI.conclusion: Global canopy height products require local validation before being used for regional carbon accounting.

title: Refin3R: Geometry-Guided Refinement for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models predict dense point maps from multiple images in a single pass. Without explicit geometric constraints, however, their predictions are often inconsistent across views and lack fine-grained precision. Recent methods incorporate geometric priors such as camera pose or depth, but use them merely as auxiliary inputs, process each view independently, or refine the geometry only where the priors are available. We present Refin3R, which refines feed-forward point maps with Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, propagating SfM geometry over the image grid. In its dual-branch architecture, a 2D branch extends SfM geometry beyond its coverage using geometry-aware backbone features, while a 3D branch reasons over the SfM points of all views, capturing multi-view structure that the image grid alone cannot represent. The two branches exchange information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view, yielding dense and accurate point maps. Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks\&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided methods in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.

AI.tldr: Refin3R is a dual-branch architecture that refines feed-forward 3D reconstruction point maps using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points to improve multi-view consistency and geometric precision.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models predict dense point maps in a single pass but often lack cross-view consistency and fine-grained precision, while existing geometry-guided methods only use priors as auxiliary inputs or refine geometry where priors exist.
AI.method: Refin3R pairs a 2D branch that extends SfM geometry over the image grid using geometry-aware backbone features with a 3D branch that reasons over SfM points across all views, exchanging information bidirectionally to jointly refine each view.
AI.result: Across ScanNet++, ETH3D, Tanks&Temples, and out-of-domain human and surgical scenes, Refin3R consistently outperforms feed-forward and geometry-guided baselines in point map accuracy while running faster than the strongest geometry-guided baseline.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional 2D-3D refinement with sparse SfM geometry enables accurate and fast dense point map reconstruction across diverse domains.

title: UnrealEvent: Synthetic Dataset Generation and Annotation for Event-Based Vision
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Neuromorphic Vision (NeVi), ECCV 2026
summary: Event-based cameras provide high temporal resolution, low power consumption, and a high dynamic range, but progress in event-based object detection remains constrained by the scarcity of annotated training data. To solve this issue, this paper introduces the tool UnrealEvent, a synthetic dataset-generation pipeline implemented in Unreal Engine 5.5. The pipeline combines a V2E-inspired event-frame generator with EasySynth semantic-rendering passes, allowing rendered level sequences to be converted into paired event representations and YOLO-format bounding-box annotations without manual labeling. Events are generated from per-pixel log-luminance differences between consecutive frames, with contrast thresholds sampled independently from a normal distribution to emulate the fabrication-induced threshold mismatch of real sensors. Using this pipeline, we provide a synthetic dataset and evaluate YOLOv8 detectors under synthetic, zero-shot real, and real fine-tuning training on eTraM. The results show strong in-domain synthetic performance but a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, especially for pedestrians. Fine-tuning on a small real subset improves real-domain performance, while the remaining gap highlights the importance of asset diversity and sensor calibration.

AI.tldr: UnrealEvent is a synthetic dataset-generation pipeline in Unreal Engine 5.5 that produces paired event-camera representations and YOLO-format bounding-box annotations without manual labeling.
AI.motivation: Event-based object detection is limited by the scarcity of annotated training data despite the high temporal resolution, low power consumption, and high dynamic range of event cameras.
AI.method: The pipeline combines a V2E-inspired event-frame generator using per-pixel log-luminance differences and normally sampled contrast thresholds with EasySynth semantic-rendering passes to output paired events and bounding boxes.
AI.result: Evaluating YOLOv8 detectors on the synthetic dataset and eTraM shows strong in-domain synthetic performance but a substantial synthetic-to-real gap, especially for pedestrians, which is improved by fine-tuning on a small real subset.
AI.conclusion: Automated synthetic event generation can bootstrap event-based detectors, though asset diversity and sensor calibration remain important for closing the sim-to-real gap.

title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
summary: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that builds a compact, reusable audio-visual memory on a server for on-device question answering.
AI.motivation: Offloading audio-visual encoding to a server while running a lightweight decoder on-device preserves question privacy, but transmitting and processing full multimodal representations remains expensive.
AI.method: The method treats video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players, estimates their importance via Monte Carlo Shapley valuation with an embedding coverage objective balancing utility, cross-modal redundancy, and unimodal diversity, and transmits the top-scoring token embeddings once.
AI.result: On Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B), the method achieves the best or tied-best accuracy among compared compression methods, improving Daily-Omni accuracy by 12.86 to 14.62 percentage points at 80% pruning with up to 1.92x decoding speedup.
AI.conclusion: Query-agnostic Shapley-based token pruning enables accurate, low-latency on-device audio-visual question answering with a single compact memory transfer.

title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
comment: Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Maritime Computer Vision (MaCVi), WACV 2027
summary: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates event-based person detection for maritime UAV search and rescue using synthetic events from MOBDrone videos and demonstrates real-time deployment on a Jetson Orin Nano.
AI.motivation: Camera motion and long exposures in low light cause motion blur on small water-surface targets during UAV maritime search, degrading frame-based person detection.
AI.method: Synthetic events are generated with the v2e simulator from MOBDrone rescue videos while retaining annotations, and the recurrent vision transformer RVT-T is compared against YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images.
AI.result: On 843 held-out test samples under 100 ms synthetic exposure, RVT-T achieves 15.63% AP50:95 versus 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18, and deployed on a Jetson Orin Nano it runs in about 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample.
AI.conclusion: Event-based detectors resist exposure-induced motion blur and can run in real time on embedded UAV hardware for maritime search.

title: FMT: Lossless Image Compression in a Fixed Number of Parallel Steps
summary: Learned lossless codecs make smaller files than common classical codecs, yet the images we archive and train on still use classical codecs. A main reason is time: a learned codec takes seconds to decode a photo that a classical codec opens in milliseconds, and their faster variants give up most of their gain in size. We argue that much of this time is spent waiting, not computing: the network waits for the values it conditions on, and the arithmetic decoder reads them one at a time. We introduce FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree), a lossless image format whose decoding order and entropy coder are designed together so that neither wait grows with the image. FMT stores an image as a coarse-to-fine tree whose steps hold independent values: a GPU predicts each step at once and decodes it in parallel rANS lanes that carry their states from step to step, so an image of any size decodes in a fixed number of sequential steps. On this tree we build a family of bit-exact codecs, from a rule with no network to large networks, and no codec we ran on the same GPU beats any of them on both size and speed. Without a network, FMT beats NVIDIA's HTJ2K on size and speed; with a large one, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61X faster than learned codecs we ran on the same A100, at the same size or smaller.

AI.tldr: FMT (Fixed-step Multiscale Tree) is a lossless image format and parallel entropy coder that decodes images of any size on a GPU in a fixed number of sequential steps.
AI.motivation: Learned lossless image codecs achieve smaller file sizes than classical codecs but take seconds to decode because neural conditioning and arithmetic decoding force sequential waiting that scales with image size.
AI.method: FMT organizes an image as a coarse-to-fine tree of independent values per step, allowing a GPU to predict each step at once and decode it in parallel rANS lanes that carry states across steps.
AI.result: Without a neural network, FMT beats NVIDIA HTJ2K on both size and speed; with a large network, it decodes Kodak photos 9 to 61x faster than other learned codecs on the same A100 GPU at equal or smaller file sizes.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing the decoding order and parallel entropy coder eliminates size-dependent sequential bottlenecks in learned lossless image compression.

title: LUTBench: Benchmarking Text-Driven Photographic Look Transfer
summary: Photographic color grading shapes the tone and color of a photograph to achieve a desired look. Text-driven photographic look transfer lets users specify these adjustments in natural language, with the goal of reproducing the requested look across photographs while preserving their content. However, prior research on text-driven color grading uses different datasets, text instructions, target definitions, and metrics. These differences make it difficult to compare how faithfully the methods reproduce the same look. To compare methods under a shared protocol, we introduce LUTBench. We collect 91 three-dimensional lookup tables (3D LUTs) and define one photographic look per LUT with a specified input conversion. Applying these looks to 5,000 MIT-Adobe FiveK photographs produces 455,000 input-target image pairs with reproducible target images. For each look, we use templates to turn measured tone and color changes on fixed color samples into candidate clauses. We use training image measurements to verify applicable clauses before composing the text description. The evaluation measures target fidelity, tests sensitivity to predefined input conversions, and separates generalization to unseen looks from reproduction of seen looks on new photographs. Across 16 methods, stronger text alignment does not guarantee target fidelity. However, most supervised variants improve fidelity on both seen and unseen looks.

AI.tldr: LUTBench is a standardized benchmark of 455,000 input-target image pairs derived from 91 3D LUTs and 5,000 MIT-Adobe FiveK photographs for evaluating text-driven photographic look transfer.
AI.motivation: Prior research on text-driven color grading uses incompatible datasets, instructions, target definitions, and metrics, preventing fair comparison of look reproduction fidelity.
AI.method: The authors define one look per 3D LUT with a specified input conversion, generate verified text descriptions from measured tone and color changes using templates, and evaluate target fidelity, conversion sensitivity, and generalization to unseen looks.
AI.result: Across 16 evaluated methods, stronger text alignment does not guarantee higher target fidelity, though most supervised variants improve fidelity on both seen and unseen looks.
AI.conclusion: LUTBench provides a reproducible protocol that separates text alignment from actual color-grading fidelity in text-driven look transfer.

title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
summary: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

AI.tldr: GameRealm is a large-scale multimodal dataset of over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of interactive gameplay across diverse view configurations with synchronized game-native supervision.
AI.motivation: Visual foundation models for physical intelligence are constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotations, and limited multimodal supervision.
AI.method: A unified data collection pipeline combining human interaction and agentic exploration captures single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic gameplay along with metric depth, camera parameters, audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse visual learning tasks show that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning.
AI.conclusion: GameRealm provides a scalable, richly annotated multimodal resource for advancing visual intelligence.

title: $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
summary: $\pi^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $\pi^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Pi^4 is a ~0.5B-parameter unified foundation model that recovers dense 4D scene geometry, camera poses, metric scale, 2D/3D point tracks, and moving-object masks in a single forward pass from uncalibrated RGB inputs.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D perception systems often require separate models or large parameter counts and struggle to jointly reconstruct geometry and motion from arbitrary single-image, unordered, or video inputs.
AI.method: The model shares a backbone across a geometry branch and a geometry-conditioned motion branch that predicts image-space correspondences and lifts them into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry.
AI.result: Pi^4 achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation and competitive 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation with less than half the parameters of most baselines, scaling to thousands of images despite training on at most 64 views.
AI.conclusion: Coupling geometry and geometry-conditioned motion in a compact shared-backbone architecture enables scalable, single-pass 4D scene perception.

title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

AI.tldr: VIVID is a video MLLM framework that preserves localized motion and event order under tight frame budgets by combining keyframes with inter-frame patch differences and entity state chains.
AI.motivation: Current video MLLMs reduce video understanding to static multi-image reasoning, which dilutes small moving targets via whole-frame pooling and erases inter-frame motion by dropping or averaging frames.
AI.method: VIVID uses Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning to select anchors from a 3 fps pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory to form Dynamic Tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion ROI and chronological Entity State Chains, adding 0.22% trainable parameters to a 27B backbone.
AI.result: Trained on 50 examples (~1.5 GPU hours), VIVID-Small beats all eleven baselines across 8,083 questions, while VIVID-Large (3,600 examples) leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
AI.conclusion: Modeling localized inter-frame differences and entity dynamics overcomes static-snapshot limitations in video MLLMs with minimal parameter overhead.

title: Attribution Through the Decoder: Prediction-Space Explanations for Structured Outputs
summary: Networks that predict angles, gaze directions, and rotations do not output these quantities directly: they emit raw coordinates that a fixed decoder, such as normalization, maps to the final prediction. Attribution methods are usually applied to the raw coordinates, so they can credit inputs for changes the decoder discards, such as rescaling a vector when only its direction matters. The resulting explanation can highlight inputs that have no effect on the prediction. We instead attribute through the decoder differential, which for normalization decoders reduces to a scaled tangent projection. We characterize invariance to output rescaling, show that every fixed smooth scalar target on a sphere has points of zero tangential sensitivity, and show that an endpoint-projected variant of Integrated Gradients can still attribute to scale-only inputs, whereas direct angular Integrated Gradients cannot. On synthetic tasks with analytically known relevance, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to an irrelevant region. On MPIIGaze validation data, tangent Grad-CAM produces 44% greater prediction displacement under 10% pixel deletion. On PASCAL3D+ with a 6D rotation decoder, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over the ambient coordinate sum and by 13.8 degrees over a decoder-invariant scalar. Results for a two-polarity tangent LayerCAM variant are mixed: it exceeds ambient-sum LayerCAM on circular regression but no difference is detected on quaternion pose. These results separate two failure sources, radial contamination and scalarization loss. The approach uses existing attribution methods with decoder-aware targets, although some variants also require changes to attribution aggregation. An invariant attribution can still miss inputs that drive the prediction, so invariance and deletion performance should each be checked.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes attributing predictions through the differential of fixed output decoders (such as normalization) rather than raw coordinates, eliminating credit assigned to discarded input variations.
AI.motivation: Standard attribution methods applied to raw network coordinates before a normalization decoder can credit inputs for scale changes that the decoder discards and have no effect on the final angular, gaze, or rotation prediction.
AI.method: The authors attribute through the decoder differential, which reduces to a scaled tangent projection for normalization decoders, and analyze invariance to output rescaling and scalarization effects across gradient and CAM-based methods.
AI.result: On synthetic tasks, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to irrelevant regions; on MPIIGaze, tangent Grad-CAM increases prediction displacement by 44% under 10% pixel deletion; on PASCAL3D+ 6D rotation, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over ambient coordinate sum.
AI.conclusion: Decoder-aware attribution separates radial contamination from scalarization loss, though both invariance and deletion performance should be verified.

title: Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 19 tables. Main text and appendices
summary: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that preference-optimized VLMs reduce object hallucinations largely by stopping earlier and losing object coverage, and proposes a training-free base-guided restoration method to recover missed categories.
AI.motivation: Preference optimization (PO) lowers object hallucination rates in VLMs, but it also reduces object coverage and yields no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR.
AI.method: The authors diagnose coverage loss using end-of-sequence (EOS) logit biasing on LLaVA-1.5-7B and propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence categories predicted only by the base model to the PO caption without training.
AI.result: Early stopping of the base model via positive EOS bias reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three PO checkpoints, while base-guided restoration brings three checkpoints within one point of base recall on held-out COCO with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model.
AI.conclusion: Much of PO's hallucination reduction stems from shorter generations, and training-free base-guided restoration can recover lost object coverage while retaining lower hallucination.

title: Any2Building: Unifying Point Clouds and Images for Building Reconstruction via Shared Spatial Queries
summary: Abstracting structured buildings from limited observations is essential for 3D urban modeling and digital twins. Partial point clouds and overhead images of the same building provide incomplete 3D surface measurements and visual cues to its footprint, roof geometry, and rooftop structures, respectively. This motivates a unified framework that aligns geometric and visual cues in 3D and reconstructs buildings from either or both modalities. Building on this connection, we present Any2Building, a unified model for Level of Detail 2 (LoD2) building reconstruction from partial point clouds, overhead images, or both, with optional coarse geometric priors. At its core is an occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries representation that organizes available observations within a common 3D grid. Supervised by complete building surface voxels, these queries connect observational evidence to target geometry, enabling a shared generator to learn structural priors across tasks and providing spatial guidance for recovering missing structure. A trained voxel conditional surface-generation and low-poly remeshing pipeline then converts the predicted structure into compact LoD2 building models. To support this framework, we introduce BuildingWorld-Image, comprising approximately one million paired samples of partial point clouds, overhead images, and LoD2 building models across 18 cities. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Any2Building outperforms existing methods in geometric reconstruction accuracy across unimodal and multimodal point-cloud completion, single-image building generation, and prior-assisted generation, while maintaining detailed and robust recovery when point cloud input modality is degraded.

AI.tldr: Any2Building is a unified model that reconstructs Level of Detail 2 (LoD2) 3D building models from partial point clouds, overhead images, or both, supported by the new BuildingWorld-Image dataset.
AI.motivation: Partial point clouds and overhead images offer complementary 3D surface and visual cues for urban building reconstruction, but existing methods lack a unified representation to align both modalities and recover missing structure.
AI.method: Any2Building organizes observations into an occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries representation on a 3D grid supervised by complete surface voxels, followed by voxel-conditional surface generation and low-poly remeshing; the authors also curate BuildingWorld-Image with roughly one million paired samples across 18 cities.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks, Any2Building outperforms existing methods in geometric reconstruction accuracy for unimodal and multimodal point-cloud completion, single-image building generation, and prior-assisted generation, remaining robust under degraded point clouds.
AI.conclusion: Shared spatial queries enable unified, modality-flexible LoD2 building reconstruction from incomplete 3D and visual observations.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
comment: Accepted in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (10/2026). Reviewed on OpenReview: this https URL
summary: Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: GRACE is a single retrieval-augmented segmentation refiner that edits predicted medical image masks using verified prior cases from a shared knowledge base, generalizing across anatomies without anatomy-specific retraining.
AI.motivation: Automated correction of residual errors in medical image segmentation typically requires training a separate corrector for each target anatomy.
AI.method: Trained once on a multi-organ corpus, GRACE uses a light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder to retrieve shape-aligned prior cases from a knowledge base and conditions a refiner on those cases to edit the input mask.
AI.result: Evaluated across 18 public CT, MRI, and ultrasound datasets and seven upstream segmentors, GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC on weak segmentors (input DSC 0.386) and supports parameter-free index extension to unseen solid organs while keeping the refiner frozen.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-conditioned refinement offers a practical, scalable alternative to anatomy-specific medical segmentation correctors.

title: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
comment: VLM safety, multimodal jailbreaks, and scene-state reasoning
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a scene-state safety vulnerability in VLMs where visual events elicit harmful assistance without explicit harmful text requests, and introduces SceneSafetyBench and the S3TA attack.
AI.motivation: Current VLM safety evaluations focus on explicit harmful prompts or text-side filters, overlooking whether models infer and assist with harmful objectives purely from visual scene states.
AI.method: The authors introduce SceneSafetyBench (375 image-question pairs across Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states) and propose S3TA, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries pairs independently, and assembles the responses.
AI.result: Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs achieve 45.6 to 72.3% attack success rates (ASR), and on seven MM-SafetyBench categories S3TA reaches 71.2% average ASR, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points despite text and visual moderation.
AI.conclusion: VLM safeguards must address harmful assistance inferred through scene-grounded reasoning rather than relying solely on input content screening.

title: Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
summary: Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.

AI.tldr: GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner) uses human gaze as a prior for visual exploration rather than full sequence imitation to improve grounded reasoning and human alignment in VLMs.
AI.motivation: Human gaze reflects systematic visual evidence extraction, but raw gaze sequences contain noise and redundancies that transfer poorly when imitated directly by VLMs.
AI.method: Using 7,109 collected human gaze trials across visual reasoning tasks, the authors train models with gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning and further apply reinforcement learning without gaze supervision.
AI.result: Across chart understanding, visual search, and counting, using gaze as a prior consistently outperforms full-sequence gaze supervision, and GGR matches or beats leading grounded-reasoning baselines while improving human alignment and visual grounding.
AI.conclusion: Human gaze is most effective when used to guide spatial exploration and shape reasoning behavior rather than as a target for complete imitation.

title: EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
summary: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.

AI.tldr: EviSlide-MIL is a class-incremental multiple instance learning framework for whole-slide image (WSI) classification that mitigates catastrophic forgetting using per-class learnable queries and a shared prediction module.
AI.motivation: Extending WSI tumor classifiers to new subtypes under limited historical data causes catastrophic forgetting when feature aggregation and prediction modules are updated.
AI.method: EviSlide-MIL assigns multiple learnable queries per class to aggregate frozen patch features while sharing a prediction module to limit parameter growth, freezing queries of previously learned classes and applying experience replay and knowledge distillation.
AI.result: Evaluated on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas, EviSlide-MIL achieves higher accuracy and lower forgetting than competing class-incremental methods across most settings.
AI.conclusion: Freezing class-specific aggregation queries alongside a shared predictor provides scalable, knowledge-preserving class-incremental WSI classification.

title: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

AI.tldr: FastFrames is a family of autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive frame-generation latency by replacing heavy VAE decoding and KV cache update operations with lightweight alternatives.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion models are too slow for interactive applications, with profiling showing that VAE decoding and KV cache updates account for over half of end-to-end latency.
AI.method: The authors replace these bottleneck components with lightweight alternatives in both 1.3B and 14B autoregressive video diffusion variants.
AI.result: The 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame (28 RPS) on a single B200 GPU while matching the quality of an ~8x slower baseline, and the 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame (22 RPS) on an 8x B200 node with superior visual quality.
AI.conclusion: Eliminating overlooked pipeline bottlenecks enables real-time interactive camera- and physics-conditioned video generation.

title: CRA: Continuous Risk Assessment for Safety-critical Visual Navigation
summary: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a vision-based continuous risk assessment (CRA) framework that estimates object-level physical risk scores from RGB and LiDAR observations for safety-critical robot navigation.
AI.motivation: Traditional safety-critical control relies on binary safe/unsafe constraints that fail to capture how real-world risk varies continuously with object motion, physical properties, and interaction context.
AI.method: The framework estimates four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) from RGB and LiDAR data, combines them into a continuous risk score per object or person, and integrates them into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field.
AI.result: The proposed safety filter is demonstrated in a simulated restaurant scene for online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation.
AI.conclusion: Continuous multi-factor risk scoring enables nuanced, context-aware safety filtering beyond binary obstacle avoidance.

title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
summary: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (this https URL).

AI.tldr: DailyBrick is a multi-stage agentic system that synthesizes physically valid LEGO models and step-by-step assembly instructions from natural language requests by generating executable construction programs.
AI.motivation: Generating LEGO models requires physical support and unblocked brick placement at every step, which strains expert LLMs when predicting long sequences of individual brick connections.
AI.method: A multi-stage agentic harness writes programs compiled by a versioned construction SDK from semantic subparts to individual bricks, while an external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the build to trace failures and route bounded repairs.
AI.result: Experiments show DailyBrick outperforms recent agentic systems on user-requested LEGO generation and supports downstream robotic assembly from generated instructions.
AI.conclusion: Framing brick assembly as verifiable program synthesis with replay-based review improves physical validity and enables robotic manipulation.

title: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
summary: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.

AI.tldr: TetherMark is a post-hoc watermarking method that enables instance-level authentication by verifying both an edit-robust payload and geometric relation consistency against cross-instance transplantation attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing robust and localized watermarks verify payload survival or content category, leaving them vulnerable to cross-instance transplantation where an attacker transfers valid watermark evidence onto a different image of the same category.
AI.method: TetherMark pairs a standard message check with a relation check that uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization, accepting only when both checks pass.
AI.result: Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark achieves 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, attaining the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under both attacks.
AI.conclusion: Combining payload verification with correspondence-based relation checks closes the cross-instance transplantation vulnerability in visual watermarking.

title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
summary: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

AI.tldr: This study models individual differences in human judgment across faces, artworks, photographs, and jokes using nested generative models, finding that the shape of disagreement varies by domain and rater sample.
AI.motivation: Prior work measured the magnitude of individual differences in judgment, but did not establish whether people merely reweight shared dimensions or reverse preferences relative to the population.
AI.method: Three nested generative models (same-sign reweighting, sign-reversing linear transform, and stimulus-specific offsets) are evaluated on held-out raters across ten public datasets totaling about 20,000 raters using 10 to 20 judgments per person.
AI.result: For faces, same-sign reweighting suffices without statistically detected reversals; for artworks, weights spread along the abstract-figurative axis with 28 percent of raters opposing the population in one sample, though far fewer in another rater sample.
AI.conclusion: Individual differences in judgment vary in geometric shape as well as size, depending on both the stimulus domain and the rater population.

title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
summary: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

AI.tldr: JointGV is a plug-in module that corrects long-horizon drift in visual world models by rolling out a parallel scene graph and coupling graph-motion context with visual state changes.
AI.motivation: Visual world models accumulate recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations over long horizons, limiting their reliability for robot planning and control.
AI.method: JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes to compute a bounded residual without backpropagating gradients into the original visual dynamics, and is attached to DINO-WM and DreamerV3.
AI.result: On 32-step DMC rollouts, JointGV reduces joint-position error by 11 to 28%; on real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, it cuts DINO-WM pole-angle error from 12.56 to 6.69 degrees; in simulated control, an actor trained on corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes versus 0 for the original.
AI.conclusion: Parallel relational graph dynamics can correct structural drift in visual world models without altering or retraining the underlying visual dynamics.

title: Technical Report of Mobile Manipulator Robot for Industrial Environments
comment: 25 pages, 22 figures, 4 tables. Technical report of Team Auriga's 2025 mobile manipulator (@Work) platform (Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Shahid Beheshti University)
summary: This paper presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' mobile manipulator robot, developed at the Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University. Hereafter, this platform is referred to as the @Work Robot. The robot targets industrial tasks, with an emphasis on improving efficiency in repetitive or hazardous work environments. It uses a 4-wheel Mecanum drive for omnidirectional movement and a 5-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper for object handling and navigation. The electronics consist of custom PCB boards built around ESP32 microcontrollers, together with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX that handles high-level processing and real-time system control. On the software side, Hector SLAM provides mapping and localization, A* handles path planning, and YOLO performs real-time object detection. These modules draw on fused sensor data to deliver robust navigation and reliable collision avoidance. Overall, the system shows effective hardware-software integration, with consistent performance in autonomous navigation, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.

AI.tldr: This technical report describes the hardware and software integration of the @Work Robot, an omnidirectional mobile manipulator developed for industrial environments.
AI.motivation: Industrial environments with repetitive or hazardous tasks require mobile manipulators capable of autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, and object handling.
AI.method: The platform combines a 4-wheel Mecanum drive, a 5-DoF manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper, custom ESP32 PCBs, and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX running Hector SLAM, A* path planning, and YOLO object detection.
AI.result: Integrated testing demonstrates consistent autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.
AI.conclusion: The @Work Robot provides a functional, integrated mobile manipulation platform for industrial automation tasks.

title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
summary: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.

AI.tldr: CaFe is a causally faithful traffic simulator that prevents private-intent leakage across agents, supported by a paired intervention test and the 531,099-scene WOMD-PACT dataset.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned traffic simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react prematurely before an instructed maneuver becomes observable.
AI.method: The authors formalize intent leakage with a paired intervention test, build WOMD-PACT with timed behavior tags via counterfactual ghost testing, and introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop to restrict inter-agent interactions to public beliefs.
AI.result: Existing conditioning designs displace 23 to 83% of nearby uninstructed agents due to intent leakage when executed motion is held fixed, whereas CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763).
AI.conclusion: Restricting inter-agent conditioning to public beliefs enforces causal faithfulness in language-steered traffic simulation without sacrificing realism.

title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows
summary: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator for CNNs that extends convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension for generalizable 3D turbulent flow super-resolution.
