AI.motivation: Existing CNN-based super-resolution methods treat physical variables as independent channels with linear mixing, neglecting nonlinear cross-variable correlations needed under sparse conditions or out-of-distribution regimes.
AI.method: The operator lifts features into a higher-dimensional manifold and constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions.
AI.result: Experiments on 3D turbulent flow super-resolution demonstrate strong reconstruction fidelity and zero-shot generalization.
AI.conclusion: Joint spatial-variable convolution provides an effective physics-aware inductive bias for modeling multi-scale turbulent flows.

title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
summary: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

AI.tldr: CodeReel is a training-free execution layer that accelerates code-to-video coding agents using exact frame reuse and blocking-aware scheduling.
AI.motivation: Coding agents building videos in a build-inspect-edit loop spend a median of 11 minutes per film, with over a third of time spent waiting on builds where 37.5% of frames were already drawn and half of builds stop at checks.
AI.method: CodeReel keys each frame by its drawing commands for exact reuse regardless of time shifts, and runs checks first while speculatively rendering at idle priority unless recent builds indicate likely failure.
AI.result: On the EditLoop benchmark, CodeReel cuts agent wait time by 36.3% against parallel Rebuild and 57.9% against Sequential, and reduces median per-build wait to 0.62x in Claude Code and 0.67x in Codex CLI across five models.
AI.conclusion: Command-keyed frame reuse and speculative scheduling substantially reduce iteration latency in code-to-video agent workflows without model changes.

title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
comment: 34 pages, 19 figures. Project Page: this https URL
summary: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.

AI.tldr: RFW-S is a dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified deformable 3D objects across 485 everyday categories, built with an automated pipeline and independent simulation verification.
AI.motivation: Robotic simulation of deformable objects is limited by 3D asset collections that focus on visual diversity while lacking scalable physical modeling and verification.
AI.method: An automated pipeline combines reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation, followed by an independent verification framework testing interactions distinct from calibration.
AI.result: Experiments validate the independent verification framework, characterize deformable responses, evaluate robotic grasping for success and object integrity, and demonstrate physical realism via sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation.
AI.conclusion: RFW-S provides a large-scale, physically verified foundation for deformable-object simulation and embodied robotic learning.

title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
summary: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

AI.tldr: TCP4D is a unified model that uses a shared 4D scene representation to both track observed tool-center-point (TCP) motion and generate future TCP trajectories from monocular RGB videos.
AI.motivation: Recovering embodiment-agnostic robot actions and gripper states from monocular RGB manipulation videos and using them to learn policies remains challenging without recorded source-robot states.
AI.method: Given monocular video and initial 2D queries, the tracker recovers metric SE(3) TCP poses, gripper states, scene geometry, and camera parameters; the generator samples local 4D features along recovered tracks with observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states, supported by a cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline.
AI.result: The tracker achieves 7.60 mm and 16.07 mm absolute trajectory error on DROID and RoboLab, adapts to new embodiments with 10 demonstrations, and the generator reaches 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin while joint training improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a 4D scene representation between TCP tracking and generation enables effective cross-embodiment robot manipulation learning from RGB videos.

title: Deal With It: On Better Schedules for Listwise Reranking
summary: Listwise LLM rerankers cannot reliably rank hundreds of documents in a single call, and rely on schedules to orchestrate their calls. Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes parallel candidate-splitting schedules for listwise LLM reranking and introduces DealRank, a round-robin dealing schedule that minimizes expected top-passage cuts.
AI.motivation: Listwise LLM rerankers use parallel group schedules with fixed advancement quotas, where contiguous or poorly balanced splits cut true top passages and trigger expensive repair calls.
AI.method: The authors prove that round-robin dealing by retriever rank minimizes expected cuts of the true top ten under equal quotas, and propose DealRank based on this analysis.
AI.result: Across six LLMs, DealRank stays within 0.1 nDCG@10 of the best schedules in two rounds, runs 1.1 to 1.4x faster than BlitzRank (and 11x faster than sliding window at 1,000 candidates), and reduces repair calls in BlitzRank from 59% to 14% without quality loss.
AI.conclusion: Round-robin dealing provides a simple, theoretically grounded schedule that improves listwise reranking latency without sacrificing ranking quality.

title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
summary: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

AI.tldr: DGF-Asym is a decentralized collective estimation method that extends the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance.
AI.motivation: Robots performing collective estimation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults must balance personal and peer information without prior noise statistics or explicit fault models.
AI.method: DGF-Asym updates peer weights asynchronously using retrospective predictive performance to form consensus without requiring fault models or noise priors.
AI.result: In simulated collective navigation under noise and time-varying faults, DGF-Asym yields more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion than three baselines, though with longer decision times and sensitivity to fault ratio, group size, and influence thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Retrospective asymmetric peer weighting enables model-free, fault-tolerant collective estimation in decentralized robot teams.

title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
comment: This publication has been submitted to NOMS2027
summary: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a reproducible QA-based benchmark on CICIDS2017 traffic to evaluate LLMs on network trace analysis, finding that protocol filtering improves accuracy and reduces prompt overhead.
AI.motivation: Automating network traffic investigation with LLMs requires understanding their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction.
AI.method: Using benign traffic from CICIDS2017 and human-generated ground truth, multiple LLMs are compared on raw textual traffic dumps versus protocol-filtered representations using a human-validated LLM-as-a-judge pipeline.
AI.result: Protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead and improves answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses across evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: Protocol-aware traffic filtering is an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network trace analysis.

title: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception?
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) enable honeypots to generate responses and deceptive artefacts on demand, yet existing approaches evaluate generated content one reply at a time and leave open whether artefacts that jointly describe a coherent event retain an attacker better than unrelated ones. This question becomes pressing as autonomous LLM-driven offensive agents emerge as realistic adversaries. This paper proposes narrative deception, a reactive strategy in which the defender maps each observed attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, selects a compatible scenario from a curated catalogue based on MITRE Engage, and deploys mutually referential artefacts (files, processes, services, and logs) on an emulated Ubuntu host while the intrusion is under way. An LLM-powered defender and an autonomous LLM attacker interact through a real SSH session, and the attacker's termination policy distinguishes abandonment due to suspected deception from abandonment due to loss of interest. A campaign of 1,150 sessions compares four conditions of increasing sophistication (Static, Same-TTP, Multi-TTP, and Chain) across four open-weight attacker models, four defender models, and three attacker skill levels. Engagement increases significantly at every step. With the same artefact budget per reaction, coherent scenarios raise the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduce their abandonment from 86% to 52%. The effect grows with attacker skill, holds across all sixteen model pairs, and comes at comparable inference cost. Nearly all sessions ended through loss of interest rather than detection, which suggests that deception should sustain meaningful findings, not only emulator fidelity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes narrative deception for LLM-driven honeypots, showing that deploying mutually referential artefacts from coherent MITRE ATT&CK scenarios significantly extends attacker engagement.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-driven honeypots generate deceptive replies one turn at a time, leaving open whether narrative coherence across artefacts better retains autonomous LLM-driven attackers.
AI.method: The defender maps observed commands to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, selects a compatible MITRE Engage scenario, and deploys mutually referential files, processes, services, and logs on an emulated Ubuntu host during live SSH sessions, evaluated across 1,150 sessions and four conditions.
AI.result: Coherent scenarios raise median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and cut abandonment from 86% to 52% at the same artefact budget and comparable inference cost, with nearly all terminations due to loss of interest rather than detection.
AI.conclusion: Sustaining coherent, meaningful findings across deceptive artefacts is more effective at retaining autonomous attackers than isolated per-turn emulator fidelity.

title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
summary: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

AI.tldr: This study presents a hierarchical modeling framework and composite synchronization metric to identify and stabilize antiphase synchronization in biomorphic spiking central pattern generators (CPGs).
AI.motivation: Systematically characterizing dynamic regimes and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in spiking neural CPGs within closed neuromuscular loops remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors define a composite metric combining phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability, and evaluate it across varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations in a closed neuromuscular loop.
AI.result: Statistical analysis shows stimulation type dominates regime determination (tonic drive yields the most robust antiphase synchronization), while reciprocal Ia interneuron weights fine-tune stability; the composite metric outperforms phase-only measures.
AI.conclusion: External drive sets the operating regime while targeted synaptic configurations tune stability, offering design guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers.

title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
summary: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a closed-loop interactive world model for autonomous driving that couples multi-agent reinforcement learning for background vehicles with per-Gaussian 3D asset diagnosis and counterfactual signal-light rendering.
AI.motivation: Existing driving world models decouple vehicle behavior from ego visual observations, leading to unrealistic closed-loop interactions and visual artifacts on under-observed vehicle views and signal lights.
AI.method: Imitation-learned background-vehicle policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent RL against an image-reactive ego planner, exposed viewpoints guide per-Gaussian color attenuation and completion on 3D vehicle assets, and an editor renders signal lights via counterfactual fine-tuning.
AI.result: On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, the method reduces interaction behavior divergence from real logs by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0 dB over the state-of-the-art world model, with rendered signal lights affecting ego behavior in a quarter of scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing closed-loop behavior, 3D asset completion, and intention-consistent light signaling improves both behavioral realism and visual fidelity in driving world models.

title: Stress Testing a Multimodal Large Language Model Grading Assistant on Kinematics Graph Reading
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recognize graph features yet award credit without sufficient graphical support. This exploratory study examines selected grading outputs for synthetic responses to four kinematics exercises, generated through visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs. Different model and prompt configurations were used. Some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from rest over a finite interval and recognized positive curvature. Yet a severely distorted velocity--time graph received full credit despite disconnected and branching traces and an unclear zero-velocity reference. Other submissions graded under the same configuration lost substantial credit. Numerical cutoffs intended to distinguish meaningful features from drawing irregularities were supplied without a coordinate convention for unnumbered graphs, leaving the basis of exact partial-credit awards unresolved. Stress testing can expose unsupported awards before classroom use. For the configurations examined, we do not recommend accepting scores as final grades without instructor review, including review of full-credit responses.

AI.tldr: This exploratory study stress-tests an MLLM grading assistant on synthetically distorted kinematics graphs, finding that it can award full credit to severely distorted graphs without sufficient graphical support.
AI.motivation: MLLMs can recognize graph features, but their reliability in awarding partial or full credit for student kinematics graphs with drawing irregularities is untested.
AI.method: Synthetic student responses to four kinematics exercises are generated via visual distortion and progressive transformation toward reference graphs, and graded across multiple model and prompt configurations.
AI.result: While some judgments correctly distinguished instantaneous zero velocity from finite rest and positive curvature, a severely distorted velocity-time graph with disconnected, branching traces still received full credit, and unnumbered graph cutoffs lacked a clear coordinate basis.
AI.conclusion: Stress testing exposes unsupported grading awards, so current MLLM scores should not be accepted as final grades without instructor review.

title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
summary: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates network-exposed configuration attacks on an LLM-controlled social robot (Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite) that bypass inference-layer prompt-injection defenses to alter physical robot behavior.
AI.motivation: Embodied LLM robots introduce security dependencies at the management and configuration layers that inference-level prompt-injection safeguards do not protect.
AI.method: The authors test unauthenticated configuration endpoints and persistent-memory sinks on Reachy Mini Lite, map weaknesses to CWE-306, CWE-1327, and CWE-352 (CVSS v3.1 6.5), and review 59 public repositories for similar patterns.
AI.result: While 11 prompt-injection attempts were resisted, both configuration-layer attack paths altered physical robot behavior; 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications in the repository survey (11 of 11 with framework defaults) lacked authentication.
AI.conclusion: Inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorized changes to model instructions when management interfaces lack authentication, highlighting a critical deployment gap in consumer embodied AI.

title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommenders decode the semantic ID of a user's next item with a language model, and post-training them with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice. The gains are mostly reported on the first ten results, yet in deployment such models hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker or reward model. We show that RL post-training has a hidden cost: it improves accuracy at the top of the list (hit@K for small K) but, on all five datasets we study, lowers the recall of the candidate list (hit@K for K in the hundreds). The model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. Controlled experiments trace the loss to the negative advantages that RL assigns to the candidates it samples, the rollout. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that RL post-training in generative recommenders improves top-K ranking accuracy at the cost of lower candidate-list recall at larger K, and introduces out-of-rollout anchoring to restore recall.
AI.motivation: Generative recommenders are routinely post-trained with RL after SFT, but evaluation focuses on top-10 metrics and overlooks whether RL degrades the recall of hundreds of candidates passed to downstream rankers.
AI.method: Controlled experiments trace recall loss to negative advantages assigned to plausible unlogged candidates in RL rollouts, and the authors add an out-of-rollout anchoring loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering outside the rollout.
AI.result: Across all five studied datasets, standard RL lowers hit@K for K in the hundreds, whereas out-of-rollout anchoring retains top-K gains and restores candidate recall to the SFT level across multiple RL configurations.
AI.conclusion: Preserving SFT ordering outside the rollout prevents RL from penalizing plausible alternatives, resolving the ranker-versus-retriever trade-off in generative recommendation.

title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
summary: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what happens when vulnerability exploitation agents continue executing after their first stop response and proposes SCoRe, a context-management method that elicits substantial additional capability.
AI.motivation: Language model agents often stop exploiting vulnerabilities even when test-time scaling budgets remain, and the behavior and potential of continuing execution beyond stopping are underexplored.
AI.method: The authors evaluate continued execution on ExploitBench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, identify unproductive continuation patterns (stop bursts and summaries retaining impossibility judgments), and propose SCoRe to compact context at stop bursts while marking impossibility judgments as unproven.
AI.result: SCoRe outperforms summary-based continuation and other context-management baselines, enabling MiMo to reach 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns compared to 32.4% under the original stopping policy and 58.6% for GPT-5.5 on 300-turn reference results.
AI.conclusion: Stopping does not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and continued execution with targeted context management can unlock significant additional capability.

title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at this https URL .

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SEAM, a benchmark of 600 cross-application OSWorld tasks where harm arises only from combining benign information across multiple screens, and shows that computer-use agents frequently execute the harm despite recognizing it.
AI.motivation: Existing safety benchmarks for computer-use agents place harm in a single instruction or single screen, failing to test whether agents detect compositional harm across multiple screens in delegated work.
AI.method: The authors construct SEAM with 600 multi-step OSWorld tasks and minimal-pair variants scored from server logs, where each instruction and individual observation is benign but their combination is harmful.
AI.result: General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents commit the harm in up to 92% of runs even though they open the decisive pages, flag the harm when asked, and often note the conflict in their reasoning, while proprietary models are markedly more cautious.
AI.conclusion: Safety recognition in computer-use agents does not reliably translate into safe execution, and agent compliance with warnings depends heavily on whether the warning appears in user instructions or on screen.

title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
summary: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

AI.tldr: This study examines how web research agents built on OpenAI and Anthropic models interpret user-stated priorities when comparing businesses, finding that they apply different underlying criteria even when focusing on the same priority.
AI.motivation: Users can specify priorities such as growth or resilience for web research agents, but without explicit evaluation criteria the agent chooses its own standards, which is poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze 36 runs comparing Microsoft and Alphabet across OpenAI- and Anthropic-based agents under growth, resilience, or no-priority prompts, examining reports, searches, returned sources, and cited sources.
AI.result: Of 24 priority-guided runs, 21 focused on the stated priority, but under growth OpenAI reports favored Microsoft using risk and predictability criteria while Anthropic reports favored Alphabet by growth pace; under resilience most named Microsoft using partly different criteria, and only Anthropic's search wording differed detectably by condition.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of web research agents should assess the criteria behind a report's judgments rather than only focus or accuracy, and interfaces could expose and allow adjustment of those criteria.

title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
summary: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BugGen 2.0, an RTL bug-synthesis pipeline that delegates structural analysis, target selection, and validation to deterministic algorithms while using LLMs only for localized semantic rewriting.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based RTL bug-synthesis tools such as BugGen 1.0 rely on LLMs for both target selection and mutation generation, which increases inference cost and produces invalid choices.
AI.method: BugGen 2.0 separates deterministic structural analysis, target selection, and validation from LLM-based semantic rewriting, and expands datasets by generating alternative mutations at accepted failure locations while simulating only a subset to estimate acceptance.
AI.result: Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 meets all quotas with 14-16 of 16 mutation types, reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x over BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x over Firefly, and skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations with 77.7% and 95.2% acceptance and 1.09% estimation error on FabScalar.
AI.conclusion: Restricting LLMs to localized semantic rewriting within a deterministic framework lowers inference and simulation costs while improving bug-synthesis consistency across models and hardware designs.

title: Inference after coding agents
summary: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that AI coding agents conducting empirical hypothesis testing cause severe selective inference distortion and proposes a subsample-replay correction procedure to restore valid p-values.
AI.motivation: Coding agents perform open-ended, human-like search over implicit estimator spaces when analyzing data, creating a new form of post-selection inference that invalidates classical hypothesis tests.
AI.method: After an agent completes its analysis, the authors reset and replay the black-box agent on data subsamples to estimate its relative selection probability, yielding an asymptotically valid and consistent conditional test without modeling the agent's internal search.
AI.result: On simulated zero-effect data, four frontier coding agents report significant p-values 54% to 98% of the time when asked for a compelling finding, and the proposed correction reduces false rejection rates to near the nominal 5% level, with illustrations on two published papers.
AI.conclusion: Subsample replay provides a model-agnostic way to detect and correct selective inference distortions introduced by AI coding agents in empirical research.

title: StringQFT: A Multiuse Textbook Resource for AI-Assisted Theoretical Physics
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures. Companion paper to an 18-volume textbook collection. Textbook PDFs: this https URL
summary: We present StringQFT as a textbook collection for string constructions of quantum field theory and as infrastructure for AI-assisted theoretical physics. The collection comprises 18 volumes, 190 chapters and 3,795 pages, covering brane probes, brane webs, geometric engineering, F-theory constructions, wrapped M5-branes and exact worldsheet constructions. Its open-book benchmark inventory contains 1,073 items, including 499 with automatic finite-answer checking. For retrieval-augmented generation, it provides 1,371 section records linked to textbook sources and PDF locations, together with a local lexical retriever. Training-data preparation is illustrated by 21 private, source-linked examples. For agents, it exposes 19 calculation tools with specified inputs and finite domains, connecting tool use to textbook derivations. We illustrate these uses through specific questions, retrieved passages and finite calculations. The textbook collection and accompanying resources are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce StringQFT, a multiuse textbook resource and benchmark infrastructure for string constructions of quantum field theory aimed at AI-assisted theoretical physics.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted theoretical physics lacks structured, source-linked textbook corpora paired with benchmarks, retrieval indices, and calculation tools for specialized domains like string constructions of quantum field theory.
AI.method: StringQFT compiles 18 volumes (190 chapters, 3,795 pages) into an open-book benchmark of 1,073 items (499 with automatic finite-answer checking), 1,371 source-linked section records with a local lexical retriever, 21 private training examples, and 19 finite-domain calculation tools.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates StringQFT's use across specific physics questions, retrieved textbook passages, and finite calculations, and releases the textbook collection and accompanying resources.
AI.conclusion: StringQFT provides an integrated benchmark, retrieval, training, and tool-use infrastructure to support AI research in theoretical physics.

title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NatBDI, an autonomous agent architecture that combines the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) reasoning cycle with natural language processing and natural language inference.
AI.motivation: Developing autonomous agents over natural language environments using pure machine learning relies on opaque models, creating challenges in developer programming interfaces, agent efficiency, and behavioral scrutiny.
AI.method: NatBDI integrates a BDI reasoning cycle with language models and natural language inference components, allowing developers to program agents using controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge.
AI.result: In empirical evaluations, instructions provided through the NatBDI interface substantially improve agent performance over a baseline agent built with a pure machine learning approach.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned language policies with intuitively engineered BDI domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains and offers a more scrutable, intuitive programming paradigm for autonomous agents.

title: Gerrymandering planar graphs

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the computational complexity and approximability of graph gerrymandering on planar graphs, establishing hardness results as well as a constant-factor approximation algorithm under specific conditions.
AI.motivation: Prior complexity work on map redistricting (gerrymandering) focused mainly on paths and trees, leaving the more realistic case of planar graphs largely open.
AI.method: The authors analyze partitioning weighted planar graphs into k connected districts, proving polynomial-time solvability for lambda-outerplanar graphs with constant candidates and polynomially bounded weights, NP-completeness and inapproximability on general planar graphs, and a constant-factor approximation algorithm for unweighted planar graphs.
AI.result: Gerrymandering is polynomial-time solvable on lambda-outerplanar graphs under constant parameters, NP-complete on general planar graphs even with two candidates, and inapproximable for many candidates unless P=NP, yet admits a constant-factor approximation on unweighted planar graphs when the number of candidates is fixed and the optimum is a sufficiently large constant.
AI.conclusion: Although planar graph gerrymandering is generally NP-complete and inapproximable in the worst case, the inapproximability barrier only holds for very small optima and can be bypassed for fixed candidate counts.

title: Benchmarking Choice Consistency in Large Language Models: A Measurement-Theoretic Analysis of Transitivity Axiom

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a measurement-theoretic framework to evaluate whether large language model (LLM) decisions satisfy the transitivity axiom of preference, revealing systematic violations across 20 models.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluations focus on benchmark accuracy rather than the structural coherence and rationalizability of model decisions, leaving preference consistency largely unexamined.
AI.method: The authors test 20 LLMs across varying question formats, generation temperatures, and contextual memory using classic choice paradigms known to induce intransitive preferences in humans.
AI.result: Many LLMs exhibit substantial and systematic transitivity violations, meaning their pairwise preferences cannot be coherently ordered, though some violation patterns partially resemble human decision behavior.
AI.conclusion: Testing the transitivity axiom provides a principled, complementary foundation for assessing the decision-making consistency of LLMs beyond standard accuracy benchmarks.

title: Differentiable Plastic Recurrent Neural Networks: A Systematic Evaluation

AI.tldr: The authors conduct a systematic, parameter-matched evaluation of 15 differentiable plastic RNNs across four task families and propose the Plastic Continuous Thought Machine (Plastic CTM).
AI.motivation: Despite many proposed plastic RNN architectures, the field lacks a unified comparison showing how methods relate, when plasticity helps, and whether learned plastic weights are actually used at inference time.
AI.method: The paper unifies existing differentiable plastic RNNs under one notation, evaluates 15 parameter-matched architectures across four task families, analyzes plasticity utilization, and introduces Plastic CTM grounded in extended neuron dynamics and population-level synchronization.
AI.result: Plastic and non-plastic architectures perform comparably on recall and continual learning, whereas plastic models—led by Plastic CTM among recurrent architectures—perform best on in-context learning, though similarly accurate models differ in whether they rely on plasticity or perform equally well with plasticity disabled.
AI.conclusion: More discriminating benchmarks, mechanistic analyses, and richer biologically inspired plasticity rules are needed to advance differentiable plastic RNNs.

title: Split Forward Gradients: Exact Head Updates and Backpropagation-Free Trunk Training

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Split Forward Gradient (Split-FG), which restricts random-direction forward-mode gradient estimation to a network trunk while computing exact analytical gradients for a tractable head.
AI.motivation: Pure forward-mode gradient estimators avoid backpropagation and activation tapes but suffer from high variance that scales with the dimension of the perturbed parameter space.
AI.method: Split-FG combines random-direction forward estimation on the trunk with analytical head gradients, yielding a conditionally unbiased estimator for disjoint parameters, and the authors derive exact variance identities and convergence guarantees for momentum-free SGD.
AI.result: Variance ratios stay within 6.8% of predictions; Split-FG outperforms pure-forward and evolution-strategy controls on eight tabular datasets, improves WikiText-103 perplexity from 668 to 387 (vs. 150 for backprop) while using 34.5% less peak CUDA memory in a tied-table GPT, and gains 31.59 and 34.60 accuracy points on CIFAR-10 over Pure FG, though a 15-minute matched-clock audit favors backprop (331.15 vs. 1004.46 perplexity).
AI.conclusion: Split-FG is an effective, lower-variance alternative to pure forward gradients when a reverse pass through the trunk is unavailable or costly, though it does not match backpropagation in equal-time quality.

title: BALF: Budgeted Activation-Aware Low-Rank Factorization for Fine-Tuning-Free Model Compression

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BALF, an end-to-end, fine-tuning-free model compression pipeline that extends activation-aware low-rank factorization to convolutional layers and allocates per-layer ranks under explicit FLOP or parameter budgets.
AI.motivation: Existing activation-aware low-rank factorization methods are mostly restricted to linear layers and rely on an implicit full-rank assumption on layer activations.
AI.method: The authors formulate a layer representation framework covering linear, standard, and grouped convolutional layers, generalize whitening-based factorization to rank-deficient activations with optimal output distortion, and allocate per-layer ranks under FLOP or parameter budgets via Lagrangian relaxation.
AI.result: Across CNNs and vision transformers on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K, BALF generally outperforms SVD-based factorization baselines at matched FLOP or parameter targets and remains competitive with other fine-tuning-free compression methods.
AI.conclusion: Extending whitening-based factorization to rank-deficient activations and convolutional layers enables effective, fine-tuning-free model compression under explicit resource budgets.
